In high spirits, Chichikov sat in his carriage, rolling along the post road for what seemed like a long time. From the previous chapter, it is clear what his principal interest and inclination were, so it is no wonder that soon he became completely immersed in it, both body and soul. The speculations, estimates, and considerations that flitted across his face were evidently very pleasant, for they left traces of a satisfied smile on his lips every moment. Absorbed in them, he paid no attention to his coachman, who, pleased with the reception at Manilov’s estate, made some shrewd comments to the bay stable horse on the right, who was quite tricky and pretended to be doing the work, while the native chestnut mare, called Zasedsatel because he had been purchased from some member of the zemstvo, worked her heart out, so that even their eyes revealed the pleasure she was receiving. "Be tricky, be tricky! I’ll outsmart you!" said Silifan, standing up and cracking the lazy horse with the whip. "You know your business, German breeches! The chestnut is a respectable horse, he fulfills his duty, and I’d gladly give him a bit extra, because he is a respectable horse, and so is Zasedsatel… Hm, why are you swishing your ears? You, fool, listen when they talk! I won’t teach you, you ignoramus. Look where he’s going!" At this, he cracked the whip again, and muttered, "Hmph, barbarian! Accursed Napoleon!" Then, addressing everyone, he said, "You, dear ones!" and whipped all of them not as a punishment, but to show that he was pleased with them. Having brought them such pleasure, he turned back to the bay: "Do you think you can hide your behavior? No, live honestly if you want respect. Just look at the good people on the estate we were at. I’d be glad to talk if the man is a good one; we’re always good friends, subtle friends, with a good man; we’d drink tea or have a snack, if he’s a good man. Every good man receives respect. That’s why everyone respects our master, because he, you hear, fulfilled his state duties, he was a colonel councilor…"

This brownish horse was cunning and showed only outwardly that he was pulling, while the original chestnut, with its own coat of chestnut, worked with all his heart, so that even in their eyes the enjoyment he was receiving was visible. Why do you shake your ears? You fool, listen up when they talk! I won’t be a teacher of the ignorant to you. See where you’re going!" At this point, he whipped him again with the whip, saying, "Ah, barbarian! Damn Napoleon!" Then, he shouted at everyone, "Hey, you lot!" and whipped all of them not as punishment, but to show that he was satisfied with them. No, he did not consider her a child! Her looks had been frightening him of late, her words as well. Sometimes it seemed to him that she was holding herself too tightly, restraining herself too much, and he recalled that this had always troubled him. True, he had tried not to think about this for the last few days, pushing away dark thoughts, but what lay hidden in that soul? That question had been tormenting him for a long time, even though he trusted that soul. And now it all had to be resolved and revealed today: the thought was awful! And again — "that woman"! Why did he always feel that that woman would come at the very last moment and unravel the whole of his destiny, like a rotten thread? Why did he always feel this, and in this he was now willing to swear it, though he was almost delirious. If he had been trying to forget about her of late, it was only because he was afraid of her. Did he love that woman or did he hate her? He had never asked himself that question today; his heart was pure: he knew whom he loved... He did not so much fear their meetings as much as the woman herself, the strangeness, the reasons for that meeting unknown to him, or its resolution in any way. He feared Natasha Filippovna. Only much later, several days later, did he remember that in those feverish hours, her eyes and gaze had almost continuously occupied his mind, her words, though strange, somehow remaining in his memory after those feverish and melancholy hours. For example, he barely remembered that Vera had brought him his lunch and that he had eaten, and whether he had slept after lunch or not, he could not recall. He only knew that he started to clearly distinguish everything that evening at the moment when Aksinya suddenly entered his terrace and he leapt from the sofa to meet her in the middle of the room, it was almost a quarter to eight. Aksinya was alone, dressed simply and hastily, in a light burnous. He replied that he had already had the good fortune to meet in an unforeseen manner; he tried to add something else, but much of it did not work out. The governor's lady spoke a few words and finally went with her daughter to the other end of the hall to other guests, while Chichikov still stood motionless in the same place, like a person who had cheerfully gone out into the street to stroll, with eyes that were ready to look at everything, and who suddenly stopped in his tracks, remembering that he had forgotten something, and became no more foolish than any other man at that moment: at once, the carefree expression slipped from his face; he struggled to remember what he had forgotten—it might have been a handkerchief, but it was in his pocket; could it be money? but money was also in his pocket, everything seemed to be with him, yet some unknown spirit whispered to him that he had forgotten something. And now he looked around nervously and embarrassingly at the moving crowd before him, at the flying carriages, the cuirasses and muskets of the passing regiment, at the signboard—and saw nothing clearly. Thus Chichikov suddenly became alien to everything happening around him. At that moment, a multitude of hints and questions, tinged with the subtlety and politeness, came to him from the sweet-scented lips of the ladies. "Is it permissible for poor residents of this land to be so bold as to ask what you are dreaming about?" "Where are those happy places where your thoughts flit?" "Is it possible to know the name of the one who has plunged you into this sweet valley of contemplation?" But he responded with decisive inattention to all, and the pleasant phrases sank, as into water. He was even so impolite that he soon went to the other side, wanting to see where the governor's lady and her daughter had gone. But the ladies, it seemed, did not want to leave him so soon; each one decided internally to use every possible weapon, so dangerous for our hearts, and to use everything that was best. As for one who has beautiful shoulders, she is sure that all young men will be completely captivated, and will repeat every now and then, when she passes by: "Oh, what wonderful shoulders she has," and do not even look at the face, the hair, the nose, the forehead, if they do, then only as something aside. When Emperor Taizong heard this in the Treasure Hall, he was very delighted, and then asked, "That monk, what are the benefits of the nine-tusked staff?" The Bodhisattva replied, "My metal staff is made of copper and iron, encased in nine rings of immortal vine that preserves youth. It is pleasing to hold, emaciated flesh grows, and it is light to carry, returning with a trail of white clouds after descending the mountain. Mahāvajra traveled through the Heavenly Palace, searching for his mother with a carrot to break the earth's barrier. It remains untainted by a trace of worldly filth, and is delighted to accompany the divine monk to the Jade Mountain." Upon hearing this, Emperor Taizong immediately ordered the robe to be spread out, and he examined it meticulously. It was indeed a fine item. He said, "Venerable Great Virtue, I must be honest with you, I am now opening the teachings of virtue widely, planting bountiful fields of good. At present, many monks gather in the Rebirth Temple to preach the scriptures. Among them is one with great virtue, whose Dharma name is Xuanzang. I have bought these two treasures for him to enjoy. How much do you ask for them?" The Bodhisattva, with Wood Staff at his side, bowed and worshipped, reciting a Buddha’s name, then bowed and said, "If there is great virtue, I, a poor monk, am willing to give them to him, and will not take money." Having said this, he turned to leave. Emperor Taizong quickly grabbed Prince Xiao Yu to hold him back, and stood on the dais and asked, "You originally said a robe for five thousand taels, and a staff for two thousand. Now that I want to buy them, you do not want money. Could it be that you think I rely on my position as a ruler to force you to part with your items? That cannot be. I will give you the original price, do not avoid it." The Bodhisattva raised his hands and said, "I have a vow beforehand, saying that if one reveres the Three Treasures, rejoices in virtue, and worships our Buddha, I will not take money and will give them to him. Now that Your Majesty is righteous and virtuous, revering our Buddhist teachings, and the high monk has great virtue and actions, spreading the great Dharma, it is appropriate to give them up, and will not take money. I wish to leave this item behind and return." Seeing the Bodhisattva’s diligence and sincerity, Emperor Taizong was very pleased, and then ordered the Office of Imperial Banquets to arrange a simple vegetarian banquet to show gratitude. The Bodhisattva again refused firmly, and left happily, returning to hide at the Temple of the Capital Land God without further mention.

K. paused and looked down at the floor. For now, he was still free; he could continue walking and through one of the three small, dark wooden doors not far from him, he could make his escape. It would simply mean that he hadn’t understood, or that he had understood but didn’t care to. If, however, he turned around, he would be held, for then he would have confessed that he had understood, that he was indeed the one summoned and that he wanted to follow. If the priest had called again, K. would certainly have left, but since nothing happened while K. waited, he turned his head slightly, wanting to see what the priest was doing now. The priest stood calmly on the pulpit as before, but it was clear to K. that he had noticed K.’s head movement. It would have been a childish game of hide-and-seek if K. had not turned completely around. He did and was called closer by the priest with a gesture of his finger. Since everything was now out in the open, K. ran toward the pulpit—out of curiosity and to cut the matter short—he took long, bounding strides. When he reached the first pews, he stopped, but the priest seemed to find the distance still too great; he stretched out his hand and pointed with his sharply lowered forefinger to a spot just in front of the pulpit. K. followed the priest’s instructions, he had to bend his head far back just to see the priest. “You are Josef K.,” said the priest, raising a hand above the rail in an indeterminate gesture. “Yes,” said K., he thought of how freely he had once given his name, but since a while, it had become a burden to him; now, too, there were people who knew his name even though they met him for the first time, how lovely it was to be introduced and then to be known. “You are accused,” said the priest, his voice even lower. “Yes,” said K., “I have been informed.” “Then you are the one I’m looking for,” said the priest. “I am the prison chaplain.” “Ah, so,” said K. “I have summoned you here,” said the priest, “to talk with you.” “I didn’t know that,” said K. “I came here to show an Italian the cathedral.” “Forget the irrelevant,” said the priest. “What are you holding in your hand? Is it a prayer book?” “No,” answered K., “it’s a guide to the city’s sights.” “Lay it down,” said the priest. K. threw it so hard that it fell open, the pages crumpled and dragged across the floor. “Do you know that your case is not going well?” the priest asked. “It seems that way to me,” said K. “I have done my best, but so far without success. To be honest, I have not yet completed my appeal.” “How do you picture the end?” the priest asked. “I used to think it would end well,” said K., “but now I often doubt it myself. I don’t know how it will end. Do you?” “No,” said the priest, “but I fear it will end badly. They hold you guilty. Your case may not go beyond a low court, but they hold at least provisionally that you are guilty.” “But I am not guilty,” said K., “it is a mistake. How can a person be guilty? We are all human, one like another.” “That is correct,” said the priest, “but that is what guilty people say.” “Do you have any prejudice against me?” asked K. “I have no prejudice against you,” said the priest. “Thank you,” said K., “but all those involved in the proceedings have prejudices against me. They pass them on to the uninvolved as well. My situation is becoming more difficult.” “You misunderstand the facts,” said the priest, “the verdict will not come all at once, the process goes slowly into the verdict.” “So it is,” said K. and lowered his head. “What are you going to do next in your case?” the priest asked. “I will seek help,” said K., lifting his head to see what the priest thought of it. “There are still some possibilities that I have not yet made use of.” “You are seeking too much outside help,” said the priest disapprovingly, “and especially from women. Don’t you realize that it is not true help?” “Sometimes and even often, I might agree with you,” said K., “but not always. Women have great power. If I could convince some of the women I know to work together for me, I would succeed. Especially at this court, which consists almost entirely of women hunters. Show a prosecutor a woman from a distance, and he rushes to the table, just in time, and the defendant.” The priest lowered his head to the rail; the canopy of the pulpit now seemed to press him down. Kolya, flushed and agitated, went on reading in a heated and excited voice: "But while our budding millionaire was, so to speak, in heaven, an entirely unexpected event occurred. One beautiful morning, a visitor arrived at his door, a man with a calm and stern expression, speaking courteously but with dignity and justice, dressed modestly yet nobly, with a marked progressive tone in his thoughts, and he explained the reason for his visit in a few words. He was a famous lawyer, entrusted with a case by one young man; he had come on his behalf. This young man was none other than the son of the late P., though he bore another name. Passionate P., having seduced a virtuous, impoverished village girl, who had been Europeanized (with, of course, baronial rights from the defunct serfdom), and foreseeing the inevitable but immediate consequences of his liaison, had hastily married her to a busy man of some nobility, who had long loved her. At first, he helped the newlyweds, but soon they were refused his help by the noble character of her husband. Some time passed, and P. gradually forgot both the girl and his son by her, and then, as is known, he died without making any provisions. Meanwhile, his son, born in lawful wedlock but raised under another name and completely adopted by the noble character of his mother's husband, who was now dead, remained with his meager means, his ailing, suffering, legless mother in one of the remote provinces; he supported himself in the capital by daily hard work as a merchant's tutor, and with these earnings he had been able to study in a gymnasium and later as a student of useful lectures, with the ultimate goal in mind. But how much can you earn from a Russian merchant for tutoring by the penny, and with a suffering, legless mother, who, by the way, did not alleviate his burden at all with her death in the remote province? The question now is: How should our heir have judged this matter justly? Of course, you, the reader, think he must have said to himself: 'I enjoyed all the gifts of P. throughout my life: on my upbringing, governesses, and the treatment of my idiocy, tens of thousands went to Switzerland. Now, I have millions, and the noble character of the son of P., who is blameless for his father's carelessness and forgetfulness, is perishing in lessons. All that went to me by right should have gone to him. These huge sums, spent on me, in reality do not belong to me. They were merely a blind stroke of fortune; they followed the son of P. and should have been used for him, not me — the result of a fanciful whim of his thoughtless and forgetful father. If I had been completely noble, delicate, and just, I would have given him half of my inheritance. But since I am primarily a calculating person and understand too well that this is not a legal matter, I will not give him half of my millions. But at the very least, it would be too low and shameless (the offspring forgot that it was also not noble) for me not to return the tens of thousands that were spent on my idiocy by P. to his son. This is a matter of conscience and justice! For what would have become of me if P. had not taken me in for upbringing and instead cared for his own son?"

There was nothing for it, Kolya, flushed and aglow, in an agitated state, went on reading in an excited voice: "But while our hasty millionaire was, as it were, in the clouds, a completely unconnected incident occurred. One fine morning a visitor appears at his door, grave and severe, speaking politely but with dignity and justice, dressed modestly and nobly, with a clearly progressive tinge to his thoughts, and in a few words explains the reason for his visit. He is a well-known lawyer; he has been entrusted with a case by a young man; he has come on his behalf. This young man is nothing more or less than the son of the late P., although he goes by a different name. Lustful P., in his youth, seduced a respectable, poor girl from the serfs, who had been raised in Europe (of course, baronial rights from the expired serfdom status were involved), but soon he realized the inevitable, immediate consequences of his liaison and hurriedly married her off to a businessman, even a man of some character, who had long been in love with this girl. At first, he helped the newlyweds, but soon he was refused aid by the noble character of her husband. Some time passed, and P. gradually forgot both the girl and his son conceived with her, and then, as is known, he died without making any will. Meanwhile, his son, born already in legal wedlock but raised under another surname and completely adopted by the noble character of his mother’s husband, remained without any means of support and with a sick, suffering, legless mother in one of the distant provinces; himself in the capital, he earned money daily by noble labor from commercial lessons, and thus supported himself in a gymnasium, then as a student of useful lectures, with the aim of furthering his education. But how much do you get from a Russian merchant for lessons at a penny, especially with a sick, legless mother, who, finally, with her death in a distant province, did not alleviate his plight in the slightest? The question now is: how should our descendant have judged fairly? Of course, you, reader, think he said to himself: 'I have enjoyed all the gifts of P. throughout my life; his money was spent on my upbringing, on governesses, and on curing my idiocy in Switzerland; and now I have millions, while the noble character of the innocent son of P., who was not guilty of his father’s thoughtless and forgetful ways, is perishing in lessons. All that went to me by right should go to him. These enormous sums, spent on me, were, in essence, not mine. This was only a blind stroke of fortune; they followed the son of P. They should have been spent on him, not on me – the offspring of a fanciful whim of the thoughtless and forgetful P. If I were completely noble, delicate, and just, I would have given him half of my entire inheritance; but since I am primarily a calculating person and very well understand that this is not a legal matter, I will not give him half my millions. But, at least, it would be shamefully and indecently low and base (the descendant forgot that it was also imprudent) for me not to return those tens of thousands that were spent on my idiocy by P. to his son. Here is only conscience and justice! For what would have become of me if P. had not taken me in for upbringing, but instead cared for his son?"

"Disciple, why don't you bow to him in return, and just stand by and laugh instead?" The Monkey said, "How would you know? Someone like him, who only shows part of himself, deserves a beating. But for the sake of the Bodhisattva, I'll forgive him and spare him the beating. He still dares to bow to this lowly孙? Since I was a ruffian from a young age, I've never learned to bow. Even if I met the Jade Emperor or the Venerable Taoist, I'd merely nod to them." The Master said, "That's not respectful! Stop talking nonsense! Get up and let's head west." The master then stood up and prepared to proceed westward.

"Disciple, why need you also kowtow to him? Stand by and mock, that is the way! Why is this so?" The Monkey said, "You don't know, for one who plays peek-a-boo, I should beat him. But for the sake of the Bodhisattva, I have spared him. He dares not pay homage to an old monk such as myself. Since my youth, I've been a ruffian and never kowtowed. Even to the Jade Emperor or the Venerable Taoist, I'd just nod." The monk said, "That's no way to behave! Stop with this nonsense! Get up and don't delay our journey." With that, the master stood up and set off westward.

"Disciple, why not refrain from paying obeisance to him and instead stand aside, only to sneer and laugh? What reason is this?" The Monkey said, "Where would you know? For one like him, who hides his head and shows his tail, he deserves a beating, but due to compassion for the Bodhisattva, I spare him a full lashing. He dares not bend his knee before me, the Old Sun. Since my childhood, I have been a tough guy and never paid obeisance to anyone. Even if I met the Jade Emperor or the Supreme Grandfather, I would merely give a nod." The Master said, "You shameless fellow! No more empty talk! Stand up and hurry on our journey." Then the master stood up to continue their journey westward.

Disciple, since I am prostrating thus, you need not prostrate to him either. Just stand by and jeer at him. What is the reason for this? The Monkey said, "You don't know, for one like him who hides his head and shows his tail, I should beat him, but because of the Bodhisattva's face, I merely beat him enough. He dares not prostrate to an old孙like me. I have been a ruffian since childhood and do not know how to prostrate to people. Even if I saw the Jade Emperor or the Taoist Supreme Ruler, I would only nod my head." The Tang Monk said, "Not a decent person! Don't talk nonsense! Get up quickly, or you will delay our journey." The master then got up and set off westward.

Disciple, since I am bowing thus, you need not bow to him either; just stand by and mock. What is the reason for this? The Monkey said, "You don't know; one who hides his head and shows his tail, should deserve a beating. But for the sake of the Bodhisattva, I spared him a beating and he’s lucky to get off with it. He still dares to bow to an old immortal like me? Since I was a rascally rascal as a child, I never knew how to bow. Even if it’s the Jade Emperor or the Taoist Supreme Ruler, I’d only nod to them." The master said, "You’re no good! Stop talking nonsense! Get up and let’s go west." The master then got up and prepared to head west.

The next morning, Emperor Taizong convened the court and assembled the officials. He wrote a document to obtain the scriptures and used the imperial seal. The Astronomer Royal then said, "Today is an auspicious day for travel; it is fitting for a long journey." Emperor Tang was very pleased. Seeing that the chamberlain was about to present him, he said, "My brother, today is a good day for your departure. Here is the document for your passage. I also have a purple-gold bowl, which you may use to solicit alms on your journey. Select two attendants and a good horse to assist you. You may now begin your journey." Tripitaka was delighted and, bowing to thank the emperor, accepted the gifts without hesitation. Emperor Tang then led the officials in seeing him off as far as the city gate, where the monks and disciples from the Hongfu Temple presented Tripitaka with his winter and summer robes. Emperor Tang, witnessing this, had his retinue pack Tripitaka’s belongings and then had servants bring out the wine. The emperor raised his cup and asked, "What is your title, my brother?" Tripitaka said, "A poor monk dares not presume to have a title." Emperor Taizong said, "The Bodhisattva said that the West has three great collections of scriptures. You might take this title of Three Collections." Tripitaka bowed again and took the imperial cup, saying, "Your Majesty, monks keep wine as their first precept. A poor monk has never drunk wine." Emperor Taizong said, "Today’s journey is different from other matters. This is plain wine, and you should drink this one cup to express my farewell sentiments." Tripitaka dared not refuse and, after receiving the wine, was about to drink when he saw the emperor lower his head and sprinkle a pinch of dust from his fingernail into the wine.

The next morning, the Emperor convened a court, assembling his ministers. He wrote a document for the journey to obtain scriptures, and used a royal seal. The Office of Astrology reported, "Today is a day when the star of good fortune shines, making it suitable for long journeys." Emperor Taizong was overjoyed. He then saw the Imperial Preceptor waiting outside the palace and called him up to the throne. "My brother," he said, "today is an auspicious day for departure. Here is the document for the journey. I also have an imperial bowl of purple gold to offer for you to use on your journey to beg for alms. Choose two attendants for the journey and a steed of silver for the road. You may proceed." Tang Sanzang was greatly pleased and thanked the Emperor, taking the items without delay. Emperor Taizong then led the officials in seeing him off to the pass. The monks from Hongfu Temple and his disciples had already brought all his summer and winter clothing to the pass. The Emperor had the attendants prepare the luggage and horses, and the officials brought wine. Emperor Taizong raised his cup and asked, "My brother, what is your title?" Tang Sanzang replied, "As a monk, I am unworthy of a title." Taizong said, "At the time, the Buddha said that the Western Heaven had three great scriptures. Could you take one and call yourself the Venerable Tripitaka?" Tang Sanzang again thanked the Emperor, took the wine, and said, "Your Majesty, monks abstain from alcohol, so I cannot drink." Taizong said, "This is a special occasion, so today you need not observe all your vows. Drink this cup of plain wine to show my respect." Tripitaka could not refuse. He took the cup and was just about to drink when he saw the Emperor bow his head, pick a pinch of dust from his finger, and sprinkle it into the wine.

The next morning, Emperor Taizong convened the imperial court, summoning the ministers of state. He wrote the edict for the journey and affixed the official seal. The Chongtian Bureau then reported, "Today is a day of good fortune for travel, especially for a long journey." Emperor Tang was overjoyed. He then saw the eunuchs report, "Your imperial brother, the Tripitaka Master, is waiting at the gate." He immediately summoned the Tripitaka Master to the throne and said, "Today is a auspicious day for travel. Here is the edict for the passage. I also have an imperial purple-gold alms bowl for you to use on your journey. I have chosen two capable attendants for you, and a silver-trimmed horse for your journey. You may depart at once." The Tripitaka Master was delighted and thanked the emperor for his gifts, showing no intention to delay. Emperor Tang and the officials accompanied him to the pass, where monks from the Hongfu Temple and their disciples had brought the Tripitaka Master’s summer and winter clothing to the pass. Upon seeing this, Emperor Tang first ordered the packing of the luggage and horses, then had a serving official pour wine. The emperor raised his cup and asked, "What is your honorable name?" The Tripitaka Master replied, "A mere monk, I dare not claim a title." The emperor said, "The Bodhisattva said that there are three collections of scriptures in the west. Might I suggest you take the name of the Three Collections?" The Tripitaka Master again thanked the emperor, then took the imperial wine and said, "Your Majesty, wine is the first taboo for monks. I have not drunk in years." The emperor said, "This journey is unlike other matters. This is plain wine, just a cup to honor my farewell." The Tripitaka Master, unable to refuse, accepted the cup. As he was about to drink, he saw the emperor lower his head and sprinkle a handful of dust from his own fingers into the wine.

The next morning, Emperor Taizong held court, summoning the scholar-officials and military leaders. He drafted a decree for the journey to fetch the scriptures, using the imperial seal of approval. The Imperial Astronomer then reported, "Today is a day of favorable stars, suitable for long journeys." Emperor Taizong was delighted. Seeing the eunuchs next, he said, "My royal brother, the Dharma Master, is waiting in the courtyard for orders." He immediately summoned the Dharma Master to the throne and said, "Today is a day for a good journey. Here is the decree for safe passage. I have also given you a purple-gold alms bowl to use on your journey. Additionally, I have selected two attendants for you and a steed of silver trotters to assist you on your long journey. You may set forth on your mission." The Dharma Master was overjoyed and immediately thanked the emperor, taking the items without delay. Emperor Taizong then arranged for the officials to prepare the Dharma Master’s luggage and horse, and had a servant pour wine. The emperor raised his cup and asked, "My royal brother, what is your Buddhist name?" The Dharma Master replied, "I am a Buddhist monk and have not dared to choose a name." Emperor Taizong continued, "The bodhisattva said that the Western Heaven has three collections of scriptures. Would you like to take these scriptures and name yourself the Three Collections?" The Dharma Master again thanked the emperor, took the imperial wine, and said, "Your Majesty, alcohol is the first taboo for Buddhist monks. I have never drunk before." Emperor Taizong said, "Today’s journey is different from other matters. This is plain wine, so please drink this cup to express my farewell." The Three Collections did not refuse. After taking the cup, he was about to drink when Emperor Taizong lowered his head and took a pinch of dust with his own fingers, sprinkling it into the wine.

The next morning, Emperor Taizong convened court and assembled his ministers to draft a document for obtaining scriptures. He used a通行宝印seal of passage. The Imperial Astronomer reported, "Today is an auspicious day for travel. It is suitable for journeying long distances." Emperor Taizong was overjoyed. He then saw the eunuch announce, "Your imperial younger brother, the Dharma Master, is waiting outside the gate." He promptly summoned him to the throne and said, "My imperial younger brother, today is a day of good omen for travel. This is the document for passage. I also have a purple-gold alms bowl to give you for alms collection on your journey. I will also select two reliable attendants for you, and a silver-jennet horse for your long journey. You may depart on this journey." The Dharma Master, Zhi Zang, was delighted and bowed to express his thanks, accepting the items without hesitation. Emperor Taizong, together with his officials, accompanied him to the pass. The monks from the Hongfu Temple and their disciples had already brought Zhi Zang's summer and winter clothing to the pass. Seeing this, Emperor Taizong first instructed that their belongings be packed and their mounts be prepared, then ordered the attendants to pour wine. Taizong raised his cup and asked, "What is your Dharma name?" Zhi Zang replied, "I am a homeless monk and do not dare to have a Dharma name." Taizong said, "The bodhisattva said that there are three sets of scriptures in the West. Could you choose a title for the scriptures, calling yourself the Three-Treasure?" Zhi Zang bowed again and accepted the imperial wine, explaining, "Your Majesty, the first precept for monks is not to drink alcohol. I have never drunk alcohol since I became a monk." Taizong replied, "This journey is different from other matters. This is plain wine. You must drink this cup to fulfill my farewell intentions." The Three-Treasure could not refuse and took the wine. As he was about to drink, Taizong bent down and sprinkled a pinch of dust from his finger into the wine.

Sages Bodhisattva led the assembly into the hall and paid respects to the Jade Emperor, then greeted Laojun and the Queen Mother, seating themselves. Then he asked, "How was the Peach Blossom Banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year, it was a grand affair. This year, however, with the chaos caused by the demonic monkey, it was a hollow honor." Sages Bodhisattva asked, "Where does the demonic monkey come from?" The Jade Emperor said, "The demonic monkey was born from a stone egg on Flower and Fruit Mountain in the Eastern Victory Land, State of Maojiao. When it was born, it emitted golden light, which shot towards the Celestial Bureaucracy. At first, we did not pay attention, but it eventually became a spirit, subduing dragons and taming tigers, erasing its name from the list of the dead. It was reported by the Dragon King and the King of Hell. I intended to capture it, but Zhengan Star reported that among the Three Realms, all who have nine orifices can become immortal. So I educated and instructed him, inviting him to Heaven to serve as the attendant of the stables. He was dissatisfied with his rank and rebelled against the Heavenly Court. I then sent Heavenly King Li and Prince Nezha to subdue him. Another decree was issued to pacify him and invite him to Heaven, where he was appointed as the ‘Great Sage Equal to Heaven,’ with a position but no salary. Due to having nothing to do, he wandered around, causing trouble. I was afraid of more disturbances and assigned him to manage the Peach Garden. He disobeyed the laws, stole the old and large peaches, and, during the banquet, as an untitled guest, tricked the Barefoot Immortal, disguised himself as him, and stole all the immortal dishes and drinks. He also stole Laojun’s elixir and an unspecified amount of imperial wine to share with his fellow monkeys in the mountain. This has caused me great distress, so I have dispatched ten thousand heavenly soldiers to trap him. I have not heard from them today and do not know the outcome."

The Bodhisattva led them into the inner chambers, paid respects to the Jade Emperor, then greeted Laozi and the Queen Mother, and they each took their seats. The Bodhisattva then asked, "How is the Peach Blossom Banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "We hold the banquet annually with great joy, but this year it was disrupted by the monkey demon, making it a mere pretense." The Bodhisattva asked, "What is the monkey demon's origin?" The Jade Emperor said, "The monkey demon originated from a stone egg on Flower and Fruit Mountain in the Eastern Victory States. When it first appeared, it radiated golden light that pierced the heavens. At first, we did not pay it any mind, but it later developed into a spirit capable of subduing dragons and tigers, and it struck its name from the records of the dead. It was then reported to me by the Dragon King and the Judge of the Soul. I intended to capture it, but Longxing Star announced that in the Three Realms, any creature with nine orifices can become a仙. So I educated and promoted him, bringing him to the celestial court and appointing him as Director of the Imperial Stables. That fiend was dissatisfied with the position and rebelled against the Heavenly Palace. I then dispatched Heavenly General Li and Prince Nezha to subdue him, and after much effort, I appointed him as 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven' without providing him with a salary. He was left to idle, wandering about. Fearing that he would cause trouble, I appointed him to oversee the peach garden. But he broke the law, stealing all the old, large peaches. When the banquet was held, as he was a non-salaried individual, he was not invited. He tricked and deceived the Barefoot Immortal and then transformed into his appearance to attend the banquet, stealing all the divine food and drinks. He also stole Laozi's elixir and many barrels of imperial wine, which he shared with his fellow monkeys on the mountain. My heart is filled with worry over this, so I have dispatched ten thousand heavenly troops to capture him. I have not heard back as of yet, and I do not know the outcome."

Bodhisattva led the crowd into the interior and, after paying respects to the Jade Emperor, greeted the Venerable Laojun and the Queen Mother of the West, then each took their seats. Bodhisattva then asked, "How was the Peach Blossom Banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "We hold this banquet annually, filled with joy, but this year it was disrupted by a monkey demon, making it a hollow affair." Bodhisattva inquired, "Where does this monkey demon come from?" The Jade Emperor answered, "This monkey demon hails from the Eastern Victory Region State of Huaguo Mountain. When it was born, it emitted golden light that pierced the celestial mansion of the Supreme Ruler of the Northern Dipper. At first, we did not take it seriously, but later it became a spirit, subduing dragons and taming tigers, removing its name from the register of the dead. The Dragon Kings and the King of Hell submitted reports to me. I wished to capture and punish it, but the Evening Star advised, ‘In the three realms, any creature with nine apertures can become immortal.’ So I educated and appointed him, summoning him to the celestial capital, and appointed him as Assistant Stable Master of the Imperial Stables. He was dissatisfied with the lowly position and rebelled against the Heavenly Palace. I then dispatched Heavenly King Li and Prince Nezha to subdue him. After that, I issued a decree of appeasement, summoning him to the celestial capital and appointing him as ‘Great Sage Equal to Heaven,’ granting him an office without stipend. Failing to find employment, he roamed the East and West. Afraid that he might cause trouble, I made him caretaker of the Peach Blossom Garden. He ignored the law and ate the old, large peaches. When the banquet was held, as he had no stipend, he did not invite him. He then lured the Barefooted Immortal, assuming his appearance and snatched the divine dishes and drinks. He also stole the Venerable Laojun's immortal elixir and several bottles of imperial wine, bringing them back to the monkeys on his mountain to enjoy. I was greatly troubled by this, so I dispatched a hundred thousand heavenly soldiers to set a trap for him. I do not know the outcome of this hunt."

The Bodhisattva led the assembly inside and, after paying respects to the Jade Emperor, greeted the Elder Immortal and Queen Mother, each taking their seat. The Bodhisattva then asked, "How was the Peach Blossom Banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year, the gathering is filled with joy. This year, however, chaos was caused by the wicked monkey, making it a mere formality." The Bodhisattva inquired, "Where does this wicked monkey come from?" The Jade Emperor explained, "The wicked monkey was born from a stone egg on Flower and Fruit Mountain in the Eastern Paradise, a region of the Eastern Great Ocean. At birth, it emitted golden light, which penetrated the palace of the stars. Initially, this was not taken seriously, but it later evolved into a spirit, subduing dragons and taming tigers, and erased its name from the register of the dead. The Dragon Kings and the阎王阎王sent an account. I intended to capture it, but Long庚星the Star of Life advised that any creature with nine orifices could become immortal. So I educated it, summoned it to the heavens, and appointed it as an Assistant Stablemaster in the Imperial Stables. The monkey disapproved of the position, rebelled against heaven, and was subdued by Heavenly General Li and Prince Nezha. A decree was then issued to pacify the monkey, who was summoned to heaven and appointed as 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven,' though he received no salary. Bored and without responsibilities, he traveled around, causing concern. I appointed him to manage the peach garden to prevent further trouble. But he did not follow the laws, and consumed all the old and large peaches. When the banquet was held, being an unpaid employee, he was not invited. He tricked and deceived the Barefoot Immortal, transformed into his appearance, entered the banquet, and stole all the immortal foods and drinks. He also stole the Elder Immortal's elixir and several bottles of imperial wine to share with the other monkeys on the mountain. This has caused me great distress, so I have mobilized ten thousand heavenly troops to ensnare him. I have not heard from them today and do not know the outcome."

The Bodhisattva led them into the inner chambers and paid their respects to the Jade Emperor. After that, they met Laojun and the Queen Mother, each taking their seats. Then he inquired, "How is the Peach Blossom Banquet proceeding?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year, we hold the banquet with joy and merriment. This year, however, a chaos was caused by the demon monkey, making it all but a farce." The Bodhisattva asked, "What is the origin of the demon monkey?" The Jade Emperor responded, "The demon monkey originated from a stone egg in the Flower and Fruit Mountain of the Eastern Regions of the Divine State of傲来国. At birth, it radiated golden light that pierced through the celestial regions. At first, we did not take it seriously, but it eventually became a spirit capable of subduing dragons and taming tigers. It removed its name from the list of the dead. At that time, the Dragon Kings and the King of Hell reported to me. I intended to capture the monkey, but Longjing Star advised that in the three realms, any creature with nine apertures can become a immortal. I thus educated the monkey, summoned it to heaven, and appointed it as a Guardian of the Imperial Stables, Prefect of the Stable Masters. The monkey was dissatisfied with the low rank and rebelled against the heavenly palace. I then sent Heavenly King Li and Prince Nezha to subdue him, but I also issued an imperial decree to pacify him, and summoned him to heaven to be appointed as ‘Great Sage Equal to Heaven,’ a position with a title but no salary. The monkey, with nothing to do, wandered around. I was afraid of further incidents and appointed him to manage the Peach Garden. But he disregarded the laws and stole ripe peaches from the old trees. When the banquet was set, as a non-paid employee, he was not invited. He then tricked the Sandalwood Monk, transformed into his appearance, and entered the banquet, stealing all the immortal food and drinks. He also stole Laojun’s elixir and a great quantity of imperial wine, which he took back to the monkeys in his mountain to enjoy. My heart was troubled by this, and thus I mobilized ten thousand heavenly troops, set up a net of heaven, and subdued him. It has been a day since they left, and I do not know the outcome."

While the servants bustled about, the master went to the common hall. Any traveler knows quite well what such common halls are like: the same walls painted with oil paint, darkened at the top from the chimney smoke and polished at the bottom by the backs of different travelers, more so from the native merchants, for merchants would come here, day after day, to drink their usual pair of teas; the same sooty ceiling; the same smoked chandelier with a multitude of hanging glass shards, which would jump and ring each time the sweeper ran up and down the worn-down linoleum, deftly swaying a tray filled with the same countless cups of tea as seagulls on a shore; the same full-wall paintings in oil, in short, everything the same as everywhere else; the only difference being that one of the paintings depicted a nymph with such enormous breasts that the reader, surely, has never seen before. Such a display of nature, however, happens on various historical paintings, unknown when, from where, or by whom they were brought to Russia, sometimes even by our nobles, art enthusiasts who had bought them in Italy according to the advice of the couriers who had carried them. The master took off his cap and unraveled the colorful shawl that his wife would prepare for him if he were married, with suitable advice on how to wrap up, and, as to whether single men wore such scarves, I cannot say, I know not who does, I have never worn such a shawl. Unraveling the shawl, the master ordered them to bring him his dinner. While he was served various ordinary fare in taverns, such as dumplings with a rolled pie specially kept for travelers over several weeks, brains with peas, sausages with cabbage, fried piglet, pickled cucumber, and the ever-ready rolled sweet pie, always ready for service; while all this was brought to him both warmed up and simply cold, he made the servant, or the sweeper, relate all sorts of nonsense: about who had run the tavern before and who now, and whether it brought much income, and what a scoundrel their landlord was; to which the sweeper, as usual, replied: "Oh, indeed, sir, a cheat." Just as in enlightened Europe, so in enlightened Russia, there are now quite a few respectable people who cannot eat in a tavern without talking to the servant, and sometimes even to jest about him. However, the traveler did not ask all empty questions; he inquired with extraordinary precision about the city's governor, the chamberlain, the prosecutor, and, in a word, did not miss a single important official; but with even greater precision, and perhaps with participation, he asked about all the important landowners: how many serfs they had, how far they lived from the city, what kind of character they had, and how often they came to the city; he inquired attentively about the state of the region: whether any epidemics had occurred in their province – widespread fevers, deadly fevers, smallpox and the like – and everything in such detail and with such precision that it showed more than just simple curiosity. In his mannerisms, the master had something dignified and sneezed very loudly. It is not known how he did it, but only his nose sounded like a trumpet. This, in my view, is a completely innocent quality, yet it gained him much respect from the tavern servant, so that every time he heard this sound, he shook his hair, straightened up more respectfully, and, bowing down from a height, asked: "Is there anything else needed?" After dinner, the master drank a cup of coffee and sat down on a divan, placing a pillow behind his back, which in Russian taverns, instead of elastic fur, is stuffed with something extremely similar to brick and stone. There he began to yawn and ordered to be taken to his room, where, lying down, he fell asleep for two hours. Having rested, he wrote on a piece of paper, as the tavern servant had asked, the rank, name, and surname to be reported to the appropriate police station. The sweeper, descending the stairs, read the note as follows: "Councillor Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov, landowner, for his own purposes." When the sweeper was still decoding the note, Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov himself went to see the city, which he seemed to be satisfied with, finding that it was no less than other provincial cities: the yellow paint on the stone houses stood out sharply, while the gray on the wooden ones darkened humbly. The houses were of one, two, and one-and-a-half stories, with a permanent mezzanine, which the provincial architects found very beautiful. Somewhere these houses seemed to be lost among the wide, like a field, street and endless wooden fences; somewhere they gathered in heaps, and here was more of a stir and liveliness of the people. There were almost washed out by rain signs with sausages and shoes, sometimes with blue pants and a sign by some Arshavsky tailor; there was a shop with hats and forage caps and a sign that read: "Foreigner Vasily Fedorov"; there was a billiard table with two players in evening coats, into which guests would come on the last act in our theaters; the players were depicted with cues aimed back, hands slightly twisted backwards, legs slightly crooked, just having finished a short scene in the air. Below all this was written: "And here is the establishment." Somewhere on the street stood tables with nuts, soap, and sweet biscuits that looked like soap; somewhere there was a tavern with a drawn thick fish with a fork stuck in it. More often, however, it was noticeable that the dark double-headed state eagles, which had now been replaced by a terse inscription: "Drinking House." The street was everywhere uneven. He peeked into the city park, which consisted of thin trees that had poorly taken root, with supports at the bottom in the form of triangles, very beautifully painted green oil paint. While the servants were busy, the master went into the common room. After thus dispelling her misgivings about him, he found the quiet tête-à-tête by the window too long; he tapped the lectern with his knuckles and then with his fist. The student glanced briefly over the woman’s shoulder at K, but was not disturbed, and even pressed closer to her and clasped her. She lowered her head deeply, as if listening attentively; he kissed her as she bent down, loudly on the neck, without interrupting his speech much. K saw in this the confirmation of the student’s tyranny, as described by the woman, and stood up, pacing back and forth in the room. He thought about how to get rid of the student as quickly as possible, and was not displeased when the student, apparently annoyed by K’s walking around, which had become almost a trampling, remarked: “If you are impatient, you can leave. You could have left earlier, no one would have missed you. Yes, you should have left immediately, and quickly.” This remark might have expressed all kinds of anger, but it also contained the arrogance of a future court official speaking to an unpleasant defendant. K stood very close to him and said smilingly, “I am indeed impatient, that is true, but this impatience can be most easily overcome by your leaving. If, however, perhaps you came here to study – I heard that you are a student – I will be glad to make way for you and leave with the woman. You will have to study much more before you become a judge, however. I know your court system only slightly, but I assume that it is not enough to do it merely with rough talk, which you know to deliver quite unseemly well.” “He shouldn’t have been allowed to walk around so freely,” the student said, as if explaining K’s offensive words to the woman, “it was a mistake. Although there was no immediate natural light, it wasn’t entirely dark, for some compartments had plain wooden lattice walls instead of uniform boards, allowing some light to pass through and allowing one to see individuals sitting at desks or standing near the lattice, peering through the slats to observe the corridor. It was likely Sunday, and there were only a few people in the corridor. They made a very modest impression. They sat in pairs on long wooden benches to either side of the corridor, at regular intervals. Though all were poorly dressed, most, based on their expressions, postures, beards, and many small, barely verifiable details, belonged to the higher classes. Since there were no coat hooks, they had placed their hats under the benches, most likely following the example of their neighbor. When the first to arrive, K. and the court officer, were spotted, the others stood to greet them, and as the subsequent ones saw them, they too stood up, so that all stood up as K. and the court officer passed. They never stood up straight; their backs were bent, their knees bent, and they stood like street beggars. K. waited for the court officer, who was slightly behind him, and said, "How humbled they must feel." "Yes," said the court officer, "they are defendants. Everyone you see here is a defendant." "Really!" said K. "Then they are my colleagues." And he turned to the next person, a large, slender, already nearly gray-haired man. "Why are you waiting here?" K. asked politely. The unexpected question threw the man into confusion, and it looked particularly awkward, since it was clear that he was an experienced person who had learned to control himself elsewhere and was not easily dislodged from his superior position over many. Here, however, he was unable to respond to such a simple question and looked at the others as if they were obligated to help him and as if no answer could be expected from him if they did not. Then the court officer came over to soothe and encourage him: "The gentleman here is only asking what you are waiting for. Answer, won’t you?" The court officer’s voice, which he likely knew, worked better: "I am waiting—," he began and then paused. Apparently, he had chosen to answer this way to respond exactly to the question, but he could not find the continuation. Several of the people waiting had approached and formed a group around them. The court officer said to them, "Away, away, clear the corridor." They moved back a little but not to their original seats. By then, the questioned man had collected himself and even answered with a small smile, "I made some evidence requests last month and am waiting for them to be addressed." "It seems you go to great lengths," said K. "Yes," said the man, "it is my matter." "Not everyone thinks as you do," said K., "I, for example, am also accused, and yet, as I hope to be saved, I have not made any evidence requests, nor have I done anything of the sort. Do you think it necessary?" "I’m not sure," said the man, again in full uncertainty; he seemed to think that K. was making a jest, so he probably would have liked to repeat his earlier answer, but K.’s impatient look prompted him to say only, "As for me, I have made evidence requests." "Do you not believe I am accused?" asked K. "Oh, please, certainly," said the man, stepping aside a little, but there was not belief but only fear in his answer. "Do you not believe me?" K. asked and, without thinking, because of the humbled man’s behavior, touched his arm as if he wanted to force him to believe. But he did not want to cause him pain; he had only lightly touched him, yet the man screamed as if K. had grabbed him with burning tongs rather than with two fingers. This ridiculous screaming made K. finally fed up with him; if one did not believe him to be accused, the better; perhaps he even thought him a judge. And he now truly grasped him and pushed him back onto the bench, then walked on. "Most defendants are so sensitive," said the court officer. Behind them, nearly all the people gathered around the man, who had already stopped screaming, and seemed to be questioning him about the incident. An armed guard came forward; he was mainly recognizable by a saber whose scabbard, at least from the color, was made of aluminum. K. was amazed and even reached out to touch it. The guard, who had come to investigate the shouting, asked about the incident. The court officer tried to soothe him with a few words, but the guard declared that he must still investigate and saluted, then walked on in quick, short, likely gout-inflicted strides.

The usher tried to reassure him with a few words, but the guard insisted on checking and saluted as he moved off with very quick, but very short, measured steps, probably due to gout.

At the entry, he nearly stumbled, as there was a step behind the door. "The audience isn’t shown much consideration," he said. "No consideration is given at all," the court attendant said, "just look at the waiting room." It was a long corridor from which crude wooden doors led to the individual compartments of the attic. Although there was no direct sunlight, it wasn’t entirely dark, for some compartments had bare wooden grilles instead of uniform planks of wood that allowed some light to seep through, enabling one to see individual officials seated at their desks or standing at the grilles, peering through the gaps to watch the people in the corridor. There were few people in the corridor, probably because it was Sunday. They looked very subdued. They sat in two rows of long wooden benches on either side of the corridor at intervals. All of them were poorly dressed, though most, judging by their facial expressions, posture, beards, and many barely noticeable small details, seemed to belong to the upper classes. Since there were no coat hooks, they had placed their hats, probably following the example of one another, under the benches. As those sitting first by the door noticed K. and the court attendant, they stood up to greet them. Seeing this, the following realized they should also greet, so that all rose when the two passed by. They never stood up straight; their backs were bent, their knees bent, and they stood like street beggars. K. waited for the court attendant, who was slightly behind him, and said, "How humiliated they must feel." "Yes," said the court attendant, "these are all defendants. All the people you see here are defendants." "Really!" said K. "Then they must be my colleagues." And he turned to the next person, a tall, slender man with almost white hair. "Why are you waiting here?" K. asked politely. The unexpected question made the man puzzled, and it seemed especially embarrassing because it was clear that he was a worldly man who, elsewhere, surely could control himself and not easily relinquish the superiority he had gained over many. Here, however, he could not answer such a simple question and looked at the others as though they were obligated to help him, as though no one could answer for him if this help was not forthcoming. Then the court attendant came over to soothe and encourage the man: "This gentleman is only asking what you’re waiting for. Answer him, please." The court attendant’s voice, which he was probably familiar with, had a better effect: "I’m waiting—“ he began and paused. Evidently, he had chosen this start to answer precisely the question, but now he could not continue. Some of those waiting had approached and formed a circle around the group. The court attendant said to them, "Out, out, clear the corridor." They moved back a bit but not to their previous seats. By now, the man had composed himself and even replied with a small smile: "I made some evidence requests in my case a month ago and am waiting for them to be processed." "It seems you go to great lengths," said K. "Yes," the man said, "it’s my case, after all." "Not everyone thinks as you do," said K., "for example, I am also charged, but, as far as I hope for salvation, I neither made evidence requests nor taken any such measures. Do you consider it necessary?" "I’m not quite sure," the man replied in total uncertainty, as though he thought K. was making a joke and, fearing to make another mistake, wanted to repeat his earlier answer, but with K.’s impatient look, he said only, "As for me, I made evidence requests." "You don’t believe I am charged, do you?" K. asked. "Oh, please, of course," said the man, stepping slightly aside, but there was no belief in his answer, only fear. "Then you don’t believe me?" K. asked and, without realizing it, due to the man’s humble nature, grasped his arm as if he wanted to compel him to believe. But he did not want to hurt him and had only lightly touched him. Nevertheless, the man cried out, as if K. had seized him not with two fingers but with a burning iron. This ridiculous screaming made K. completely weary of him. If they did not believe him that he was charged, it was even better; perhaps he even considered him a judge. And he now really held the man firmly, pushed him back on the bench, and went on. "Most defendants are so sensitive," the court attendant said. Now almost all those waiting gathered around the man who had already stopped screaming and seemed to be interrogating him about the incident. A guard came up to them, who was primarily recognizable by a saber, the sheath of which, at least by color, was made of aluminum. K. was surprised and even touched his hand. The guard, who had come because of the screaming, asked about the incident. The court attendant tried to soothe him with a few words, but the guard insisted on investigating it himself, saluted, and walked off with very quick, very short, apparently gout-induced steps.

He whistled and leaped into the air, his fiery eyes shielding his gaze as he scanned the surroundings. Finding no sign of their horse, he reported, "Master, our horse must have been devoured by that dragon; we cannot see it anywhere." The monk replied, "Disciple, how could that beast have a mouth so large to swallow not only the horse but also the saddle and bridle? Perhaps it ran off into a nearby valley. You must look once more." The monkey replied, "You do not know my abilities. I can usually see a thousand li in every direction. Even a dragonfly’s fluttering wings within that range are visible to me, yet I cannot see this horse!" The monk said, "If he ate the horse, how shall we proceed? Alas! This mountain and river journey, how can we go on?" Saying this, tears began to stream down his face. Seeing the monk weep, the monkey could not contain his irritation and roared, "Master, do not be such a coward! Sit there and let me go find that beast and have him return our horse!" The monk held him back, saying, "Disciple, where do you intend to look for him?"

"Uncle," said K., "excitement is so useless, it's useless on your side and would be useless on mine. With excitement, one does not win the proceedings, let my practical experiences count as well, just as you count yours, even if they surprise me, always and especially now, pay attention to them. Since you say that the family would also be involved in the proceedings – which I, for one, can hardly comprehend, but that is a side issue – I will gladly follow you in everything. Only the rural stay, I hold not for advantageous in your sense, for that would mean flight and a sense of guilt. Moreover, although I am pursued more here, I can also advance the case more myself." "Right," said the uncle in a tone as if they were finally getting closer, "I only made the suggestion because I feared that, if you stayed here, the matter would be jeopardized by your indifference, and it seemed better if I worked for you instead of you. But if you want to take the matter on with all your might, it is of course much better." "We are in agreement on that," said K. "And do you now have a suggestion for what I should do first?" "I must consider the matter first," said the uncle, "you must consider that I have been practically on the land for twenty years now, and my sense of smell for such matters is weakening. Various important connections with people who might know more here have loosened on their own. I am somewhat neglected in the country, you know that. Only in such situations does one realize it. Partly, my case also came unexpectedly, although I somehow sensed something similar in Erna's letter, and now, with your appearance, I almost know it with certainty. But that is irrelevant; the most important thing now is not to lose any time." While he was speaking, he stood on his tiptoes, waved to a car, and now, while simultaneously shouting the address to the driver, he pulled K. behind him into the car. "We are going now to Attorney Huld," he said, "he was my schoolmate. You know the name, don't you? No? That is rather curious. He does have a great reputation as a defender and legal aid. But I have, as a person, the greatest trust in him." "Everything you do is fine with me," said K., though the uncle's urgent and pressing manner caused him some discomfort. It was not particularly pleasant to be driven to an attorney's office as a defendant. "I did not know," he said, "that one could also enlist an attorney in such a matter." "But of course," said the uncle, "that is only natural. Why not? And now, tell me everything that has happened so that I can be thoroughly informed about the matter." K. began to recount everything immediately, without omitting anything, his complete openness being the only protest he could make against the uncle's opinion that the trial was a great shame. He mentioned Frau Bürstner's name only once, briefly, but this did not affect his openness because Frau Bürstner had no connection to the case. As he spoke, he looked out the window and observed that they were approaching the suburb where the court offices were located. He pointed this out to the uncle, but the uncle did not find it particularly remarkable. The car pulled up in front of a dark house. The uncle rang the bell at the first door on the ground floor; while they waited, he grinned and whispered, "Eight o'clock, an unusual time for visitors. But Huld won't mind." Two large, black eyes appeared in the peephole, stared at the two guests for a while, and then disappeared; the door did not open. The uncle and K. confirmed to each other that they had seen two eyes. "A new maid who is afraid of strangers," said the uncle and knocked again. The eyes appeared again, and one could almost think they looked sad, though perhaps this was just an illusion caused by the gas flame that hissed loudly above their heads but gave little light. "Open up," the uncle called out and pounded with his fist against the door, "it's friends of the gentleman attorney!" "The gentleman attorney is ill," whispered someone behind them. At the other end of the short hallway stood a man in a nightshirt who made this announcement with a very soft voice. The uncle, already irritable due to the long wait, turned around abruptly, called, "Ill? You say he is ill?" and moved almost threateningly toward the man, as if the man was the illness. "Someone has already opened the door," said the man, pointed to the door of the attorney, pulled his nightshirt together, and disappeared. The door had indeed been opened; a young girl – K. recognized the dark, slightly bulging eyes again – stood in a long white apron in the anteroom and held a candle in her hand. "You will open earlier next time," said the uncle without any greeting, while the girl made a small curtsey. "Come, Josef," said the uncle, and then K. followed the girl slowly past her. "The gentleman attorney is ill," said the girl as the uncle, without stopping, hurried toward a door. K. still looked at the girl as she turned around to lock the door to the apartment, for she had a round, doll-like face, not only the pale cheeks but also the jaw, the temples, and the forehead. "Josef!" the uncle called again, and he asked the girl, "Is it heart trouble?" "I believe it is," said the girl, finding time to carry the candle forward and open the door to the room. In a corner of the room, where the candlelight had not yet reached, a face with a long beard rose from the bed. "Leni, who's that?" asked the attorney, blinded by the candle and not recognizing the guests. "Albert, your old friend is here," said the uncle. "Ach, Albert," said the attorney and sank back on the pillows, requiring no pretense before this visit. "Is it really so bad?" asked the uncle and sat on the edge of the bed. "I do not think so. It is an attack of my heart trouble, and it will pass like the earlier ones," the attorney said softly. "Possible," said the attorney, "but it is worse than ever before. I breathe heavily, I do not sleep, and I lose strength daily." "So," said the uncle and pressed the Panama hat tightly against his knee with his large hand. "These are bad news. Have you the proper care? It is already sad enough here, so dark. It has been a long time since I was here last, and then it seemed friendlier. Your little Miss here does not seem very cheerful, or is she pretending?" The girl still stood with the candle near the door; to the extent that K. could discern with her hazy gaze, she looked more at K. than at the uncle, even as he spoke to her. K. leaned against a chair that he had pushed near the girl. "When one is as ill as I am," said the attorney, "one must rest. I am not sad." After a short pause, he added, "And Leni cares for me well; she is good." But this did not convince the uncle, who was prejudiced against the caregiver and although he did not say anything to the patient, he followed the caregiver with a stern gaze as she now went to the bed, placed the candle on the nightstand, bent over the patient, and whispered to him as she rearranged the pillows. He forgot almost all concern for the patient, stood up, and walked back and forth behind the caregiver. K. would not have been surprised if he had grabbed the girl by her skirts and pulled her away from the bed. K. himself watched everything calmly; even the attorney's illness was not entirely unwelcome to him, for he could not oppose the uncle's zeal for his cause, and the diversion this zeal now brought him without his consent he was happy to take. Then the uncle said, perhaps only to provoke the caregiver, "Miss, please let us have a moment alone, I have a personal matter to discuss with my friend." The caregiver, who was still bent over the patient and smoothing the sheet on the wall, turned her head only and said very calmly, which was a stark contrast to the uncle's previously agitated and then overwrought speech: "You see, the gentleman is so ill that he cannot discuss matters." She had probably repeated the uncle's words out of convenience, but even from an unbiased observer, they could be seen as mocking. The uncle, however, reacted like a man with a stake in the matter, "You damn wench," he said in a first flurried whisper, to K.'s alarm, even though he had expected something similar, and he rushed to the uncle, with the determined intention of covering his mouth with both hands. Fortunately, the patient behind the girl rose, the uncle made a dark face, as if he were swallowing something repulsive, and then said more calmly, "Of course, we still have our wits. If what I ask is not possible, I would not ask. Please, go now!" The caregiver stood upright at the bed, fully facing the uncle, and with one hand, she seemed to stroke the hand of the attorney as K. thought. "You can say anything in front of Leni," said the patient, in all likelihood in a tone of urgent entreaty. "It does not concern me," said the uncle, "it is not my secret." And he turned around as if he no longer intended to discuss the matter further, but still gave a little time to think. "Who does it concern then?" the attorney asked with a fading voice and lay back down again. "My nephew," said the uncle, "I have brought him with me." And he introduced: "Procurator Josef K." Listen to my reply to all your letters: for the first time I felt sorry for Prince Lev Nikolayevich the very day I met him, and when I learned all that happened at your evening. I felt sorry for him because he is such a simple person and believed in his simplicity that he could be happy... with a woman... of that sort. What I feared for him has come true: you could not love him, you tormented him and left him. You see the Monkey King splitting the waterway, straight back to the Iron Board Bridge, leaping up. Only to see four old monkeys, leading the other monkeys: all waiting by the bridge. Suddenly, they saw Sun Wukong jump out of the waves, not a speck of water on him, golden and radiant, walking onto the bridge. The monkeys were all frightened and knelt down, saying, "King, what splendid colors! What splendid colors!" Sun Wukong, with a pleasant smile, climbed onto the throne, holding the iron rod in the middle. The other monkeys, unaware of their manners, all came to grab that treasure, but it was like a dragonfly trying to shake an iron tree; they couldn't budge it at all. They all bit their fingers and stuck out their tongues, saying, "Grandfather! So heavy, how did you manage to bring it?" Sun Wukong approached, stretched out his hand, and grabbed it, laughing and saying, "Every object has its owner. This treasure was sealed in the ocean for thousands of years, and just so happened to shine brightly this year. The Dragon King thought it was just a piece of black iron and called it the divine treasure at the bottom of the天河. None of those fellows could lift it, so they asked me to go and take it. At that time, the treasure was over two丈long and as thick as a bushel; I grabbed it, thought it was too big, and it became much smaller; when I asked for it to be smaller, it became even smaller; when I asked for it to be smaller again, it became even smaller. Hurrying to look at the light, it had a line of characters on top: '如意金箍棒, 一万三千五百斤.' All of you step back, and let me show you how it can change again." He tossed the treasure in his hand, saying, "Smaller! Smaller! Smaller!" Instantly, it became as small as a needle for embroidery, which could be stuffed inside the ear. The monkeys were startled, calling out, "King, give it back for us to play with!" Sun Wukong really went into his ear and took it out, holding it in his palm, calling, "Bigger! Bigger! Bigger!" Immediately, it grew to the size of a bushel and two丈long. In the joy of his demonstration, he leaped onto the bridge, walked out of the cave, held the treasure in his hand, used his celestial mimicry divine power, and bent his waist, calling, "Long!" And he grew to ten thousand feet, his head like a mountain, waist like a steep mountain, eyes like lightning, mouth like a blood basin, and teeth like swords and spears. In his hand, that rod touched the thirty-three heavens above and reached the eighteen layers of hell below, frightening all the tigers, leopards, wolves, and foxes, all the creatures of the mountain, the seventy-two cave kings, to prostrate and greet. In an instant, he gathered his power, changed the treasure back to a needle for embroidery, and hid it in his ear, returning to his cave. All the cave kings were terrified and came to congratulate him.

The monkeys, not knowing how to behave, all tried to grab the treasure, but it was as if a dragonfly were trying to shake a cypress tree—impossible to move it. Monkey King advanced, stretched out his hands, and picked up the rod, smiling as he said, "Every object has its owner. This treasure has lain hidden at the bottom of the sea for thousands of years. Only this year did it emit light. The dragon kings thought it was just a lump of black iron, calling it the divine treasure at the bottom of the天河. None of them could lift it, so they asked me to go get it. At the time, the rod was over two zhang long, as thick as a choushi (a measurement), and quite heavy. When I grabbed it, I felt it was too big and made it smaller. When I asked for it to be even smaller, it became smaller. When I asked for it to be even smaller, it became even smaller. It grew to the size of a dou (measurement), and two zhang long. When he was in a jovial mood, he jumped onto the bridge, walked out to the cave entrance, and held the rod in his hand. Using his divine power to transform, he bent his waist and said, "Grow!" He grew to a height of ten thousand feet, his head like Mount Tai, his waist like a steep ridge, his eyes like lightning, his mouth like a blood bowl, his teeth like swords.
