"Oh no," said the painter in defense of his window, "by not being able to open it, although it is a simple pane, the warmth is better retained here than through double glazing. If I want to ventilate, which is not very necessary, as air can enter through the gaps in the beams, I can open one of my doors or even both." K., somewhat comforted by this explanation, looked around to find the second door. The painter noticed this and said, "It’s behind you, I had to block it with the bed." Only now did K. notice the small door in the wall. "It’s just that everything is much too small for an atelier here," said the painter, preempting a possible criticism from K. "I had to settle with what I could. The bed in front of the door, of course, stands in a very bad place. The judge, for example, whom I am currently painting, always comes through the door near the bed, and I gave him a key to this door so that he could wait for me in the atelier, even if I am not at home. Now he usually comes early in the morning while I am still asleep. It naturally wakes me from the deepest sleep when the door next to the bed opens. You would lose all respect for the judges if you heard the curses with which I greet him when he climbs over my bed in the morning. I could take away the key, but that would only make things worse. All doors here can be broken out with the slightest effort." While the painter was speaking, K. considered whether to remove his coat. But in the end, he realized that if he did not do so, he would not be able to stay here much longer. So, he removed his coat and put it over his knees so that he could put it back on if the meeting ended. As soon as he had taken off his coat, one of the girls cried out, "He has already taken off his coat!" and one heard how everyone pressed themselves to the cracks to see the spectacle. "The girls, you see, believe that I will be painting you and that you will therefore take off your coat," said the painter. "So," said K., only slightly amused, for he felt no better than before, sitting here in his shirt sleeves. Almost grumpily, he asked, "What did you call the other two options?" He had already forgotten the expressions. "The semblance of acquittal and postponement," said the painter. "You can choose which one you want. Both are accessible through my help, of course not without effort. The difference here is that the semblance of acquittal is a collective and temporary one, while postponement is a much smaller but lasting one. First, the semblance of acquittal. If you desire this, I will write a statement of your innocence on a piece of paper. The text for such a statement was passed down to me by my father and is unassailable. With this statement, I now make a tour among the judges I know. I will begin, for example, by presenting the statement to the judge whom I am currently painting, when he arrives for the session today. I present the statement, explain that you are innocent, and stand surety for your innocence. This is not only a superficial but a real and binding guarantee." There was reproach in the painter’s gaze as if he was troubled that K. wanted to burden him with such a guarantee. "That would be very kind," said K. "And the judge would believe you, yet still not acquit me?" "As I said," answered the painter. "By the way, it is not entirely safe that everyone would believe me. Some judges, for example, will demand that you be brought to him yourself. Then you would have to come once. However, in such a case, the matter is already half won, especially since I would certainly prepare you beforehand on how to behave in front of the relevant judge. Things are worse for the judges who – this will happen – immediately reject me. We must do without these, but we may, for individual judges cannot decide the matter here. If I now have sufficient signatures of judges on this statement, I will take it to the judge who is handling your trial. Perhaps I have also his signature, then everything will develop a bit faster than usual. In general, there will then be no more obstacles, and for the accused, it is the time of highest confidence. It is curious, but true, that people are more confident in this time than after an acquittal. No special effort is needed anymore. The judge has the guarantee of a number of judges in the statement and can acquit you without concern. He will do so, although after the fulfillment of various formalities, I and other acquaintances will be pleased." "Then I am free," said K. hesitantly. "Yes," said the painter, "but only apparently free or, better put, temporarily free. The lower judges, to whom my acquaintances belong, have no right to make a final acquittal. This right is reserved for the highest, the unreachable court for you, for me, and for us all. How it is there, we do not know and do not want to know. Therefore, our judges do not have the great right to free one from the accusation, but they do have the right to release one from the accusation. That means, if you are acquitted in this way, you will be free for the moment, but the accusation still hovers over you and can be brought up again.

This orderly presentation initially surprised K., but then he spoke just as softly as the painter: "I believe you are contradicting yourself." "How so?" the painter asked patiently, leaning back with a smile. This smile gave K. the feeling that he was about to begin uncovering contradictions not in the painter's words, but in the judicial proceedings themselves. Nevertheless, K. did not back down and said: "You once remarked that the court is inaccessible to evidence, later you confined this to the public court, and now you even say that the innocent need no help before the court. This is already a contradiction. Moreover, you earlier stated that it is possible to influence the judges personally, but now you doubt that genuine acquittal, as you call it, can ever be achieved through personal influence. This is the second contradiction." "These contradictions are easily resolved," said the painter. "We are speaking of two different things here: what is stipulated in the law and what I have personally experienced. You must not confuse them. In the law, I may not have read it, but it certainly states that the innocent are acquitted. On the other hand, it does not say that the judges can be influenced. Now, I have, on the contrary, experienced the opposite. I know of no real acquittal, but I have heard of many influences. It is of course possible that in all the cases I know, there was no innocence. But isn't that unlikely? In so many cases, not a single one of innocence? When I was a child, I listened carefully to my father when he talked about trials at home. Even the judges who came to my studio talked about the courts. We never talked about anything else; as soon as I had the chance to go to court myself, I always took it, and I have heard countless trials and followed them as far as I could observe, and – I have to admit – I have never experienced a genuine acquittal." "No genuine acquittals then," said K., as if talking to himself and his hopes. "This confirms my view of the court. It is thus also pointless from this perspective. A single executioner could replace the whole court." "You must not generalize," said the painter unhappily. "I was only speaking from my experiences." "That's enough," said K., "or have you heard of any acquittals from earlier times?" "Such acquittals," the painter replied, "did indeed exist. But it is very difficult to prove them. The final decisions of the court are not published and are not even accessible to the judges. Thus, only legends have survived about old cases. These do, however, contain actual acquittals, and one can believe them, but they are not provable. Nevertheless, one must not entirely ignore them; they certainly contain some truth, and they are very beautiful. I have even painted some pictures with such legends as their subject." "Legends do not change my opinion," said K., "one cannot appeal to them in court, can one?" The painter laughed. "No, you cannot," he said. "Then it is useless to discuss it," said K., wanting for the moment to accept all the painter's opinions, even if he found them unlikely and contradictory to other reports. He had no time to verify the truth of everything the painter said or to refute it. It was already the utmost when he managed to persuade the painter to help him, even if only in some unimportant way. Therefore, he said: "Let us leave aside the actual acquittal for the moment. You mentioned two other possibilities." "The apparent acquittal and the postponement. These are the only possibilities," said the painter. "Would you mind removing your robe? You seem to be sweating a lot." "Yes," said K., who had hitherto paid attention only to the painter's explanations and who, now that he was reminded of the heat, broke out in a strong sweat on his forehead. "It is almost unbearable." The painter nodded, as if he understood K.'s discomfort very well. "Could we not open the window?" K. asked. "No," said the painter. "It is merely a fixed glass pane; it cannot be opened." Now K. realized that he had been hoping the whole time that the painter or he would suddenly go to the window and break it open. He was prepared to inhale the fog with open mouth. The feeling of being completely sealed off from the air caused him to feel dizzy. He lightly struck the feather bed next to him and said in a weak voice: "This is quite uncomfortable and unhealthy." "Oh no," said the painter in defense of his window. "Since it cannot be opened, the heat is better retained here, even though it is just a simple pane, than in a double window. When I want to ventilate, which is not very necessary, since air can enter through the cracks in the beams, I can open one of my doors, or even both." K., somewhat comforted by this explanation, looked around to find the second door. The painter noticed and said: "It is behind you; I had to hide it behind the bed." Only then did K. see the small door in the wall. "It is just that everything is too small for an atelier here," the painter said, preempting any criticism from K. "I had to do the best I could. The bed in front of the door, of course, stands in a very bad place. The judge, whom I am now painting, always comes in through the door by the bed, and I gave him a key to this door so that he could wait for me in the atelier even if I am not here. But he usually comes early in the morning while I am still asleep. It always wakes me out of the deepest sleep when the door opens next to the bed. You would lose all respect for the judges if you heard the curses I let fly when he climbs over my bed in the early morning. However, I could take away his key, but it would only make things worse. All the doors here can be broken out of their hinges with the slightest effort." While the painter was speaking, K. considered whether he should remove his robe, but finally realized that if he did not, he would not be able to stay here much longer. He therefore took off his robe and draped it over his knees, so that he could put it back on if the discussion was over. Hardly had he taken off his robe when one of the girls called out: "He has already taken off his robe!" and they could be heard crowding around the cracks to see the spectacle. "The girls believe," the painter said, "that I will paint you and that you will therefore take off your robe." "So," said K., only slightly amused, for he did not feel much better than before, now sitting in his shirt sleeves. Almost glumly, he asked: "What did you call the other two possibilities?" He had already forgotten the terms. "The apparent acquittal and the postponement," said the painter. "It is up to you which one you choose. Both are achievable with my help, of course, not without effort. The difference lies in the fact that the apparent acquittal is a temporary, collected effort, whereas the postponement is a smaller, but permanent, sustained effort. First, the apparent acquittal. If you wish to have this, I will write a statement of your innocence on a sheet of paper. The text for such a statement was handed down to me by my father and is completely unassailable. With this statement, I now make a tour among the judges I know. So, I start with the judge I am now painting, and I will present the statement to him this evening when he comes for the session. I will present the statement to him, explain that you are innocent, and guarantee your innocence. This is not just a formal guarantee, but a binding one. "There is reproach in the painter's eyes as though he found it burdensome to make K. responsible for such a guarantee. "That would be very kind," said K. "And the judge would believe you and still not really acquit me?" "As I already said," answered the painter. "Moreover, it is not at all certain that everyone would believe me. Some judges, for example, will require that I bring you to them myself. Then you would have to come with me once. However, in such a case, the matter is already half won, especially since I would naturally give you thorough instructions beforehand on how to behave with the relevant judge. It is worse with judges who, as will happen from time to time, reject me outright. We must then, although I will not hesitate to make several attempts, do without them, but we can afford to do so since individual judges cannot decide the outcome here. If I now have enough signatures on this statement from the judges, I will take this statement to the judge who is presiding over your trial. Perhaps I will also have his signature, then the process will be a little faster. In any case, there will be no more obstacles, and for the accused, this is the time of highest hope. It is remarkable, but true, that people are more hopeful at this time than after an acquittal. There is now no need for special effort. The judge has the guarantee of several judges in the statement and can acquit you with complete security. He will do so, of course, after the necessary formalities, but it will please him and others as well. You will then leave the court and be free." "Then I am free," said K. hesitantly. "Yes," said the painter, "but only apparently free, or, more accurately, temporarily free. The lower judges, to whom my acquaintances belong, do not have the right to give a final acquittal. This right only belongs to the highest, for you, for me, and for all of us, unreachable, court. We do not know what it is like there and, besides, do not want to know. Thus, our judges do not have the great right to be freed from the accusation, but they do have the right to be released from the accusation. That means, if you are acquitted in this manner, you are temporarily released from the accusation, but it still hovers over you and can continue to haunt you.

— I, gentlemen, am speaking of the times when famines were frequent. I have heard of them, though I know little of history. But it seems it should have been that way. When I came to the Swiss mountains, I was amazed at the ruins of old knightly castles built on the slopes of the mountains, on steep cliffs, and at least a mile in height (which means several miles by trails). It is known that the castle is nothing but a heap of stones. The work was terrible, impossible! And this, of course, these poor people, vassals, must have built. Furthermore, they had to pay various taxes and support the clergy. Where was there anything to feed themselves and cultivate the land? There must have been very few of them then, and they must have died of starvation in horrifying numbers, and there may have been nothing to eat at all. Sometimes I even wondered: how did this people not die out completely then and something not happen to them, how could they have endured and survived? That there were cannibals, and perhaps many, this is undoubtedly true; Lebedev is right. Only I do not know why exactly he involved monks and what he means by that.

About the evening gathering at the Epanshin country estate, where Belokonskaya was expected, Varvara Arkadyevna also reported accurately to her brother; the guests were scheduled for the same evening. However, she expressed herself somewhat more sharply than was necessary. It was true that the matter had been arranged too hastily, even with a bit of unnecessary agitation, precisely because in this family "everything was done as no one else did." Everything was explained by the impatience of "no longer doubting" Madame Lizaveta Prokofyevna and the fervent joys of both parents' hearts about the happiness of their beloved daughter. Besides, Belokonskaya was indeed about to leave; and since her patronage really counted in society and they hoped she would be favorable to the prince, the parents reckoned on "society" accepting Aglaya's fiancé directly from the hands of the all-powerful "old lady," so that if anything strange was to be found in it, it would appear much less strange under such a protectorate. The point was that the parents could not decide for themselves: "Is there something strange in all this, and to what extent? Or is there nothing at all strange?" The friendly and candid opinion of people of authority and expertise would have been suitable at this moment, when, thanks to Aglaya, nothing was decided definitively. In any case, the prince had to be introduced to the society he knew nothing about. In short, he was to be "shown." However, the evening was planned simply: only "family friends" were expected, in the smallest numbers possible. Besides Belokonskaya, one important lady was also expected, the wife of a high-ranking nobleman. Among the young people, they hoped to see Eugene Pavlovich, and he was to come along with Belokonskaya.

Someone must have slandered Josef K., for although he had done nothing wrong, he was arrested one morning. Mrs. Grubach’s housekeeper, who brought him his breakfast at eight every morning, did not come this time. This had never happened before. K. waited for a while, seeing the old lady across the way, who was observing him with an unusually curious interest. Then, at the same time, annoyed and hungry, he rang the bell. Immediately there was a knock and a man entered whom he had never seen before in that apartment. He was slim but strongly built, wearing a close-fitting black outfit similar to a traveling suit, adorned with various pleats, pockets, buckles, buttons, and a belt, so that one did not quite know what its use was, but it seemed very practical. “Who are you?” asked K. and sat half up in bed. But the man ignored the question and only said, “Did you ring?” “Anna is to bring me my breakfast,” said K. and tried to deduce, without saying anything, who the man really was, through attention and speculation. But the stranger did not linger under his gaze, but turned to the door, which he opened slightly to tell someone standing just behind it, “He wants Anna to bring him his breakfast.” A little laugh followed from the next room, but it was not certain from the sound whether more than one person was involved. Although the stranger could not have learned anything new from this, he now told K. in a matter-of-fact tone, “It is impossible.” “That would be new,” said K., and jumped out of bed, quickly putting on his trousers. “I want to see who’s in the next room and how Frau Grubach will answer for this interruption to me.” It occurred to him that he had no need to say this aloud and that he had unwittingly given the stranger the right to supervise him, but it did not seem to matter. The stranger took this to heart, however, and said, “Why don’t you stay here?” “I want neither to stay here nor to be addressed by you until you introduce yourself.” “It was meant well,” said the stranger and now opened the door himself. K., entering the next room more slowly than he wanted to, saw at first glance that it looked almost exactly as it had the night before. It was the living room of Frau Grubach, perhaps there was a bit more space in this furniture-filled room today, but one could not tell at once, especially not because the main change was the presence of a man sitting at the open window with a book, which he put down now and looked up. “You should have stayed in your room! Didn’t Franz tell you that?” “Yes, what do you want?” said K. and looked from the stranger to Franz, who had stopped in the doorway, and back again. Through the open window, the old woman could be seen again, with her truly ancient curiosity, now standing at the opposite window to see everything. “I want to see Frau Grubach,” said K., made a move as if trying to pull away from the two men who were standing far from him, and wanted to continue. “No,” said the man at the window, closed the book and stood up. “You are not to leave, you are under arrest.” “It looks that way,” said K. “And why?” he asked. “We are not supposed to tell you that. Go back to your room and wait. The proceedings have been initiated, and you will learn everything in good time. I am going beyond my instructions by speaking to you so kindly. But I hope no one else overhears us, especially not Franz, who is himself unusually friendly to you. If you are as fortunate as you were in the selection of your guards, then you can be confident. ” K. wanted to sit down, but now he noticed there was no place to sit in the entire room, except for the chair by the window. “You will soon see how true this is,” said Franz and came to him together with the other man. The latter, in particular, was much taller than K. and often patted him on the shoulder. Both inspected K.’s nightshirt and said he would now have to put on a much worse shirt, but that they would keep his nightshirt and all his other clothes and would return them if his case turned out favorably. “It’s better to hand over the things to us as they go into storage,” they said, “because there are often swindlers in the storage depot, and they also sell off the clothes after a certain time without regard to whether the proceedings have ended or not. And how long do such cases last, especially in recent times! You would get the proceeds from the depot eventually, but this would be relatively small, for the amount is not decided by the highest bid, but by the highest bribe. Furthermore, such proceeds are known to decrease as they are passed from hand to hand and from year to year.” K. barely paid attention to these words. He did not highly value the right of disposal over his belongings; what mattered much more was clarity about his situation. Oh, morality! I'm not a boy anymore, I know that myself, — Ganya fiercely interjected, — and I started this conversation with you, my prince, for that very reason. I wouldn't have taken this step for profit, for I would surely have erred, given my inexperience and inchoate character. I am venturing into this darkness out of passion and impulse, because I have a solid goal. You think I'm going to get seventy-five thousand and immediately buy a carriage. No, I would wear an old, third-hand coat and break off all my social connections. We have few principled people, despite the fact that we are all moneylenders, and I want to be one of them. The main thing is to see it through to the end—this is the whole challenge! Pytonin slept in the street at seventeen, selling pocketknives, and started with a kopeck; now he has sixty thousand, but after what kind of a struggle! I will cut straight through all that and start from a position of wealth; in fifteen years, people will say, "Here's Ivolygin, the king of the Jews." You say I'm not an original. Take note, dear prince, that there's nothing more hurtful to a person of our age and generation than to be told that they are not original, lacking in character, and without special talents, that they are just an ordinary person. You didn't even consider me a good scoundrel, and you know, I wanted to eat you alive for that! You've offended me more than Epanchintsev, who sees me as capable of selling his wife (without any coaxing, in all sincerity, take note of this)! This, father, has been bothering me for a long time, and I want money. After making money, I'll be the most original person. Money is the most base and hateful precisely because it even gives talent. No, I would then wear a three-year-old coat and abandon all my club acquaintances. There are few steadfast souls amidst all the usurers, but I want to be one. The main thing is to see it through to the end—that's the challenge! Putilin slept on the street at seventeen, hawking pocketknives, and started with a kopek; now he has sixty thousand, but only after what trials! I will leap over all his trials and start from scratch with capital. In fifteen years they will say, 'There's Ivolgin, the Jewish king.' When you tell me I'm not an original, you wound me deeply—there's nothing more hurtful to a person of our time and lineage. You did not even consider me a good scoundrel, and you know, I wanted to eat you up just now for that! You've wronged me more than Epanchin, who considers me (without any coaxing or temptation, and with all honesty, note this) capable of selling my wife to him! This, Father, bothers me more than anything else, and I want money. By earning money, I will be the most original person. Money is the basest and most hateful thing because it even gives talents. It will continue to do so until the end of the world. You'll say that all of this is childish or perhaps poetic, but the more childish or poetic, the more fun it is for me, and the matter will still be resolved. I will see it through and endure. The last laugh is the best laugh![7] Why does Epanchin offend me so? Out of malice, you say? Not at all. Simply because I am too insignificant. Well, then... However, enough, and it's time. Kolya has already invited me to dinner twice; he's summoning you to supper. I will be leaving from the courtyard. Sometimes I will drop by. It will be well with you there; now you will be welcomed into the family circle. Just don't give it away. I think we will either be friends or enemies. As for you, Your Highness, what do you think—if I had kissed your hand yesterday (as I was eagerly offering to do), would I become your enemy later for that?"

"Oh, morality! I know I'm still a boy, that's for sure," Ganya hotly interrupted, "and at least I've started this conversation with you. I, Prince, am not going into this darkness for calculation—I would certainly make a mistake if I did, because my head and character are still not solid. I am going by passion and inclination, because I have a solid goal. You think I'll get seventy-five thousand and buy a carriage right away. No, I'll wear that old three-year suit for a while and drop all my club acquaintances. We have few people who can withstand hardship, even though we're all usurers, and I want to withstand it. The main thing is to see it through to the end—that's the whole task! Putilin slept on the street at seventeen, trading pocketknives and starting with a kopek; now he has sixty thousand, but only after what a tough time! I'm going to skip all that tough time and start right from capital; in fifteen years they'll say: 'Here's Ivolgin, the king of the Jews.' You tell me I'm not an original person. Mind you, my dear Prince, nothing is more offensive to a man of our time and race than to say he is not original, lacks character, has no special talents, and is an ordinary man. You even didn't consider me a good rascal, and you know what, I wanted to eat you up for that yesterday! You offended me worse than Epanchinsky, who considers me (without any talk of temptation, in plain sincerity, notice this) capable of selling my wife to him! This, Father, annoys me greatly, and I want money. Having earned money, you'll see, I'll be the most original person. Money is the most despicable and hateful thing precisely because it even gives talents. And they will continue to give until the end of time. You'll say this is all childishly naive or, perhaps, poetry, but to me that's just what makes it more fun, and the matter will still be done. I'll see it through and endure. He who laughs last laughs best![7] Why is it Epanchin who offends me so much? Out of spite? Never. Simply because I'm too insignificant. Well, then... But, however, enough, and it's time. Kolya has already invited you to dinner twice: he's calling you to dinner. I'll be leaving from the courtyard. I'll drop by sometimes. Things will go well for you now; they will actually welcome you into the family. Watch it, don't let it slip. I think we'll either be friends or enemies. And what do you think, Prince, if I had kissed your hand yesterday (as I was earnestly proposing), would I have become your enemy because of it later?"

The Great Supreme Ruler summoned all the literary and military deities and asked, "How many years did this monkey spirit take to mature, in which generation was it born, and how did it acquire such virtue?" Before the words were finished, a figure stepped forward, identified as Thousand-Mile Eye and Wind-Ear, and said, "This monkey is a stone monkey that was born three hundred years ago. Initially, we did not pay much attention, but we now know that it has spent the past years cultivating and has become immortal, subduing dragons and taming tigers, thus erasing its name from the register of the dead." The Jade Emperor said, "Which celestial guards should descend to subdue it?" Before the words were finished, another figure stepped forward, identified as Senior White Star, and bowed to report, "In this Three Realms, any being with nine orifices can become immortal. However, this monkey is a being nurtured by heaven and earth, a body formed by the sun and moon. It has walked on heaven and earth, feasted on dew and dined on mist; now that it has attained immortality and has the power to subdue dragons and tame tigers, how is it any different from a human? I advise Your Majesty to show mercy and compassion from its origins, and send down an edict of amnesty to summon it here, bestowing upon it a minor official post, registering it in the register, and restraining it here. If it fulfills the heavenly mandate, it will be rewarded; if it defies the heavenly mandate, it will be captured. This will neither disturb the multitude nor exhaust the armies, and will also subdue a celestial being with great virtue." The Jade Emperor was very pleased upon hearing this, and said, "As you suggest." He immediately had the Literary Star Official draft the edict and instructed Senior White Star to bring the amnesty.

The Supreme Lord summoned all the officials of the imperial court and asked, "How many years did this demon monkey take to mature, and in what generation did it appear, to be so virtuous and enlightened?" No sooner had the question been posed than Kwantseye and Ventorsea stepped forward and said, "This monkey was born three hundred years ago from a celestial stone. We did not pay it heed at the time, and we do not know where it has been refining itself to become immortal, subduing dragons and taming tigers, striking off death from the record." The Jade Emperor replied, "Which heavenly warrior should be sent to subdue it?" No sooner had the question been asked than Taidengxing appeared and, bowing his head, said, "In all three realms, any living being with nine apertures may seek immortality. Yet this monkey was nurtured by the heavens and the earth, born from the sun and moon. He stands heaven tall and treads earth firmly, drinking dew and feasting on the morning mist. Now that he has attained immortality, and can subdue dragons and tame tigers, what is he different from a human? I advise your majesty to consider the kindness of his creation and issue an imperial decree to bring him up, granting him a minor position so that his name can be inscribed. This will keep him in check, and if he serves the heavens, he can be further rewarded. If he defies the heavens, he can be apprehended. Thus, you will not trouble the masses and the army, and an immortal of such ability can be acquired." Hearing this, the Jade Emperor was pleased and said, "As you have suggested." He then ordered Wenchuguangxingsheng to draft the imperial decree and summon Taiyinjinxing to grant the monkey his position.

The Grand Supreme Ruler summoned the gathered officials and asked, "How long does this妖monkey take to gestate, from which generation did it come, and how has it acquired such wisdom so early?" The Jade Emperor asked, "Which god will descend to subdue it?" Before he could finish, Taibai Xingzheng stepped forward and said, "Among the three realms, any creature with nine openings can become immortal. However, this monkey is a body formed by the heavens and earth and a body conceived by the sun and moon; it upholds the sky and treads on the earth, living on dew and feasting on mist. Now that it has attained immortality, with the ability to subdue dragons and tame tigers, what difference is there from human beings? He then ordered the Star of Literary Curation to draft a decree and assigned Taibai Golden-star to effect the proclamation of amnesty.

The Supreme Heavenly Venerable summoned all the officials of the court and asked, "How many years has this demonic monkey existed, and which generation was he born in, for him to have attained such Daoist cultivation?" Before the words were finished, the Thousand-Mile Eye and the Breezy-Ear stepped forward and said, "This monkey was born three hundred years ago from the heaven-spawned stone. The Jade Emperor asked, "Which deity should go down to subdue him?" Before the words were finished, the Star of Tai Bai stepped forward and knelt to report, "Your Supremeness, among the three realms, any being with nine orifices can become a仙. Thus, we will not mobilize a great army and we can subdue a deity with cultivation." 

Upon hearing this, the Jade Emperor was very pleased and said, "As per your suggestion." He then instructed the Star of Wen Que to draft the imperial decree and ordered the Star of Tai Bai to recruit and bring him up.

The Great Heavenly Ruler summoned all the ministers and officials, and asked, "How many years did this demon monkey take to be born, and which generation did it belong to, that it is now so virtuous?" Before the words were fully spoken, the Thousand-mile Eye and the Wind-顺风耳 whispered, "This monkey is a stone monkey produced by heaven three hundred years ago. When the yellow notice reached Hai Zhou, there was a man surnamed Chen, named Er, with the courtesy name Guang Rui. Seeing this notice, he immediately went home and told his mother Zhang Si, "The imperial court has issued a yellow notice, calling for the provincial examinations to select talented scholars. I wish to go and take the exam. If I can obtain even a minor official position, it would bring honor to my family and fame to myself, as well as secure a wife and provide benefits for my descendants. I wish to inform you of this before I leave." Zhang Si said, "My son, as a scholar, you should 'study when young and act when grown', which is exactly what you should do. When you go to take the exam, be cautious on your journey, and return home as soon as you receive a position." Guang Rui then instructed his servant to pack his luggage and immediately took leave of his mother, hurrying forward. When he reached Chang An, the provincial examinations were just beginning. Guang Rui entered the examination hall. After the exams, he was selected, and his answers in the three policy essays were personally selected by Emperor Tang, who bestowed the title of状元, allowing him to ride a horse and parade through the streets for three days. Unforeseen was the fact that on the third day, he passed by Chancellor Yin Kai Shan’s residence, where his daughter, named Wen Jiao, or alternatively, Manor Beauty, had just set up a decorated pavilion to throw a silk ball to choose a husband. As Chen Guang Rui was passing the pavilion, the young lady was delighted by his remarkable appearance and knew that he was the new状元. She threw the silk ball, which struck Guang Rui’s black hat. Hearing the sound of the stringed and wind instruments, a dozen or so maids and concubines came down from the pavilion, led Guang Rui to the residence, and welcomed the状元into the marriage. The chancellor and his wife immediately left their hall, calling the attendants to perform the marriage rituals, and matched the young lady with Guang Rui. After bowing to heaven and earth and exchanging marriage vows, they also bowed to Guang Rui’s father-in-law and mother-in-law. The chancellor then instructed them to prepare a feast, and they feasted for the night.

The notice had reached Haizhou, where there lived a man named Chen Yuhui, styled Guangrui. Seeing the imperial edict, he promptly went home and informed his wife Zhang Si: "The court has issued a yellow notice, inviting scholars to the national examination to select talented individuals. I wish to take this opportunity to sit the examination. If I manage to obtain even a minor position, I can honor our family and earn fame, and my children will be protected and our family will flourish. This is my ambition. I wish to inform you of my intention to leave now." Zhang Si said, "My son, as a scholar, you should 'study from a young age and put it into practice in your adulthood,' which is exactly what you should do. But be careful on your journey, and if you manage to obtain an official post, return as soon as possible." Guangrui then instructed his servant to pack his belongings and bid farewell to his mother, setting off at a rapid pace. He arrived in Chang'an just as the imperial examination was opening. Guangrui entered the examination hall and passed the preliminary test, as well as the third imperial test of policy advice. Emperor Tang personally wrote the names of the successful candidates and bestowed the title of Jinshi upon Guangrui, who rode his horse through the streets for three days. Unbeknownst to him, during his parade, the procession passed the residence of Chancellor Yin Kaishan. The chancellor's daughter, named Wen Jiao, also known as Full-Glorious Beauty, who had not yet been married, was celebrating in her brightly decorated pavilion, throwing embroidered balls to choose a husband. Coincidentally, as Guangrui passed below, the lady saw his distinguished appearance and knew he was the new Jinshi. She was delighted and threw the ball, which hit Guangrui's black hat. At that moment, a loud melody of flutes and strings was heard, and several maids rushed down the stairs to pull Guangrui’s horse, bringing him into the chancellor's residence to marry the lady. The chancellor and his wife immediately came out to see and, with the help of a wedding officiant, arranged the marriage between the lady and Guangrui. They honored heaven and earth, exchanged vows, and then bowed to the father and mother-in-law. The chancellor then ordered a feast to be prepared, and they feasted for the night.

Three years had passed when the Patriarch again took his seat and spoke to the assembly. He spoke of public cases and parables, and argued over outer appearances. Then he asked, "Where is Sun Wukong?" Wukong stepped forward and kneeled, saying, "Master, your servant is here." The Patriarch said, "What sort of way have you been cultivating of late?" Wukong replied, "Since my recent training, my fundamental nature has become quite open, and my foundation has grown more solid." The Patriarch said, "Now that you have opened your fundamental nature and solidified your foundation, you should guard against the 'Three Disasters and Their Harms'." Upon hearing this, Wukong pondered for a long moment and said, "Master's words are incorrect. I have often heard that a great sage has high morals and lives as long as heaven, both water and fire being in harmony, and yet not a single illness can touch him. How can there be such a thing as the 'Three Disasters and Their Harms'?" The Patriarch said, "This is a most extraordinary way: it steals the secrets of heaven and plunders the mysteries of the sun and moon. When the elixir is completed, even the gods and demons cannot endure it. Though it can make you youthful and long-lived, in five hundred years, you will be struck by a thunderstorm. You must cultivate your true nature and clarify your heart to avoid this. If you can escape it, your lifespan will be as long as the heavens; if you cannot, your life will be ended. In another five hundred years, a fire will descend from heaven to burn you. This fire is not a heavenly fire nor is it a mundane fire, but is called the 'hidden fire'. It starts from the涌泉穴 at your feet and burns straight through to the泥垣宫, reducing your organs to ashes and your limbs to rot, turning your millennium of suffering into an illusion. In another five hundred years, a wind will descend. This wind is neither east, west, south, nor north wind, nor is it a gentle breeze, a northerly wind, a floral breeze, or a wind from bamboo, trees, or grass. It is called the 'great wind'. This wind enters from your forehead and passes through your viscera, through your dan tian, and out through your nine orifices, causing your flesh and bones to wither, and your body to dissolve. That is why you must avoid it." Wukong heard this and shuddered, bowing his head and kneeling, saying, "Mighty Master, if you pity me, teach me the method to avoid the Three Disasters, and I will not forget your kindness." The Patriarch said, "It is not difficult, but since you are different from others, I cannot teach you this." Wukong said, "Though my head is round and touches the sky, and my feet are square and press the earth, and I have nine orifices and four limbs like everyone else, why am I different?" The Patriarch said, "Though you look like a person, you have fewer cheeks than others." In fact, the monkey had a single cheek and an elongated, pointed mouth. Wukong reached out to feel and laughed, saying, "Master, you have no foresight! I may have fewer cheeks, but I have this fleshy apron, which can be compensated for." The Patriarch said, "Very well, which art do you wish to learn? There is the art of the 36 Heavenly Strokes, and there is the art of the 72 Earthly Strokes." Wukong said, "Master, I wish to learn the 72 Earthly Strokes." The Patriarch said, "Very well, come forward and I shall teach you the formula." He whispered something in Wukong's ear, whose secrets were known to none. This monkey also learned everything with a single insight, and after learning the formula, he practiced and cultivated, mastering all 72 transformations.

Three years had passed before the Patriarch once more ascended the dais to discourse with his disciples. He spoke of parables and metaphors, and discussed the outer forms. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is Monkey?" Monkey advanced and knelt, saying, "Disciple is here." The Patriarch said, "What practice have you been engaged in of late?" Monkey replied, "Disciple has recently attained a profound understanding of the Dharmic nature and a sturdy foundation." The Patriarch said, "Since you have mastered the Dharmic nature and achieved a solid foundation, you are imbued with divine essence. However, you must guard against the 'Three Disastrous Calamities.'" Upon hearing this, Monkey reflected for a while and said, "Master's words are mistaken. I often heard that a sage attains longevity equal to that of heaven, and that water and fire are subdued; thus, no illnesses should arise. How, then, are there these three disastrous calamities?" The Patriarch said, "This is an extraordinary path: it seizes the workings of heaven and earth, and invades the profound mechanisms of the sun and moon; after the elixir is completed, the gods will not tolerate it. Although you have halted aging and increased your lifespan, in five hundred years, a lightning disaster shall befall you. You must awaken to your true nature and pre-emptively seek shelter. Should you avoid it, you will live as long as heaven; should you not, your life will be cut short. In another five hundred years, a fire disaster will descend upon you. This fire is neither celestial nor mundane, but a 'yin fire.' It will rise from the涌泉穴, pass through the mud wall palace, burn your five viscera to ashes, rot your four limbs, and render all your thousand-year austerities an illusion. In yet another five hundred years, a wind disaster will blow upon you. This wind is not the east, west, south, or north wind; it is not the balmy spring breeze or the chilly winter wind; it is not the breezes of plum blossoms, willow catkins, or pine and bamboo. It is called the 'bodily wind.' It will enter from the top of your head, pass through your six腑, the dantian, and your nine orifices, causing the flesh to decay and the body to disintegrate. Therefore, you must avoid these disasters." Monkey heard this and shuddered, then bowed and knelt, saying, "Sage, grant mercy and teach me the method of avoiding the three disasters, for I shall never forget your kindness." The Patriarch said, "There is no difficulty in this, but since you are different from others, I cannot impart it." Monkey said, "I too have a round head and a sky as my crown, and a square body and earth as my foundation; I have the same nine orifices and four limbs, the same five viscera and six腑, so why am I different?" The Patriarch said, "Though you resemble a human, you lack a chin." The monkey, with a recessed face and pointed mouth, was indeed chinless. Monkey touched his chin and laughed, saying, "Master lacks foresight! Though I lack a chin, I have this white sack, which may be a compensation." The Patriarch said, "Well then, which art do you wish to learn? There is an art of thirty-six heavenly strikes, and there is an art of seventy-two earthly strikes." Monkey said, "I wish to learn the art of seventy-two earthly strikes." The Patriarch said, "Since that is so, come forward, and I shall impart the secret." Then, he leaned in and whispered something, unknown to anyone. This Monkey King, with one understanding, mastered all others. He then practiced and refined the art, mastering all seventy-two transformations.

Yet three years had passed before the Master reoccupied his throne to expound the Dharma to the assembly. He spoke of cases and similes, and argued about outer forms and coverings. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is Sun Wukong?" Wukong stepped forward and kneeled, "Student is here." The Master said, "What practice have you been engaged in of late?" Wukong replied, "Student has recently thoroughly understood the dharma and fortified the root." The Master said, "Since you understand the dharma, have mastered the root, and have infused your body with spirit, you must beware the three calamities." Upon hearing this, Wukong pondered for a long moment and said, "Master, your words are erroneous. I have often heard that one who is highly revered and of great virtue lives as long as heaven, that the body is tempered by fire and water, and that no illness arises, so how can there be three calamities?" The Master said, "This is an extraordinary path: it appropriates the creation of heaven and earth, usurps the mysteries of the moon and sun; after the elixir is completed, the gods and spirits will not tolerate it. Although it preserves your youth and extends your life, in five hundred years, heaven will send a thunderstorm to strike you; you must purify your mind and preserve your essence to avoid it. If you avoid it, your lifespan will be as long as heaven’s; if you do not, your life will end here. In five hundred years, a fire from the underworld will be sent to burn you. This fire is not a heavenly fire nor is it a mortal fire; it is called yin fire. It rises from your涌泉穴 (yǒng quán xué) and passes through the mud wall palace, burning your five viscera to ashes and rotting your four limbs, making all your austerities a delusion. In another five hundred years, a wind from heaven will be sent to blow you. This wind is neither the southeast, northwest, warm nor cold, nor the wind of flowers, willows, pines, or bamboos; it is called the leviathan wind. It enters through the crown of your head, passes through your six organs, through the dantian, and out through your nine orifices, disintegrating your flesh and bones, and making your body disintegrate. That is why you must avoid them." Wukong, hearing this, shuddered and knelt, bowing his head and saying, "Respected Master, have mercy on me and teach me the way to avoid the three calamities, and I will not forget your kindness." The Master said, "This is not difficult, but you are different from others, hence you cannot learn it." Wukong said, "Though I have a round head and a heaven, and square feet and a ground, I have the same nine orifices, four limbs, and five viscera and six organs, why am I different?" The Master said, "Though you look like a human, you are lacking cheeks." The original monkey had a squashed face, a pointed mouth, and a malformed jaw. Wukong reached out and touched it, laughing and saying, "Master, you are not thoughtful! Though I lack cheeks, I have this fur bag, which can be used as a substitute." The Master said, "Very well, what do you wish to learn? There is a method of heaven with thirty-six techniques, and a method of earth with seventy-two techniques." Wukong said, "I am willing to learn the seventy-two techniques." The Master said, "Since that is so, come forward, and I shall teach you the secret." He leaned in and whispered, unknown words of secret art into the monkey’s ear. The monkey king understood one thing, and all else became clear. Then and there, he practiced the secret art and learned to transform himself into seventy-two forms.

Three years had passed when the Master ascended the dais once more to discourse with his disciples. The topic was cases and comparisons, and he discussed externals and surface traits. He suddenly asked, "Where is Monkey?" Monkey advanced and knelt, "Your disciple is here." The Master said, "What have you been up to lately?" Monkey replied, "Lately, my Dharmic nature has become clear, and my roots have become steadily firm." The Master said, "Since your Dharmic nature is clear and your roots are firm, you have infused your body with divine essence. But you must guard against the ‘Three Disasters and Their Harmful Effects.’" Monkey, upon hearing this, reflected deeply for a long time and said, "Master, your words are incorrect. I have often heard that high virtue and great dignity bring longevity akin to that of heaven, and that water and fire can be brought to a balance, leading to no illness. How can there be such a thing as the Three Disasters and Their Harmful Effects?" The Master said, "This is an extraordinary path: it seizes the secrets of creation from heaven and the mysteries of the sun and moon. Once the elixir is complete, even the gods and spirits cannot tolerate it. Although it may preserve your youth and add to your lifespan, after five hundred years, you will be struck by lightning. You must awaken to the nature of your mind and act accordingly to avoid it. If you can avoid it, your life will be as long as heaven; if you cannot, you will die. After another five hundred years, you will be incinerated by fire. This fire is not from heaven or from the mundane world; it is called the ‘Yin Fire.’ It starts from your涌泉穴 (yǒng quán xué,涌泉穴 is a acupuncture point on the sole of the foot) and rises through the dantian to the nine orifices, reducing your organs to ash and your limbs to dust, rendering all your ascetic practices illusory. Another five hundred years later, a wind disaster will blow upon you. This wind is not east, west, south, or north, nor is it gentle, nor is it from the flowers, trees, or bamboo. It is called the ‘Least Wind.’ It enters from the top of your head, passes through your organs, crosses your dantian, and exits through your nine orifices, causing your body to disintegrate. Therefore, you must avoid it." Monkey heard this and was deeply alarmed, bowing and kneeling, saying, "O Grandmaster, if you pity me, please impart the methods to avoid the Three Disasters. I will not forget your kindness." The Master said, "This is not difficult, but you are different from others, so I cannot teach you." Monkey said, "I have a round head and a high forehead, and flat feet grounded to the earth, just like others with nine apertures and ten limbs, five viscera and six organs. Why am I different?" The Master said, "Though you resemble a person, you have no chin." The original monkey had a one-eyed, sunken face with a pointed mouth. Monkey reached out and touched himself, smiling and saying, "Master, your calculations are wrong! Although I lack a chin, I have this pouch on the side, which can be offset." The Master said, "Very well, then. Which of the two paths do you want to learn? One is the Heavenly Technique, which has 36 transformations, and the other is the Earthly Technique, which has 72 transformations." Monkey said, "I am willing to learn the Earthly Technique." The Master said, "Then come forward, and I will teach you the秘诀 (secret). " So he whispered in his ear, and it is unknown what wonderful techniques were imparted. This Monkey King, with one kung opening everything, learned the secret, practiced and cultivated himself, and mastered the 72 transformations.

Three years had passed before the Master ascended the dais again to expound the Dharma to his disciples. He spoke of koans and parables, and then addressed the outer form and the false coverings. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is Sun Wukong?" Wukong approached and knelt, saying, "My master, I am here." The Master said, "What have you been practicing of late?" Wukong replied, "My master, of late my fundamental nature has been enlightened, and my source strengthened." The Master said, "Since you have attained enlightenment and the root of your nature, your body has taken on divine substance. Yet you must guard against the 'three disasters and calamities.'" Upon hearing this, Wukong pondered for a long while and said, "Master, your words are in error. I have often heard of a sage who has attained high virtue and long life, whose body is impervious to fire and water, and who is free from sickness. How can there be such things as the three disasters and calamities?" The Master said, "This is extraordinary doctrine: to usurp the processes of heaven and earth, to invade the secrets of the sun and moon; when the elixir is complete, it becomes a transgression even for the gods. Although it can preserve your youth and prolong your life, in five hundred years the heavens will send a thunderstorm to strike you. You must awaken to your true nature and be mindful of your heart to avoid it. If you can avoid it, your life will be as long as the heavens; if not, you will die. Five hundred years later, the heavens will send a firestorm to burn you. This fire is neither heaven-sent nor from this world, but called 'yin fire.' It will rise from the涌泉穴 and burn through the palace of mud and clay, reducing your organs to ashes and your limbs to decay, rendering all your austerities in vain. Five hundred years later, a windstorm will descend. This wind is not east, west, south, or north; it is not the gentle zephyrs of spring or the biting blasts of winter; nor is it the winds of the flowers and trees, but called 'de wind.' It will enter through the fontanelle, pass through the six organs, and pierce the dan tian, the nine orifices, and the bones and flesh, causing your body to disintegrate. Therefore, you must avoid these disasters." Wukong heard this and felt his bones shudder, then he knelt and bowed, saying, "Lord, have mercy and teach me the way to avoid these three disasters. I will never forget your kindness." The Master said, "This is not difficult, but since you are unlike others, I cannot teach you this." Wukong said, "I have a round head and a flat ground, and I have the same nine orifices, four limbs, and five organs and six intestines as others. How am I unlike others?" The Master said, "Although you resemble a human, you lack the cheekbones." It turned out that the monkey had a single cheek and a concave face and sharp mouth. Wukong stretched out his hand and poked, smiling, "Master, your calculations are off! Although I lack cheekbones, I have this white pouch. This can be considered a compensation." The Master said, "Well, then, what do you wish to learn? There is one set of heavenly triple numbers, amounting to thirty-six transformations, and one set of earthly single numbers, amounting to seventy-two transformations." Wukong said, "My master, I wish to learn the seventy-two transformations." The Master said, "Very well, come forward, and I will impart the秘诀 to you." He whispered into the monkey’s ear, and Wukong learned the method. He practiced and refined it himself, mastering the seventy-two transformations.

"A Russian heart can even discern a great man in its very enemy, its own homeland!" That is, to be honest, I don’t remember if I actually said it that way... I was just a child... but the meaning was certainly that! Napoleon was moved. He pondered for a moment and said to his retinue, "I love the pride of this child! But if all the Russians think like this child...?"—he left the sentence unfinished as he entered the palace. I immediately intervened with the retinue and ran after him. By now, the retinue was parting for me and looking at me as a favorite. But all of that was fleeting... I only remember that, entering the first hall, the Emperor suddenly stopped before a portrait of Empress Catherine and stared at it in thought for a long time before finally saying, "This was a great woman!" and walked past it. Two days later, everyone in the palace and the Kremlin already knew me and called me "le petit boyard." I only went home at night. At home, they nearly went mad with excitement. Two days after that, the chamber page to Napoleon, Baron de Bazanкур, who could not endure the campaign, died. Napoleon remembered me; they took me, brought me in without explaining the reason, dressed me in the deceased page’s uniform—a twelve-year-old boy—and when they brought me to the Emperor in uniform and he nodded his head, they informed me that I had been honored and promoted to chamber page to his Majesty. I was delighted. I really felt a warm sympathy for him, and for a long time... well, and let’s agree that a shiny uniform means a lot to a child... I wore a dark green frock coat with long and narrow tails; gold buttons, red cuffs with gold embroidery, a high standing collar embroidered in gold, embroidery on the tails; tight white tights, a silk waistcoat, silk stockings, gaiters with buckles... and during the Emperor’s horseback rides, and if I was part of his retinue, tall boots. Although the position was not glamorous and ominous misfortunes were already anticipated, the etiquette was observed as much as possible, and even more meticulously the more ominous the misfortunes seemed to be.
