The next day, three ministers gathered the monks in the Mountain and River Altar to conduct a thorough search. They selected a virtuous elder from among them. You wonder who he is? His name is Jin Chan, a knowledgeable monk, who, due to a lack of interest in Buddhist teachings, had reincarnated into the mortal world to endure hardship. He was born into a noble family; his father was Mian Qiaorui, the top scholar of the sea prefecture, and his maternal grandfather was the chief administrator of the empire. His birth star indicated he would die in water, and he was raised by the monk named Qian'an on a small island. At the age of eighteen, he was reunited with his mother and went to the capital to seek his maternal grandfather. The chief administrator mobilized a large army to clear the mountain, and after defeating bandits in Hongzhou, scholar Mian successfully escaped the trap and reunited with his son. The emperor bestowed him with high offices and allowed him to renounce worldly life. He chose to become a monk and was given the title of Master Chenzang. His childhood name was Jiangliu, and his Dharma name was Chen Zangzang. On that day, the three ministers recommended Master Zangzang to the emperor. This man had become a monk since childhood, and as soon as he was born, he had kept a vow of celibacy and precepts. His maternal grandfather, Yinxikaishan, was the commander of the imperial army, and his father, Mian Qiaorui, was a top scholar and a grand secretary of the Literary Treasure Hall. He was uninterested in worldly glory and only enjoyed religious practices. They found him to be of good origin and high moral character. He was proficient in thousands of scriptures, and could recite Buddhist and immortal verses with ease. The three ministers led him to the emperor, who welcomed him and bowed, saying, "We have found a virtuous elder named Chen Zangzang as per your command." Emperor Taizong thought for a while and asked, "Is this scholar Mian Qiaorui's son, Zangzang?" Jiangliu knelt and replied, "I am." The emperor was delighted and said, "You were indeed a worthy choice. You are truly a virtuous elder with a pure heart. I hereby bestow upon you the positions of Left and Right Monastic Chief and the Grand Monastic Chief of the Empire." Zangzang bowed and accepted the high position. The emperor then bestowed upon him a five-colored brocade robe and a hat with the image of Vairocana Buddha. He instructed Zangzang to select the principal monks and establish a hierarchy, and to organize the scripture recitation on a auspicious day in theizing temple. The ceremony began on the ninth day of the ninth month, a day favorable for rituals, and Zangzang conducted a 49-day water and land religious festival. A report was made to the emperor and his ministers, and all the imperial relatives and nobles were invited to attend and listen to the scriptures. It remains to be seen what the emperor’s intentions are, and we shall continue in the next chapter.

The next day, the three officials gathered the assembly of monks in the Mountain and River Altar to conduct a thorough selection. Among them, they chose a virtuous high monk. You may ask who he is: his true name is Golden Cicada, named Ingenious by the Buddha. He listened to no Buddhist teachings, only to suffer in the secular world, to be captured in a net, and to face perils and malevolent groups. He was born and met ill fortune at the moment of birth, before even leaving the womb. His father was Mencius, the Chief Scholar of Hainan, and his maternal grandfather was the Grand Governor and Vizier of the imperial court. His birth stars were tainted by a star of being washed away by the flood, so he was carried along with the flow. He had a great connection to Mount Gold and Island, where Big Ocean Temple resides, and was raised by Big Ocean Temple's monk, Big Ancestor. When he was eighteen, he sought his biological mother and travelled to the capital to visit his maternal grandfather. The maternal grandfather mobilised the army to march to Hongzhou, to suppress bandits and eliminate evil, and scholar Mencius escaped the net. Father and son were reunited, and were greeted with rejoicing. After paying respects to the current emperor, his gratitude was acknowledged, and his name was inscribed on the Hall of Eminent Officials. He declined the imperial honours and wished to become a monk. With great good fortune, he became a Buddhist monk. He was called Flowing River, and his Dharma name was Tripitaka Chen. On that day, the three officials recommended Master Tripitaka. This man had become a monk from childhood, observing fasting and taking the vows at the moment of birth. His maternal grandfather was Marshal Yin Kai Shān, the present-day head of the imperial army, and his father, Scholar Mencius, had become the Chancellor, Master of the College of Literature, and Scholar Mencius had always despised worldly honours and cherished spiritual discipline. The officials found that he was of good descent and great virtue. He was proficient in all scriptures and texts, and skilled in reciting and chanting Buddhist scriptures. The three officials led him to the emperor, who was dusting and dancing, and after the prostrations, they reported, "We, officials Rú, have selected the monk Chen Tripitaka as ordered." Emperor Taizong reflected for a moment and asked, "Is he Scholar Mencius's son, Tripitaka?" Flowing River prostrated and said, "Your Majesty, I am." Emperor Taizong said joyfully, "Indeed, your choice was right. You are a monk of great virtue and compassion. I bestow upon you the positions of left and right heads of the Buddhist clergy and head of the entire nation's Buddhist clergy." Tripitaka bowed his head and thanked the emperor, and received the high office. The emperor then bestowed upon him a five-colored brocade and gold Buddhist robe, and a hat adorned with the Dharmakāya. He was instructed to carefully choose masters of ceremonies, head his ordination line, write and issue imperial orders, and proceed to Bodhi Birth Temple to select a good day and time to expound the teachings. Tripitaka bowed and accepted the imperial command, and then went to Bodhi Birth Temple. There, he gathered many monks and prepared Buddha seats, constructed ritual platforms, and arranged music. He selected a total of one thousand two hundred enlightened monks, and distributed them into upper, middle, and lower halls. All the Buddha statues and objects before them were complete, arranged in order. On the third day of the ninth month, the emperor chose a favorable date, and the Water and Land Great Feast for forty-nine days was initiated. A report was sent to the emperor and the officials, and all the imperial relatives, the ministers, and the royal clan were invited to attend and offer incense and listen to the teachings. The outcome of the emperor's intention will be revealed in the next chapter.

The next day, the three court officials gathered the monks and gathered in the Mountain and River Altar, one by one, checking from the beginning to select a virtuous high monk among them. You may ask, who is he? The name of this enlightened being is Jin Chan by his original surname and name. He merely could not bear to listen to Buddha’s teachings and thus transmigrated into secular life to undergo hardship. Born into the world, he was entangled and trapped. He was about to be born when he met with misfortune, and before leaving the womb, he encountered a gang of evildoers. His father was the Imperial Scholar Chen Guangrui of Haizhou, and his maternal grandfather was the Grand Inspector of the Ministry of War. He was born under the stars of misfortune, destined to be carried by the current and drift with the waves. He had great karmic connection with the Island of Gold Mountain, where he was raised by the monk named Chuan An. At the age of eighteen, he was recognized as his mother’s son and went to the capital to seek his maternal grandfather. The Grand Inspector dispatched his troops to eliminate the bandits, and Imperial Scholar Guangrui escaped the encirclement. Father and son met and were rejoiced at their reunion. They again paid homage to the emperor, receiving imperial favors, and his reputation was echoed in the hall of illustrious men. He did not accept the official position but desired to become a monk, seeking great fortune as a Buddhist monk. His nickname is Riverflow, and his dharma name is Chen Xuanzang. The court officials then recommended Xuanzang as the virtuous monk. This person has been a monk since childhood, born to his mother, he kept斋 and took the precepts. His maternal grandfather, Yan Kaishan, is the current inspector general, and his father, Chen Guangrui, is an imperial scholar and a university chancellor. He did not love worldly glory and only cherished spiritual cultivation and extinction. After checking his lineage and virtuous conduct, they decided to invite him to the imperial court. He raised dust and danced, bowed, and said, "We, your servants, were honored with the imperial decree to select a virtuous monk, Chen Xuanzang." Emperor Taizong, upon hearing this name, pondered for a while and asked, "Is this the son of the scholar Chen Guangrui, Xuanzang?" Riverflow fell to his knees and said, "This servant is he." Emperor Taizong said with joy, "Surely this is the right choice; you truly are a monk of virtue and a heart imbued with Zen. I shall grant you the ranks of Left Grand Preceptor, Right Grand Preceptor, and Grand Preceptor of the Whole World." Xuanzang bowed in thanks and accepted the great rank. He was also bestowed with a five-colored golden robe and a Vairocana cap. He was instructed to instruct the junior monks, arrange the preceptor position, and draft the imperial decree, then proceed to the Birth Transformation Temple to choose a favorable date and time to preach the scriptures. Xuanzang bowed and accepted the edict, then arrived at Birth Transformation Temple, gathered many monks, and prepared the meditation couches, decorated the halls, and arranged the music. He selected a total of one thousand two hundred junior monks, divided into upper, middle, and lower ranks. All objects before the Buddha were prepared in order. On the ninth day of the ninth month of that year, a favorable day on the Yellow Dao, the Water and Land General Ceremony was opened for forty-nine days. He then prepared a report and submitted it to the emperor, who, along with the ministers, princes, and imperial relatives, attended the ceremony on the appointed day, burned incense, and listened to the teachings. One does not know how the emperor’s intentions will be, so please wait for the next chapter to find out.

The next day, three court officials convened a gathering of monks in the Mountain and River Altar, carefully examining them one by one. Among them, they selected a high monk with virtue. Who was this person? His name, according to his dharma name, was Jin Chan. Due to his lack of interest in Buddhist teachings, he was reborn in the mortal world, enduring hardships, and was born into the world to face trials. His father was the imperial scholar Chen Guangrui of Hai Zhou, and his maternal grandfather was the chief grand secretary in charge of state affairs. Born under the influence of the star of the falling river, his fate was to drift like a reed in water. By chance, he had great affinity with the island and the golden mountain, and was raised by Master Qian An. When he was eighteen, he reunited with his mother and set out for the capital to seek his maternal grandfather. The maternal grandfather dispatched his army to clear the way, and Chen Guangrui, the imperial scholar, escaped the trap and reunited with his son. He was bestowed with the imperial favor, and his name rang through the Lingyan Pavilion. However, he did not accept official positions but wished to be a monk, and became a devout monk with the dharma name Hengzang. On that day, the three court officials recommended Hengzang. He had been a monk since childhood, and upon birth, he adhered to vegetarianism and took his vows. His maternal grandfather was the imperial grand secretary Yan Kaishan, and his father Chen Guangrui, the imperial scholar. He did not love worldly glory but only sought tranquility in practice. They found his roots excellent and his virtues high. He had no gaps in his knowledge of the thousands of sutras and had mastered all musical and recitative arts. The three then led him to the imperial presence, dusting off their sleeves and performing a dance before bowing and saying, "Your Majesty, we have selected the monk Hengzang." The Emperor, upon hearing his name, thought for a while and asked, "Is this the son of the scholar Chen Guangrui, Hengzang?" The river child knelt and said, "I am he." The Emperor said, "Indeed, you have been well selected. You are a monk with virtue and a true heart. I hereby grant you the positions of Chief Superior Monk on the Left, Chief Superior Monk on the Right, and Supreme Chief Superior Monk of the Land." Hengzang bowed his head in gratitude and accepted the high office. He was also given a five-colored brocade monk robe and a Pulu hat. He was instructed to teach the monks below him, organize the chief monks, and draft the imperial decree, then proceed to the Palace of Birth to choose a favorable day and time to hold a 49-day water and land religious gathering. He prepared a report and submitted it to the Emperor, who, along with all the officials, princes, and nobles, attended the ceremony to offer incense and listen to the teachings. Whether the Emperor's intentions would be fulfilled remains to be seen, and we shall continue in the next chapter.

The next day, three court ministers gathered a crowd of monks in the Altar of Mountains and Rivers and proceeded to examine them one by one. Among them, they chose a virtuous high monk. You might ask who he was. His dharma name was Jin Chan, originally named Ling Tong. Due to having no interest in listening to Buddha's teachings, he reincarnated into the secular world to endure tribulations, born into the mortal world, ensnared by worldly affairs. His father was the Sea Prefecture Jin Kuang Rui, and his maternal grandfather was the Grand Governor of the Imperial Office. Born under the star of drowning, he followed the current and tumbled with the waves. He was raised by the monk Jien an on Mountain Jin. At the age of eighteen, he met his birth mother and traveled to the capital to seek his maternal grandfather. The maternal grandfather mobilized the troops and led a grand campaign. Jinguang Rui defeated the bandits in Hongzhou and was reunited with his son, a cause for celebration. He then paid homage to the current emperor and accepted his favor, becoming renowned in the Hall of the Wholly Eminent. Dissatisfied with worldly honors, he wished to become a monk and visit the Buddha. With great blessings, he adopted the monastic name of Jiangliu and dharma name of Chen Xuanzang. On that day, the court ministers presented Xuanzang as the chosen monk. This person had become a monk since childhood, taking the precepts and observing vegetarianism from birth. His maternal grandfather was the Imperial Commissioner Yan Kaishan, and his father, Jin Kuang Rui, was a Jinshi scholar, serving as a vice chancellor of the Daming Hall of Literature. He had no love for worldly honors but only enjoyed pursuing spiritual perfection. The ministers found him to be well-grounded and of high moral character. He was knowledgeable in all thousand scriptures and could recite all Buddhist and Taoist incantations. The three ministers brought him before the emperor, dusting themselves off as they bowed and reported, "Your Majesty, we have found a high monk named Chen Xuanzang as per Your Highness's command." Upon hearing this name, the emperor pondered for a long time before asking, "Is this scholar Chen Kuang Rui's son, Xuanzang?" Xuanzang prostrated himself and replied, "Your Majesty, I am he." The emperor said with joy, "Indeed, you were chosen correctly. You are truly a monk with virtue and a pure heart. I hereby appoint you as the left and right heads of Buddhist clergy, and the Grand Priest of the Great Illumination." Xuanzang prostrated himself in gratitude, accepted the official post, and was then given a five-color silk robe and a pheasant crown. He was instructed to select and instruct junior monks, organize a group of Dharmas, arrange the musical accompaniment, and proceed to Birthplace Temple. On an auspicious date, they would hold a four-ninety day water and land scripture exposition. A memorial was submitted to the emperor and the ministers, as well as the nobles and relatives, who were all invited to attend. They would offer incense and listen to the scriptures. It remains to be seen what the emperor's intentions are; the next chapter will unfold these details.

I was very surprised why the prince had guessed so accurately that I was having "bad dreams" the other day; he literally said that in Pavlovsk "my agitation and dreams" will change. And why dreams? He must be either a doctor or of truly unusual intelligence and can predict a lot of things. (But it is certain that in the end he is an idiot.) As if on purpose, right before his arrival, I had one nice dream (though now they visit me by the hundreds). I fell asleep, I think an hour before he came, and saw that I was in one room (but not in mine). The room was bigger and higher than mine, more furnished, and brighter; a wardrobe, a dresser, a couch, and my large, wide bed, covered with a green quilted silk blanket. But in this room I noticed a terrible animal, some kind of monster. It was like a scorpion, but not a scorpion, but worse and more terrifying, and, as it seemed, precisely because such animals do not exist in nature, and it came purposely for me, and this was somehow a secret. I looked at it very carefully: it was brown and scaly, a crawling creature about four fingers long, two fingers thick at the head, narrowing to the tail, so that the tip of the tail was no thicker than a tenth of a finger. From the head, at a forty-five degree angle, two legs came out, one on each side, two fingers long, so that the whole creature, viewed from above, appeared like a trident. I did not see the head, but I saw two short feelers, sturdy like two pins, also brown. There were two such feelers on the end of the tail and on the end of each leg, making a total of eight feelers. The animal ran through the room very fast, using its legs and tail, and when it ran, its body and legs wriggled like snakes, extremely fast despite the hard shell, which was very unsettling to watch. I was terribly afraid that it would sting me; they told me it was venomous, but what I suffered most from was who sent it to my room, what they wanted to do to me, and what secret was in it? It hid under the dresser, under the wardrobe, crawled into the corners. I sat on a chair with my legs drawn up. The animal quickly crossed the entire room diagonally and disappeared somewhere near my chair. I looked around in fear, but as I was sitting with my legs drawn up, I hoped that it would not climb onto the chair. Suddenly, I heard a crackling rustle behind me, near my head. I turned around and saw that the creature was climbing the wall, already at the level of my head, and its tail was touching my hair, which it whipped and wriggled with incredible speed. I leapt up and the creature disappeared. I did not dare to lie on the bed, in case it got under the pillow. My mother and one of her acquaintances came into the room. They started catching the creature, but they were calmer than I was, and even did not fear it. But they did not understand anything. Suddenly, the creature reappeared; it crawled very quietly this time, as if with a special purpose, slowly wriggling, which was even more repulsive, diagonally across the room toward the door. Then my mother opened the door and called Norma, our huge black terrier, who had died five years ago. She rushed into the room and stood like a statue over the creature. The creature stopped, but it was still wriggling and clicking its legs and tail on the floor. Animals cannot feel a mystical fear, if I am not mistaken; but at that moment it seemed to me that Norma's fear was something very unusual, almost mystical, and that she, like me, sensed that in the creature there was something fatal and some secret. She slowly retreated before the creature, which crept on her silently and cautiously; it seemed to want to suddenly attack and sting her. But, despite her fear, Norma looked terribly angry, although she was trembling all over. Suddenly, she slowly bared her terrible teeth, opened her huge red mouth, and, after positioning and struggling, decided to catch the creature with her teeth. It must have pulled hard to try to escape, so Norma caught it again in the air, bit it twice with her whole mouth, and swallowed it all in one go, in the air, as if it was gulping it down. The shell broke on her teeth; the tail and the legs that came out of her mouth were wriggling with terrifying speed. Suddenly, Norma let out a pitiful whine: the creature had stung her tongue. With a scream and a howl of pain, she opened her mouth from the pain, and I saw that the chewed creature was still wriggling across her mouth, releasing a lot of white fluid, like the juice of a crushed black cockroach, from its crushed body onto her tongue... Then I woke up, and the prince came in.

It was a very rainy and stormy morning when K., full of anger at the day ahead, arrived at the office at seven, just to finish some work before the visitor would take over everything. He was very tired, for he had spent half the night studying Italian grammar to prepare a bit; the window, where he had often sat of late, beckoned more than his desk, but he resisted and sat down to work. Unfortunately, the servant entered just then and reported that the director had sent him to see if the prokurist was already there; if so, he should go to the reception room, for the Italian was already there. "I'll come right away," said K., put a small dictionary in his pocket, took up an album of the city's sights, which he had prepared for the visitor, and went through the deputy director’s office into the director’s room. He was glad to have arrived so early and to be immediately available; it was not something that anyone had seriously expected. The deputy director’s office was still empty, as in the middle of the night; perhaps the servant had also called him to the reception room, but unsuccessfully. When K. entered the reception room, the two men stood up from their deep armchairs. The director smiled friendly, clearly very pleased with K’s arrival; he immediately introduced everyone, the Italian shook K’s hand firmly and laughed, calling someone a morning lark. K did not fully understand who he meant; it was, besides, a peculiar word whose meaning K only figured out after a while. K answered with some smooth sentences, which the Italian took with another laugh, repeatedly running his nervous hand over his gray, bushy moustache. This moustache was obviously perfumed; one was almost tempted to approach and smell it. As everyone took their seats and a preliminary conversation began, K felt great unease, understanding the Italian only in fragments. When he spoke slowly, K understood almost entirely, but these were rare exceptions; mostly, the words spilled out of his mouth, and he shook his head as if in delight over them. During such speeches, he invariably got entangled in some dialect that was no longer Italian to K, but the director understood and spoke it, which K could have predicted, since the Italian came from Southern Italy, where the director had also spent several years. Anyways, K realized that his ability to communicate with the Italian was largely taken away, since even the latter’s French was difficult to understand, and his moustache concealed his mouth movements, whose sight might have helped in comprehension. K began to anticipate many difficulties, but for the moment, he gave up trying to understand the Italian—in the director’s presence, where he understood so easily, it would be unnecessary effort—and limited himself to observing him irritably, as he comfortably reclined in the armchair, often tugging at his short, sharply cut frock coat, and once gesturing with raised arms and loose hands at something K could not grasp, even though he leaned forward and did not take his eyes off his hands. Finally, K, who had been mechanically following the ebb and flow of the conversation, due to his earlier fatigue, felt a wave of drowsiness approaching. He caught himself once, to his horror, just in time, about to stand up, turn around, and leave. Finally, the Italian looked at his watch and jumped up. After bidding farewell to the director, he pressed himself close to K, so much so that K had to push back his armchair to be able to move. The director, who surely recognized K’s predicament from his eyes, intervened in the conversation in such a clever and delicate way that it seemed he was only giving minor advice while, in reality, he quickly made the Italian’s words clear to K. K learned from him that the Italian still had some errands to run, that he would have little time in total, that he did not plan to rush through all the sights, but rather, would—though only if K agreed—decide to thoroughly inspect only the cathedral. He was immensely happy to be able to conduct this inspection in the company of such a learned and charming man—meaning K, who was only listening to the Italian, quickly grasping the words of the director. The Italian asked K if the time suited him, to meet in the cathedral at around ten, and that he would surely be there by then. K replied with appropriate comments. The Italian first shook hands with the director, then with K, and then again with the director, before leaving, followed by both, half facing them, still talking non-stop. If he spoke very quietly, he almost understood him, which was a rare exception, for the Italian usually spoke so much that he shook his head as if in joy. In such cases, he would invariably slip into some dialect that meant nothing to K. but that the director understood and even spoke, which K. could have predicted since the Italian came from Southern Italy, where the director had also spent several years. In recent years, all three of General Epanchina's daughters—Alexander, Adelaide, and Aglaya—had grown and matured. True, they were all Epanchinas, but their mothers were of noble birth, bringing substantial dowries with them. Their father claimed to aspire to a very high position in the future, and what was equally important, all three were strikingly beautiful, not to mention the eldest, Alexander, who was already twenty-five. The middle one was twenty-three, and the youngest, Aglaya, had just turned twenty. This youngest one was even considered beautiful and was beginning to attract significant attention in society. But this was not all: all three were well-educated, intelligent, and talented. It was known that they loved each other dearly and supported each other. Even mentions of supposed donations from the two older ones to their younger sister as a common idol in the family were made. In society, they did not like to draw attention to themselves and were, in fact, too modest. No one could reproach them for arrogance and haughtiness, yet it was known that they were proud and knew their worth. The eldest was a musician, and the middle one was an excellent painter; but for many years, few knew about this, and it was only revealed recently, and even then accidentally. In short, much good was said about them. But there were also those who disliked them.

It turned out, therefore, that one had to calm down, look coldly and wait. But alas, calmness did not last for even ten minutes. The first blow to composure came from news about what happened on Kamen Island while Mama was away. (Liza Prokofievna’s trip took place on the very morning after the count, the day before, had come at one o’clock instead of ten.) The sisters, responding very detailed to Mama’s impatient inquiries, first said that “nothing really happened while Mama was away, as far as they could tell,” that the count had come, that Aglaya did not come out to see him for half an hour, then came out and immediately offered the count to play chess; that the count did not know how to play chess and that Aglaya beat him right away; that she became very cheerful and utterly ashamed the count for his inability, laughed so much at him that it was pitiful to look at him. Then she offered to play cards, “dummet.” But here everything went in the opposite direction: the count turned out to be such a skilled player in “dummet” as a professor; Aglaya tried to cheat, swapped cards, and even stole small change right under his nose, yet every time he left her in “dummet” and won five times in a row. Aglaya went berserk and completely lost it; she said to the count such biting and impertinent things that he stopped laughing and turned ashen when she finally told him that “her foot will not be in this room as long as he stays here, and that it is utterly shameless of him to come to them, and especially at night, at one in the morning, after everything that happened.” Then she slammed the door and went out. The count left like from a funeral despite all their reassurances. Suddenly, a quarter of an hour after the count left, Aglaya ran down from upstairs onto the terrace with such urgency that she didn’t even wipe her eyes, which were all red from crying; she ran there because Kolya had come and brought an hedgehog. They all started to look at the hedgehog; in response to their questions, Kolya explained that it was not his, that he and a schoolmate, Kostya Lebedev, were now going together because Kostya remained outside and was ashamed to come in with an axe, because he was carrying it; that they had just bought the hedgehog and the axe from a passing peasant for fifty kopecks, and that they had already convinced the peasant to sell the axe, as it was handy and very good. K. stared at the guard. Here, he received schoolboy lessons from someone perhaps younger than himself? For his openness, he was punished with a reprimand? And about the reason for his arrest and its sponsors, he learned nothing? He grew somewhat agitated, walked back and forth, something no one prevented him from doing, rolled back his cuffs, ran his hand over his chest, combed his hair, passed by the three men, said, "It's all pointless," and as they turned towards him, he added, "in a friendly manner but seriously," and finally stopped before the guard's desk. "State Attorney Hasterer is a good friend of mine," he said, "may I call him?" "Of course," the guard replied, "but I don't see the point, unless you have some private matter to discuss with him." "What point?" K. cried, more dismayed than vexed. "Who are you, anyway? You talk about a point, when you're engaging in the most pointless activity there is? Is this not in bad taste? First, you men attacked me, and now you're standing around here letting me ride the high school over you. What point could there be in calling the State Attorney if I'm supposedly under arrest? Fine, I won't call." "But yes," the guard said, stretching out his hand towards the anteroom where the telephone was, "please, do call." "No, I don't want to," said K. and walked towards the window. There, the group was still at the window, seemingly disturbed only by K.'s approach. The elders wanted to rise, but the man behind them calmed them down. "Those are also such spectators," K. shouted loudly at the guard, pointing with his finger. "Away from there," he then shouted. They all took a few steps back, the two elders even more behind the man, who covered them with his broad body and, judging from his mouth movements, said something incomprehensible from a distance. They did not vanish entirely, though, but seemed to wait for the moment when they could approach the window unnoticed. "Intrusive, thoughtless people!" said K. as he turned back into the room. The guard may have agreed with him, as K. thought from a sidelong glance. But it was equally possible that he had not listened, for he had his hand pressed firmly on the desk and seemed to be comparing the lengths of his fingers. The two guards sat on a box covered with a lace curtain and rubbed their knees. The three young men had their hands on their hips and looked around vacantly. It was as silent as in some forgotten office. "Now, gentlemen," K. shouted, as if carrying the weight of all the world on his shoulders, "based on your appearance, my case seems to be concluded. I believe it's best not to think anymore about the legitimacy or lack thereof of your actions and to close the matter with a friendly handshake. If you agree, then –" and he approached the guard's desk and extended his hand. The guard lifted his eyes, bit his lips, and looked at K.'s outstretched hand; K. still thought the guard would strike. But the guard stood up, put on a hard, round hat that lay on Miss Bürstner's bed, and carefully put it on with both hands, as one tries with a new hat. "How simple everything seems to you!" he said to K. "we should close the matter with a friendly handshake, did you mean? No, no, that really can't happen. But by no means am I saying you should despair. No, why? You are only under arrest, nothing more. That was what I wanted to tell you, and I have told you, and I have seen how you received it. That's enough for today, and we can say our goodbyes, although only temporarily. You will probably want to go to the bank now, won't you?" "To the bank?" K. asked, "I thought I was under arrest." K. asked with a certain defiance, for even though his handshake was not accepted, he felt more independent of these people now that the guard had stood up. He was playing with them. He intended to run to the door and offer his arrest if they left. Therefore, he repeated, "How can I go to the bank if I'm under arrest?" "Oh, so," said the guard, who was already at the door, "you misunderstood me. You are under arrest, certainly, but that shouldn't prevent you from fulfilling your duties. You shouldn't be hindered from your usual way of life either." "Then being under arrest isn't very serious," said K. and moved close to the guard. "That was never my intention," said the guard. "But it seems the announcement of your arrest wasn't even necessary," said K. and moved closer. The others had also approached. Now, all of them were gathered in a small space by the door. "It was my duty," said the guard. "A foolish duty," said K. obstinately. "May be," answered the guard, "but we shouldn't waste our time with such talk. I thought you wanted to go to the bank. Since you are paying such close attention to my words, I add that I don't force you to go to the bank; I only assumed you wanted to. And to make your arrival at the bank as unobtrusive as possible, I kept these three colleagues of yours at your disposal." "What?" K. exclaimed and looked at the three men. These uncharacteristic, bloodless, young men, whom K. only recalled as a group in photographs, were actually guards from his bank, not colleagues, which was too much to say and proved a gap in the guard's omniscience, but they were indeed subordinates from the bank. How could K. have overlooked that? How could he have accepted the guard and the guards without recognizing these three! The stiff, arm-swinging Rabensteiner, the blond Kullich with his deep-set eyes, and the perpetually grinning Kaminer with his characteristic smile due to chronic muscle spasms. "Good morning!" said K. after a moment and shook hands with the correctly bowing men. "I didn't recognize you at all. So we'll go to work now, right?" The men nodded laughingly and enthusiastically, as if they had been waiting for this all along, until K. realized his missing hat, which had remained in his room, and they all ran in a line to fetch it, which suggested some embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them through the two open doors. The last was, of course, the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had just started a smart walk. Kaminer handed over the hat, and K. had to explicitly state, as was often necessary in the bank, that Kaminer's smile was not intentional, that he couldn't smile at all. Then Mrs. Grubach, who did not look particularly guilty, opened the apartment door for the entire group, and K. saw, as he often did, the apron band that cut into her ample body unnaturally deep. At the bottom, K. decided to take an automobile, in hand, to avoid increasing the already half-hour delay. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch the car, the other two tried to distract K., but suddenly Kullich pointed at the opposite door, where the large man with the blonde mustache had just appeared and, in the first moment, a little embarrassed that he now showed his full height, stepped back and leaned against the wall. The elders were probably still on the stairs. K. was irritated with Kullich for making the man visible, whom he had seen earlier, even expected. "Don't look!" he exclaimed, not noticing how unusual such a statement was to independent men. It was not even necessary to explain, for the car arrived at that moment. They got in and drove off. Only then did K. remember that he did not notice the guard and the guards leaving, the guard had hidden the three men, and now the men hid the guard. This did not require much presence of mind, and K. resolved to observe himself more carefully in this respect. But he still involuntarily turned around and leaned over the back seat of the car to possibly see the guard and the guards again. But immediately, he turned back and comfortably leaned against the car, making no attempt to search for someone. Although it did not seem so, he needed consolation just then, but the gentlemen seemed to be tired. Rabensteiner looked out of the car to the right, Kullich to the left, and only Kaminer stood at his disposal with his grin, over which making a joke was unfortunately against humanity.

The more he thought, the angrier he grew, unable to bear the insult, gritting his teeth as he rushed out and shouted, "Who are you, coming from somewhere, to bully me like this!" The Monkey King replied, "You need not know where I come from. Just give me the horse, and I’ll spare your life!" The dragon retorted, "Your horse is in my stomach. How can I spit it out? What are you going to do about it?" "If you won’t give me the horse, you’ll feel this stick!" the Monkey King said, "Only after I’ve killed you will your horse have its life repaid!" The two then continued to fight beneath the cliff. After a few exchanges, the demon dragon, unable to withstand the blows, transformed into a water snake and slithered into the grass.

The Monkey King took a step forward and leaped to the edge of the ravine. With his powers to stir up the sea, he stirred the once-clear waters of Eagle Fright Ravine, making them surge like the turbulent Yellow River. The demon dragon, who had been lying and resting in the depths of the ravine, thought to himself, “Misfortune never comes alone, and happiness never visits twice. I escaped the judgment of death not long ago, and in less than a year, this devil has appeared to trouble me!” The more he thought about it, the more infuriated he became. Unable to endure the injustice, he gritted his teeth and charged out, shouting, "Where are you from, you filthy demon? Why do you dare to intimidate me?" The Monkey King replied, "I don’t care where you are from, but you must return the horse, or your life will not be spared!" The dragon retorted, "Your horse is in my stomach, how can I spit it out? If I don’t give it back, what will you do about it?" The Monkey King retorted, "If you don’t return the horse, I’ll beat you to death, and you’ll pay for your horse’s life!" The two continued to fight fiercely at the base of the cliff. After a few exchanges, the young dragon found himself unable to withstand the onslaught and transformed into a water snake, slithering into the grass.

Tripitaka could not stop praising: "You are truly a mountain god!" Berqin said, "What power do I have that you praise me thus? This is all thanks to the senior monk's great blessings. Come along! We'll skin the beast early, boil some meat, and treat you to it." He held the fork in one hand and dragged the tiger by the other, leading the way. Tripitaka led the horse, following behind. They trudged up the hill, and suddenly came upon a village. There, indeed, were: ancient trees towering in the distance, wild vines sprawling on the paths. The winds whispered through a thousand gorges, the mists hung over a thousand cliffs. A path covered with wildflowers carried a faint scent; a few bamboos swayed in the breeze. The thatched cottage had a stone-paved entrance, a fenced yard with neat walls. In autumn, the scene was bleak yet refreshing, the outlook elevated. Yellow leaves fluttered by the roadside, and clouds drifted on the hills. In the sparse woods, birds chirped incessantly; outside the courtyard, a small dog barked eagerly. Berqin reached the door and tossed the dead tiger down, calling, "Where are the servants?" Out came three or four maids, ugly in appearance, who dragged the tiger away. Berqin instructed them, "Skin it early and prepare it for our guest." He turned to greet Tripitaka inside. They both greeted each other, and Tripitaka thanked Berqin for his great kindness in saving his life. Berqin said, "We are fellow villagers; no need for thanks." They sat and sipped tea. Then an old woman, accompanied by a young wife, greeted Tripitaka. Berqin said, "This is my mother and wife." Tripitaka replied, "Please let me greet your mother." The old woman said, "The senior monk is a far guest; let us each take care of our own. No need to bow." Berqin said to his mother, "Mama, he is a monk sent by the emperor of Tang to travel westward to see the Buddha and seek scriptures. He met our son on the hill just now and asked him to bring him home to rest before sending him on his way tomorrow." Upon hearing this, the old woman was overjoyed, saying, "Good! Good! Good! If not for inviting him, we would not have this. Tomorrow is your father’s memorial day, so you may invite the monk to do some good deeds and chant scriptures for him. Then, send him off on the day after tomorrow." Although Berqin was a tiger slayer and the town’s guardian, he had a kind heart, and hearing his mother, he immediately prepared incense and paper to keep the monk.

— As for life in prison, one can disagree on that, — said the prince. — I heard a story from a man who had been in prison for twelve years; he was one of my professor’s patients and was being treated. He had seizures and was sometimes agitated, wept, and even tried once to kill himself. His life in prison was very sad, I assure you, but it certainly wasn’t a pittance. But his only company was a spider and a sapling that grew under the window... But I will tell you about another encounter I had with a person last year. There was a strange circumstance there, — strange precisely because such a case is rarely encountered. This man was on the gallows, along with others, and was sentenced to death by shooting for a political crime. Twenty minutes later, the pardon was read, and a different penalty was assigned; but between the two sentences, the twenty minutes, or at least a quarter hour, he lived under the certainty that he would die in a few minutes. I was extremely eager to hear when he sometimes recalled his impressions from those moments, and I questioned him several times. He remembered everything with extraordinary clarity and said that he would never forget those minutes. About twenty paces from the gallows, where the crowd and the soldiers stood, three posts were driven in, since there were several criminals. The first three were led to the posts, tied up, and put on their death garments (long white robes), and white caps were placed over their eyes so that they could not see the guns. Then a squad of several soldiers lined up against each post. My acquaintance was eighth in line, so he had to go to the posts in the third group. The priest passed by all with a cross. It turned out that he would have five more minutes, not more. He said that these five minutes seemed to him an endless span, a vast wealth; he felt as though in those five minutes he would live as many lives as it would be pointless to think about the last moment. So he made various arrangements: he calculated the time to say goodbye to his comrades, putting aside two minutes, then two minutes to think in private, and then to look around one last time. He remembered very well that he had made these three arrangements and calculated them exactly. He was dying at twenty-seven, healthy and strong; when he said goodbye to his comrades, he remembered asking one of them a rather offhand question and being very interested in the answer. Then, when he said goodbye to his comrades, the two minutes he had counted for private thought came. He knew beforehand what he would think about: he wanted to imagine as quickly and vividly as possible how it was that he now was and lived, and in three minutes he would be something or someone else—so who? where? All this he resolved in those two minutes! A church was nearby, and the golden-topped spire of the cathedral glittered in the bright sun. He remembered that he stared so intently at the spire and the rays that shone from it that he could not tear his gaze away; it seemed to him that these rays were his new nature, and that in three minutes he would somehow merge with them... The unknown and the repulsion from this new, which was about to arrive and would arrive, were terrifying; but he said that at that moment nothing was as heavy for him as the unceasing thought: “What if not to die! What if to turn back life—what an infinity! And all of this would be mine! I would then turn every minute into an entire century, I would not lose a moment, I would count every minute and not squander a single one!” He said that this thought eventually transformed into such a hate that he wanted to be shot as soon as possible.

About prison life, one might still disagree, said the prince. I heard a story from a man who spent twelve years in prison. He was one of my professor’s patients and was being treated for his illness. He had fits and was sometimes troubled, wept, and even tried to commit suicide once. His life in prison was very sad, I assure you, but it certainly wasn’t worthless. His company in prison was only a spider and a little tree that grew under his window... But I will tell you about another meeting I had last year with a man. There was one strange circumstance – it was strange in that such a case rarely occurs. He knew in advance what he would think about: he wanted to imagine as quickly and vividly as possible how it was possible that he was alive now, and in three minutes he would already be something, someone or something. Who and where? He thought about all this in those two minutes! Not far away was a church, and the gilded roof of its spire shone on the bright sun. He remembered that he looked very intently at the roof and the beams that sparkled from it, could not tear his gaze away from the beams, and thought that these beams would be his new nature, that in three minutes he would somehow merge with them... The uncertainty and repulsion from this new, which would be and was about to come, were horrific; but he said that nothing was as heavy for him at that time as the unceasing thought: "What if I were not to die! What if I were to reverse life, what an infinity! And all of this would be mine! Then I would turn each minute into a century, not lose anything, count each minute, and not squander a single moment!" He said that this thought had finally evolved into such malice that he wanted to be shot as quickly as possible.

—"We can still disagree about life in prison," said the prince. "I heard a story from a man who spent twelve years there. He was one of my professor's patients and was being treated. He had fits, sometimes was agitated, wept, and even attempted to commit suicide once. His life in prison was very sad, I assure you, but certainly not uneventful. He had acquaintance only with a spider and a little tree that grew under the window." But I'll tell you about another meeting I had with a man last year. The strange circumstance was, this strange fact happens very rarely. He was among several people who were once set to be hanged. A death sentence by shooting for a political crime was read out. Twenty minutes later, a pardon was read and a lesser sentence was assigned. But during the twenty minutes, or at least a quarter hour, between the two sentences, he lived under the indubitable certainty that he would die in a few minutes. I was terribly eager to hear when he sometimes recounted his then impressions, and I asked him about it several times. He remembered everything with an unusual clarity and said he would never forget these minutes. Twenty yards from the gallows, where the people and soldiers were standing, were three posts, as there were several offenders. The first three were led to the posts, tied up, given white long gowns, and their eyes covered with white caps so that they couldn't see the guns. Then soldiers formed a squad of several men for each post. My acquaintance was eighth in line, so he had to go to the posts in the third group. A priest had gone around all of them with a cross. It turned out that he had five minutes left, at most. He said these five minutes seemed to him an infinite time, a huge wealth; he felt that in these five minutes he would live as many lives as it would not be worth thinking about the last moment now; and so he made different arrangements: he timed it to kiss his comrades, for two minutes, then two more minutes to think about himself in the last moment, and then to look around one more time. Immediately after the greeting—when K. invited him to sit in the armchair, he had no time for it—they spoke of a private meeting. "It is necessary," he said, swallowing with difficulty, "it is necessary for my peace of mind." K. sent the servants out of the room, instructing them not to let anyone in. "What have I heard, Josef?" shouted the uncle when they were alone, and sat down on the table, shoving various papers under himself without looking to find a more comfortable position. K. was silent, knowing what was coming, but, suddenly relaxed from the tiring work, he succumbed to a pleasant lethargy and looked out the window at the opposite street, where only a small triangular patch was visible from his vantage point, a piece of empty building wall between two shop displays. "You are looking out the window!" shouted the uncle, his arms upraised, "for God's sake, Josef, answer me! Is it true? Can it be true?" "Dear Uncle," said K., rousing himself from his distraction, "I really don't know what you want of me." "Josef," the uncle warned, "you have always told the truth, as far as I know. Should I take your last words as a bad sign?" "I sense what you want," said K., acquiescing, "you must have heard about my trial." "That's so," answered the uncle, nodding slowly, "I heard about your trial." "From whom?" asked K. "Erna wrote to me about it," said the uncle, "she hasn't been in contact with you, you don't bother with her much, even so she found out. Today I received the letter and came straight here. For no other reason, but it seems a good enough reason. I can read you the relevant part of the letter." He pulled the letter from his wallet. "Here it is." She writes: "I haven't seen Josef for a long time. Last week I was at the bank, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't allowed in. I waited for almost an hour and then had to go home because I had piano lessons. I wanted to speak to him, maybe an opportunity will present itself soon. For my birthday, he sent me a large box of chocolate, it was very thoughtful. I had forgotten to write about it, only now, when you asked, do I remember. You see, chocolate disappears immediately at the pension, as soon as one realizes one has been given chocolate, it is gone. But as for Josef, I wanted to say something more. As mentioned, I wasn't allowed in because he was negotiating with a gentleman. After a while of waiting, I asked a servant whether the negotiations would last much longer. He said probably, for the matter dealt with was the trial against the Prokurist. I asked whether this was really a trial, whether he might be mistaken, but he said he was not mistaken, it was a trial and a serious one, but he did not know any more. He would like to help the Prokurist, for he is a good and fair man, but did not know how to begin, and hoped that influential people would take the matter up. This would certainly happen, and the matter would, as he could tell from the Prokurist's mood, not be going well. I did not attach much importance to this, sought to calm the simpleton, forbade him from mentioning it to others, and considered it mere idle chatter. Still, perhaps it would be good if you, dear father, looked into the matter on your next visit, it would be easy to get a precise account, and if anything had to be done, you could intervene with your powerful acquaintances. But if nothing needs to be done, which is most likely, your daughter will have the opportunity soon to hug you, which she would be happy about." – What a good girl," said the uncle, after finishing the reading, and wiped a few tears from his eyes. K. nodded, he had completely forgotten Erna because of the distractions of recent times, even her birthday, and the chocolate story seemed to have been invented only to shield him from Uncle and Aunt. It was touching, but the theater tickets he was going to start sending her regularly would hardly be sufficient compensation, and he now felt unqualified for visits to the pension and conversations with an eighteen-year-old gymnasium student. "And what do you say now?" the uncle asked, having forgotten all haste and excitement in the letter and rereading it. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it is true." "True?" the uncle exclaimed.

— Yes, exactly, it belongs to Vakharment Deribin. Can you imagine, what joy Deribin's aunt must be feeling: she quarreled with her son because he married a former serf, and now she has bequeathed him all his property. I was thinking to myself, wouldn't it be a stroke of luck to have an aunt like that for further adventures! But you, brother, have gone so far from everyone, you don't even visit anymore? Of course, I know that you sometimes devote yourself to scholarly pursuits and enjoy reading (though, why Nоздрев concluded that our hero is engaged in scholarly pursuits and loves reading, we cannot say for certain, and certainly not as much as Chaadayev). Oh, Brother Chaadayev, if only you could see... there would certainly be food for your satirical wit (why Chaadayev had a satirical mind is also a mystery). Can you imagine, brother, the merchants of Likhachev playing at ball? There was real laughter there! Perpendev, who was with me, said, "Look, if only Chichikov were here now, it would be perfect for him!" (meanwhile, Chichikov had never even heard of Perpendev). And, let's admit it, brother, you really did me a disservice then; remember when we played checkers, I won... Yes, brother, you simply baited me. But I, who knows why, can never stay angry. The guests continued to be amazed, whispering and glancing at each other, but it became perfectly clear that all this was planned and staged in advance, and that now, however crazy Nastasya Filippovna might be—she was certainly going mad—it was impossible to upset her. Everyone was terrified by an incredible curiosity. Besides, there was really no one to be afraid of. Only two ladies were present: Daria Alexandrovna, a lively lady of the world who had seen it all and was hard to embarrass, and a lovely but silent stranger. The silent stranger probably understood nothing: she was a newcomer and knew no Russian and, moreover, was as simple as she was beautiful. She was new, and she was already being invited to the well-known evenings in an elegant costume, coiffured like for an exhibition, and placed like a charming picture to brighten up the evening—just as others might borrow for their evenings a painting, a vase, a statue, or a screen from a friend. As for the men, Ptičyn, for example, was a friend of Rogozhin; Ferdyshchenko was as at home as a fish in water; Ganchev could not come to his senses yet, but he vaguely and irresistibly felt a feverish need to reach the end of his shameful stake; the old teacher, who did not understand the situation, was almost in tears and shivered in terror at the extraordinary anxiety that prevailed and especially in Nastasya Filippovna, whom he loved as his own granddaughter; but he would sooner die than leave her in such a moment. As for Afanasy Ivanovich, of course, he could not risk compromising himself in such a situation; but he was too much interested in the matter, even though it had taken such a crazy turn; besides, Nastasya Filippovna had dropped a couple of words about him that made it impossible to leave without clarifying the matter. He resolved to stay to the end and remained silent, becoming just an observer, which was, of course, what his dignity required. Only General Epanchin, recently and shamelessly insulted by the return of his gift, could be even more outraged by all these eccentricities, or perhaps the appearance of Rogozhin; but a man of his rank, who had already stooped to sit next to Ptičyn and Ferdyshchenko, was at the limit of his tolerance. But what passion could do, could be overcome by a sense of duty, a feeling of obligation, rank, importance, and in general by self-respect, so that Rogozhin with his group, at any rate in the presence of his Excellency, was impossible.

As K. passed one of the following evenings through the corridor separating his office from the main staircase — he went home almost last that time, only two servants were still at work in the small light of a bulb — he heard, behind a door where he had always only imagined a dusty storeroom, a sigh. He paused in astonishment and listened again to verify that he had not imagined it — for a moment there was silence, but then there were sighs again. At first, he wanted to summon one of the servants; maybe a witness was needed. Then, however, an uncontrollable curiosity seized him, and he flung the door wide open. It was as he had suspected, a storeroom. Old, useless printing forms, overturned empty earthenware ink bottles lay at the threshold. Inside the room, however, three men were hunched in the low space. A candle fastened to a shelf gave them light. "What are you doing here?" K. asked, agitated but not loud. One man, who apparently commanded the others and directed his gaze toward himself, was dressed in a kind of dark leather garment that exposed his neck and the entire length of his arms to the cold. He did not answer. But the other two cried out, "Mister! We are to be beaten because you complained to the examining magistrate about us." Now K. recognized that it was really the guards Franz and Willem, and that the third man had a whip in his hand with which to beat them. "Well," said K. and stared at them, "I did not complain; I only said how things had been in my office. And you certainly did not misbehave." "Mister," said Willem, as Franz sought to shield himself behind him from the third, "if you only knew how little we are paid, you would judge us better. I have a family to support, and Franz here wants to marry; we try to enrich ourselves as best we can, through sheer hard work alone does not succeed, especially with the most strenuous efforts. Your fine linen lured me, of course, it is forbidden to the guards to act thus, it was wrong, but it is a tradition that the linen belongs to the guards, it has always been so, believe me; it is understandable too, what do such things mean for the one who is so unfortunate as to be arrested? If he brings it up publicly, though, the punishment must follow." "What you are saying now, I did not know; I did not even demand that you be punished, I was concerned about a principle." "Franz," Willem addressed the other guard, "I told you that the master did not want us to be punished? Now you hear that he did not even know that we would be punished." "Do not let such talk trouble you," said the third to K., "the punishment is both just and inevitable." "Do not listen to him," said Willem, pausing only to press the hand that had been struck with the whip to his mouth, "we are only being punished because you reported us. Nothing would have happened to us otherwise, even if it had been discovered what we had done. Can that be called justice? We, especially I, had been a good guard for a long time — you must admit that, from the point of view of the authorities, we kept a good watch — we had a chance to advance, and we would certainly soon have become like that one, who had the luck not to be reported, since such a report is very rare. Now, sir, everything is lost, our careers are over, we must perform much more subordinate tasks than guarding, and besides, we are getting these awful beatings now." "Can that whip cause such pain?" K. asked, checking the whip that the punisher was brandishing. "We will have to strip naked," said Willem. "Oh, so," said K. and studied the punisher closely; he was as brown as a sailor and had a wild, fresh face. "Is there no way to spare the two of them their punishment?" he asked the punisher. "No," said the punisher and shook his head with a smile. "Strip!" he ordered the guards. And to K. he said, "You need not believe them; they are somewhat deluded by the fear of the beatings. What this one, for instance," he pointed to Willem, "said about his career possibilities is sheer nonsense. Look at how fat he is; the first strokes will simply go into the fat. — Do you know how he became so fat? He eats the breakfast of every prisoner. Did he not also eat your breakfast? Well, I told you. But a man with such a belly can never be a whipsman, that is out of the question." "There are also whipsmen like that," asserted Willem, as he began to unbutton his trousers. "No," said the punisher and struck him so sharply on the neck with the whip that he flinched, "listen, but strip." "I would reward you well if you let them go," said K. and, without even looking at the punisher again — such business is best conducted with lowered eyes from both sides — took out his wallet. "Do you want to report me too," said the punisher, "and subject me to these beatings? No, no!" "Be reasonable," said K., "if I had wanted them punished, I would not be buying them off now. I could simply shut the door here, not see or hear anything, and go home. But I do not do that now; I am really concerned about freeing them. If I had known that they were to be punished or could be punished, I would never have mentioned their names. I do not even think they are guilty; guilty is the organization, guilty are the high officials." "That's right!" the guards cried and immediately received a blow on their already undressed backs. "If you had a high magistrate here under your whip," said K. and pressed down on the whip, which wanted to rise again, "I would certainly not hinder you from striking, no, I would even give you more money to support the good cause." "What you say sounds convincing," said the punisher, "but I cannot be bribed. I am hired to strike, so I will strike." The guard Franz, who had been somewhat restrained in his expectations of K.'s intervention, now, naked except for his trousers, knelt at the door and whispered, "If you cannot spare us both, at least free me. Willem is older than I, he is less sensitive in every respect, and he was already given a light beating a few years ago, but I have not yet been disgraced and have only been brought to this by Willem, who has been my teacher for both good and bad. My poor bride is waiting at the bank, I am so ashamed." He dried his tears with K.'s coat. "I will not wait any longer," said the punisher, seized the whip, and struck Franz, while Willem, in a corner, watched secretly, daring not to look away. At that moment, a scream arose from Franz, unbroken and unchanging, as if it came not from a human but from a tortured instrument. The whole corridor resounded with it, and the whole house must have heard it. "Do not scream," K. cried, unable to hold back, and as he anxiously looked in the direction from which the servants must come, he pushed at Franz, not strongly, but strong enough that the insensible one fell to the ground and searched the floor in convulsions; the blows did not miss him either, striking him even on the ground as he writhed under them. And already, in the distance, a servant appeared, and a few steps behind him, another. K. had quickly slammed the door and moved to a window, opening it. The screaming had completely stopped. To prevent the servants from coming closer, he shouted, "It's me!" "Good evening, Mr. Procurator!" they called back. "Did something happen?" "No, no," answered K., "a dog is just howling on the yard." When the servants did not move, he added, "You can stay at your work." To avoid any conversation with the servants, he bent out the window. When he looked out into the corridor after a while, they were gone. K. remained at the window, not daring to go into the storeroom and not wanting to go home. Below him was a small quadrangle yard; all the office rooms were around it, and all the windows were now dark, but the upper ones reflected the moonlight. K. strained his eyes in the darkness of a yard corner where several carts were parked. It tormented him that he had not been able to prevent the beating, but it was not his fault that it had not succeeded — Franz had cried out, of course, and he had undoubtedly felt great pain, but at the crucial moment one had to control oneself. If he had not cried out, K. would have, at least very likely, found another way to persuade the punisher. If the whole lower administration was riddled with riffraff, why should the punisher, who had such an inhuman task, be an exception? K. had noticed how his eyes had sparkled at the sight of the note and had apparently only taken the beating seriously to increase the bribe. And K. would not have stinted; he really did want to free the guards. If he had already begun to fight the corruption of this judicial system, it was self-evident that he would also intervene from this side.

On one of the following evenings as K. passed through the corridor that separated his office from the main staircase – he went this time almost as the last person home, only the two servants were still working in the small light of a bulb – he heard from behind a door where he had always only assumed to be a storage closet, which he had never actually seen, a sigh being emitted. He stood surprised and listened again to confirm that he was not mistaken – there was a brief silence, then the sighs did come through again. – At first, he wanted to call one of the servants, perhaps a witness could be useful, but then an irresistible curiosity seized him and he flung the door open. It was, as he had correctly suspected, a storage closet. Unusable, old printing type, overturned empty earthen ink bottles lay behind the threshold. But in the room itself, three men stood hunched over in the low space. A candle fixed to a shelf gave them light. "What are you doing here?" asked K., his excitement overwhelming him, but not his voice. The man who seemed to be in command and first drew the attention to himself, dressed in a kind of dark leather clothing that left his neck and entire arms bare down to the chest, did not respond. But the other two cried out: "Master! We are to be beaten because you complained about us to the investigating judge." And now K. realized that they were indeed the guards Franz and Willem, and that the third held a whip in his hand to beat them. "Now," said K. and stared at them, "I did not complain, I only said what had happened in my room. And you have certainly behaved correctly. "Master," said Willem, while Franz, behind him, sought to secure himself from the third, "if you knew how little we are paid, you would judge us better. I have a family to feed, and Franz here wanted to marry – one enriches oneself somehow, but not through mere work, no matter how strenuous. Your fine underwear tempted me – it is of course forbidden to the guards to do such things, but it was customary for the laundry to belong to the guards – it has always been so, believe me – it is understandable for someone so unlucky as to be arrested to think about such things. But when he brings it up publicly, then punishment must follow." "What you are saying now, I did not know, I did not ask for your punishment, I was concerned only with a principle," K. said and looked at them. "Franz," Willem said to the other guard, "didn't I tell you that the master did not request your punishment? Now you see that he did not even know that we were to be punished." "Don't be swayed by such talk," said the third to K., "the punishment is just as unavoidable as it is just." "Don't listen to him," said Willem and paused only to bring the hand, which had received a lash, to his mouth, "we are only being punished because you reported us. Otherwise nothing would have happened, even if they had found out what we had done. Can that be called justice? We two, and especially me, have served as guards for a long time and proved ourselves – you yourself must admit that, from the point of view of the authorities, we have done a good job of guarding – we had prospects for advancement and would certainly soon have become floggers like this one, who, by the way, had the good fortune not to be reported by anyone, for such reports rarely happen. Now, Master, all is lost, our careers are over, we will have to take on much more menial work than guarding, and moreover, we will receive these terrible, painful lashes." "Can a whip really cause such pain?" asked K. and examined the whip held out in front of him by the flogger. "We will have to take off our clothes completely," said Willem. "Ah, so," said K. and looked closely at the flogger, he was tanned like a sailor and had a wild, fresh face. "Is there no way to spare the two of them the lashes?" he asked him. "No," said the flogger and smiled and shook his head. "Get undressed!" ordered him the guards. And to K., he said, "You don't have to believe everything they say, they are already somewhat insane from fear of the lashes. What this one, for example, has just said about his career is laughable. Look at how fat he is – the first lashes will simply be lost in the fat. – Do you know how he became so fat? He eats the breakfasts of all the detainees. Has he not eaten your breakfast as well? Well, I said so. But a man with such a belly can never become a flogger, it is completely impossible." "There are also floggers like that," declared Willem, as he unfastened his belt. "No," said the flogger and struck him across the neck with the whip in such a way that he flinched, "you mustn't listen, but undress." "I would reward you well if you let them go," said K. and without once looking at the flogger – such transactions are best conducted with lowered eyes by both parties – drew his wallet from his pocket. "You will perhaps report me then and administer lashes to me as well," said the flogger, "no, no!" "Be reasonable," said K., "if I had wanted these two to be punished, I would not be trying to buy them off now. I could simply have closed this door, seen and heard nothing more, and gone home. But I am not doing that now, rather, I am seriously concerned with freeing them; had I known that they were to be punished or could be punished, I would not have mentioned their names. I do not hold them guilty at all, guilty is the organization, guilty are the higher officials." "That's right!" the guards cried and received immediately a lash on their already undressed backs. "If you had a high judge under your whip here," said K., while he pressed the whip, which wanted to rise again, down, "I would not hinder you from striking, on the contrary, I would give you more money to strike for a good cause." "What you say sounds convincing," said the flogger, "but I am not to be bribed. I am hired to flog, so I flog." The guard Franz, who had so far been rather reticent in the hope that K.'s intervention would be successful, now, only in his trousers, knelt at the door and whispered to K., "If you cannot bring about leniency for us both, at least try to save me. Willem is older than I, less sensitive in every respect, and has already received a mild beating a few years ago, I, however, have not been disgraced and was only led into this by Willem, who has been my teacher in the good and bad. My poor fiancée is waiting outside the bank, I am so ashamed. "He dried his face, which was dripping with tears, with K.'s coat. "I wait no longer," said the flogger, seized the whip with both hands, and lashed out at Franz, while Willem crouched in a corner and secretly watched without daring to turn his head. A scream came from Franz, unbroken and unchanging, it seemed to come not from a man, but from a tortured instrument, it resounded through the whole corridor, the whole house must have heard it. It tormented him that he had not managed to prevent the beating, but it was not his fault that he had not succeeded – Franz had screamed – of course, it must have hurt very much, but in a decisive moment one must master oneself – if he had not screamed, K. would have, at least very probably, found a way to persuade the flogger. If the whole lower echelon of officials was scum, why should the flogger, who had the most inhumane office, make an exception? K. had observed well that his eyes had gleamed when he saw the note, he had only taken the beating seriously to increase the bribe amount a little more. And K. had not been stingy, it was really about freeing the guards; if he now had already begun to fight the corruption of this judicial system, it was of course obvious that he would also fight it from this side.

As K. passed one of the next evenings through the corridor that separated his office from the main staircase—this time, he was almost the last to leave, for two servants were still working in the small light of a filament lamp in the storeroom—, he heard behind a door, behind which he had always assumed there was only a storage closet, which he had never seen, sighs being let out. As he had rightly suspected, it was a storage closet. Unusable, old typesetting plates, overturned empty earthenware ink bottles lay at the threshold. But inside the room stood three men, bent over in the low space. A candle fastened to the shelf gave them light. "What are you doing here?" K. asked, excited but not loudly. The man who seemed to dominate the others and first directed his gaze, dressed in a kind of dark leather clothing that left his neck and whole arms bare, did not answer. But the other two cried out: "Master! We should be beaten because you complained about us to the examining judge." And now K. recognized that they were indeed the guards Franz and Willem, and the third man held a stick to beat them. I have a family to support, and Franz here wanted to marry; everyone seeks to enrich himself, it’s just not possible through work alone, even with the hardest effort. Your fine linen tempted me, of course it’s forbidden for guards to act like that, it was wrong, but the custom is that the linen belongs to the guards, it’s always been that way, believe me; it’s understandable for the unhappy prisoner, what can such things mean to him? "Can a stick really cause such pain?" asked K., inspecting the stick the flogger held in front of him. "We will have to take off our clothes completely," said Willem. "Ah, so," said K. and carefully examined the flogger. He was tanned like a sailor and had a wild, fresh face. "Is there no way to spare the two of them from the flogging?" he asked the flogger. "No," said the flogger and shook his head with a smile, "step out!" he ordered the guards. To K., he said, "You needn’t believe everything they say, they have become a little mad with the fear of the flogging. What this one, for example," he indicated Willem— "says about his career is truly laughable. Look at how fat he is—the first blows will be lost in the fat. Do you know why he has become so fat? He eats the breakfast of every prisoner. Didn’t he eat your breakfast too? I told you so. But a man with such a belly can never be a flogger, it’s out of the question." "Do you think then that I would report you and get flogged too?" said the flogger, "no, no!" "Be reasonable," said K., "if I wanted to punish these two, I would not release them now. It does not matter if his face and the whole image did not flit about like a living entity before the eyes; instead, the soul would not be agitated after reading, and one could return to the card table, which amuses all of Russia. Yes, my dear readers, you would not have wanted to see the exposed human poverty. Why, you ask, do we need this? Do we not already know that life is full of contemptible and stupid things?
