One day, the Master and his disciples were playing before the Three Stars Cave. The Master said, "Wukong, have you finished your task?" Wukong replied, "Thanks to your great kindness, my discipleship is complete, and I am now capable of ascending on clouds." The Master said, "Try ascending on clouds for me." Wukong showed his skill, leaping into the air with a somersault, and rose several dozen feet. He rode the clouds for a while, a while being the time it takes to have a meal, but he did not travel more than a few miles. Returning, he landed and clasped his hands before the Master, saying, "Teacher, this is ascending on clouds, is it not?" The Master smiled and said, "This is not considered ascending on clouds. It is just crawling on clouds. It is said in ancient texts, 'Celestial beings travel north to the Bohai Sea and south to Mount Aofu in one day.' If it takes you a whole day to travel a few miles, you are still considered crawling on clouds." Wukong asked, "What does that mean, 'north to the Bohai Sea and south to Mount Aofu in one day'?" The Master replied, "When ascending on clouds, one starts in the Bohai Sea in the morning, passes through the East Sea, the West Sea, and the South Sea, and then returns to Mount Aofu. Mount Aofu is a play on words for the Northern Zero-Yang in the Bohai Sea. To travel around the entire world in a day is considered ascending on clouds." Wukong said, "This is difficult! This is difficult!" The Master said, "There is nothing difficult in this world, for those who are determined." Hearing these words, Wukong prostrated himself and said, "Teacher, one must strive for perfection. Please grant me your great compassion and teach me this method of ascending on clouds, without fail, for I will never forget your kindness." The Master said, "When other immortals ascend on clouds, they take off by stamping their feet. You do it differently. I saw you jump and somersault up. I will now teach you the somersault cloud." Wukong again prostrated himself and begged, and the Master taught him a formula, saying, "With this cloud, recite the spell, gather your fist tightly, and when you shake it, you will have traveled ten-hundred thousand eight thousand miles in one somersault!" The disciples heard this and all laughed, saying, "Wukong, what a stroke of luck! If you learn this, you can earn a living as a messenger, delivering documents, and wherever you go, you can find food." That night, the master and disciples each returned to their abode. That night, Wukong practiced, and he mastered the somersault cloud. Henceforth, he could do as he pleased, free and without restraint, enjoying the bliss of eternal life.

As the old saying goes: 'A immortal travels north in the early morning to Mount Heng and south to Mount Lu at night.' Wukong asked, "Then what does ‘north in the early morning to Mount Heng and south to Mount Lu at night’ mean?" The master said, "Those who soar in the clouds usually rise in the early morning from the North Sea, travel to the East, South, and West Seas, and then return to Mount Heng in the evening. Mount Heng is nothing but the speech of the North Sea's Lingling. To travel the four seas in a day is what it means to soar in the clouds." Wukong said, "That is hard! It is hard!" The master said, "There is no difficult thing in the world; one only fears the person without a will." Hearing this, Wukong bowed and said, "Master, a person must be thorough. K. did not linger over him or the crowd on the hallway, particularly since he spotted a way to veer right through an unframed opening halfway down the hall. He consulted with the usher about whether this was indeed the right path, and the usher nodded. So K. turned there. It was annoying that he had to take one or two steps ahead of the usher; at least it could appear as if he were being led to his detention. He waited often for the usher, but this man would always fall behind. Finally, K. said to put an end to his discomfort: "Now I have seen how it is here, I want to leave." "You have not seen everything," the usher said, completely nonchalantly. "I do not want to see everything," K. said, who in truth was feeling quite weary, "I want to leave, how do I get to the exit?" "You must not have got lost yet?" the usher said in surprise, "Just go straight to the corner and then take the right passage down the hallway to the door." "Come with me," K. said, "show me the way, I will get lost with so many passages here." "There is only one way," the usher said now reproachfully, "I cannot go back with you again, I must present my report, and I have already lost a lot of time on your account." "Come with me!" K. repeated more sharply, as if he had finally caught the usher in a lie. "Do not shout so," the usher whispered, "there are offices all around. If you do not want to go back alone, you can walk a little with me or wait here until I finish my report, then I will be happy to go back with you." "No, no," K. said, "I will not wait and you must go with me now." K. had not even bothered to look around in the room in which he was standing; only now, when one of the many wooden doors lining the room opened, did he look. A girl, presumably summoned by his loud voice, entered and asked, "What does the gentleman want?" Beyond her, in the dimness, a man was approaching. K. looked at the usher. This man had said no one would attend to K., and now two were here. It would not take much for the civil service to take notice of him, to want an explanation of his presence. The only sensible and acceptable explanation would be that he was the defendant and wanted to know the date of his next hearing, and this explanation he did not want to give, especially since it was not true. He had only come out of curiosity, or, what was even more improbable, to determine that the interior of this judicial system was as repulsive as its exterior. And it seemed that he was right to think so. He did not want to go in further; he was sufficiently cramped by what he had already seen. He was not in the mood to confront a higher official behind every door. He wanted to leave, either with the usher or alone if he had to.

For a long time he sat there, not knowing what exactly was worrying him, only occasionally glancing nervously over his shoulder towards the door of the ante-room, where he had mistakenly thought he had heard a sound. But as no one came, he grew calmer, went to the washbasin, washed his face with cold water, and returned to his window seat with a clearer head. The decision to take his own defense proved more formidable than he had originally assumed. While he had been largely untouched by the trial as long as he had entrusted his defense to his lawyer, he had observed it from a distance and had been scarcely affected by it, he could have checked how his case was going whenever he wanted, and he could also have withdrawn his head whenever he wanted. Now, however, if he would take his own defense, he would have to – at least for the moment – entirely expose himself to the court, and the success of that should be his complete and final liberation, but in order to achieve that, he would have to put himself in considerably greater danger than before. If he had had any doubts, his meeting with the director-substitute and the manufacturer today would have been more than enough to dispel them. How had he sat there, utterly dazed by the mere decision to defend himself? What would become of him later? What days lay ahead! Would he find his way through everything to a good end? Did not a careful defense – and everything else was meaningless – at the same time mean the necessity of joining with everything else as closely as possible? Would he be able to survive that? And how would the implementation of that succeed in the bank? It was not only about the entry, for which a holiday might have sufficed, although asking for a holiday at this time would have been a great risk, it was about a whole trial whose duration was beyond estimation. What sudden obstacle had been thrown into K.'s career path!

Xuanzang wept as he returned to the temple and told his master. He then took leave and set out directly for Hongzhou. Upon arriving at Flower Shop Village, he asked Liu Xia'er, the owner, "Last year, Mr. Chen from Jiangzhou stayed at your inn with his mother. Is she well?" Liu Xia'er replied, "She used to stay here, but later she lost her sight. She hasn't paid me any rent in three or four years. She is now in a dilapidated earthen kiln by the South Gate, begging on the streets for a living. That guest has been gone for a long time, and there has been no news of him." Xuanzang, upon hearing this, immediately went to the South Gate to the dilapidated earthen kiln and found the grandmother. The grandmother said, "Your voice sounds like my son, Chen Guangrui." Xuanzang said, "I am not Chen Guangrui, but his son. Wen娇 Miss is my mother." The grandmother asked, "Why hasn't your father and mother come?" Xuanzang replied, "My father was murdered by bandits, and my mother was forced to marry one of them." The grandmother asked, "How do you know you should look for me?" Xuanzang answered, "My mother sent me to find you. She has a letter and a ring of incense with her." The grandmother accepted the letter and ring and cried aloud, "My son came seeking his fortune, and I thought he had forgotten his duties and obligations. Who would have known he was murdered by others! But it is a relief to know that heaven has not forsaken my son, and that my grandson has come to find me." Xuanzang asked, "Why are your eyes all cloudy?" The grandmother replied, "I grieved for your father day and night, never seeing him come back, which is why my eyesight deteriorated." Xuanzang then knelt and prayed to heaven, "O Xuanzang, at eighteen, I could not avenge my parents' deaths. Today, I come to find you as per my mother's command. May heaven have pity on my sincerity and restore my grandmother's eyesight!" After the prayer, he licked his tongue to the grandmother's eyes. In a short while, her eyes were opened, and she saw the young monk.

How adept the Deputy Director was at appropriating everything K. was now compelled to give up! Did K. not retain more than was strictly necessary? As he rushed off to an unknown painter with vague and, as he admitted to himself, very slim hopes, his reputation suffered an irreparable injury here. It would probably have been much better for K. to take off his overcoat again and at least try to win back the two gentlemen who still had to wait next door. K. might have done so too if he had not seen the Deputy Director in his room, searching through the bookshelf as if it were his own, looking for something. As K. hurried toward the door, he called out, "Oh, you haven’t left yet!" K. took a step forward, but the Deputy Director said, "Thank you, I’ve already found it," and returned to his room with a large bundle of papers, which undoubtedly contained much more than just the contract copy.

"Bring him the soup first," he said, "let him have the strength to talk with me after eating, he will need it." "You are also a client of the lawyer," said the trader, in a low voice from his corner as a matter of fact. It was not well received. "What does it matter to you?" said K, and Leni said, "Be quiet. – Then I will bring him the soup first," said Leni to K and poured the soup into a plate. "It will only be feared that he will fall asleep after eating, he will probably fall asleep soon." "What I have to say to him will keep him awake," said K, he always wanted to hint that he had something important to discuss with the lawyer and would want to be asked by Leni what it was and then only ask for her advice. But she fulfilled the given orders punctually. When she passed him with the cup, she nudged him gently and whispered, "When he has finished the soup, I'll register you at once so that I can get you back as soon as possible." "Go on then," said K, "go on." "Be kind," she said and turned around in the doorway with the cup.

The first ring at the lawyer’s front door was, as usual, in vain. "Leni could be nimbler," K thought. But it was a benefit if the other side did not intervene, as they often did, whether the man in the dressing gown or someone else began to harass him. As K pressed the bell for the second time, he looked back at the other door, which remained closed as well. Finally, two eyes appeared at the lawyer’s window, but they were not Leni’s eyes. Someone opened the door but held it partly shut, shouted back into the apartment: "It’s him!" and only then fully opened it. K had pushed against the door, for he could hear the other door of the neighboring apartment’s key being turned hastily. When the door before him finally opened, he stormed straight into the antechamber and saw Leni, who had been warned by the door opener, running off in her nightshirt through the corridor that led between the rooms. He watched her for a moment, then looked around for the door opener. It was a small, thin man with a full beard, holding a candle. "Are you employed here?" K asked. "No," the man replied. "I’m a stranger here; the lawyer is only my agent. I’m here about a legal matter." "Without a coat?" K asked, gesturing with his hand at the man’s lack of proper attire. "Oh, forgive me!" said the man and lit the candle to see his own state for the first time. "Is Leni your lover?" K asked shortly. He had spread his legs slightly, entwining his hands at the back where he held his hat. With the possession of a heavy overcoat, he felt he was very superior to the gaunt little man. "Oh God," the man said, raising one hand in frightened denial to his face, "no, no, what do you think?" "You look credible," K said with a smile, "nevertheless, come." He waved him with his hat and made him go ahead. "What is your name?" K asked on the way. "Block, merchant Block," the little man said and turned around when thinking of this, but K did not let him stand still. "Is that your real name?" K asked. "Certainly," was the answer, "why do you doubt?" "I thought you might have reason to hide your name," K said. He felt so free, as one only is when speaking with low people in a foreign place, keeping everything that concerns himself to himself, talking only calmly about the interests of others, thereby elevating himself, but also being able to fall back at will. At the door to the lawyer’s office, K stopped, opened the door, and shouted to the merchant, who had obediently continued walking, "Not so fast! Light up here!" K thought Leni might be hiding here, so he made the merchant search every corner, but the room was empty. In front of the judge’s portrait, K held the merchant back by the waistband of his trousers. "Do you know him?" K asked, pointing with his finger upward. The merchant raised the candle, squinted up, and said, "It’s a judge." "A high-ranking judge?" K asked, stepping to the side to observe the impression the portrait made on him. The merchant looked up in admiration. "It’s a high-ranking judge," he said. "You don’t have much insight," said K. "Among the low examining judges, he’s the lowest." "Now I remember," said the merchant and lowered the candle, "I’ve heard that too." "But of course," K shouted, "I forgot, of course you must have heard it too." "But why, why, why," said the merchant, being confused by the contradictory commands. "You probably think you’re very clever," said K, "so guide me!" In the kitchen, K had never been before; it was unexpectedly large and well-equipped. The stove was three times as large as usual; one could not see the rest of it because the kitchen was now only lit by a small lamp hanging at the entrance. Leni, in her white apron as always, stood at the stove, emptying eggs into a pot over a spirit stove. "Good evening, Josef," she said with a sideways glance. "Good evening," said K, gesturing with his hand to a chair beside the stove, which the merchant sat on. But K walked very close behind Leni, bent over her shoulder, and asked, "Who is this man?" Leni grabbed K with one hand, the other stirring the soup, pulling him forward and saying, "He’s a pitiable man, a poor merchant, a certain Block. Look at him." They both turned back. The merchant, sitting on the chair K had pointed to, had blown out the candle whose light was no longer needed and pressed the wick with his fingers to prevent smoke. "You were in your nightshirt," said K and turned her head back to the stove with his hand. She remained silent. "Is he your lover?" K asked. She wanted to grab the soup pot, but K took her both hands and said, "Now answer!" She said, "Come into the office and I’ll explain everything." "No," said K, "I want you to explain it here." She clung to him and wanted to kiss him. K repelled her and said, "I don’t want you to kiss me now." "Josef," said Leni, looking at K beseechingly and open-eyed, "you won’t be jealous of Mr. Block, will you. – Rudi," she then said, turning to the merchant, "help me, you can see I’m being accused, let go of the candle." It might have seemed that he hadn’t paid attention, but he was completely in the know. "I wouldn’t know why you should be jealous," he said in a somewhat unfunny manner. "I don’t either," said K, looking at the merchant with a smile. Leni laughed loudly, took advantage of K’s inattention, and hung herself in his arm, whispering, "Let him go, you can see what kind of a man he is. I took to him a bit because he’s a big client for the lawyer, for no other reason. And you? Are you going to speak with the lawyer today? He’s very ill today, but if you want, I’ll register you. You must stay with me tonight, though, certainly. You haven’t been with us for so long, even the lawyer has inquired about you. Don’t neglect the case! I have something to tell you too, what I’ve learned. But first take off your coat!" She helped him undress, took his hat off, ran with the clothes into the antechamber, hanged them up, then returned and looked at the soup. "Shall I register you first or bring him the soup first?" "Register me first," said K. He was annoyed; he had originally intended to discuss his affair with Leni, particularly the pending termination, but the presence of the merchant had taken his desire away. But he felt his matter was too important to be left to this small merchant, and so he called Leni, who was already in the corridor. "Bring him the soup first," he said, "he should eat before he talks to me, he will need it." "You’re also a client of the lawyer," the merchant said softly, as a matter of fact, from his corner. It was not well received. "What does that matter to you?" said K, and Leni said, "Be quiet." – "Then I’ll bring him the soup first," Leni said to K and poured the soup into a bowl. "It’s only to be expected that he’ll fall asleep soon after eating, he usually falls asleep soon after." "What I will tell him will keep him awake," said K, wanting always to make it seem that he had something important to discuss with the lawyer, wanting to be asked by Leni what it was and then only ask her for advice. But she faithfully fulfilled only the stated commands. When she passed with the cup in front of him, she deliberately nudged him gently and whispered, "When he has finished the soup, register me straight away so I can get you back as soon as possible." "Go on," said K, "go on." "Be kinder," she said and turned around completely in the door with the cup.

I don't want to lie: reality had caught me on the hook these past six months and occasionally enthralled me so much that I would forget about my sentence or, better yet, didn't want to think about it and even went about my business. By the way, about my then environment. When I became very ill eight months ago, I stopped all my dealings and severed ties with all my former friends. Since I was always rather moody, my friends soon forgot about me; of course, they would have forgotten me anyway without that circumstance. The atmosphere in my home, that is, 'in the family,' was also isolated. Five months ago, I locked myself inside and completely separated myself from the family room. I was always obeyed, and no one was allowed into my room except to clean it at a specific time and to bring me lunch. My mother trembled at my commands and even hesitated to nag me when I sometimes allowed her to come in. She constantly beat my children to keep them quiet and from bothering me; I often complained to her about their crying; perhaps, now they love me! "Reliable Kolya," whom I had nicknamed, I probably tormented quite a bit as well. Recently, he was tormenting me: all of this was natural, for people are created to torment one another. But I noticed that he endured my irritability as though he had vowed to spare the sick. Naturally, this irritated me; but it seemed to me that he had decided to emulate the Prince in his "Christian meekness," which was already rather amusing. This was a young, fiery boy who certainly followed every example; but I sometimes felt that he should live by his own wits. I love him very much. I also tormented Sukhov, who lived above me and ran around all day long on other people's errands; I constantly proved to him that he was to blame for his poverty, so he eventually became afraid and stopped coming to see me. This is a very meek person, the meekest of creatures (NB. They say meekness is a terrible power; I should ask the Prince about this, as it is his own expression); but when I, in March, went up to see how they had "frozen" the child, as he said, and inadvertently laughed at the body of his child, because I was explaining to Sukhov again that he was "to blame," the little button's lips began to tremble. With one hand, he grabbed me by the shoulder, pointed to the door with the other, and said to me softly, almost in a whisper: "Go away!" I left and found it very pleasing, even in that very moment, as he was showing me out; but his words left me with a heavy impression of some strange pity that I did not wish to feel for a long time, even on reflection. Even at such an insult (I do indeed feel that I offended him, even though I did not mean to), even then, this man could not get angry! His lips did not quiver with anger, I swear; he grabbed me by the hand and uttered his splendid "go away" without being angry at all. It was a display of dignity, even too much dignity, which was not becoming to him at all (therefore, in truth, it was much comical here), but there was no anger. Perhaps, he simply suddenly began to despise me. Twice or three times, when I met him on the stairs, he started removing his hat before me, something he had never done before, but he no longer stopped, as before, but hurried past me, embarrassed. If he did despise me, then only in his own way: he "meekly despised." Or perhaps, he removed his hat out of fear, like a son of his creditor's, because he was always indebted to my mother and could not extricate himself from his debts. And the latter is the most probable... I wanted to have a conversation with him, and I know for sure that he would have begged for my forgiveness in ten minutes; but I decided it was better not to trouble him.

—"Enough, Mr. Terentiev, enough," Ardalionovich managed to interject. "Calm down, don’t irritate yourself; it seems you are very unwell? I sympathize with you. In that case, if you wish, I shall conclude, that is, I shall be compelled to report only in brief the facts which, in my opinion, it would not be amiss for everyone concerned in the matter to know in full." Noting a certain general movement, akin to impatience, he added: "I wish only to state, with evidence, for the information of all those concerned, that your mother, Mr. Burdovskiy, enjoyed the affection and care of Pavliatsev exclusively because she was the sister of the country girl in whom Nikolay Andreievich Pavliatsev was in love in his earliest youth, but had to marry her absolutely, if she had not died suddenly. I have evidence that this family fact, entirely accurate and true, is known to very few, and is even forgotten. Furthermore, I could explain how your mother, a ten-year-old child, was taken in for upbringing by Mr. Pavliatsev instead of a relative, how she was given a considerable dowry, and how all these attentions gave rise to extremely anxious rumors among the numerous Pavliatsev relatives; it was even thought that he would marry his ward, but in the end she married a land-surveyor, Mr. Burdovskiy, at the age of twenty, by inclination (and this I could prove with the utmost accuracy). Here I have gathered several more precise facts to substantiate that your father, Mr. Burdovskiy, being quite unbusinesslike, with fifteen thousand rubles as dowry for your mother, abandoned his service, entered commercial ventures, was cheated, lost his capital, could not endure the pain, began to drink, fell ill, and died prematurely, eight years after his marriage to your mother. Then, by her own testimony, your mother remained in poverty and would have perished entirely without constant and generous help from Pavliatsev, who provided her with six hundred rubles a year in aid. Then there are countless testimonies that you, the child, were very dear to him. By these testimonies and again by your mother’s own confirmation, it appears that he loved you particularly because you had the appearance of a slow-talking, a cripple, a wretched child (and I deduced from accurate evidence that Pavliatsev had throughout his life a special tender inclination toward everything oppressed and injured by nature, especially in children, a fact, in my opinion, of the utmost importance for our affair). Finally, I can boast of the most precise research into the main fact: how this extraordinary attachment of Pavliatsev to you (due to which you entered the gymnasium and studied under special supervision) gradually engendered among the relatives and servants of Pavliatsev the notion that you were his son and that your father was only a cheated husband. But the main point is that this idea strengthened to absolute and universal conviction only in the last years of Pavliatsev’s life, when everyone was afraid for the will and the initial facts had been forgotten, and inquiries were impossible. Undoubtedly, this idea reached you as well, Mr. Burdovskiy, and took hold of you completely. Your mother, whom I had the honor to know personally, although she knew all these rumors, does not even know to this day (I too kept this from her), that you, her son, were under the spell of this rumor. I found your much esteemed mother in Pskov in illness and utter poverty, into which she fell upon the death of Pavliatsev. With tears of gratitude, she told me that she only lives in this world through you and your help; she expects much from you in the future and fervently believes in your future success...

Varvara Ardalionovna was a girl of twenty-three, of medium height and rather slender, her face not exactly beautiful but full of a mysterious charm that could captivate without beauty, and which at times was positively magnetic. She looked very much like her mother, dressed almost the same way, out of sheer laziness. Her gray eyes could be very cheerful and kind, but they were usually serious and thoughtful, often too much so, especially in recent times. Firmness and resolution were evident in her face, and there was a sense that this firmness might be even more enterprising than her mother's. Varvara Ardalionova was somewhat quick-tempered, and her brother sometimes even feared her quick temper. The guest seated now at their house, Ivan Petrovich Ptytsyn, also feared her quick temper. This was a rather young man, in his mid-thirties, modest yet elegantly dressed, with agreeable but somehow too dignified manners. His dark beard indicated that he was not in the service. He was able to talk intelligently and interestingly, but he was often silent. In general, he made an agreeable impression. He was clearly not indifferent to Varvara Ardalionova and did not hide his feelings. Varvara Ardalionova treated him with friendliness, but she often hesitated to answer his questions and even disliked them; Ptytsyn, however, was not at all disheartened. Nina Alexandrovna was kind to him and, in recent times, began to trust him even more. It was known, however, that he specialized in making money by lending it at high interest on collateral that was at least somewhat sound. He was a particularly good friend with Ganya.

"Please don't cry, Mrs. Grubach," said K, and looked out the window. He was only thinking of Miss Bürstner and how she had taken in a foreign girl. "Well, yes, it is as you say," said K, and now, judging by Mrs. Grubach's behavior, that she had not told the captain anything, he added: "Do you really think I would quarrel with you over a foreign girl?" "That is precisely why, Mr. K," said Mrs. Grubach. It was her misfortune that, as soon as she felt at all at ease, she blurted something clumsy. "I wondered all the time why Mr. K. is so interested in Miss Bürstner. Why does he quarrel with me because of her, even though he knows that every harsh word of his keeps me awake? I have only said what I saw with my own eyes." K said nothing in response. He should have rushed her out the door with the first word, but he didn't want to. He settled for drinking the coffee and letting Mrs. Grubach feel the weight of her unnecessary presence. Outside, they heard the slow step of Miss Monday crossing the whole anteroom. "Do you hear that?" asked K, pointing toward the door. "Yes," said Mrs. Grubach, sighing, "I wanted to help her and had the servant help as well, but she is stubborn and wants to move everything herself. I wonder about Miss Bürstner. I haven't said anything about Miss Bürstner except what I saw with my own eyes." K said nothing to that. He should have driven her from the room at the first word, but he didn't. He contented himself with drinking the coffee and allowing Mrs. Grubach to feel the discomfort of the situation. Outside, the heavy footfall of Miss Monday could again be heard as she passed through the anteroom. "Do you hear it?" asked K, indicating the door with a hand. "Yes," said Mrs. Grubach, and sighed. "I wanted to help her and have the maid help her too, but she is obstinate and wants to move everything herself. I find it odd about Miss Bürstner. It's often troublesome for me that I have Miss Monday in my rooms on rent, but Miss Bürstner even takes her into her room." That needn't trouble you at all, said K, pressing the remnants of sugar in his cup. "Do you suffer any loss from that?" "No," said Mrs. Grubach. "It's quite welcome for me. I get a room free and can put my nephew, the Hauptmann, in it. I was already afraid that he might have been a nuisance to you in the past few days, while I had to house him in the living room next door." "What imaginings!" said K, getting up. "That's not the case. You must think I'm oversensitive because I can't abide Miss Monday's wanderings—now she's going back—while you're here. "Mrs. Grubach felt quite impotent. "Should I, Mr. K, tell her to postpone the rest of the move? If you want, I can do that right away." "But she must move to Miss Bürstner's!" said K. "Yes," said Mrs. Grubach, not quite understanding what K meant. "Well, then," said K, "she'll have to carry her things over." Mrs. Grubach merely nodded. This silent helplessness, which looked from the outside like defiance, irritated K even more. He began pacing the room from window to door, thus robbing Mrs. Grubach of the possibility to move away, which she would probably have done otherwise.

While they were feasting merrily, someone reported, "Your Majesty, two One-Horned Demon Kings are outside the door, seeking an audience with Your Majesty." The Monkey King said, "Bid them enter." The Two-Horned Demon King straightened his clothes and rushed into the cave, falling to his knees and bowing. The Handsome Monkey King asked, "Why do you come to see me?" The Demon King replied, "I have long heard that Your Majesty is seeking talents, but have not had an opportunity to meet. Now that Your Majesty has been granted a position in heaven and has returned in glory, I specially bring a robe of imperial yellow to celebrate with Your Majesty. If Your Majesty will not disdain me and accept me, I can also serve Your Majesty as a humble dog or horse." The Monkey King was overjoyed, putting on the robe of imperial yellow. All the others were delighted as they lined up to pay homage, and the Demon King was promptly appointed as the Vanguard General of the Front Line. After bowing to receive his thanks, the Demon King asked, "How long has Your Majesty been in heaven, and what position has been granted?" The Monkey King said, "Heaven's Highness looked down on me, and has made me a mere 'Guardian of the Horses'!" Upon hearing this, the Demon King continued, "Your Majesty possesses such great abilities, why not serve heaven as the 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven'? Is there any reason not to do so?" The Monkey King was overjoyed, saying, "Good! Good! Good!" and told his four chief bodyguards to quickly prepare banners with the four characters "Great Sage Equal to Heaven" on them, to be raised on a pole and displayed. From this point forward, they were to refer to him as "Great Sage Equal to Heaven" and not "Great King" any longer. He also instructed that this should be communicated to all the other demon kings in the various caves, so that they too would be aware. This was beyond the scope of the matter at hand.

Crossing himself in the Russian manner, he set about his task. Under the pretext of choosing a place to settle and for other pretexts, he sought to inspect all corners of our realm, and particularly those most afflicted by misfortunes, famines, deaths, and the like—wherever it might be more convenient and cheaper to procure the needed peasants. He did not approach every landlord at random, but chose people to his liking or with whom he could more easily conduct such transactions, always seeking first to become acquainted, to win their favor, to acquire them more through friendship than through purchase. Therefore, readers should not be displeased if, until now, the characters who have appeared did not satisfy them; this is the fault of Chichikov, who is here the master, and wherever his fancy takes him, there we must follow. On our part, if the characters are indeed pale and unsightly, let us simply say that at the outset one cannot see the entire scope of a matter. The entry into any city, even a capital, always begins indifferently; at first, everything is grey and monotonous: endless factories and smoky factories stretch out, and only then do the corners of six-story buildings, shops, signs, and vast streets, all filled with spires, columns, statues, towers, shine with the glitter, noise, and boom of human handiwork and mind. How the first purchases were made, the reader already knows; how things will proceed, what successes and failures the hero will have, what more difficult obstacles he will have to overcome, how the colossal images will appear, how the hidden levers of the broad narrative will move, how its horizon will stretch far, and how it will take on a majestic lyrical flow—this, the reader will see later. There is still much to travel before the entire caravan consisting of a middle-aged gentleman, a bachelor's barouche, the footman Petrushka, the coachman Selifan, and the already known trio of horses, from the Convener to the black knave, all travel together. Thus, here is our hero, as he is! But one might demand a final characterization in a single trait: what kind of person is he, morally speaking? That he is not a hero full of perfection and virtues is obvious. What kind of person is he, then? A villain? Why should he be so harsh on others? Nowadays, we do not have villains; we have good-natured, pleasant people, but it will be hard to find two or three who would show their faces for a public slap. Such people are even spoken of as virtuous. The most fitting characterization is that he is a possessor, an acquirer. Acquisition is his guilt; because of it, such business was done, which the light of day has given the name of not very pure. Indeed, there is already something repulsive about such a character, and the same reader who will be friendly to such a person on his life's journey, who will share bread and salt with him, will look at him askance if he should become the hero of a drama or a poem. But he who does not shy away from any character and, with a probing gaze, investigates its root cause is wise. Everything in a person rapidly transforms; you will not even have time to look around before a terrible worm grows inside, self-willed and drawing all the life juices to itself. Often, not only a broad passion but even a small passion for something petty could swell in the one who was destined for great deeds, forcing him to forget great and holy duties and see the great and holy in trifles. Human passions are countless, like sea sands, and all are different from each other; all are both low and beautiful, submissive to a person at first and later becoming fearsome masters of him. Blessed is the one who chooses from all the most beautiful passion; his happiness grows and multiplies with each hour and minute, and he sinks deeper and deeper into the infinite paradise of his soul. But there are passions that are not chosen by a person. They were born with him at his birth into the light, and he is not strong enough to turn away from them. They are guided by the highest precepts, and there is something eternally calling in them, unceasing in his entire life. The earthly great journey is destined for them: it matters not whether they stride in a dark form or swiftly appear in a bright manifestation, delighting the world, for they are called to unknown human good. And perhaps, it is this very passion in Chichikov that is not his own, and the coldness of his existence contains what will later bring a person to his knees before the wisdom of heaven. And there is still a mystery why this image appeared in the poem that now appears on the stage of the world.

Crossing himself according to Russian custom, he set about his task. Pretending to choose a place for settlement or under other pretexts, he began to poke into every corner of our state, and especially into those which had suffered most from disasters, famines, and deaths, and so on, in short, wherever it would be easiest and cheaper to acquire the needed population. He did not approach just any landlord at random, but chose people more to his liking, or with whom such deals could be made more easily, striving first to familiarize himself and win their favor, in order, if possible, to acquire the peasants by friendship, not by purchase. Therefore, readers should not fault the author if the persons thus far presented do not suit his taste; this is the fault of Plyushkin, who here is the master and can go wherever he pleases. As for us, if blame falls on the paleness and unattractiveness of the characters, we can say that at the beginning one does not see the whole extent of the matter. The entrance into any city, even the capital, always starts colorlessly; at first, everything is gray and monotonous: endless factories and smoke-stained chimneys, and then only the angles of six-story buildings, shops, signs, gigantic perspectives of streets with their spires, columns, statues, and towers, and the whole urban splendor, noise, and hubbub, everything that the human hand and mind have produced. How the first purchases were made, the reader has already seen; how the matter will proceed, what successes and failures the hero will have, how he will have to resolve and overcome more difficult obstacles, how colossal forms will appear, how the hidden levers of the broad narrative will move, how its horizon will stretch far and wide, and how the whole thing will take on a majestic lyrical flow, that the reader will see later. There is still much to travel for the camp coach, consisting of a middle-aged gentleman, a bachelor's cab, a footman named Peter, a coachman named Selifan, and a team of horses already known by name from the chairmen to the black traitor. Thus, here is our hero as he is! But it may be demanded, perhaps, that a single stroke provide the final definition: what sort of a man is he, morally speaking? That he is not a hero, full of perfection and virtues, is evident. Who, then, is he? A scoundrel, you may say? Why a scoundrel, why be so strict with others? Nowadays there are no scoundrels; there are good-natured and pleasant people, and there are only two or three who would publicly display their physiognomy for a public slap. It is more just to call him a purchaser, an acquirer. Acquisition is the crime; for it, affairs have been carried out, which the light of day names not very pure. True, there is already something repulsive in such a character, and the same reader, who on his life's journey will be a friend with such a person, will share bread and salt with him and spend pleasant time with him, will look at him askance if he becomes a hero in a drama or poem. But a wise man is he who is not ashamed of any character, but, with a probing look, probes it to its original causes. Everything changes quickly in a person; you have not looked around when a terrible worm has grown inside, taking possession of all the life juices. Not only broad passions, but even a small passion for something petty, can grow in the one born for great deeds, making him forget great and holy duties and see greatness and sanctity in trifles. Human passions are as countless as seashells, and none are alike, and all, though lowly and noble, are at first submissive to man and later become terrible masters of him. Blessed is the one who chooses from all the most beautiful passions; his bliss grows and multiplies every hour and minute, and he sinks deeper and deeper into the infinite paradise of his soul. But there are passions chosen not by the person. They are already born with him at the moment of his birth, and it is not given to him to deviate from them. They are dictated by the highest decrees, and there is in them something forever calling, unceasing throughout life. The earthly great field is destined for them: whether in a dark guise or as a bright manifestation, rejoicing the world, they are equally summoned for unknown human good. And perhaps in this very Plyushkin's passion that pulls him is not from him, and the coldness of his existence contains what will one day throw a human being to the ground before heavenly wisdom. And there is still a mystery as to why this image has appeared in the poem now emerging into the light.

As K. entered, Miss Monday approached him from the window side, along the opposite side of the table. They greeted each other silently. Then Miss Monday said, always with her head held unusually erect: "I don't know if you know me." K. looked at her with narrowed eyes. "Of course," he said, "you've been staying with Frau Grubach for some time now." "But I don't seem to bother much with the pension, I believe," said Miss Monday. "No," said K. "Would you mind sitting down?" said Miss Monday. Both of them silently pulled two chairs from the very end of the table and sat facing each other. But Miss Monday rose again immediately, for she had left her handbag on the window sill and went to fetch it, dragging herself across the whole room. When she returned, swinging her handbag lightly, she said: "I only want to speak to you a few words on behalf of a friend of mine. She wanted to come herself, but she doesn't feel too well today. Please excuse her and listen to me instead. She could have told you nothing more than I will tell you. On the contrary, I think I can tell you even more, since I am relatively uninvolved. Don't you agree?"

The farewell service made a strong and painful impression on the prince; in church, he whispered to Lefedeva, in reply to some question of his, that it was the first time he was present at a Russian farewell service, and he only vaguely remembered another one in a village church when he was a child.

The lady maid entered the temple, bowed to the Bodhisattva, and then set up a grand meal for the monks, instructing her maids to carry the monk's sandals and socks on a tray. She then came to the Dharma Hall and, after lighting incense, bowed to the Bodhisattva once more, instructing the Elder Dharmamitra to distribute it to the monks. When the monks had dispersed and no one remained in the Dharma Hall, she knelt forward. The lady maid asked him to remove his sandals and socks, and he saw that his left foot indeed lacked a little finger. At that point, the two of them held each other and wept, thanking the elder for his care. Dharmamitra said, "Now that you and your mother have reunited, fear that the villain will learn of it. You should depart quickly and return, lest you suffer harm." The lady maid said, "My son, I give you a tiny amulet. You must go directly to a place northwest of Hongzhou, approximately one thousand five hundred miles away. There is a flower village named Hundred Blossom Village, where your grandmother Zhang resides; she is your father's mother. I shall also write a letter for you and have you go straight to the inner city of the Tang emperor's palace, to the left of the golden throne, to the home of Emperor Cheng's minister Yan. He is your mother's father. Deliver this letter to your uncle and ask him to present it to the emperor. Command the troops to capture the villain and avenge your father's death, then come and save your mother. I must not tarry any longer, for fear that the villain will be angry if I return too late." She then left the temple and boarded a boat.

—"Do you know what?" the prince took up the challenge eagerly. "You have noticed this, and everyone else has noticed it in the same way, and that's why the machine was invented—the guillotine. But then I had an idea: what if it's even worse than that? You find it funny, you think it's absurd, but with a bit of imagination, such a thought can pop into your head. Think about it: for example, if you were to suffer a punishment, say, torture; if there were suffering, wounds, and physical pain, and consequently, it all distracted from the mental anguish, so that you suffer only from the wounds until you die. But maybe the greatest pain isn't in the wounds, but rather that you know for sure that in an hour, or ten minutes, or thirty seconds, or right now, your soul will fly out of your body, and you won't be a person anymore, and that's for sure. The main thing is that it's for sure. Just imagine laying your head under the blade and hearing the knife slide over your head; those mere quarter seconds are the most terrifying. You know, this isn't just my imagination, but what many people have said? I believe in this so much that I will state my opinion directly. It is disproportionate to punish a murderer with a greater punishment than the crime itself. A sentence of death is even more horrifying than a spontaneous murder. The one whom bandits kill is cut down in the middle of the night in a forest or somewhere else, and he always clings to the hope of escape until the very last moment. There were cases where the throat was already slit, but he still clung to hope, running away or begging. But here, all the hope that makes dying ten times easier is taken away for sure; the sentence and the inevitability of it—those are the most terrible pains, and there is nothing worse than them in the world. Imagine bringing a soldier right up to the cannon at a battle and shooting him, and he will still be hopeful, but if you read a soldier his death sentence, he will go mad or cry. Who said that human nature can endure this without madness? Why this cursing, this ugly, unnecessary, and futile ridicule? Perhaps there is such a person who was read the sentence, made to suffer, and then was told, "Go, you are pardoned." It is only such a person who might be able to tell the story. Christ spoke of this pain and this horror. No, this is not how one should treat a person!

He entered, closed the door, looked at me silently, and quietly went to a corner to a table that stood almost under the lamp. I was very surprised and looked in anticipation; Rogozhin leaned against the table and began to look at me silently. Thus passed two or three minutes, and I remember that his silence offended and annoyed me greatly. Why doesn’t he want to speak? The fact that he came so late at night seemed strange to me, of course, but I remember that I was not at all amazed by that. On the contrary: although I did not express my thoughts clearly to him in the morning, I know that he understood them; and such thoughts could warrant another conversation, even very late. I thought that he had come for that very reason. We had parted from each other rather hostilely in the morning, and I even remember that he glanced at me twice in a mocking manner. It was this mocking glance that now offended me. As for my not doubting at all that this was really Rogozhin, not a delusion or a hallucination, I did not have the slightest doubt about it. Nor did I even suspect it.

He entered, closed the door, looked at me silently, and silently crept into the corner to that table which stood almost under the lamp. I was very surprised and looked on in anticipation; Rogozhin leaned against the small table and stared at me silently. Two or three minutes passed in this silence, and I remember that his silence deeply offended and annoyed me. Why doesn't he want to speak? The fact that he came so late, of course, seemed strange to me, but I recall that I was not particularly astonished by this. On the contrary: although I had not clearly expressed my thoughts to him in the morning, I knew that he understood them; and those thoughts were such that one could indeed come to discuss them even late at night. I thought that was why he had come. We had parted rather mistrustfully that morning, and even now I remember that he looked at me with a sneer twice. This same sneer I read into his gaze now, and it offended me. As for the fact that it really was Rogozhin and not some illusion, I had no doubt whatsoever at first. It did not even occur to me to doubt it.

It was already known that Chichikov was deeply concerned about his descendants. Such a sensitive issue! Another might have ventured only a little more, had he not been struck by a question that somehow came to mind of its own accord: what would the children think? And so the future founder of the family, like a cautious cat, glanced sideways with only one eye, as if checking whether a master was around, snatched up anything that was close by: a bar of soap, candles, lard, a canary—indeed, nothing was left out. Our hero lamented and wept bitterly, yet his activity did not cease in his head; everything there was geared toward building something and awaiting only a plan. He shriveled up once again, embarked on a hard life, limited himself in everything once more, fell, as it were, from purity and respectability into a mire and a base existence. And in anticipation of better times, he was even compelled to take up the rank of court commissioner, a title not yet granted citizenship and pushed from all sides, disdained by petty officialdom, even by those who trusted him, condemned to crawl on all fours in the front ranks, to endure rudeness and the like; but necessity forced him to resort to everything. One of the tasks assigned to him as a court commissioner was to get some hundreds of peasants pledged to the committee of guardians. The estate was in a wretched state. It had been ravaged by livestock epidemics, tricked by factor plotters, ruined by crop failures, laid waste by sweeping diseases that had claimed the best workers, and, finally, rendered futile by the owner himself, who, in his efforts to furnish a house in Moscow to the last detail, had squandered all his wealth down to the last kopek, leaving him nothing with which to subsist. For this reason, he was finally forced to pledge what was left of the estate to the treasury. This kind of pledge to the treasury was still a novelty, and one was not without trepidation when one resolved to take it on. Chichikov, as a court commissioner, first put everyone in the mood (as is known, even a simple inquiry or a passport can be obtained only if one has made everyone in the right frame of mind, and it would take a bottle of Madeira to bring about this change in anyone), so, having made everyone amenable, he explained that here was a circumstance, among other things: half the peasants had died out, so there would be no question of any claims being attached to them.

Wukong laughed and said, "Prince, you are still teething and your down has yet to fade. How dare you speak such grand words? I shall spare your life for now, but do not challenge me. Tell the Jade Emperor what is written on my banners: if the titles match, no need for conflict, I will submit; if they do not, I will battle the Ling霄 Palace."

Nezha raised his head and saw the characters "Supreme Sage of Heaven." He said, "This monkey dares to call himself Supreme Sage! Do not be afraid! I will slash you with my sword!"

Wukong replied, "I shall stand still and let you strike as many times as you wish."

Enraged, Nezha shouted, "Transform!" He immediately turned into a three-headed, six-armed figure, his ferocity daunting, wielding six weapons: the Sword of Vengeful Demons, the Saber of Vengeful Demons, the Rope of Vengeful Demons, the Staff of Vengeful Demons, the绣球 of Vengeful Demons, and the Wheel of Vengeful Demons. The Great Sage shouted, "Transform!" He also transformed into a three-headed, six-armed figure, waving his golden cudgel, which became three. With six hands, he held three cudgels to counter Nezha's assault. This battle shook the heavens and earth, a true spectacle of ferocity.

The prince finally emerged from the dark park, where he had wandered about for so long, as he had the day before. The light, transparent night seemed even brighter than usual; "is it still so early?" he wondered. (He had forgotten to bring his watch.) Somewhere, it seemed to him he heard distant music; "it must be at the station," he thought again, "of course, they didn't go there today." Realizing this, he saw that he was standing right in front of their villa; he knew that he would have to end up here eventually, and, his heart beating fast, he stepped onto the terrace. No one met him, and the terrace was empty. He waited and opened the door to the hall. "This door is never closed," he thought, but the hall was also empty; it was nearly dark. Time passed swiftly. One day, Lord Liu Hong went out on official business, and the young miss in the hall thought of her mother and husband, lamenting in the flower pavilion. Suddenly, she felt her body grow weary, and pain in her abdomen, and she fainted to the ground, giving birth to a son. Someone whispered in her ear, "Mighty Beauty, listen to my words. I am the Southern Pole Star Deity, sent by the Bodhisattva Guanyin on divine mandate to deliver this child to you. In the future, your fame will spread far and wide, not like ordinary folk. If Lord Liu returns, he will surely harm this child. You must protect him with all your might. Your husband is already rescued by the Dragon King, and in the future you shall reunite with your husband and child, and avenge the wrongs done to you. Remember my words, wake up quickly!" With that, the voice faded away. The young miss awoke, remembering every word, and embraced the child, at a loss what to do. Suddenly, Liu Hong returned. Seeing the child, he wanted to drown it. The young miss said, "It is already late, let me wait until tomorrow to throw it into the river." Thankfully, the next morning, Liu Hong suddenly had urgent official business and had to leave. The young miss thought, "If I wait for that man to return, my child's life will be in danger! I must throw it into the river as soon as possible, letting fate decide its fate. Perhaps Heaven will show mercy and someone will find and take care of the child, and we might meet again someday." Afraid that she might not recognize the child later, she bit her finger and wrote a blood-stained note with the child's parents' names and the circumstances, and also bit off the little finger of the child's left foot to serve as a mark. She took her own undergarment, wrapped the child inside, and carried it out of the official residence. Thankfully, the official residence was not far from the river. When the young miss reached the riverbank, she cried bitterly. Just as she was about to throw the child in, she saw a piece of wood floating by the riverside. The young miss turned to the sky and prayed, placed the child on the board, tied it down, and attached the blood-stained note to her chest. She then pushed the board into the river, leaving it to its fate. The young miss carried on her tears back to the official residence.

The preparations for the party took up more than two hours, and there was such meticulous attention to dress, especially on the newcomer, that it was hardly seen anywhere else. After a light nap, he ordered to be washed and used the lather to scrub his cheeks inside for an unusually long time. Then, taking a towel from the inn's servant, he thoroughly wiped his entire face, beginning behind his ears and made two odd snorting sounds directly at the inn's servant. Then he put on a frock coat in front of the mirror, plucked two hairs from his nose, and immediately afterwards appeared in a dark red frock coat with a spark. Thus dressed, he rolled out in his carriage along endlessly wide streets, lit by meager lamps from the few ocean-starved lanterns flickering here and there. However, the governor's house was as well-lit as for a ball; the carriage was attended by two guardsmen, and cries of the forester rang out in the distance—the same as needed. Upon entering the hall, Chichikov had to blink for a moment due to the glare from the wax candles, lanterns, and the ladies' dresses. Everything was bathed in light. Black frock coats darted and flitted apart and in groups here and there, like flies on a white sugary confection during a hot July day when an old housekeeper chops and divides it before an open window, and the children gather around to watch the motions of her rough hands raising the mallet, while the airy squadrons of flies, lifted by the light breeze, boldly enter as if they were full owners, using the old lady's blindness and the sun's blinding rays to sprinkle the delicious pieces here and there, in thick heaps. Satisfied by the abundant summer sweetness and already setting out to distribute the luscious fare wherever they stepped, they entered not to eat but to show off, walking back and forth on the sugar pile, rubbing one leg against the other, or scratching under their wings, or extending both forelegs to rub them above their heads, turning around, and flying off again, only to return with new pestilential squadrons. Chichikov had not even had a chance to look around when he was already seized by the governor and introduced to the governor's wife immediately. The newcomer did not disgrace himself: he said a compliment suitable for a man in his middle years with a rank that was neither too high nor too low. When the couples who had already started dancing pressed everyone against the walls, he, crossing his arms behind his back, watched them intently for two minutes. Many of the ladies were well-dressed and in fashion, while others were dressed in whatever they had managed to get in the provincial town. The men were of two sorts: some thin and ever circling around the ladies; some were of such a kind that they were barely distinguishable from the Petersburg men, had their sideburns very thoughtfully and tastefully brushed or just smooth-shaved oval faces, and leaned on the ladies just as the Petersburg men did, teasing them just as they did in the capital. The other sort of men were thick, or such as Chichikov, that is, neither too fat nor too thin. These, on the contrary, would eye and sidle away from the ladies and only look around, checking whether the governor's servant had laid out a green table for cards. Their faces were round and full, some even had warts, some were warty, none wore their hair in topknots, curls, or 'devil take me,' as the French say, but their hair was either short or combed straight, with softer, more rounded features. These were the honored officials in the city. Alas! the fat men handle their affairs better in this world than the thin men. The thin men serve more for special commissions or merely on the roster, with their existence being too light, airy, and altogether unreliable. The fat, however, never occupy backhanded positions but always direct ones. And even if they do sit down, they sit firmly and securely, so that it is the place that cracks and bends under them, and they do not fall. They do not care for outward glitter; the frock coats do not fit them as neatly as the thin men's, but the wealth is in the box. In three years, the thin man has no one left who is not mortgaged to a pawnbroker; the fat man, look, and behold—there is a house somewhere at the end of the city in his wife's name, then another house in another end, then a village near the city, then a village with all its land. Finally, having served God and the state, having earned universal respect, he leaves his service, moves, and becomes a nobleman, a hospitable Russian master, a bread-and-butter man, and lives, and lives well. And then his thin descendants, in accordance with Russian custom, let their father's possessions go down the line through couriers. One cannot hide that such thoughts were preoccupying Chichikov at the time he was observing the society, and the result was that he finally joined the fat men, where he met almost all the familiar faces: the procurator with thick, dark, and hirsute brows, who winked his left eye as if to say: "Come, brother, into another room, I have something to tell you," a serious and taciturn man; the postmaster, a short man, but a wit and philosopher; the president of the court, a very thoughtful and amiable person—all greeted him like an old acquaintance, to which Chichikov gave a slight bow, not without pleasure. There, he acquainted himself with the very attentive and courteous landowner, Manilov, and somewhat awkwardly, as he appeared to be at first glance, Sobakevich, who, at his first attempt, apologized when he had trodden on his foot: "Please forgive me." There, they thrust a card for cards into his hands, which he received with a respectful bow. They sat down at the green table and did not stand up until dinner. All conversation ceased completely, as always when they devoted themselves to something practical. Although the postmaster was very talkative, even with the cards in his hands, he immediately exhibited a thinking face, covered his lower lip with his upper, and maintained that position throughout the game. When he exited from a figure, he slapped the table firmly with his hand, saying "Go, old witch!" if it was a queen, and "Go, Tambov peasant!" if it was a king. The president said, "I'll scrub his beard! I'll scrub her beard!" Occasionally, exclamations burst forth from the cards on the table: "Ah! here's no use, so to the trumps!" or simply "clubs! wormwood! picnion! " or "picniondrass! picchurushuk! picchur!" and even just "picchuk!"—the names under which they christened the suits in their society. After the game, they debated quite loudly, as was customary. Our newcomer also debated, but in a way that was extremely skillful, so that everyone saw that he was debating and yet was enjoying himself. He never said "You went wrong," but "You decided to go," "I had the honor to cover your double," and the like. To further convince his opponents of something, he would always offer them his silver snuffbox, in the bottom of which two violets were noticed, placed there for the aroma. The newcomer's attention was particularly engaged by the landowners Manilov and Sobakevich, about whom he was just mentioned. He immediately inquired about them, drawing the president and the postmaster aside. A few questions revealed in the guest not only curiosity but also thoroughness; he first asked how many peasants each had and in what state their estates were, and then inquired about their name and patronymic. In a short time, he completely charmed them. The not-yet-old landowner Manilov, with sweet eyes like sugar, which he squinted every time he laughed, was completely under his spell. He shook his hand for a long time and earnestly asked him to pay him a visit in the village, which, according to his words, was only fifteen versts from the city gate. To which Chichikov, with a very respectful inclination of his head and a sincere handshake, replied that he was not only with great eagerness ready to do so.

The stranger, it seemed, avoided speaking much about himself; if he did talk, it was in clichés, with noticeable modesty, and his conversation took on a somewhat bookish turn: he was a mere worm of this world, not worth much concern, he had experienced much in his lifetime, endured trials in his service for the truth, had many enemies who even attempted to take his life, and now, seeking to find peace, was looking for a place to settle. Upon arriving in this city, he felt it was his duty to pay his respects to its first officials. This was all that the city learned about this new face, which was soon enough on display at the governor’s reception. Preparing for this reception took more than two hours, and the stranger showed such meticulous attention to his attire that such care was seldom seen. After a short nap, he ordered to be dressed, and he spent an unusually long time lathering his cheeks with soap, supporting them from within with his tongue; then, taking a towel from the tavern servant’s shoulder, he thoroughly wiped his face, starting behind his ears and flaring his nose twice at the tavern servant. He then donned a lacy undershirt in front of the mirror, plucked two stray hairs from his nose, and soon found himself in a dark berry-colored frock coat with a sparkling trim. Thus dressed, he rolled out in his carriage along endlessly wide avenues, lit by meager illumination from the occasional ocean. However, the governor’s mansion was as brightly lit as for a ball; the carriage with lanterns, two mounted soldiers at the entrance, and the shouts of pageboys in the distance — everything was as it should be. Entering the hall, Chichikov had to momentarily close his eyes because the glare from the candles, lamps, and ladies’ gowns was overpowering. Everything was bathed in light. Black coats flickered and swirled separately and in clusters, like flies on a gleaming, shimmering confection on a sweltering July day, when the old housekeeper cuts and shares it into glinting fragments through an open window; children gather around, curiously watching the movements of her hard hands raising the mallet, while the airy squadrons of flies, lifted by the light breeze, confidently enter as full masters, and, taking advantage of the old lady’s nearsightedness and the sun blinding her eyes, rain down their desirable morsels here and there, in random heaps or thick clusters. Overfed by the summer, and already spreading enticing dishes everywhere, they flew in not to eat, but just to show themselves, strolling back and forth on the sugar pile, rubbing one leg against another, or scratching under their wings, or, stretching both front legs, rubbing them over their heads, turning around, and flying away, followed by new squadrons of annoying insects. Before Chichikov could take in his surroundings, he was already being pulled by the hand by the governor, who immediately presented him to the governor’s wife. The stranger did not lower himself on this occasion: he said a compliment, rather suitable for a middle-aged man with a rank not too small or too great. When the couples in the ballroom started to push everyone against the walls, he, with his hands behind his back, stared at them attentively for two whole minutes. Many ladies were well-dressed and up-to-date, while others dressed as best they could for the provincial town. The other category consisted of fat men, or such as Chichikov, neither too fat nor too thin. These men looked askance and dodged the ladies, glancing around for where the governor’s servants might have set up a green table for cards. These were the respectable officials in the city. Sadly, the fat men are more adept at conducting business in this world than the thin ones. The thin ones serve mostly for specific missions or are only on the books, swaying back and forth; their existence is too light, airy, and unreliable. The fat ones never occupy secondary positions but always hold important posts, and once they sit somewhere, they do so securely and firmly, so that the place cracks and bends under them, but they do not fall off. He said he was a negligible worm in the world, unworthy of much concern, that he had experienced much in his lifetime, had endured many hardships on service for the truth, had many enemies who had even tried to take his life, and that now, wishing to rest, he was seeking to find a place to live, and that having arrived in this city, he felt it was his duty to greet the city’s first dignitaries. This was all that the city learned about this new face, which did not fail to show itself at the governor’s soirée. The preparation for this soirée took more than two hours, and in the stranger there was such attention to grooming that it was not seen everywhere. After a short post-luncheon nap, he ordered to be washed and spent an extremely long time scrubbing both cheeks with lather, propping them up with his tongue inside. Then, taking a handkerchief from the inn servant’s shoulder, he wiped his whole face from all sides, starting from behind his ears and even burping twice at the inn servant’s face. Then he donned a frock coat in front of a mirror, plucked two stray hairs from his nose, and shortly thereafter appeared in a dark cherry evening coat with a spark. In this way dressed, he rolled off in his own carriage along the infinitely wide streets, lit by meager lighting from now and then visible oceans. However, the governor’s house was illuminated even for a ball; a carriage with lanterns, two mounted guards at the entrance, and far-off calls of the outriders—everything was as it should be. Upon entering the hall, Chichikov had to blink for a moment because the light from the candles, lamps, and ladies’ dresses was terrifying. Everything was bathed in light. Black evening coats flashed and swarmed apart and in clusters, like flies on a shiny sugar heap in a hot July, when the old matron is slicing and cutting it into sparkling fragments before an open window; children gathered around, watching with interest the movements of her stiff hands lifting the hammer, while the air squadrons of flies, stirred by the light breeze, boldly entered, acting as true masters, taking advantage of the old lady’s poor eyesight and the sun’s glare, covering the sugary lumps with bites and clusters. The children were replete with summer’s wealth, setting out tables at every step with sugary delicacies, not so much to eat, but only to show themselves, to stroll back and forth over the sugar heap, to rub their hind or front legs together, to scratch under their wings, or, stretching out both front legs, to rub them on top of their heads, to turn around and fly off, and then to come back with new, pestering squadrons. No sooner had Chichikov had a look around than he was already being gripped by the governor, who introduced him to the governor’s wife on the spot. The stranger did not lose his dignity at this: he said a rather decent compliment for a man of middle years, holding a rank neither too high nor too low. When the couples of established dancers pressed everyone against the wall, he folded his hands behind his back and looked at them attentively for two minutes. Many ladies were well-dressed and in fashion, while others dressed in what providence had provided for the provincial city. Men, as everywhere, were of two kinds: some slender, who fluttered about the ladies; some of whom were of such a sort that it was hard to tell them apart from the St. Petersburg types, had their sideburns very thoughtfully and tastefully combed, or were just decently shaved oval faces, who as well leaned in to the ladies, spoke French, and amused the ladies in the same way as in St. Petersburg. Another kind were stout, or like Chichikov, not too stout, yet not slender. These, on the contrary, kept their distance from the ladies and looked around, only checking if the governor’s servant had set up a green table for whist. Their faces were round and plump, with warts on some, and were dotted with smallpox; they did not wear their hair in queues, curls, or in the way of “damn me,” as the French say—hair was either cut short or combed, and their faces were more rounded and strong. These were the honored officials in the city. Alas! the stout manage business better in this world than the slender. The slender serve more on special commissions, or just number and waddle about; their existence is too light, airy, and entirely unreliable. The stout, on the contrary, never occupy indirect positions, but only direct ones, and when they sit somewhere, they sit firmly and securely, so that it’s the seat that cracks and bends under them, but they won’t fall. They don’t love outward brilliance; their frocks are not as neatly tailored as the slender’s, but in their boxes the blessings of God are. In three years, a thin man has no soul left to pawn at the pawnshop; a stout man appears, somewhere at the end of the city, a house bought in his wife’s name, then in the other end of the city another house, then a village near the city, then a village with all its fields. Finally, having served God and the state and earned general respect, the stout man retires, moves, and becomes a wealthy Russian nobleman, a host, and lives, and lives well. And after him, his thin successors once again pass down their entire father’s fortune as per Russian custom on couriers. One cannot help but think that such thoughts occupied Chichikov at the time he was observing the gathering, which led to him joining the stout, where he met almost all familiar faces: the procurator with very dark, thick eyebrows, and a slight wink of the left eye, as if to say: “Come, brother, let’s go to another room, I have something to tell you,” a serious and silent man; the postmaster, a short man, but a wit and a philosopher; the president of the chamber, a very judicious and amiable person, who all greeted him as an old acquaintance, to which Chichikov slightly bowed to the side, not without pleasure. He also met the accommodating and polite landowner Manilov and the somewhat clumsy, as seen, Sobakevich, who immediately stepped on his foot, saying: “Excuse me.” Here, he was offered a whist card, which he took with the same polite bow. They sat at a green table and did not rise until dinner. All conversation ceased completely, as it always happens when one finally engages in something useful. Although the postmaster was very talkative, as soon as he took up the cards, he immediately had a thinking expression on his face, covered his lower lip with his upper one, and kept that position throughout the game. Exiting from a card, he struck the table hard with his hand, muttering if it was a queen: “There you go, old hag!” if it was a king: “There you go, Tamanian peasant!” The president, however, would say: “I’ll give you a beard! I’ll give you a beard!” Occasionally, after striking the cards on the table, expressions would emerge: “Ah! in for a penny, in for a pound, no point, so with diamonds!” Or simply exclamations: “Spades! bleeding spades! hearts! spades! and then hearts! imprecations! spades! poking stick! poking stick! poking stick!”—the names under which they had baptized the suits in their society. After the game, they argued, as usual, rather loudly. Our stranger also argued, but in a most skillful way, so that everyone saw that he was arguing, but pleasantly. He never said: “you went wrong,” but: “you were pleased to go,” “I had the honor to cover your double,” and the like. To further agree with his opponents on something, he would present them with his silver tobacco box decorated with finework, where two violets had been placed at the bottom for scent. The stranger’s attention was particularly captured by the landowners Manilov and Sobakevich, whom he had just mentioned. He immediately inquired about them, drawing the president and the postmaster aside. A few questions he asked showed in the guest not only curiosity but also a firm grasp; he first asked about the number of peasant souls each of them had and the state of their estates, and then asked for their names and surnames. In a short time, he thoroughly charmed them. The landowner Manilov, not very old, with sweet eyes like sugar, which he squinted whenever he smiled, was hopelessly smitten by him. He held his hand for a long time, asking him to come to his village, which, according to his words, was only fifteen versts from the city gate. To which Chichikov, with a very polite nod of his head and sincere handshake, replied that he was more than willing to fulfill this.

Bhante Xuanzang is greatly blessed, fitting for this task. Like a living arhat from the Pure Land, surpassing true cultivators of the Western Paradise. His crosier jingles with nine rings, his Vairocana hat rich and sumptuous. Truly a son of Buddha, without falsehood, superior to Bodhi without deceit. At the threshold, the courtiers and guards roared in approval; Emperor Taizong was overjoyed and had the bhante put on the robe and hold the precious crosier, granting two escort parties. He had the officials see him off at the city gate, then proceed down the main street to the temple as if celebrating an imperial examination success. Xuanzang fell to his knees to thank the emperor, then, on the street, he moved with a grand procession. Look at the city of Chang'an, merchants, craftsmen, princes and nobles, scholars and poets, young and old—none did not gather to admire and praise, all exclaiming, "What a bhante! Truly a living arhat has descended, a living bodhisattva has appeared in the world." Xuanzang reached the temple; the monks came to welcome him. Seeing him in the robe and holding the crosier, they all believed the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha had arrived, each revering and attending to him. Xuanzang ascended the altar, burned incense, and paid respect to the Buddha, then recounted the emperor's grace to the assembly, after which they returned to their seats. Unconsciously, the sun began to set. This was the time when: the smoke and haze from the grass and trees enshrouded the city, the imperial drums and gongs sounded; the jingles of the evening bell cut through the evening air, and the imperial court was quiet. The temple was bright with lanterns, while the village was desolate and silent. The monks entered meditation, finishing their sutras; it was the perfect time for subduing demons and cultivating the self.
