Thus, the monk was served by the Monkey as he journeyed west, and after a few days, it was the dead of winter, with cold winds biting and the ground slippery with ice. The road was a winding path through steep cliffs and rugged hills, with craggy mountains and layered peaks. Master Tripitaka, on his horse, heard a loud, howling sound and turned to ask, "Wukong, where is that water noise coming from?" The Monkey replied, "I remember this place as Snake-Coil Mountain Eagle-Worry Ravine. The sound must be from the water in the ravine." Not long after, the horse arrived at the ravine. Master Tripitaka reined in his mount to have a look. He saw: a stream of cold water flowed between the clouds, while clear, red water glittered in the sunlight. The sound of the water at night echoed through the ravine, while at dawn, the water’s reflection seemed to dazzle the sky. The water burst from great heights and gushed out like shattered jade, its roar like the wind. The water flowed to the boundless distance and the seabirds and cranes were so engrossed in it that they had forgotten fishing. As the master and his companion were admiring the scene, the water in the ravine burst with a loud sound, and a dragon emerged. It pushed the water, leapt over the cliff, and lunged at the master. The Monkey dropped the luggage and grabbed the master from his saddle, then turned to run. The dragon, unable to catch up, swallowed the master’s horse and saddle in one bite and hid in the water again. The Monkey put Master Tripitaka down on a high hill and went to retrieve the horse and luggage. There was only one pack with no horse. He brought the pack to the master and said, "Master, the monster dragon has disappeared, and it has only chased away my horse." The master said, "What will we do to find the horse?" The Monkey replied, "Worry not, worry not, let me go and see."

And so, as the Monkey King attended Tang Sanzang on his western journey, they traveled for several days, reaching the snowy month of winter, with biting cold winds and icy paths. The road was a series of steep cliffs and rugged paths, with tiered mountains and layered ridges of daunting heights. As Tang Sanzang rode on the horse, he heard the whirling sound of water and called out, "Monkey, where does that water sound come from?" The Monkey King replied, "I remember this place is called Snake-Coiled Mountain Eagle-Fear Ravine, so the sound must be from the ravine." Not long after, the horse reached the edge of the ravine, and Tang Sanzang reined in the horse to take a look. There he saw: a stream of cold water slicing through the clouds, clear waves shimmering under the sun. Its sound stirred the night rain in the remote valleys, while the splendor of the morning clouds dazzled the vast sky. Thousand-foot waves spewed like shattered jade, while the one pond of water roared and howled in the breeze. The stream flowed to the vast expanse of misty waters, where the seagulls and egrets forgot their fishing. As the master and disciple were admiring the scene, a loud splash was heard from the middle of the ravine, and a dragon emerged, pushing the waves and leaping from the cliff to snatch the master. The Monkey King, startled, dropped the baggage and carried the master off the horse, turning to flee. The dragon could not catch up and swallowed the horse, saddle and all, into its belly, then vanished beneath the water. The Monkey King brought the master to a high spot to sit down and then went to retrieve the horse and the luggage, finding only a single pack of baggage, the horse gone. He brought the luggage to the master and said, "Master, I cannot see any trace of the monster, but it has merely frightened away your horse." Tang Sanzang said, "How shall we find the horse?" The Monkey King replied, "Don't worry, don't worry, I will go to look."

But the monk was served by the Wukong as they journeyed westward for many days, through the month of winter, with cold winds biting and ice everywhere. The path was over sheer cliffs and craggy paths, over high hills and layered mountains. As Tang僧 rode, he heard a loud rushing sound and called, "Wukong, what is that rushing sound?" Wukong replied, "I remember this place is called Snake-Circle Mountain Eagle-Fear Ravine. The sound is probably from the ravine." Before they could finish speaking, the horse reached the ravine. Tang僧 pulled on the reins to see, and he saw: A thin stream of cold water flowing through the clouds, clear waves reflecting the sun’s red glow. The sound of the night rain echoed in the deep valley, rainbow colors flashing in the sky at dawn. Thousand-foot waves burst like shattered jade, a single pool’s roar shaking the cool wind. Flowing into the vast sea, the seagulls forgot the fishing net. As the master and disciple gazed at the scene, the middle of the ravine gave a loud sound, and a dragon appeared, pushing and leaping over the waves, jumping over the cliff, snatching the elder. Startled, Wukong dropped the luggage, seized the monk and pushed him from the horse, then turned to flee. The dragon could not catch up and swallowed his horse and saddle whole, then sank back into the water. Wukong set the monk on a high mound and came to pick up the horse and luggage, but only one set of luggage remained, with no horse. He brought the luggage to the master and said, "Master, the demon dragon is nowhere to be seen, but it has frightened away my horse." Tang僧 said, "What will we do now to find the horse?" Wukong replied, "Rest assured, rest assured, I’ll go and look."

But it was said that when the Monkey King served Tang僧 on his journey westward, they traveled for several days, and it was just that cold month of winter. The wind was piercing, the ground icy, and the path was over rugged cliffs and steep mountains. The Three Palms were covered in dense layers of towering peaks. As Tang僧 rode, he heard a rumbling sound and turned to ask, "Monkey, where is that water sound coming from?" The Monkey replied, "I remember the place being called Snake-Coiled Mountain Eagle Frightening Gorge. It must be the sound of the stream there." Not long after, their horse reached the edge of the gorge, and Tang僧 pulled back on the reins to look. There, he saw: A stream of icy water trickling through the clouds, clear waves reflecting the sun's red glow. Night rain’s whispers were echoed in the depths, and dawn’s colors dazzled in the sky. Thousand-foot waves spewed like shattered jade, a single pool roared with the sound of a clear wind. The water flowed away over vast expanses of misty waters, where gulls and herons were indifferent to fishing. As the two disciples gazed, a rumbling echoed in the center of the ravine. A dragon emerged, churning waves, leaping over the cliffs, and seizing the elder. Monkey dropped the luggage, scooped up his master from the horse, and turned to flee. The dragon could not catch up, and swallowed the horse and saddle whole, then vanished beneath the water. Monkey placed his master on a high, open area and came back to retrieve the horse and luggage, but only one load remained, the horse having vanished. He brought the luggage to the master and said, "Master, the fiendish dragon has no trace, it only scared away my horse." Tang僧 said, "Disciple, how can we find our horse?" Monkey replied, "Relax, relax, let me go and find it."

But as the Traveler Monkey attended the Tripitaka on their westward journey, after several days, it was the coldest month of winter, with piercing winds and icy conditions. The path was rugged and treacherous, through sheer cliffs and towering mountains. The Master on his horse heard a roaring sound and turning back called out, "Monkey, what is that noise?" Monkey replied, "I remember this place is called Snake-Circling Mountain Eagle-Fear Valley; surely it is the creek waters making that sound." Not long after, the horse reached the creek edge. The Master reined the reins to look, and he saw: the cold spring water sliced through the clouds, the clear waves glinted red under the sun. The sound shook the night rains heard in the depths of the valley, colored like dawn’s rising sun aglow in the heavens. Torrents of water flew like shattered jade, echoing the clear wind in their cries. Flowing to the boundless, misty waters, the seagulls and herons no longer remembered their fishing. As the Master and his companion were admiring the view, the middle of the creek suddenly roared, and a dragon emerged. It stirred the waves and leaped out from the cliff, rushing to seize the elder. Monkey, startled, dropped the luggage, held the Master off the horse, and turned to run. But the dragon could not catch up, swallowing the Master’s horse and saddlebag in one gulp before sinking back under the water. Monkey brought the Master to a high hill and left his luggage beside him, then went to retrieve his horse and pack, leaving only the luggage behind, the horse gone. He carried the luggage back to the Master and said, "Master, no sign of that monster; it only startled away your horse." The Master said, "What can we do to find our horse?" Monkey replied, "Relax, relax, I will go and look."

But as he sat in his hard chairs, troubled by thoughts and insomnia, entertaining Nosdrev and his whole family, a greasy candle flickered before him, the candlestick having long been covered with a black, smoke-stained cap, threatening to go out at any moment. The blind, dark night peered through his windows, ready to turn blue as dawn approached. In the far-off distance, roosters crowed, and in the completely asleep city, perhaps somewhere a friezed pelisse was being woven by a wretched person of unknown class and rank, knowing only (alas!) the path well-worn by the Russian people—just when, at the other end of the city, an event occurred that was about to increase the difficulty of our hero’s situation. Specifically, in the remote streets and alleyways of the city, a very strange conveyance creaked, causing puzzlement about its name. It did not resemble a tarantass, a carriage, or a brougham, but was more like a thick-waisted, bulging watermelon set on wheels. The cheeks of this watermelon, or the doors, which bore traces of yellow paint, could not be closed properly due to the poor condition of the handles and locks, clumsily tied with ropes. The watermelon was filled with cotton cushion-pouches, pillows, and simple pillows, stuffed with sacks of bread, kozhukh, kozhurka, skorodumka, and krendel made of puff pastry. Even the kurnic and rassolnik puffs peeked out from above. The saddlebags were occupied by the face of a livery servant, wearing a homemade checkered jacket, with an unshaven beard, slightly flecked with gray, known as "the small one." The noise and squeaking from the iron shackles and rusty bolts woke up a baker at the other end of the city, who, raising his halberd, groggily shouted: "Who’s there?" but, seeing no one walking, only hearing the distant clattering, caught a beast on his neck and, approaching the lantern, executed it right there on his finger. Afterward, putting away his halberd, he fell asleep again according to the rituals of his knighthood. The horses fell to their forelegs time and again, since they were not shod, and it was clear that the old city pavement was unfamiliar to them. After making a few turns from street to street, the conveyance finally turned into a dark alley, passing by a small church of St. Nicholas Without-Borders, and stopped before the gates of the protopop’s house. A girl, with a scarf on her head and a parka, hit the gates with both fists so hard that even a man (the small one in the checkered jacket was already dragged out by his legs, as he had fallen fast asleep) would have felt it. Dogs barked, and the gates, finally opening with difficulty, swallowed this awkward roadwork. The carriage drove into a narrow courtyard piled with wood, coops, and various cages; a lady emerged from the carriage: this lady was a landowner, a collegiate secretary, Korablechka. The old woman was soon worried about the possibility of trickery from him after he left, not having slept for three nights in a row, and decided to travel to the city despite the horses not being shod, to find out for sure how much dead souls cost and to ensure that she had not sold them, God forbid, for three times their worth. What the arrival of this caused can be learned from a single conversation between two ladies. This conversation… but perhaps it would be better for this conversation to be in the next chapter.

In a certain sense, Nosegade was a historical figure. At every meeting where he was present, there was always a story. Some story or other inevitably transpired: either he would be led out of the hall by the police under arm, or his own friends would have to push him out. If this didn’t happen, then something else would still occur that wouldn’t happen elsewhere: either he would cut his finger at the buffet in such a way that only amusement was the result, or he would lose so miserably that he would feel ashamed even himself. He would invent complete nonsense without any need: all of a sudden, he would recount that he had a horse with some kind of blue or pink hair, and other such rubbish that the listeners would finally move away, saying, “Well, brother, it seems you’ve started shooting your words.” There are people who have a penchant for defaming others, often for no reason at all. One, for instance, even a man of high rank, with a noble appearance, a star on his chest, would shake your hand and chat with you about profound topics that inspire thought, only to defame you right there, before your very eyes, with the savagery of a mere clerk, not the way a man of high rank would do it while discussing topics that inspire thought. One can only stand there and shake one’s head in wonder. Nosegade had a similar strange passion. The closer someone was to him, the more he defamed that person: he spread ridiculous lies, making someone’s wedding or a business deal a shambles, and considered himself no enemy of that person; on the contrary, if the chance arose for him to meet you again, he would behave as a friend and even say, “You’re such a cad, you never come around to see me.” Nosegade was multifaceted in many ways, a man for all occasions. At the same instant, he would invite you to go anywhere, even to the ends of the earth, to join any enterprise, and to exchange everything you had for whatever you wanted. A gun, a dog, a horse—everything was an object of exchange, not for gain, but from some restless, bustling character. If he was lucky to encounter a simpleton at a fair and beat him, he would buy up everything that caught his eye at the stalls: bridles, smoking candles, nurses’ handkerchiefs, a colt, raisins, a silver basin, Dutch canvas, coarsely ground flour, tobacco, pistols, herring, paintings, a sharpening tool, pots, boots, porcelain dishes—whatever he could afford. However, this was rarely brought home; it was usually sold off on the same day to a more fortunate player, sometimes even with his own pipe, tobacco pouch, and mouthpiece, and other times with the entire team: the carriage and the coachman, so that the owner himself would go out in his waistcoat or with a caftan to look for a friend in order to use his carriage. Such was Nosegade! Perhaps some would call his character trite, and say that there is no longer such a person as Nosegade. Alas! It would be unjust to say so. Nosegade would still not be extinguished from the world. He is everywhere among us and perhaps only wears another caftan; but people who are carefree and without insight consider a man in another caftan to be a different man.

Nozdryov was in some respects a historical figure. At no gathering where he was present would fail to have an anecdote. Some anecdote was bound to take place: either the police would drag him out of the hall by the arm, or they would be forced to push out one of his own acquaintances. If that didn’t happen, something else would surely occur that wouldn’t happen with anyone else: he might, for instance, cut a piece of cake in such a way that only those present would laugh, or he might behave in the most shameless manner, to the point where he himself would feel ashamed. And he would make up outright nonsense: suddenly he would say that he had a horse with blue or pink hair, and such nonsense that in the end the listeners would all go away, saying, “Well, brother, it seems you’ve already started to spew filth.” There are people who have a penchant to cause mischief to others, sometimes for no reason at all. One, for example, might be a man of rank, with a noble appearance, a star on his chest; he might shake your hand, talk to you about deep subjects that provoke reflection, and then, looking at you, would do exactly the same thing. He would do it in the manner of a mere registrar, not as someone with a star on his chest, discussing subjects that provoke reflection, so that you are only left standing there, shrugging your shoulders, and that’s all. Nozdryov had such a strange inclination as well. The closer someone was to him, the more they would be the target of his mischief: he would spread outright lies, the falsity of which is difficult to imagine, he would ruin weddings and business deals, and he did not consider you his enemy; on the contrary, if an opportunity arose to meet again, he would behave as a friend and even say, “You’re such a scoundrel, you never come to see me.” Nozdryov was a versatile man in many ways, a jack-of-all-trades. He would immediately offer you a ride anywhere, even to the ends of the earth, to enter any enterprise, to exchange everything for anything you wanted. A gun, a dog, a horse—everything could be traded, but not to gain anything: it was just from some restless and sprightly character. If he won a simpleton at the fair, he would buy everything that caught his eye in the stores: bridles, smoking candles, baby caps, a colt, currants, a silver basin, Dutch canvas, coarse flour, tobacco, pistols, herring, paintings, a sharpening tool, pots, boots, porcelain dishes, as much as the money would last. However, rarely did it all make it home; almost immediately, it was all given to someone else, the luckiest player, sometimes even adding his own pipe, tobacco pouch, and mouthpiece, or a whole team: with a carriage and coachman, so that the owner himself would go in his short coat or arhalyk to seek a friend to use his carriage. That was Nozdryov! Perhaps his character is considered hackneyed, and people will say that Nozdryov no longer exists. Alas! Those who say so are unjust. Nozdryov will long remain in the world. He is among us everywhere and, perhaps, just wears another kaftan; but frivolous and unperceptive people see a different man in a different kaftan.

Nоздрев was in a certain sense a historical figure. At no gathering where he was present would there be any lack of history. Some incident would inevitably take place: either the gendarmes would drag him out of the hall under arm, or they would be forced to push out one of his own acquaintances. If that did not happen, then something else would certainly occur that could not be replicated elsewhere: either he would slice something in the buffet in a way that only amused, or he would be completely humiliated to the point where he himself would feel ashamed. And he would invent completely unnecessary falsehoods: at some moment, he would tell you that he had a horse with blue or pink hair, and similar nonsense, such that the listeners would eventually retreat, saying, “Well, brother, it seems you’ve started shooting off your mouth.” There are people who enjoy spoiling others, sometimes without any reason at all. For instance, a man of some rank, with a noble appearance, a star on his chest, will shake your hand, engage you in a conversation about profound topics that prompt reflection, and then, right before your eyes, proceed to ruin you. He would do so as thoroughly as a simple registrar would, and not as someone of such rank who speaks about topics that prompt reflection. You would stand there, shrugging your shoulders in wonder, and that would be all. Nоздрев had such a strange habit. The closer one became to him, the more he would stab the person in the back: spreading untruths, more ridiculous than one could imagine, ruining weddings, business deals, and did not consider his acquaintance an enemy; on the contrary, if a chance brought him face to face with the person again, he would treat him with friendship and even say, “You’re such a scoundrel, you never drop by.” Nоздрев was a versatile person in many ways, that is, a person for all occasions. At that very moment, he would offer you to go anywhere, even to the ends of the earth, to enter any venture, to exchange all that you had for what you desired. A gun, a dog, a horse—all were subjects of exchange, but not with the intent of profiting: this was simply due to some restless, sprightly nature. If he were to encounter a simpleton at a fair and defeat him, he would buy a large quantity of whatever had caught his eye in the shops: harnesses, smoking candles, nanny’s handkerchiefs, a stallion, raisins, a silver washbasin, Dutch canvas, coarse flour, tobacco, pistols, herring, paintings, a whetstone, pots, boots, porcelain dishes, to the extent that his money would allow. However, it rarely happened that all of this was brought home; in the same day, it would all be transferred to another, luckier player, sometimes even with his own pipe, pouch, and mouthpiece, and on another occasion, the entire team, including the carriage and coachman, such that the owner himself would travel around in a short coat or a kaftan to look for a friend who would allow him to use his carriage. This was Nоздрев! Perhaps, he might be called a tired old character, and people might say that there is no longer a Nоздрев. Alas! Those who say this are unfair. Nоздрев will not be eradicated from the world for a long time. He is among us everywhere, and perhaps only wears a different kaftan; but those who are light-minded and unperceptive cannot grasp that a person in another kaftan is the same person.

In some respects, Ostrovsky was a historical figure. At no gathering where he was present did any history fail to unfold. Something invariably occurred: either he would be escorted from the hall by mounted police, or they would be forced to push out one of his own acquaintances. If this didn’t happen, something else would: he might get so drunk at the buffet that he ended up laughing at his own misfortune, or he would be so thoroughly humiliated that he would feel ashamed. He would also invent stories completely without cause: suddenly, he would tell you that he had a horse with blue or pink hair, and other such nonsense, until the listeners finally withdrew, saying, “Well, brother, it seems you’ve started firing blanks.” There are people who enjoy, for no reason at all, putting others in a bad light. One might be a man of rank, of noble bearing, with a star on his chest; he might shake your hand, engage you in deep, thought-provoking conversation, and then, right before your eyes, would go and embarrass you. He would do it with the subtlety of a mere clerk, not the sophistication of a man with a star on his chest engaging in deep, thought-provoking conversation. You would only stand there and shrug, and that would be it. Ostrovsky possessed such a peculiar obsession. The closer someone got to him, the more likely they were to be the recipient of his slander: he would spread false rumors, farcical in nature, and would not even consider himself your enemy; on the contrary, should a chance arise for them to meet again, he would treat them with renewed friendliness and even say, “You’re such a scoundrel, never dropping by.” Ostrovsky was a multifaceted individual, a man for all occasions. At the very moment, he would offer you a ride anywhere, even to the ends of the earth, to join any enterprise, and to exchange anything for anything you desired. A gun, a dog, a horse—everything could be traded, but not with the aim of winning: this was simply due to his restless, eager nature. If he happened to encounter a simpleton on the fair and outplay him, he would buy everything that had caught his eye in the shops: bridles, smoking candles, nurses’ handkerchiefs, a stallion, raisins, a silver basin, Dutch cloth, groats, tobacco, pistols, herring, paintings, a tool for sharpening, pots, boots, porcelain dishes—until his money ran out. However, rarely was this brought home; almost immediately, all of it would be passed on to another, luckier player, sometimes even adding his own pipe and tobacco pouch, and at another time the entire carriage with the coachman, so that the original owner would have to seek out a friend to use his carriage. Such was Ostrovsky! Perhaps he is considered a hack, and some might say that there is no longer an Ostrovsky. Alas! Those who would say so are being unfair. Ostrovsky will not soon disappear from the world. He is among us everywhere, perhaps only in another coat; but those who are hasty and lacking in insight mistake him for someone else.

But did it come to pass? But was it justified? Why is he trembling again, breaking out in cold sweat, enveloped in darkness and inner coldness? Is it because he just now saw those eyes again? But didn’t he walk from the Summer Garden solely to see them? That was the crux of his “sudden idea.” He persistently wanted to see those “yesterday’s eyes” to finally convince himself that he would definitely meet them at that house. This was his spasmodic desire, and why is he now so dispirited and struck that he actually saw them just now? As if he didn’t expect it! Yes, these were indeed the same eyes (and there is now no longer any doubt that these were the very same eyes!) that had flashed at him in the crowd in the morning when he was exiting the train; those same eyes (the exact same ones!), the look of which he caught the other day behind him while sitting in Rogozhin’s parlor. Rogozhin had recanted: he asked with a twisted, chilling smile, “Whose eyes were they, then?” And the prince had an awful urge, just a short while ago, at the Tsarskoe Selo railway station, when he was boarding the train to go to Aglaya and suddenly saw those eyes for the third time that day—to approach Rogozhin and tell him, “Whose were those eyes!” But he dashed out of the station and only woke up when he stood in front of a cutlery shop, assessing a piece for sixty kopecks, with an antler handle. A strange and terrifying demon had finally latched onto him and no longer wanted to leave him. This demon whispered to him in the Summer Garden, when he was lost in thought under a linden tree, that if Rogozhin had been following him since morning and catching him at every step, and learned that he was not going to Pavlovsk (which, of course, was a fateful revelation for Rogozhin), then Rogozhin would inevitably go to that house on Peterhof Street and would inevitably watch over the prince, who had given him his word that morning not to see her and that he had come to St. Petersburg for no other reason. And so the prince hurriedly rushes to that house, and what is there to be surprised about if he does indeed meet Rogozhin there? He only saw a wretched man, whose mood was dark but very understandable. This wretched man was not even trying to hide now. Yes, Rogozhin had locked himself in and lied before, but at the station he stood almost openly. Rather, the prince was the one who was hiding, not Rogozhin. Now, standing across the street from the house, fifty paces away at an angle, on the opposite sidewalk, with his arms crossed, and waiting. Here he was fully in plain sight and, it seems, deliberately wanted to be noticed. He stood as if he were a judge and an accuser, and not... and not someone else?

"I have just ordered the Imperial Medical Institute to procure some medicine. I wonder how it turned out." He then instructed the concubines to enter the palace and fetch her. The palace mistress cried out from within, "What medicine do I need? This is not my home! My house is a cool tile-roofed cottage, not this yellowish disease-ridden building with its patterned doors and windows! Let me out! Let me out!" As she was being escorted to the throne, the King of Tang asked, "Do you recognize your husband?" Yu Ying replied, "What nonsense is this? We have been husband and wife since we were young, and we have even given birth to children together. How could I not recognize him?" The king instructed his attendants to lead her down. The palace mistress descended the jade steps and stopped in front of Liu Quan, where she grabbed his arms and said, "Husband, why are you going without waiting for me? I tripped and was surrounded by unreasonable people who were shouting at me. What is going on here!" Liu Quan, hearing his wife's words and seeing her face, did not dare to recognize her. The king said, "This is indeed a case where a man must be moved by a tale to believe it, and a husband and wife must be reunited after a long separation!" The wise king then presented the dowry, clothing, and jewelry of his sister-in-law to Liu Quan, as if they were her own dowry. He also bestowed upon him an imperial decree exempting him from all future taxes and duties, and sent him off with his sister-in-law. The couple thanked the king and returned home, elated. There is a verse that bears witness to this: Life and death are predetermined by fate, each with their allotted span. Liu Quan brings back the melon from the underworld, and Li Cuilien returns to life through another's body. The couple bid farewell to the king and returned directly to Junzhou, where they found their children and home in good condition. They both proclaimed their good fortune without further ado.

"I have just sent for the Imperial Medical Institute to fetch medicine, and I do not know how it went," said the emperor. He then ordered the ladies-in-waiting to enter the palace to summon the man. My home is a cool tile-roofed house, not this yellow-disease-infested building, with its shabby and foppish doors and windows! Let me out! Let me out!" Just as she was screaming, four or five female officials and two or three eunuchs came to support her and brought her to the throne. Emperor Tang asked, "Do you recognize your husband?" Yu Ying replied, "How can you say such a thing? We are husband and wife from our childhood, and we have given birth to sons and daughters. How could I not recognize him?" The emperor ordered the eunuchs to lead her down. I tripped and was surrounded by those unreasonable people who bellowed at me. What is the meaning of this!" Liu Quan, upon hearing her words, recognized his wife by her voice but dared not acknowledge her because of her appearance. Emperor Tang said, "This is a rare case of mountain collapse and earth upheaval where someone witnesses it, but it is hard to find a case of capturing a live person to replace a dead one!" This virtuous king rewarded Liu Quan with his late sister's jewelry, clothes, and accessories as dowry, as if she were his own wife, and bestowed on him an edict exempting him from labor taxes, sending him back with his sister. The couple thanked the emperor and returned home joyfully. A poem serves as a witness: Life and death are fate, each with their time. Liu Quan brought back the melon from the underworld, and Li Cuilien's body was restored through a borrowed soul. They publicized the good fortune of their return, without further mention.

The prince did not even notice that others were speaking and being polite to Aglaya; sometimes he almost forgot that he himself was sitting beside her. At times he wanted to go somewhere, to disappear entirely from here, and even a gloomy, desolate place would have suited him, just to be alone with his thoughts, so that no one knew where he was. Or at least to be at home, on the terrace, but with no one there, neither Lebedev nor the children; to throw himself onto his couch, bury his face in a pillow, and lie like that for a day, for a night, and another day. For moments he longed for the mountains, and a particular familiar spot in the mountains that he always liked to recall and that he used to visit when he still lived there, to look down from there at the village, at the barely visible white thread of the waterfall below, at the white clouds, at the deserted old castle. Oh, how he wished he could be there now and think about only one thing—oh, to think about it all his life—that would be enough for a thousand years! And let them forget him entirely here. Oh, it would even be better if he were unknown to everyone and this whole vision was just a dream. What does it matter, after all, whether in a dream or in reality! K. was interrupted by a scream from the rear of the hall. He shaded his eyes to see, as the dull daylight turned the mist white and blinded him. It was the laundress, whom K. had recognized as a significant disturbance upon her entry. Whether she was guilty or not could not be determined. K. only saw that a man had pulled her into a corner near the door and was pressing her against him there. But it was not she who screamed, but the man, who had opened his mouth wide and was looking up at the ceiling. A small circle had gathered around them; the gallery spectators nearby seemed delighted that the seriousness K. had brought to the meeting was being interrupted in such a way. K. was about to rush over at first impression, thinking that everyone would want to restore order and at least drive the couple out of the hall. But the first rows in front of him remained solid; no one moved, and no one let K. through. On the contrary, he was impeded; elderly men held their arms out, and some hand – he had no time to turn around – grabbed him by the collar. K. did not really think about the couple anymore; it felt as if his freedom was being restricted, as if the arrest was being taken seriously, and he jumped down from the podium without consideration. Now he was face to face with the crowd. Had he not judged the people correctly? Had he attributed too much impact to his speech? Had people feigned a distance while he was speaking, and now that he was concluding, did they want to stop pretending? What faces surrounded him! Small, black eyes darted about; the cheeks hung down, as if from drunkenness, long beards were stiff and sparse, and if you reached in, it felt like you were touching claws, not beards. But beneath the beards – and this was K.'s discovery – patches of insignias of different sizes and colors were visible at the collars of their coats. Everyone seemed to have these insignias as far as he could see. Everyone belonged to each other, the supposed parties on the left and right; and when he suddenly turned around, he saw the same insignias on the collar of the examining judge, who sat quietly with his hands in his lap. "So," K. shouted, raising his arms, the sudden realization demanding space, "you are all officials, as I see it, you are the corrupt gang against whom I spoke, you pushed your way here as listeners and snoops, formed supposed parties, and one applauded to test me, you wanted to learn how to seduce the innocent! Well, you were not in vain here, I hope, either you talked about someone expecting a defense of the innocence from you, or – let me go or I'll hit you," K. shouted at an elderly man who had pushed close to him. "Or you really did learn something." With that, K. wished them all good luck in their profession. He quickly picked up his hat, which was lying on the edge of the table, and pushed his way through the general silence, or the silence of the greatest possible surprise. The examining judge, however, seemed to have been even quicker than K., for he was waiting for him at the door. "A moment," he said. K. stopped but did not look at the examining judge; instead, he looked at the door, whose handle he had already grasped. "I just wanted to remind you," said the examining judge, "that you deprived yourself today – it may not have occurred to you yet – of the advantage that a hearing represents for the person arrested in any case." K. laughed at the door. "You scum," he shouted, "I'll give you all interrogations," opened the door, and rushed down the stairs. Behind him, the noise of the revived assembly rose, which probably began to discuss the incidents in the manner of students.

He was still free. "May I?" he said, and hurried between the guards into his room. "He seems reasonable," he heard someone say behind him. In his room, he immediately opened the drawers of his desk; everything was in order, but in his excitement, he could not find the identification papers he was looking for right away. Finally, he found his cycling license and was about to go to the guards with it, but then he thought it was too insignificant and continued searching until he found his birth certificate. When he returned to the adjacent room, the door opposite opened, and Frau Grubach was about to enter. They could only see her for a moment, for as soon as she recognized K., she seemed embarrassed and apologized, then disappeared and shut the door very carefully. "Come in," K. had just been able to say. Now, however, he stood in the middle of the room with his papers, looked back at the door that did not open again, and was only roused from his thoughts by the guards calling him from the little table by the open window, where they were now eating his breakfast, as K. now realized. "Why didn’t she come in?" he asked. "She’s not allowed to," said the tall guard. "You’re under arrest." "How can I be under arrest in this manner?" "Now you’re starting again," said the guard, dipping a piece of bread into the honey pot. "Questions like that we don’t answer." "You will have to answer them," said K. "Here are my identification papers. Show me yours and, in particular, the arrest order." "Good heavens!" said the guard. "You cannot adapt to your situation and seem to be trying to irritate us, the ones who, presumably, are now closest to you of all your fellow humans!" "It’s so, believe me," said Franz, did not bring the coffee cup he was holding to his lips, but looked at K. with a long, probably meaningful but incomprehensible glance. K., without meaning to, was drawn into a gaze duel with Franz, then turned back to his papers and said: "Here are my identification papers." "What do we care about that?" shouted the tall guard now. "You’re behaving worse than a child. What do you want? Do you think you can end your ridiculous trial quickly by arguing with us, the guards, about identification papers and an arrest order? We’re low-level employees who don’t know much about identification papers and have nothing to do with your case except to stand guard for ten hours a day and get paid for it. That’s all we are, yet we are capable of understanding that the higher authorities, to whom we report, before they make a decision on an arrest, will thoroughly investigate the reasons for the arrest and the person of the arrested. There is no error in that. My knowledge of our department, to which I am only privy of the lower ranks, is that it does not seek guilt in the population but, as the law says, is drawn to the guilty and must send out the guards. That is the law. Where could there be an error?" "I don’t know this law," said K. "The worse for you," said the guard. "It probably exists only in your heads," said K., wanting somehow to penetrate the thoughts of the guards, to win them over, or to become a part of them. But the guard only replied dismissively: "You’ll feel the consequences." Franz intervened and said: "Look, Willem, he admits that he doesn’t know the law and at the same time claims to be innocent." "You’re right, but he can’t be reasoned with," said the other. K. did not reply any longer; he thought, should I, through the chatter of these lowest organs – they themselves admit to being that – be further confounded? They are, after all, talking about things they don’t understand. Their security rests only on their own foolishness. A few words with someone of my equals – they themselves admit to being that – would make everything incomparably clearer than the longest speeches with these. He walked several times up and down the empty space of the room, over there he saw the old woman who had pulled an even older man to the window and held him in her arms. K. had to put an end to this spectacle: "Take me to your superior," he said. "Only if he wishes; not earlier," said the guard called Willem. "And now I advise you," he added, "to go back to your room, behave calmly, and wait for what will be decided about you. Bo Qin recounted the dreams of the three to Tripitaka, who was also delighted. They early served a simple vegetarian meal and prepared one tael of silver as a gift. Tripitaka did not accept a single coin. Despite their earnest pleas, he did not take a single coin but said, "That you are willing to send me on my way with mercy is more than enough." Bo Qin and his wife and mother had no choice but to quickly prepare some coarse cakes for the journey and bid Bo Qin see the master off. Tripitaka was delighted to accept. Taibao, following his mother’s orders, called for a few servants, each armed with hunting gear, and together they headed for the main road, where they enjoyed the wild scenery of the mountains and the picturesque view from the hills. After half a day, they saw in the distance a great mountain that truly touched the heavens, towering and perilous. Before long, Tripitaka reached the edge. Taibao climbed this mountain as if it were flat land. Just as they reached the middle of the mountain, Bo Qin turned around, standing by the side of the road and said, "Master, you go forward, and I will bid you farewell." Hearing this, Tripitaka dismounted and said, "Please, no matter what, do me the favor of seeing me a little further!" As they were bidding farewell and praying to each other, they heard from below the mountain a voice like thunder calling out, "My master is here! My master is here!" This frightened Tripitaka and Bo Qin to a stupor. It was not clear who was shouting; the story continues in the next episode.

The poem says: Great Emperor Tang has issued an edict, 
Dispatching Tang Sanzang with a quest to seek Zen's truth.
With steadfast heart, he seeks the treasure's hidden lair,
With zeal, he strives, bound for Mount Jiufeng.
Crossing borders, far and wide, visiting many nations,
Climbing mountains and crossing rivers, traversing thousands of miles.
From now on, as you embark upon the journey west,
Hold to the teaching, seek enlightenment, and comprehend the vast void.
As for Tang Sanzang, since the ninth day before the full moon of the thirteenth month of the year of Zhen Guan,
He was escorted out of Chang'an by Emperor Tang and officials.
For a few days, the horses traveled without pause,
Reaching Famen Temple early.
The abbot, a senior monk, led over five hundred monks in welcoming him inside,
Whereupon they all greeted and offered tea.
After the tea, they retired for dinner, and as evening drew near, it was:
Shadows moving as the stars draw near, bright moon without a speck of dust.
Wild geese calling from afar in the heavens, pounding cloths echoing in the neighbor's courtyard.
Birds returning and perching on withered trees, monks chanting scriptures.
On a mat of woven reeds, seated through the night.

The poem says: Great Emperor Tang, issuing imperial edicts, appointed the Venerable Xuanzang to seek the Dharma. With steadfast heart, he searched for the dragon’s nest; with sincere effort, he ascended to Mount Grouse. Many lands lie beyond the border; countless layers of mountains and clouds lie ahead. From now on, he sets out westward, carrying the teachings and vows to fathom the great void. As for the Tripitaka, from the ninth month, third day before the full moon of the thirteenth year of Zhen Guan, he was escorted out of the pass of Chang'an by Emperor Tang and his ministers. For the next two days, he rode without pause, reaching the Dharma Gate Temple. The abbot of the temple, a senior elder, led more than five hundred monks to greet him. They lined up on both sides, ushering him inside, where they all greeted and offered tea. After tea, the meal followed, and before long, the night grew deep: shadows flitted as the stars grew near, and the moon’s light shone bright without a speck of dust. The cry of the geese echoed through the distant heavens, and the sound of pounding clothes spread to the neighboring dwellings. The birds flew to roost in the withered trees, while the monks spoke of their Buddhist teachings. Seated on a single pillow of reed mat, he sat until the night drew to an end. The monks discussed the true purpose of their Buddhist path and the reason for seeking the scriptures from the West. Some spoke of the water’s vastness and the mountains’ heights, while others mentioned the presence of tigers and leopards along the way. Some spoke of perilous ridges and steep cliffs that were hard to traverse, and others spoke of ferocious demons that were hard to subdue. The Tripitaka did not speak but instead pointed to his heart and nodded several times. The monks did not understand his meaning and respectfully asked, “Master, what does pointing to your heart and nodding signify?” The Tripitaka replied, “Where there is a heart, there are various demons; where there is no heart, there are no demons. I made vows at the Dharmachakra Temple to seek the scriptures from the West. I cannot help but fulfill my heart’s wish. This journey, I must go to the Western Heaven to see the Buddha and obtain the scriptures to ensure the transformation of the Buddhist law, wishing the holy ruler’s empire to be long-lasting.” The monks were all filled with admiration and praised him endlessly, calling him the loyal and virtuous great Tripitaka Master.

Moonlit night, no dust,  
Falcon calls echo through the distant sky,  
Sounding of pounding cloths at the neighbor’s west,  
Retreating birds rest in withered trees,  
Zen monks discourse on Buddhist doctrine,  
On the mat of reed mats,  
Sitting till the night wanes.  
The monks discuss the purposes of the Buddhist teachings under the light of lamps,  
The reasons for traveling to the West to seek the scriptures.  
Some say the journey is far, mountains are high,  
Others say the path is dangerous, with tigers and leopards,  
Some say the mountains are steep, cliffs are dangerous,  
Others say demons and evil spirits are hard to subdue.  
Silent, the Three Saints do not speak,  
Only pointing to their hearts and nodding several times.  
The monks cannot understand their meaning,  
Folding their hands, they ask, "Why do the master point to his heart and nod?"  
The master replied, "When the mind arises, so do all kinds of demons;  
When the mind ceases, all kinds of demons cease.  
I vowed at Fawang Temple to seek the scriptures,  
This is why I cannot avoid fulfilling this vow.  
This time, I must surely go to the Western Heavens, see Buddha and seek the scriptures,  
To bring the Buddhist teachings back and restore the holy realm."  
The monks heard these words, each praised and admired,  
Each praising endlessly, calling the master "loyal and brave Tripitaka,"  
Lauding him without end, inviting the master to rest.

The poem says: Great Emperor Tang issued imperial edicts to seal,  
And specially sent Zen Zang to investigate Chan's core.  
With steadfast heart, he seeks the dragon's lair,  
And with concerted effort, ascends Mount Juefeng.  
Traversing many kingdoms far from the borders,  
Through countless layers of clouds and mountains.  
From now on, embarking on this journey west,  
Holding the teachings, gaining enlightenment in the void.  
As for the Three-Treasure since the third day before the full moon of the ninth month of the贞观fourteenth year,  
Bestowed by Emperor Tang and officials, they were sent beyond the Chang'an gate.  
In a day or two, without respite, reaching Famen Temple.  
The abbot and over five hundred monks of the temple stood arrayed,  
Greeting them inside, offering tea and greetings.  
After the tea, they ate, and as the evening approached, it was just as:
Shadows sway as the stars draw near,  
Moonlight shines, dustless and clear.  
Distant yaks call in the Milky Way,  
The pounding of the loom rings out, near and far.  
Retiring birds rest in withered trees,  
Monks preach the Dharma's words.  
On the mat of reed mats, they sit until night falls.  
The monks discuss the true purpose of their Buddhist mission,  
The reasons for seeking the scriptures in the West.  
Some say the distance is vast, the mountains high,  
Others say the path is fraught with tigers and leopards.  
Some say the cliffs are perilous, too steep to climb,  
Others say the demons are vicious and hard to subdue.  
The Three-Treasure clamps his mouth shut and does not speak,  
Only pointing to his heart and nodding several times.  
The monks do not understand the meaning,  
Bowing to ask: "Why does Master point to his heart and nod?"  
The Three-Treasure answered: "A heart gives rise to various demons,  
A heart extinguished, various demons vanish.  
I made a great vow in the Hua Shan Si, setting my mind before the Buddha,  
Thus I cannot ignore this heart.  
This journey, without fail, will reach the Western Heavens,  
To see the Buddha and seek the scriptures,  
So that the Dharma may cycle and turn,  
May the Holy Emperor's rule endure forever."  
Upon hearing these words, every monk praised and admired,  
All calling him the "loyal and red-hearted Great Emanating Master,"  
Struggling to express their praise.  
Inviting the Master to rest on the bed.

The verse says: "Great Tang King issues imperial decree to封玄奘,  
his钦差to seek禅宗.  
With steadfast heart, he searches for the dragon's den,  
and with zeal, ascends Mount Vulture.  
Traversing distant lands, crossing numerous kingdoms,  
through countless mountains and rivers.  
From now on, you will set off to the west,  
holding the teachings to attain great emptiness."  

The Three-Saddharmapuṣpadanta Sutra continued: 
In the thirteenth month of the year of Zhen Guan, three days before the full moon, 
the Three-Saddharmapuṣpadanta Sutra was escorted by Emperor Taizong and his officials out of the city gate of Chang'an.  
For two or three days, they journeyed without stopping.  
Soon, they reached Famen Temple.  
The senior elder in charge of the temple, with over five hundred monks, 
lined up on both sides to greet them and led them into the temple.  
After a tea ceremony, it was already late.  
The scene was this:  
The stars seemed closer as shadows moved,  
the bright moon without a speck of dust.  
The distant sky echoed with the sound of geese,  
the neighboring cottage with the sound of pounding clothes.  
Birds roosted in withered trees,  
monks talked of the Dharma.  
On the cushion, they sat until the night was half over.  
The monks discussed the purpose of their mission to the Western Heavens to seek the scriptures,  
some saying the journey was too long and the mountains too high,  
others saying it was dangerous with many tigers and leopards along the way,  
some saying the paths were full of perilous cliffs and steep mountains,  
and others saying the demons and monsters were too fierce to subdue.  
Silent, the Three-Saddharmapuṣpadanta Sutra nodded his head several times,  
but said nothing.  
The monks could not understand the meaning,  
and all folded their palms,  
asking, "Master, what does your pointing at your heart and nodding mean?"  
The Three-Saddharmapuṣpadanta Sutra replied, "Thoughts give birth to various evils;  
thoughts are extinguished, various evils are extinguished.  
I made a great vow in the Hua Sheng Temple,  
and I cannot help but fulfill this vow.  
This journey, I must reach the Western Heavens,  
seek the scriptures from the Buddha,  
so that the Dharma may turn, 
may the Emperor's reign be eternal."  
The monks marveled at his words,  
praising him endlessly,  
and called him "loyal and righteous Great Dharma Master, "  
and had no words to praise him further,  
leading him to his bed to rest.

"I don’t know what you mean," said the merchant, "in business legal matters – I run a grain business – he has represented me ever since I took over the business, so that would be about twenty years. In my own lawsuit, which you probably allude to, he has represented me from the beginning. It’s been longer than five years, it’s been more than that." Then he added, and pulled out an old wallet, "I have everything written down here; if you want, I can tell you the exact dates. It’s hard to keep track of everything. My lawsuit has probably been going on for much longer, it began shortly after my wife’s death, and that was more than five and a half years ago." K. leaned closer. "Does the lawyer also handle everyday legal matters?" he asked. This connection of the courts and legal studies seemed to greatly reassure K. "Of course," said the merchant, and then whispered to K., "they even say he’s better at these everyday matters than at anything else." But then it seemed he regretted what he had said, he laid a hand on K.’s shoulder and said, "Please, don’t tell on me." K. patted him on the thigh and said, "No, I’m no traitor." "He is vengeful," said the merchant. "He will do nothing to such a loyal client," said K. "Oh, yes," said the merchant, "when he’s upset, he knows no boundaries, and anyway, I’m not really loyal to him." "Why not?" asked K. "Will you trust me with this?" asked the merchant doubtfully. "I think you may," said K. "Well," said the merchant, "I will tell you part of it, but you must also tell me a secret so that we can both stand by each other in front of the lawyer." "You are very cautious," said K., "but I will tell you a secret that will fully reassure you. So, what is your disloyalty to the lawyer?" "I," said the merchant hesitantly and in a tone as though he was admitting something shameful, "I have other lawyers apart from him." "That’s nothing so terrible," said K., a little disappointed. "Here, it is," said the merchant, who was still breathing heavily from his confession, but whose confidence was now somewhat restored thanks to K.’s remark. "It’s not allowed. And certainly not to take corner lawyers alongside a so-called lawyer. And exactly that is what I did, I have five corner lawyers apart from him." "Five!" cried K., struck by the number first, "five lawyers apart from this one?" The merchant nodded, "I’m even negotiating with a sixth one." "But why do you need so many lawyers?" asked K. "I need all of them," said the merchant. "Will you explain why?" asked K. "Of course," said the merchant. "Above all, I don’t want to lose my case, that’s clear. Therefore, I can’t neglect anything that might help me; even if the hope of such help seems slight in a particular case, I can’t discard it. I’ve therefore used everything I own for my case. For instance, I’ve withdrawn all the money from my business, earlier my business offices filled an entire floor, today I suffice with a small room in a back building where I work with an apprentice. This decline, of course, has not been caused solely by withdrawing the money, but more so by withdrawing my own labor power. When you want to do something for your case, you can barely manage other things." "You work yourself in court, too?" asked K. "I would like to know more about that." "I can only say little about that," said the merchant, "I might have done it at the beginning, but I quickly gave it up. It’s too exhausting and brings little success. Even sitting and negotiating there, for me, has turned out to be impossible. Just sitting and waiting there is already a great exertion. You know the heavy atmosphere in the offices." "Why do you know I was there?" asked K. "I was just in the waiting room when you went through." "What a coincidence!" exclaimed K., completely taken in and forgetting the earlier merchant’s ridicule. "You saw me, didn’t you? You were in the waiting room when I went through. Yes, I went through there once." "That’s no coincidence," said the merchant, "I’m there almost every day." "Good that you remind me," said the merchant, "you are a new person, a young one. Your lawsuit is half a year old, isn't it? Yes, I heard about it. Such a young lawsuit! But I've thought about these matters countless times, they are the most natural things in the world to me." "Are you happy that your lawsuit is so far advanced?" asked K., he didn't want to ask outright about the merchant's situation. But he didn't get a clear answer. "Yes," said the merchant, and lowered his head, "it's not a small achievement to have my lawsuit lasting five years." He was silent for a while. K. listened to see if Leni was already coming. On the one hand, he didn't want her to come because he had much to ask and didn't want to be caught in this intimate conversation with the merchant by Leni, but on the other hand, he was annoyed that she stayed so long at the lawyer's, much longer than was necessary to fetch the soup. "I remember exactly when that time was," the merchant began again, and K. was immediately all attention, "when my lawsuit was about as old as your lawsuit now. I had only this lawyer then, but I wasn't very satisfied with him." Here, I am learning everything, thought K. and nodded vigorously, as if he could thereby encourage the merchant to tell everything. "My lawsuit," the merchant continued, "wasn't advancing; although there were investigations, I attended each of them, gathered material, and submitted my business books to the court, which, as I later found out, wasn't necessary. I kept going to the lawyer, who also submitted various submissions—." "Various submissions?"

K. turned around, barely noticed by the merchant, who was about to stand up. "Stay seated," said K. and pulled a chair beside him. "Are you already a long-standing client of the lawyer?" K. asked. "Yes," said the merchant, "a very long-standing client." "For how many years has he represented you?" K. asked. "I don’t know what you mean," said the merchant, "in business law matters—my grain business—the lawyer has represented me since I took over the business, so about twenty years. In my own case, he has represented me since the beginning; it’s been more than five years. Actually, it’s been well over five years," he added, pulling out an old wallet, "I have everything written down here; if you want, I can tell you the exact dates. It’s hard to remember everything. My case probably started just after my wife’s death, and that was more than five and a half years ago." K. leaned closer. "Does the lawyer also take care of regular legal matters?" he asked. This connection of the courts and legal sciences seemed to K. exceedingly reassuring. "Certainly," said the merchant and whispered to K., "they even say he’s better at these matters than at the others." But then he seemed to regret what he had said, he laid a hand on K.’s shoulder and said, "Please, don’t betray me." K. patted his thigh for reassurance and said, "No, I’m no traitor." "He is vengeful," said the merchant. "Against such a loyal client, he will certainly do nothing," said K. "Oh, yes," said the merchant, "when he’s upset, he knows no distinction; anyway, I’m not really loyal to him." "Why not?" asked K. "Do you want to confide in me?" asked the merchant doubtfully. "I think you can," said K. "Well," said the merchant, "I will confide in you in part, but you must also keep a secret from me so we can both stand up to the lawyer." "You are very careful," said K., "but I will tell you a secret that will completely reassure you. What is your unfaithfulness to the lawyer about?" "I have," said the merchant hesitantly, as if confessing something dishonorable, "I have other lawyers as well." "That’s not so terrible," said K., a little disappointed. "Here, yes," said the merchant, who was still panting heavily from his confession but now felt more trust due to K.’s remark. "It is not allowed. And certainly not allowed to have corner lawyers in addition to a so-called lawyer. And that is exactly what I did, I have five corner lawyers in addition to him." "Five!" cried K., surprised by the number, "five lawyers in addition to him?" The merchant nodded: "I am still negotiating with a sixth." "But why do you need so many lawyers?" asked K. "I need all of them," said the merchant. "Won’t you explain that to me?" asked K. "Of course," said the merchant. "Above all, I don’t want to lose my case, that is, of course, self-evident. Therefore, I can’t overlook anything that might be of use to me. Even if the hope of benefit in a particular case is very slim, I can’t dismiss it. That’s why I’ve used everything I have for the case. For example, I have taken all the money out of my business. Earlier, the offices of my business filled a whole floor, now it’s enough to have a small room in the back of the building where I work with an apprentice. Of course, this decline wasn’t only due to the withdrawal of the money, but also to the withdrawal of my working power. If you want to do something for your case, you can hardly do anything else." "You work at the court yourself, too?" asked K. "That’s exactly what I would like to know about." "I can only tell you little about that," said the merchant, "at first, I did try, but soon gave it up. It’s too exhausting and brings little success. Even to work and negotiate there has proved entirely impossible for me. Just sitting and waiting there is already an enormous effort. You know the heavy air in the law offices yourself." "Why do you know that I was there?" asked K. "I was just in the waiting room when you passed through." "What a coincidence!" exclaimed K., taken aback and completely forgetting the earlier laughable behavior of the merchant. "You saw me, didn’t you? You were in the waiting room when I passed through. Yes, I went through there once." "It’s no great coincidence," said the merchant, "I’m there almost every day." "I will probably have to go there more often now," said K., "but I won’t be so honorably received as I was before. Everyone stood up. They probably thought I was a judge." "No," said the merchant, "we greeted the court officer. We knew you were the defendant. Such news spreads very quickly." "You knew about me then," said K., "and perhaps thought my behavior arrogant. Wasn’t that talked about?" "No," said the merchant, "on the contrary. But it’s nonsense." "What nonsense?" asked K. "Why are you asking about that?" said the merchant angrily. "You don’t seem to know the people there and might misinterpret them. You must consider that in this procedure, many things are discussed for which reason is not enough. One is simply too tired and distracted for much, and superstition takes over. I speak about others, but I’m no better. One such superstition is that many believe they can judge the outcome of the case from the shape of the accused’s face, especially the contours of the lips. These people claimed that from the contours of your lips, they could see that you would be certainly and soon found guilty. I repeat, it’s a laughable superstition and mostly contradicted by the facts, but living in that company, it’s hard to escape such opinions. Think of how strong this superstition can be. You did talk to someone there, didn’t you? He could hardly answer you. Of course, there are many reasons to be confused there, but one of them was also the sight of your lips. He later said he had seen the sign of his own conviction on your lips." "My lips?" asked K., took out a pocket mirror, and looked at them. "I can’t see anything special on my lips. And you?" "I can’t see anything either," said the merchant, "absolutely nothing." "How superstitious these people are!" exclaimed K. "Did I not say so?" asked the merchant. "Do they talk to each other much and exchange their opinions?" said K. "I have so far stayed completely apart," said the merchant, "it would not be possible, there are so many. There are also few common interests. Sometimes in a group, a belief in a common interest arises, but it is quickly seen as wrong. Nothing can be achieved against the court collectively. Each case is examined separately, after all, it is the most careful court. So, nothing can be achieved collectively, but sometimes an individual can achieve something secretly; only when it is achieved, the others learn about it. So, there is no commonality. We come together now and then in the waiting rooms, but little is discussed there. The superstitions have been around for a long time and multiply on their own." "I saw the gentlemen in the waiting room," said K., "their waiting seemed pointless to me." "Waiting is not pointless," said the merchant, "only independent intervention is. I have already said that I now have five lawyers in addition to this one. One might think – and I first did – that I could leave the matter entirely to them. But that would be completely wrong. I can entrust them with less than if I only had one. Don’t you understand that?" "No," said K., and laid his hand to calm the merchant, "I only ask you to speak a little slower. These are all very important things for me, and I can’t follow you." "Good that you remind me," said the merchant, "you are a new, young man. Your case is half a year old, right? Yes, I have heard about it. A young case! But I have thought about these things countless times. They are the most self-evident things in the world to me." "Yes, I have been dragging my case for five years," said the merchant and lowered his head, "it’s no small feat." Then he was silent for a while. K. listened, wondering if Leni was already there. On one hand, he didn’t want her to come, for he had still much to ask and didn’t want to be caught in this confidential conversation with the merchant by Leni, on the other hand, he was annoyed that she stayed so long with the lawyer despite his presence, much longer than needed for the soup. "I still remember the time," the merchant began again, and K. was fully attentive, "when my case was as old as your current case. I only had this lawyer then, but I wasn’t very satisfied with him." There were indeed investigations, I attended every one, I collected materials, I submitted all my business books to the court, which, as I later learned, wasn’t even necessary, I kept going back to the lawyer, he made different submissions—." "Different submissions?"

Chichikov fell into a bad mood and tossed his traveling saber, which had been used to instill due fear on appropriate occasions, onto the floor. He spent more than a quarter of an hour with the blacksmiths, trying to get the job done, because, as usual, they were blatant rogues and, realizing that the job was urgent, raised the price sixfold. No matter how much he fumed, calling them cheats, robbers, and highwaymen, hinting even at a terrible judgment, the blacksmiths were not swayed: they stood their ground and even delayed the job, instead of two hours, for five and a half. During this time, he had the pleasure of experiencing the delightful moments familiar to every traveler when everything is neatly packed in the suitcase, and the room is left with only ropes, papers, and miscellaneous items, when a person does not belong to the road or to the seat, when he sees from the window people walking by, discussing their fortunes, and raising their eyes in some silly curiosity, to then continue their journey, which only further irritates the unhappy, journeyless traveler. Everything around him, everything he sees: the shop opposite his window, the head of the old woman living in the house opposite, approaching with short curtains—everything fills him with aversion, but he does not leave the window. He stands there, sometimes lost in thought, sometimes focusing with a dulled attention on everything that moves and everything that does not, and irritates himself with some fly buzzing and beating against the glass under his fingers. But all good things must come to an end, and the desired moment arrived: everything was ready, the carriage was properly equipped, the wheel was wrapped with a new cover, the horses had been brought from the watering place, and the blacksmiths had gone, counting their whole rubles and wishing each other well. Finally, the carriage was packed, and the two fresh loaves of bread, just bought, were placed inside; Selifan already had something for himself in the pocket by the horse's harness, and our hero, with a wave of the servant's hat, dressed in the same overcoat as before, with tavern and foreign footmen gathered there to yawn, finally got into the carriage, and the carriage, which had long been idle in the city and, perhaps, bored the reader, finally rolled out of the inn gate. "Glory be to God," thought Chichikov and crossed himself. Selifan cracked the whip; first, Petroshka, who had been hanging around for a while on the running board, got in, and our hero, sitting more comfortably on the Georgian carpet, placed a leather pillow behind his back, and pressed the two warm loaves of bread, and the carriage began to dance and sway again thanks to the cobbled street, which, as was known, had a jumping force. He watched the houses, walls, fences, and streets with some indeterminate feeling, which, as if kicking, slowly receded behind him and which he might or might not see again in the course of his life. When the carriage had to stop at a corner, a endless funeral procession was passing along its entire length. Chichikov, sticking his head out, told Petroshka to find out who was being buried and learned that the prosector was being buried. Overcome with unpleasant sensations, he immediately hid in a corner, covered himself with a blanket, and drew the curtains. At that moment, when the carriage was stopped, Selifan and Petroshka, reverently taking off their hats, observed who, how, in what, and on what was traveling, counting the number of both walking and riding, and the master, having instructed them not to recognize or bow to any of the familiar footmen, also began to cautiously observe through the glass in the leather curtains: all the officials were walking behind the coffin, their hats off. He began to fear that his carriage might be recognized, but they were not bothered by that. They did not even engage in the usual everyday conversations that grieving friends often have when seeing off a deceased person. All their thoughts were concentrated on themselves: they were thinking about the new governor-general, how he would take office, and how he would treat them. Behind the walking officials came carriages from which ladies in mourning bonnets were peering out. From the movements of their lips and hands, it was clear that they were involved in a lively conversation; perhaps they were also talking about the arrival of the new governor-general and making guesses about the balls he would give and were busy with their eternal fringes and epaulettes. Finally, after the carriages came a few empty phaetons in a row, and after them, nothing remained, and our hero could go. He opened the leather curtains and sighed, saying with feeling, "So, the prosector! lived, lived, and then died! And they will print in the papers that he died, to the sorrow of his subordinates and the whole humanity, a respectable citizen, a rare father, a model husband, and will write all sorts of nonsense; they will probably add that he was accompanied by weeping widows and orphans; but if you look carefully, you'll see that the whole thing was just a thick mustache." Then he told Selifan to hurry up and, meanwhile, thought to himself, "It's good that we met the funeral; they say it's good luck if you meet a dead person."

Chichikov was in no mood and tossed his saber, which had traveled with him for intimidation purposes, onto the floor. For more than a quarter of an hour, he busied himself with the blacksmiths, managing to resolve the issue only because the blacksmiths, as usual, were incorrigible scoundrels and, realizing that the job needed to be done in a hurry, hiked the price sixfold. No matter how much he fumed, calling them frauds, robbers, and highwaymen, even hinting at a terrible trial, they remained unmoved: they held their ground with their prices and spent five and a half hours working instead of two. Throughout this time, he had the pleasure of experiencing the delightful moments known to every traveler, when everything is packed in a suitcase and in the room there are only ropes, pieces of paper, and miscellaneous odds and ends, when a man is neither on the road nor at his seat, sees passersby plodding along the street, chatting about their fortunes, and raising their eyes with some foolish curiosity to look at him before resuming their journey, which only aggravates the discontent of the unfortunate traveler who is neither in the road nor at home. Everything he sees now: the shop opposite his window, the old woman from the house across, with short curtains, approaching the window—everything displeases him, though he does not leave the window. He stands there, now losing himself in reverie, now focusing on the movement or stillness of whatever is before him, and chokes on his annoyance as a fly buzzes and flies into the glass under his finger. But all comes to an end, and the desired moment arrived: everything was ready, the carriage was set up, the wheels were wrapped in a new tire, the horses were led from the watering trough, and the scoundrel blacksmiths, after counting the received kopecks, wished him well and departed. Finally, the carriage was loaded, and two scorching hot cakes, just purchased, were put inside. Selyanin already had something for himself in his purse, which was on the kibitka, and the hero, finally, after a dramatic gesture by the stable boy, standing in the same frock coat as the other hired stable hands and lacqueys, gathered to doze, took his seat, and, putting a leather cushion behind him on a Caucasian rug, hugged the hot cakes. The carriage began to dance and rock as it moved along the rutted street, which, as is known, had a jolting effect. He watched the houses, walls, fences, and streets with a vague sense of feeling, as if they, too, were jumping and slowly receding, and it was a wonder if his fate would allow him to see them again during his life. At a turn into one of the streets, the carriage had to stop because a seemingly endless funeral procession filled its entire length. Chichikov stuck his head out, told Peter to ask who was being buried, and learned that the prosecutor was being laid to rest. Displeased, he immediately huddled in a corner, covered himself with his cloak, and drew the curtains. While the carriage was stopped, Selyanin and Peter took off their hats and, devoutly, observed how many people and how many were walking, reckoning the number of those on foot and in carriages, while the master, ordering his men not to recognize or greet any of his known lacqueys, likewise peered cautiously through the glass in the leather curtains, behind which the officials walked with their hats off. He began to fear that his carriage would be recognized, but they did not care. They did not even engage in the usual lively conversations of those bidding farewell to the dead. All their thoughts were concentrated on themselves at that moment: they wondered how the new general-governor would behave, what he would do, and how he would treat them. After the officials walked by, ladies in mourning hats appeared in the windows of carriages, their movements and gestures showing that they were having a lively conversation. Perhaps they were talking about the arrival of the new general-governor, making guesses about the balls he would give and worried about their eternal fringes and epaulettes. Finally, a few empty kibitkas followed in a line, and then nothing remained, and the hero could continue his journey. He opened the leather curtains, sighed, and said with feeling, “There goes the prosecutor! Lived, lived, and then died! And then they’ll print in the papers that he died, to the sorrow of his subordinates and the whole human race, a distinguished citizen, a rare father, a model husband, and will write all sorts of nonsense; and, perhaps, they’ll add that he was accompanied by the tears of widows and orphans; but if you look into it carefully, the truth is that he had just thick eyebrows.” Then he ordered Selyanin to go faster and, meanwhile, thought to himself, “Well, it’s good that the funeral procession met us; they say it’s good luck to meet a corpse.”

And the coach, in which bachelors travel, which had long been idle in town and, perhaps, annoyed the reader, finally left the inn’s gates. “Glory be to Thee, Lord,” Chichikov thought and made the sign of the cross. The carriage began to bounce and sway with the road, which, as everyone knows, has a bouncing power. Embarrassed, he immediately ducked into a corner, covered himself with a blanket, and drew the curtains. At that moment, when the carriage was thus stopped, Selifan and Petrushka, having removed their hats with solemnity, observed who, how, what, and how they were traveling, counting how many there were in total, walking and in carriages. Tripitaka saw them and joyfully accepted them, instructing the Monkey to carry them and place them on the horse to see if they were a good fit. The Monkey climbed forward and examined each item, finding them indeed to be excellent. There was a poem to attest to this:
Jade-hued saddle, silver stars gleam,
Golden threads flash on the jeweled seat.
Layered with velvet, cushioned and soft,
Three strands of purple silk secure.
Flower patterns on the reins, splendid and fine,
Fan-shaped trappings, golden, inlaid with beasts.
Bit crafted from refined iron, polished and bright,
Two hanging tassels, wet with water’s light.

The Monkey was secretly delighted, placing the saddle and bridle on the horse, as if made specifically for it. Tripitaka bowed in gratitude to the old man, who hurriedly pulled him up and said, "Be alarmed! Be alarmed! There is no need for such thanks." The old man did not stay, but instead bid them ride. When the monk came out, he mounted the horse and patted its flanks. The Monkey took up the baggage. The old man, from his sleeve, produced a whip made of slender strips of aromatic vine and tiger sinews, and offered it to the monk, saying, "Saint, I also have a rein. Take this with the rest." Tripitaka, on his horse, took it and said, "Many thanks for your generosity! Many thanks!" As he was about to bow, the old man was already gone, and when he looked back, the land where the shrine stood was a barren place. Hearing someone from the sky say, "Saint, forgive my discourtesy. I am the mountain spirit of Lague Mountain, sent by the Bodhisattva to provide you with this saddle and bridle. Proceed on your journey with determination, do not slacken," Tripitaka dismounted, fell to his knees in the air, and said, "Disciple, ignorant and unworthy, did not recognize the divine form. Pardon the offense, and pray convey the Bodhisattva's blessings." Seeing this, the Monkey laughed joyfully, while the Monkey King was overjoyed, and said to Tripitaka, "Master, you need not continue to kneel.
