To the side, the living monkey and lively monkey laughed heartily as they watched; impatiently happy, they tugged at their master's sleeve. "Master, rise now, he is far away and can no longer hear your prayers or see your kowtows," said the living monkey. "Only continue with your journey, and show your gratitude as you go."

"Master, the saddle and bridle are presented." Seeing this, Tripitaka was delighted and accepted them, instructing the disciple to take them and put them on the horse to see if they fit. The disciple walked up and examined each piece, finding them indeed to be excellent. A poem attests to this, saying: 

The gilded saddle glimmers with silver stars,  
The padded bench shines with golden threads.  
Several layers of plush cloths cushion the seat,  
Three strands of purple silk tie the reins.  
The bridle is adorned with brocade, shining brightly,  
The cloud fan, gilded and decorated with dancing beasts.  
The bit is crafted from tempered iron,  
Two tassels, dipped in water, hang from the ends.

The disciple's heart was secretly pleased, and he placed the saddle and bridle on the horse, as if they had been custom-made. Tripitaka bowed in gratitude to the old man, who hastily helped him up and said, "Be wary! Be wary! No need for such thanks." The old man did not linger further, but invited Tripitaka to mount the horse. When the elder came out and mounted his horse, the disciple took the luggage. The old man then took another length of rope from his sleeve, a stick made of incense-cane, with a thong of tiger sinew tied to the end, and held it out, saying, "Saint, I have one more bit of rope. I shall send it with you."

Tripitaka received it on the horse and said, "Thank you for your generosity! Thank you for your generosity!" As he saluted, the old man was nowhere to be seen. And when he looked back, there was nothing left but an open space where the shrine stood. Suddenly, he heard someone speaking from the sky, "Saint, I am sorry for the rudeness. I am the Mountain God of L落伽山, sent by the Bodhisattva to provide the saddle and bridle for you. Proceed westward with effort, and do not slacken." Tripitaka dismounted, fell to his knees, and worshipped the heavens, saying, "My eyes are those of an ordinary man, unable to recognize your holy face. I ask for your forgiveness. Please convey my gratitude to the Bodhisattva, for your benevolence is profound." He continued to kneel, prostrating himself without cease, but to the amusement of the living孙大圣and the delight of the merry美猴王, who came forward and pulled at Tripitaka, saying, "Master, get up. He has gone far away. He cannot hear your prayers or see your prostrations. What more is there to do?" The elder said,

Disciple, the saddles and bridles are here." Seeing this, Tripitaka was delighted and accepted them, instructing the monk to carry them and put them on the horse to see if they fit. The monk walked forward and examined each one carefully, indeed finding them to be fine. A poem attests to this: 

The carved saddle glitters with silver stars,  
The jeweled bench shines with golden threads.  
Several layers of velvet cloths are cushioned inside,  
Three strands of purple silk make the reins.  
The bridle's leather headstall is inlaid with floral patterns,  
The cloud fan is adorned with golden beasts.  
The bit is forged from tempered iron,  
Two tassels hang down, glistening with moisture.  
The monk secretly rejoiced, putting the saddles and bridles on the horse, feeling as if they were made just for it. Tripitaka thanked the old man, who hurriedly pulled him up and said, "Frightened! Frightened! No need for thanks." The old man did not stay, and Tripitaka mounted the horse. The elder came out, grabbed the saddle, and the monk carried the luggage. The old man then took out a whip from his sleeve, a fine piece of intertwined stingy vines and tiger sinew, and offered it to the monk saying, "Sage, I have a handle to match, let me give it to you as well." Tripitaka got off the horse, mounted, and took the whip, thanking the old man profusely. The monk kept bowing and knocking his head to the ground, not knowing how many times, while Monkey and his companion laughed and were overjoyed, pulling Tripitaka up and saying, "Master, get up, he's already far away, he can't hear your prayers or see your headbanging."

"Ashrama, the saddle and bridle are now in your hands." Seeing this, Tripitaka was delighted and gratefully accepted them, instructing the pilgrim to mount the horse and see if they fitted. The pilgrim ascended and, taking each item in turn to inspect, found them to be of excellent quality. The poem speaks of this:

Carved saddles gleam with silver stars,
Jeweled benches flash with golden threads.
Multiple layers of velvet linings,
Threefold purple silk reins.
Embellished harnesses, flowered in groups,
Fans of gold, beastly dancers take flight.
Bit and mouthpiece forged from tempered iron,
Pendant water-dripping tassels below.

Overjoyed, the pilgrim placed the saddle and bridle on the horse, fitting them perfectly as if custom-made. Tripitaka thanked the old man, who hurried to his aid, saying, "Fancy! Fancy! There is no need for such gratitude." The old man did not linger, but rather bade them farewell, urging them to mount the horse. The elder exited, mounted the horse, while the pilgrim carried the belongings. The old man then emerged from his sleeve a whip made of bark-dyed leather with tiger sinew lash, presented to the pilgrim. "Holy pilgrim," he said, "I have one more whip for you. May I offer it with this one?" Tripitaka dismounted and received the whip, bowing in gratitude. "I thank you! I thank you!" The old man was already out of sight, and when Tripitaka looked back at the temple, there was nothing but open land. From above, a voice called out, "Holy pilgrim, my apologies for the inconvenience. I am the mountain deity of L落伽山, dispatched by the Bodhisattva to bring saddle and bridle. I wish you a safe journey to the West. Do not slacken." Astonished, Tripitaka dismounted and knelt to the sky. "Disciple has unsighted eyes, and did not recognize the honor of your presence. Pray accept my apologies. I beg you to convey my deepest gratitude to the Bodhisattva." He continued to bow repeatedly, but the Monkey King beside him was laughing, while the pilgrim's heart was already filled with joy, pulling on Tripitaka's sleeve. "Master, let's get up. He is long gone. He won't hear you or see your bowing." The elder, still kneeling, said, "I was just speaking to the heavens."

The rumble of excitement about the affair reached the church with incredible swiftness. As Keller approached the prince, a multitude of unfamiliar people began to interrogate him. There was loud talk, headshaking, even laughter; nobody left the church; all were awaiting the prince's reaction to the news. He paled, but took the news quietly, murmuring almost inaudibly, "I was afraid; but I did not think it would be... " Then, after a brief pause, he added, "Well, in her condition... it is quite natural." Such a reaction, Keller later called it "unparalleled philosophy." The prince left the church apparently calm and vigorous; indeed, many noticed this and would later recount it. It seemed to him that he very much wanted to get home and be alone as soon as possible; but this was not to be. Some of the invited guests, including Putilin and Grigory Ardalionovich, and the doctor as well, who had no intention of leaving, entered the room after him. The whole house was besieged by idle crowds. From the terrace, the prince heard that Keller and Lebedev were involved in a fierce argument with some unknown officials, who were determined to enter the terrace at all costs. The prince approached the disputants, inquired what the matter was, and politely dismissed Lebedev and Keller, then politely addressed a rather rotund, silver-haired gentleman standing on the steps, at the head of several others who wished to enter, and invited him to do the prince the honor of accepting his invitation. The gentleman blushed but, however, went in; after him, another, then a third. Out of the entire crowd, some seven or eight visitors managed to enter, trying to do so as unreservedly as possible; but more eager ones did not turn up, and soon, in the crowd, they began to criticize the interlopers. The guests were seated, a conversation began, tea was served—everything was extraordinarily proper, modest, somewhat surprising to the guests. There were, of course, several attempts to liven up the conversation and bring it to a “proper” topic; some impertinent questions were asked, and some rude remarks were made. The prince answered everyone simply and hospitably, but at the same time with such dignity and trust in the honorability of his guests that the impertinent questions ceased of their own accord. Gradually, the conversation began to take on almost a serious tone. A certain gentleman, attached to the conversation, suddenly swore, in great indignation, that he would never sell his estate, no matter what happened; that, on the contrary, he would wait and see and that “enterprises are better than money”; "see, Your Excellency, here is my economic system, you can learn about it." Since he was speaking to the prince, the prince warmly praised him, despite Lebedev's whispered remarks that this gentleman had neither a squire nor a yard, and had never owned an estate. Almost an hour passed, the tea was drunk, and finally, after the tea, the guests felt ashamed of sitting on any longer. The doctor and the silver-haired gentleman warmly said goodbye to the prince; everyone said goodbye with warmth and enthusiasm. Respective sentiments and opinions were expressed, such as, "There is nothing to mourn about, and it may be for the best," and so on. Indeed, there were attempts to order champagne, but the older guests stopped the younger ones. When everyone had departed, Keller leaned over to Lebedev and said, "We would have made a commotion, fought, been a fool, and called the police; but he made some new friends, and such good ones; I know them!" Lebedev, who was rather ready for it, sighed and said, "He kept the wise and the prudent in the dark and enlightened the infants; I've been saying this about him before, but now I add that the very infant was saved from the abyss and is safe with all the saints!"

His appearance at the ball produced an extraordinary effect. Everything and everyone turned to meet him. Some came with their cards in hand, others interrupted the most interesting parts of their conversations to exclaim, "The district court replies as follows…", but what the district court replies was quickly set aside as they hastened to greet the hero of the story. "Pavel Ivanovich! Oh my God, Pavel Ivanovich! Dear Pavel Ivanovich! Honored Pavel Ivanovich! My soul, Pavel Ivanovich! There you are, Pavel Ivanovich! There he is, our Pavel Ivanovich! Let me embrace you, Pavel Ivanovich! Come here, Pavel Ivanovich, I'll kiss you more closely, my dear Pavel Ivanovich!" Chichikov suddenly found himself in several embraces at once. Before he could quite extricate himself from the embrace of the chairman, he was already in the arms of the police major. The police major handed him over to the medical inspector, who then passed him on to the tax farmer, who passed him on to the architect… The governor, who at the time was standing by the ladies, holding a confectionery ticket in one hand and a dalmatian in the other, dropped both the ticket and the dalmatian when he saw him; only his little dog barked; in any case, he spread extraordinary joy and merriment. There was no face that didn't reflect pleasure or, at the very least, an echo of general pleasure. Such is the way it happens with officials during an inspection by the overseeing superior: after the first fear has passed, they see that much pleases him and that he has even deigned to jest, i.e., to say something with a pleasant smile. Those surrounding him began to laugh in response, more than doubling the merriment. Those who had just heard his words poorly laughed as well. Finally, the policeman standing at the door near the exit, who had never laughed in his entire life and had just shaken his fist at the crowd, also expressed some kind of smile on his face, though it more resembled the action of someone clearing their throat after a strong cigar. The hero replied to everyone and felt an extraordinary nimbleness: he bowed left and right, a bit to the side, but with perfect ease, charming everyone. The ladies immediately surrounded him with a blazing garland and with them came clouds of all sorts of fragrances: one exhaled roses, another smelled of spring and violets, and a third was entirely filled with hyacinth. Chichikov only raised his nose and sniffed. Their dresses were a complete mishmash: muslins, silks, and veils were of such pale, fashionable colors that they could not be named (the taste was so subtle). Ribbons and floral garlands flew around their dresses in the most picturesque disorder, although an orderly mind had labored over this disorder. Hatted head coverings clung only to their ears, as though saying, "Hey, I’ll fly away, but it’s a pity I won’t be able to take a beauty along!" Their waists were tightly cinched, and they had the most elegant forms for the eye to behold (it should be noted that all the ladies of city N. were somewhat plump, but were laced up so artfully and had such a pleasant manner that one couldn’t notice the thickness). Everything was prepared and foreseen with extraordinary care; their necks and shoulders were exposed precisely as much as was needed, and no more; each revealed her territory until she felt, by her own conviction, that it was capable of destroying a man; everything else was hidden with extraordinary taste: either a delicate ribboned cravat, or a scarf lighter than a confection known as a kiss, or fine gossamer in the form of little battlements from fine batiste, known as modesty. These modesties hid what could no longer harm a man in front and back, but made one suspect that it was precisely there that the harm lay. Long gloves were not pulled up to the sleeves, but were thoughtfully left bare up to the elbows, which many wore with impressive plumpness; on others, even the sable gloves burst, compelled to descend further, in short, it seemed as though everything were written: no, it’s not a province, it’s the capital, it’s Paris itself! Only now and then would a hitherto unseen hat or even a peacock feather, in defiance of all fashions, pop out, according to one’s own taste. But without this, it couldn’t do, such was the nature of the provincial city: it would surely end somewhere. Chichikov, standing before them, thought, "Which one, however, is the author of the letter?" and was about to stick out his nose; but a whole row of elbows, cuffs, sleeves, ends of ribbons, fragrant petticoats, and dresses tugged at his nose. The gallop was in full swing: the postmistress, the captain-coroner, the lady with the blue feather, the lady with the white feather, the Georgian prince Chipkaykhilidze, a Petersburg official, a Moscow official, the Frenchman Couque, Perhunovskiy, Berebendovskiy—everyone was on their feet and galloped.

Allow me to embrace you, Pavel Ivanovich! Come here, let me kiss you, my beloved Pavel Ivanovich!" Chernyya felt himself enveloped in several embraces at once. He barely managed to extricate himself from the embrace of the president, when he found himself in the arms of the police commissioner; the police commissioner handed him over to the medical inspector, who passed him on to the contractor, who handed him to the architect… The governor, who was standing by the ladies with a confectionery ticket in one hand and a bologna sausage in the other, upon seeing him, dropped both the ticket and the sausage, only for his little dog to start barking; in short, he spread an extraordinary joy and merriment. There was not a single face that did not reflect pleasure or, at the very least, the general air of pleasure. Such is the way with officials' faces when a visiting superior officer inspects their charge: after the initial fear subsides, they see that much pleases him and that he even indulges in a joke or two, as it were, uttering a few words with a pleasant smile. His attendants chuckled twice in response; those who, to be sure, only half-heard what he said, chuckled heartily; and the policeman standing near the exit, who had never laughed in his life and had just shaken a fist at the crowd, suddenly expressed a smile on his face, albeit one that looked more like someone who was about to sneeze after a puff of tobacco. The hero responded to everyone and felt an extraordinary nimbleness: he greeted left and right, leaning a little to one side, but with such ease that he captivated everyone. The ladies surrounded him in a sparkling garland and left behind whole clouds of various scents: one smelled of roses, another of spring and violets, and another was soaked through with bitter almonds; Chernyya only raised his nose to sniff. Their taste in clothing was a mystery: silks, velvets, and tulle in the palest of fashionable hues, so pale that it was almost impossible to give them a name (to such a degree had their taste for the subtle reached). Ribboned bow ties and floral bouquets fluttered about in the most picturesque disorder, although a considerable head had been at work to organize this disorder. A light hat was perched precariously on his ears, as if it said: "Well, I'll fly away, only pity I can't take a beauty with me!" Their waists were tightly corseted and had the most graceful and pleasing forms to the eye (it must be noted that all the ladies in the city of N. were somewhat full, but were so artfully laced and had such pleasant manners that the extra weight could not be noticed). Everything was prepared with a degree of extraordinary care; their necks and shoulders were bare just enough and no further; each exposed her delights until she felt they could ruin a man; the rest was concealed with extraordinary taste: a light ribboned bow tie, or a scarf lighter than a confection known as "a kiss," or little lattice-like walls of fine batiste known as "modesties." These "modesties" hid what could no longer do any harm, but made one suspect that it was there that the ruin lay. Long gloves were not pulled up to the sleeves, but left a little of the exciting parts of their arms exposed above the elbows, which, in some cases, breathed with impressive fullness; in others, even the sable gloves had split, compelled to move further up—indeed, it seemed as though everything were written: no, this is not a province, this is the capital, this is Paris itself! Here in my explanation, I note all these numbers and figures. Of course, it will make no difference to me, but now (and, perhaps, only at this moment) I wish that those who will judge my action could clearly see from which chain of logical deductions my "final conviction" stemmed. I wrote above that the final resolve, which was lacking for me to fulfill my "final conviction," seemed to arise in me not from a logical deduction, but from some strange impulse, from one strange circumstance, which, perhaps, had nothing to do with the course of events. Ten days ago, Rogozhin came to me on some matter of his, which it would be superfluous to expand upon here. I had never seen Rogozhin before, but I had heard a great deal about him. I gave him all the necessary information, and he soon left, for he had only come for information, and so the matter would have ended between us. But he intrigued me too much, and the whole day I was under the influence of strange thoughts, so that I resolved to go to him the next day to pay him a visit. Rogozhin was obviously not pleased to see me and even "delicately" hinted that there was nothing for us to continue our acquaintance; but still, I spent a very interesting hour, as he, in all likelihood, did as well. There was such a contrast between us that it could not fail to be noticeable to us both, especially to me: I was a man who had already counted the days of my life, while he was living the fullest, immediate life, in the present moment, without a care for "final" deductions, figures, or anything not pertaining to what... what... well, let it be whatever he was obsessed with; let Mr. Rogozhin forgive me this expression, even though I am perhaps a bad writer unable to express my thoughts. Despite all his unfriendliness, I seemed to think that he was a man of intelligence and could understand much, even though not much from the outside interested him. I did not hint at my "final conviction," but for some reason I felt that he, listening to me, had guessed it. He did not speak, he was frightfully silent. I hinted at this to him as I was leaving, that despite the whole difference and all the opposites between us, les extrémités se touchent (I explained this to him in Russian), so that he, perhaps, was not as far from my "final conviction" as he seemed. To this, he responded with a very gloomy and sour expression, stood up, fetched my cap for me as if I were leaving, and simply took me out of his dark house under the pretense of seeing me off out of courtesy. His house struck me; it seemed like a cemetery, and he, apparently, liked that, which, of course, was understandable: such a full, immediate life, which he lived, was too full in itself to need an atmosphere.

But our hero was already in his middle years and of a character that was cautious and somewhat cold. He too fell into thought and pondered, but his thoughts were more positive, less unthinking, and even somewhat very solid. "What a fine woman!" he said, opening his snuffbox and taking a whiff of the tobacco. "But what’s most important about her is that she’s good? It’s good that she appears to have just come out of some pension or institute, that there’s still nothing womanly about her, that is, precisely the worst of what they have. She’s still a child, everything about her is simple. She will say what she pleases, she will laugh wherever she feels like laughing. You could do anything with her; she could be a wonder, or she could turn out to be dross, and that’s exactly what will happen! Just wait and see how the mama’s and aunts will take to her. They will fill her up with all sorts of womanly nonsense in a single year that her father won’t recognize her. Where will the air-headedness and priggishness come from? She will start to behave according to conventional advice, to rack her brains and think up whom she should talk to, how, and for how long, always dreading to say more than necessary. She will eventually get entangled and will finally have to lie all her life, and end up as something altogether unpredictable!" He fell silent for a moment and then added, "It would be interesting to know her background. Is her father a wealthy landowner with good character, or just a thinking man with a capital earned through his career? If, for example, this girl were to be given two hundred thousand as a dowry, she could very well turn out to be a very desirable piece. This could constitute, as it were, the happiness of a decent person." Two hundred thousand dollars began to appear so enticing in his mind that he started to regret that during the fuss over carriages he hadn’t bothered to ask the coachman or coach driver about the passengers. However, the village of Sobakevich that soon appeared soon drove his thoughts back to their constant subject.

It turned out that the Four Guarding Generals and the seventy-two cave kings were practicing martial arts. Sun Wukong called out from high, "Lads! I'm here!" The monsters put down their weapons and knelt, saying, "Master Wukong, you have such a kind heart! You've left us for a long time without coming to visit!" Sun Wukong said, "Not long at all! Not long at all!" He continued talking and walking until he reached the deepest part of the cave. The Four Guarding Generals cleaned and tidied the place, then knelt to pay their respects. They all said, "Master Wukong, you were in Heaven for over a hundred years. What important posts did you hold?" Sun Wukong laughed, "I can only remember half a year. How can you say I've been there for a hundred years?" The generals said, "One day in Heaven equals one year down here." Sun Wukong said, "Fortunately, the Jade Emperor favors me this time and has appointed me as 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' A Que Tian Temple was built for me, and I was given the positions of Chief of Tranquil Resolutions and Chief of Peaceful Aspiration, with celestial officials and guards. Later, when I had nothing to do, I was tasked with guarding the Penglai Peach Garden. Recently, the Queen Mother of the West held a Peach Banquet and did not invite me. I did not wait for an invitation but went to the Jade Pool by myself, stealing the divine fruits and wines. I stumbled out of the Jade Pool and accidentally entered Laozi's palace, where I stole the five golden elixirs from the alchemical jars. I am afraid that the Jade Emperor will be angry, which is why I came out of the Heavenly Gate just now."

The Four Guards cleaned the quarters, finished their prostrations, and saluted. They all said, "Master has been in the heavens for these hundred years, what kind of post did you hold?" The Monkey King laughed, "I remember it was only a few months ago; how can you say a hundred years?" The Guards replied, "In the heavens, a day is equivalent to a year below." The Monkey King said, "It is fortunate that the Jade Emperor favors me and indeed conferred the title 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' A temple of the same name was erected for me, and two offices, Quietness and Tranquility, were established, with celestial officials to protect and serve. Later, when I had nothing to do, he assigned me to guard the Penglai Peach Grove. Recently, due to the Queen Mother of the West's 'Peach Banquet,' she did not invite me. I did not wait for her invitation and first attended the Jade Hall. I ate all the immortals' delicacies and immortal wine that she had. After leaving the Jade Hall, I stumbled and strayed into Laojun's palace, where I also ate the five golden elixirs from his five alchemical crucibles. I fear the Jade Emperor might hold me responsible, so I have just left the heavens."

Yesterday morning, the prince came to see me; among other things, he persuaded me to move to his dacha. I knew all along that he would insist on this and was sure that he would flatly tell me that it would be “easier to die among people and trees,” as he puts it. But instead of saying die, he said “it will be easier to live,” which is pretty much the same thing for me in my current state. I asked him what he meant by his constant “trees” and why he was pushing me to go there, and to my surprise, he told me that I myself had supposedly mentioned on that evening that I had come to Pavlovsk for the last time to look at the trees. When I pointed out to him that it was all the same whether I died under the trees or just looked at my bricks through a window, and that there was no need to fuss for two weeks, he immediately agreed. However, in his opinion, the greenery and fresh air would surely produce some physical change in me, and my agitation and dreams would change and perhaps ease up. I jokingly remarked to him that he was speaking like a materialist. He answered me with his smile that he had always been a materialist. Since he never lies, these words must mean something. His smile is nice; I now examined him more closely. I do not know whether I like or dislike him now; I have no time to deal with this. My five-month hatred towards him, which was evident at the end of the month, has almost faded away. Who knows, maybe I came to Pavlovsk mainly to see him. But... why did I leave my room then? A man condemned to die should not leave his room; and if I had not reached a final decision now but decided to wait until the last hour, I would surely not have left my room for anything and would not have accepted his offer to move to Pavlovsk “to die.”

Eternity already seemed to have spread its dark wing over him. Sometimes, at night, we would spend entire hours in silence together—Rustum, the mameluke, would snore in the next room; this man slept incredibly soundly. "But he is faithful to me and to the dynasty," Napoleon used to say about him. One day I felt a terrible pain, and suddenly he noticed the tears in my eyes; he looked at me with tenderness: "You pity me!" he cried, "You, the child, and perhaps another child, my son, the King of Rome; everyone else hates me, and the brothers would sell me out in my distress!" I wept and threw myself into his arms; he could not withstand it either; we embraced, and our tears mingled. "Write, write a letter to Empress Joséphine!" I sobbed to him. Napoleon shuddered, thought for a moment, and said to me, "You have reminded me of the third heart that loves me; thank you, my friend!" Then he sat down and wrote that letter to Joséphine, which was sent off with Constant the next day.

A thousand officials in jade pendants circled in front and back, five guards' banners and flags lined the sides. Holding golden gourds, bearing axes in pairs, facing each other. Red gauze candles, imperial incense burners, smoke rising in thick, majestic clouds. Dragons flying, phoenixes dancing. A wise and virtuous emperor, loyal and righteous ministers. May good fortune continue for a thousand years, surpassing the rule of Yu and Shun. May peace and prosperity last for ten thousand generations, outshining the reigns of Yao and Shun. Then I see the curled umbrellas, embroidered robes, shining with reflected light. Jade rings, colored phoenix fans, auspicious clouds swirling. Pearl crowns, jade belts, purple sashes, golden seals. A thousand guards escort, two lines of attendants. This emperor bathes in sincere respect for the Buddha, embracing good deeds and taking pleasure in incense. The Tang King arrives early at the temple, ordering the music and instruments to stop, dismounting from his carriage, leading all officials in offering incense and prayers. Three rounds complete, lifting his head to behold, truly a magnificent gathering, as seen: banners and flags fluttering, precious canopies gleaming. Banners and flags wave, condensing to bright rays of colored clouds; precious canopies shine, reflecting radiant red lightning. Golden Sakyamuni's countenance is radiant, arhats' faces are powerful. Bottles holding divine flowers, incense burners burning sandalwood. Bottles holding divine flowers, flowering trees shining in the jeweled temple; incense burners burning sandalwood, fragrant clouds filling the clear sky. Fresh fruits are piled on crimson dishes, unusual sugar pastries on colorful cases. High monks lined up reciting true scriptures, praying for the liberation of wandering souls. Both the crown prince and his military attendants offer incense, bowing before the Buddha and prostrating before the arhats. Then I see Great Evident Maitreya Dharma Master Chen Xuanzang leading the monks in bowing to the Tang King. After the ceremony, they take their places, the Dharma Master presenting a memorial for the liberation of spirits to the Tang King to read. It reads: Vast and mysterious is the virtue, silent and extinguished is the dharma. Pure and clear, flowing through the three realms. Innumerable transformations, mastering yin and yang. True and constant in essence and use, endless and boundless. Observing those wandering souls, it is fitting to pity them. Following the emperor's command: collect many monks, practice dhyana and expound the law. Open the path of easy access, spread the boat of boundless compassion, widely liberate the suffering in the ocean of suffering, release those suffering from six paths. Guide them to the true path, explore the primordial origins; moving without effort, integrated with the pure and simple. Relying on this good cause, invite blessings to the clear capital and crimson palaces; taking advantage of my glorious gathering, escape from hell and the ordinary cage. Ascend to extreme happiness and enjoy freedom, travel to the west following your own will. Poem: One incense burner for eternal longevity, several scrolls of scriptures for rebirth. Boundless wonderful doctrines proclaimed, boundless heavenly grace bestowed. All hatreds eliminated, wandering souls freed from prison. May this bless our nation and peace for ten thousand years. The Tang King reads with joy, turning to the monks and saying: "With loyal hearts, do not neglect the Buddha's teachings. After completing the task, each will receive their due reward, I will give generous rewards, not leaving you in vain." The thousand two hundred monks bow together in thanks.

Seeing the curving canopies, dragons embroidered on robes, radiating light; jade-linked rings, peacock fans, spreading auspicious clouds. Pearl crowns and jade belts, purple sashes and golden seals. A thousand troops of soldiers protecting the imperial chariot, two rows of generals supporting the imperial canopy. This emperor, deeply pious and reverent, worships Buddha, rejoicing in the fruits of goodness, holding incense. The Tang emperor, early at the temple gate, halted the music and carriage, leading all the officials in worship. Bowing to Buddha, holding incense. After three circuits, he raised his head to gaze, indeed a magnificent Dharma assembly. To behold: banners and flags fluttering, precious canopies shining. Banners and flags fluttering, casting down multicolored rainbows in the sky; precious canopies shining, reflecting red lightning beneath the sun. The golden image of the World Honored One is majestic, the Arhats powerful and fierce. Vessels of divine flowers, incense burning in sacred vats. Vessels of divine flowers, beautiful trees reflecting in the precious shrine; incense burning in sacred vats, fragrant clouds permeating the clear sky. Fresh fruits laid out on crimson platters, exotic sugar pastries piled on colorful tables. Monks arranged, reciting true scriptures, praying for the release of wayward souls from suffering. Both the Taizong and his officials held incense, respectfully bowing to the Golden Buddha, bowing to the Arhats. Seeing that Great Dharmaraja Chan Master Tripitaka Maitreya led the monks in bowing to the Tang emperor. After the ceremony, they took their respective places, the master presenting a list of wishes for the release of the dead to Taizong. The proclamation read: "In infinite virtue, the dharma remains silent. Pure and clear, traversing the three realms. Infinite transformations, embracing yin and yang. Essence and function eternal, boundless and without end. Observing these lost souls, compassion calls. By the grace of the sovereign, select and gather monks, engage in dharma lectures. Open the door of easy access, extend the boat of compassion, rescue all living beings from suffering, freeing them from the six hells. Guide them to the true path, revel in primordial nature; cease striving, becoming one with pure simplicity. This virtuous cause, invite blessings from the Clear Capital and Crimson Palace; participating in this wondrous gathering, escape the realms of suffering. Ascend to bliss in the West, enjoy free will. Poem: A perpetual life incense, a few scrolls of deliverance. Endless wondrous teachings, boundless divine grace. Expunge all karmic debts, release souls from the prison of sorrow. May my nation be blessed with peace and prosperity for a thousand years." Taizong, reading with joy, said to the monks, "You must uphold your loyalty, and not neglect Buddhist affairs. When the work is completed, each will receive due reward, and I shall surely honor you." All one thousand two hundred monks bowed their heads in gratitude and thanks.

The Buddha's golden statue, serene and lifelike, arhats with jade faces, awe-inspiring. Vases filled with divine flowers, incense burners burning incense and sandalwood. Vases filled with divine flowers, dazzling blossoms enveloping the Buddhist temple; incense burners burning incense and sandalwood, fragrant clouds wafting into the clear sky. Fresh fruits laid out on red trays, exotic candies and pastries piled on colored trays. Monks arranged, chanting true scriptures, praying to rescue lost souls from suffering. Both war and civil officials, holding incense and bowing to the Buddha, paying homage to the Buddha and the arhats. Then, the Great Sage and Upholder of the Dharma, Master Chen Xuanzang, leads the monks in bowing to the Tang emperor. The ceremony complete, the monks take their places in their ranks, and the master presents a memorial for releasing the lost souls to the emperor, written as follows: "Endless virtue, silent Zen. Pure and clear, flowing through the three realms. A myriad of changes, mastering yin and yang. True and constant in use, boundless and without end. Viewing those lost souls, deep pity is due. This, in accordance with the emperor's command, selects a gathering of monks, practicing Zen and preaching dharma. Greatly opening convenient entrances, widely spreading the ferry of compassion, universally saving the suffering across the sea of distress, freeing from the six paths of suffering. Leading the way to the true path, wandering through the original void; moving without purpose, becoming pure and true. Relying on this good cause, inviting rewards in the clear capital and purple palaces; taking part in this superior gathering, escaping from hell and worldly prisons. Swiftly ascending to pure bliss and enjoying freedom, coming and going to the western paradise with ease. Verse: A furnace of longevity incense, a few scrolls of salvation scriptures. Boundless wonderful teachings proclaimed, boundless divine grace showered. Vengeful spirits entirely removed, lost souls all released from prison. May I protect my country, enjoying perpetual peace and prosperity. The emperor, upon reading, was overjoyed, turning to the monks and saying, "You all stand firm with your hearts of sincerity, never neglecting Buddhist practices. After the work is completed, each shall have his own reward, and I will reward you generously, not leaving any labor unrewarded." The one thousand two hundred monks bowed their heads in gratitude and praise.

Around the emperor in front and back were the officials with their ceremonial accessories; on both sides stood the five regiments with banners and flags. Holding golden gourds and bearing axes in pairs, they stood in order. Red silk candles and incense from the imperial incense burner filled the hall. Dragons and phoenixes flew in elegance, while eagles and fowls displayed their might. Under the rule of a wise and bright emperor, with loyal and righteous ministers, blessings would endure for a thousand years, surpassing the times of Yu and Shun, and prosperity would continue for ten thousand generations, outshining the reigns of Yao and Tang. Also seen were the curved canopy umbrellas, rolling dragon robes, and their brilliant rays; jade rings, colored phoenix fans, and auspicious clouds swaying. With jade crowns and jade belts, and purple sashes and golden seals, a thousand soldiers guarded the imperial chariot, and two rows of officers supported the imperial canopy. This emperor bathed in sincerity and respect, turning to Buddhism, rejoicing in the virtuous fruits of planting good seeds. Emperor Taizong, the Tang king, arrived early at the temple, halting the music and carriages, leading the officials to worship Buddha and plant incense. After three rounds of worship, he raised his head to gaze, truly a magnificent Dharma assembly. As seen: pennants fluttered, and the precious canopies shone. Pennants fluttered, casting streaks of colorful clouds in the sky; the precious canopies shone, illuminating the sun with vivid red lightning. The golden image of the Buddha was sublime, while the jade-faced Arhats were awe-inspiring. Flowers in vases, incense in the burners, radiating splendor. Flowers in vases, blossoming in the precious temple; incense in the burners, permeating the clear sky. Fresh fruits were arranged on red platters, and colorful sugar pastries piled on decorated trays. High-ranking monks stood in order, reciting the true scriptures, praying for the release of lonely souls from suffering. Emperor Taizong, both in martial and civil aspects, planted incense and worshipped, venerating the Buddha and paying homage to the Arhats. Then saw the Great Dharma Marshal Chen Xuanzang, the Venerable Master, leading the monks to worship Emperor Taizong. After the ceremony, the monks took their places in order, the Venerable Master presented to Emperor Taizong a notice of mercy, reading: "Eternal virtue, silent Chan; purity and penetration, circulating through the three worlds. Infinite changes, controlling Yin and Yang; true and constant, beyond bounds. Gazing upon these lonely souls, deep compassion is due. By the emperor's imperial command, select various monks, practice and expound Chan Dharma. Opening broad gates of convenience, vast ferry of compassion, rescuing all suffering in the sea of suffering, freeing them from the six paths of rebirth. Guiding them to the true path, exploring the great cosmos; actions and inactions, becoming pure and unadulterated. With this good cause, inviting rewards in the clear purple palaces; boarding my felicitous assembly, escaping the hells and mundane cages. Ascend to the pure land for freedom, journeying to the West following one's will. Poem: One incense for eternal life, several scrolls for rebirth. Boundless wonderful Dharma proclaimed, boundless heavenly grace bestowed. All ills of past lives eliminated, lonely souls all released from captivity. May the nation and its people be protected, enjoying peace for ten thousand years." Emperor Taizong was overjoyed after reading, addressing the monks, "You all hold true intentions, do not neglect Buddhist services. Once the work is completed, each of you will receive due rewards, and I will reward you richly, not allowing your efforts to be in vain." The thousand two hundred monks bowed in unison to express their gratitude.

Thousand officials in jade accessories formed a ring before and behind, five guards with banners lined the two sides. Holding golden gourds, bearing axes, in pairs they stood; red gauze candles, imperial incense, fragrant and majestic. Dragons flying, phoenixes dancing, woodpeckers defending, eagles flourishing. A wise and virtuous emperor, loyal and righteous ministers. Prosperity lasting a thousand years surpassing Yu and Shun, peace for generations emulating Yao and Tang. Then there were the curved umbrellas, embroidered robes, shining and reflecting; jade rings, colorful phoenix fans, auspicious clouds floating. Bejeweled crowns, jade belts, purple sashes, golden seals. Protecting the emperor, a thousand teams of guards; supporting the emperor’s carriage, two rows of generals. This emperor bathed, sincere and respectful, venerating Buddha, embracing virtue, delighted to hold incense. Emperor Tang arrived early at the temple gate, ordered the music and instruments to cease, and alighted from his carriage, leading all officials to worship Buddha and offer incense. Three circumambulations completed, he looked up and saw indeed a splendid Dharma assembly: banners fluttering, treasure canopies shining. Banners fluttering, blanketing the sky with streamers of rainbow; treasure canopies shining, reflecting red lightning on the sun. The golden Buddha statue was incomparable in form, the arhats fierce and formidable. Vases with immortal flowers, incense burning in treasure braziers. Vases with immortal flowers, bright flowers radiating in the temple; incense burning in treasure braziers, fragrant clouds penetrating the clear sky. Fresh fruits arranged on crimson platters, exotic sugar pastries piled on colorful trays. High-ranking monks in line chanting the true scriptures, wishing to free lost souls from suffering. The Tathagata, both martial and civil, each offered incense, bowed to the Buddha’s golden image, and venerated the arhats. Then Master Chenshen, Chen Hui-zang, the great Dharma preceptor, led the monks in paying respects to Emperor Tang. After the ceremony, they took their places in order, the preceptor presented a decree for the release of souls to the emperor, which read: Utmost virtue, silent Chan. Clear and pure, traversing the three realms. Infinite transformations, controlling yin and yang. True and constant, boundless and eternal. Observing those lost souls, pity is due. This is in accordance with the emperor’s command: assembling monks to practice Chan and discuss the Dharma. Opening the path of great convenience, extending the boat of compassion, saving all living beings in the sea of suffering, rescuing the sick from the six paths. Leading them to the true path, playing with the primordial universe; movement and cessation, achieving a state of pure simplicity. With this good cause, inviting blessings from the clear and crimson palaces; participating in this magnificent assembly, escaping from the hells and mundane cages. Ascending to bliss in the Western Pure Land, freely traveling to the West. Poem: A single incense burner of eternal life, several scrolls of scriptures for the living. Ineffable methods revealed, boundless grace bestowed. Evil and debt completely erased, lost souls freed from prison. May it protect our nation and state, enjoying peace for a thousand years. The emperor was delighted and said to the monks, "You all uphold sincere loyalty, do not slacken in your Buddhist duties. When the task is complete, each shall receive due reward, and I will not overlook your efforts." The thousand and two hundred monks bowed their heads in unison, expressing their gratitude.

Is it not so, O Russia, that you are carried by a spirited, uncatchable troika? The road smokes beneath you, the bridges resound—everything falls behind. A mesmerized worshipper, struck by a divine wonder, stops: is this not a thunderbolt thrown from the heavens? What does this terrifying movement mean? And what unknown power lies within these unknown, light-flecked horses? Alas, horses, horses, what horses! Whirlwinds sit in your manes? Sensitive ears, glowing in each of your sinews? Hearing a familiar tune from above, you strain your copper chests together, barely touching the earth with your hooves, and transform into lines stretched for flight, soaring through the air, and the inspired land rushes on! O Russia, where are you rushing to? Answer me. It does not answer. The bell chimes in a pleasant resonance; the torn air, shattered into fragments, resounds like wind; everything passing on the earth flies by, and other nations and states step aside, yielding to its path.

Is it not so, O Rus', that your brisk, uncatchable troika races on? The road smokes beneath you, bridges resound – all fall behind and are left behind. The astonished contemplator, struck by divine wonder, stops: is this not a lightning bolt cast from heaven? What does this terrifying movement mean? What secret power lies within these unseen steeds? Ah, horses, horses, what horses! Whirlwinds sit in your manes? Sensitive ears burn in every one of your veins? From on high, you hear a familiar song, and together, you tense your coppery flanks and, scarcely touching the earth with your hooves, transform into single stretched lines, flying through the air, and the inspired Rus' speeds on! O Rus', where are you going? Give an answer. It does not give an answer. The chime of the bell rings out melodiously; the torn air becomes a roar and a wind; all that exists on earth flies past; and, sidestepping, other nations and states give way to her.

Is it not so, O Russia, that your lively, unstoppable troika rushes on? The road smokes beneath you, the bridges resound, all is left behind, all is left in the dust. Stunned, the observer, struck by a divine wonder, contemplates: is this not a thunderbolt fallen from heaven? What means this fearful motion? And what unknown force is pent up in these unknown steeds of darkness? Ah, horses, horses! Are tempests seated in your manes? Is a keen sense of hearing burning in every one of your veins? Hearing a familiar song from on high, you lift your copper-flaring flanks in unison and, scarcely touching the earth with your hooves, you transform into extended lines, gliding through the air, and the whole inspired people rushes on! Russia, where are you rushing to? Give an answer. No answer is given. The tinkling of the chime bell echoes in a marvel of sound; the rent air roars and becomes a wind; all that is on earth flies past, and turning aside, other peoples and states make way for it.

Is it not so, O Russia, that the quick, unstoppable troika dashes along? The road smokes beneath you, the bridges resound—everything falls behind and stays behind. A marvel-struck beholder has halted: is this not a bolt of lightning cast down from heaven? What does this terrifying motion mean? And what unknown force is imprisoned in these unseen steeds? Ah, horses, horses, what horses! Whirlwinds sit in your manes? Sensitive ears burn in every one of your veins? From a height, you catch a familiar song, you brace your copper chests together, scarcely touching the ground with your hooves, you transform into stretched-out lines that soar through the air, and the inspired Russia darts on!... Russia, where are you rushing to? Answer. No answer is given. The jingling of the bell resounds with a miraculous peal; the air, rent into fragments, roars and becomes a wind; everything passing by makes way, and other peoples and states step aside and yield to it.

Is it not so, O Rus, that your fleet uncatchable trio gallops on? The road smokes beneath you, bridges resound, all falls behind. A struck observer, filled with divine wonder, pauses: is this not a lightning bolt, cast from the heavens? What does this terrifying movement mean? And what unknown force dwells in these shadowed horses? Ah, horses, horses, what horses! Do whirlwinds sit in your manes? Do you burn with a sensitive ear in every vein? Hearing the familiar song from above, you strain your bronzed chests in unison, barely touching the earth with your hooves, transforming into one stretched line, flying through the air, and the inspired land races on! O Rus, where do you go? Give an answer. No answer is given. A chime bellows with a mystical clang; shattered air resounds like wind; all that is on earth passes by, veering aside and yielding to her, and other peoples and states give way as she passes.

—"And let us go, the evening is delightful!" exclaimed Eugene Pавлович. —But to prove to you that this time I spoke entirely in earnest, and, above all, to prove it to the prince (Your Highness, you have greatly interested me, and I swear to you that I am not quite as empty a person as I must certainly appear to be—although, in truth, I am an empty person! ), and... if you will allow, gentlemen, I shall ask the prince one last question out of pure curiosity, and we shall end with it. This question occurred to me quite by accident two hours ago (see, Your Highness, I do think seriously about some things as well); I have decided on my answer, but let's see what the prince will say. They just spoke of a "private case." This word is very significant for us; it is often heard. Not long ago everyone was talking and writing about this terrible murder of six people by this... young man, and about the defense speech, in which it is said that when a criminal is in a bad situation, it is natural for him to think of killing these six people. This is not literal, but the meaning, I think, fits this or something similar. But in my personal opinion, the defense lawyer, by making such a strange statement, was convinced that he was saying the most liberal, the most humane, and the most progressive thing one could possibly say in our time. Well, then, from your point of view, is this a perversion of concepts and convictions, this possibility of such a twisted and remarkable view of the case, whether it is a private or a general case?

— And let us go, the beautiful evening! — cried Eugene Pavlovich. — But to prove to you that this time I spoke quite seriously, and above all to prove it to the prince (your highness interested me extraordinarily, and I swear to you that I am not as empty a person as I must necessarily appear — though I am in fact an empty person! ), and... if you will permit, gentlemen, I will ask the prince one more final question out of mere curiosity and conclude with it. This question somehow occurred to me two hours ago (you see, your highness, I do sometimes think seriously too); I decided it, but let us see what the prince will say. They mentioned a "private case" just now. That word is very significant for us; it is often heard. Recently everyone was talking and writing about that awful murder of six people by that... young man and about the strange speech of the defense attorney, in which it is said that it was natural for a poor criminal to think of killing those six people. This is not literal, but the meaning seems to fit the case or something like it. But in my personal opinion, the defense attorney, stating such an odd idea, was fully convinced that he was saying the most liberal, the most humane, and the most progressive thing one could say in our time. Well, then, according to your opinion, is this an perversion of concepts and convictions, this possibility of such a distorted and remarkable view of the matter, whether it is a private or a general case?

"But in order to prove to you that this time I was absolutely serious, and, above all, to prove it to the prince (Your Highness, you have greatly interested me, and I swear to you that I am not as empty a person as I necessarily must appear—though I am actually a very empty person!), and... if you will permit, gentlemen, I will ask the prince one last question, out of idle curiosity, and will end with it. "But to prove to you that this time I was speaking quite seriously, and, above all, to prove it to the Count (Your Highness, you have greatly interested me, and I swear to you that I am not quite the empty person that I must inevitably appear—although, to be honest, I am an empty person! ), and... if you will permit, gentlemen, I will make one final question to the Count, purely out of curiosity, and end with it. This question came to me quite accidentally two hours ago (see, Your Highness, I do also sometimes think seriously about matters); I have decided on an answer, but let us see what Your Highness will say. They spoke just now about a 'private case.' This word is very significant to us; it is one we often hear. Recently everyone was talking and writing about that terrible murder of six people by this... young man, and about the strange defense speech, where the defense claimed that to a poor defendant it was natural that he would come to the idea of killing these six people. It is not literal, but the meaning, I think, is more or less the same. But, in my personal opinion, the defense, by putting forth such a strange idea, was convinced that he was speaking the most liberal, the most humane, and the most progressive thing one could say in our times. Well, then, what do you think: is this an perversion of ideas and convictions, this possibility of such a twisted and remarkable view of the case, whether it is a private or general case?

Still, there would come accusations from so-called patriots, who comfortably sit in their corners, engaged in completely unrelated matters, amassing their capital, arranging their destiny on the backs of others; but as soon as something happens, according to their opinion, that is offensive to their homeland, some book would appear with bitter truths sometimes conveyed. They would rush out from all corners like spiders at the sight of a fly caught in a web, and suddenly raise a clamor: "Is it good to bring this to light, to proclaim it? After all, everything described here is ours—how can this be good? And what would foreigners say? Isn't it unpleasant to hear a bad opinion about oneself? They think, can this not hurt? They think, are we not patriots?" Indeed, such astute remarks, especially about foreign opinion, one cannot really refute. But then, there were two dwellers in a remote corner of Russia. One was a family man named Kifa Mokyevich, a man of mild character, who led his life in a slack manner. He did not concern himself with his family; his existence was more inclined towards contemplation, and he was preoccupied with what he called a philosophical question: "For example, an animal is born naked—why naked? Why not like a bird, why not hatch from an egg? How to explain the nature, the deeper one probes into it!" This was how Kifa Mokyevich thought. But this was not the main point. The other dweller was Mokyevich Kifaevich, his own son. He was considered a hero in Russia, and while his father was occupied with the birth of an animal, his twenty-year-old, broad-shouldered figure was eager to spread its wings. He was unable to do anything without great effort: either someone’s hand would crack, or a boil would appear on someone’s nose. Everyone in the house and neighborhood, from the maidservant to the household dog, would run away upon seeing him; even in the bedroom, he had torn his own bed apart. Such was Mokyevich Kifaevich, but he was a kind-hearted soul. But this was not the main point. The main point was: "Oh Lord, father Kifa Mokyevich, — said both the master and the servants to their father, — what kind of Mokyevich Kifaevich do you have? He gives no peace to anyone, he is such a pest!" "Yes, he is mischievous, mischievous, — his father would usually say, — but what can one do: it is late to fight with him, and they would accuse me of cruelty; but he is ambitious, and if someone reprimands him, he will settle down, but alas, publicity—what a bother! The town will learn of him and call him a dog. What do they think, do I not feel it? am I not a father? If I am so engrossed in philosophy that I do not have time for anything else, am I not a father? Yet I am, father! father, damn it, father! Mokyevich Kifaevich is sitting right here in my heart! — Then, Kifa Mokyevich would strike his chest very hard with his fist and fall into a complete frenzy. — If he is to remain a dog, let it not be known from me, let it not be me who reveals him." Showing such fatherly feelings, he left Mokyevich Kifaevich to continue his heroic exploits and returned to his favorite topic, setting himself a question like this: "What if an elephant hatched from an egg, the shell would be so thick, no musket could penetrate it; one must invent some new firearm." Thus, the two dwellers of a peaceful corner spent their lives, only to unexpectedly appear at the end of our poem, peeking out to modestly answer accusations from some fervent patriots, who, at ease, were engrossed in some philosophy or the addition of their beloved homeland’s capital, thinking not about not doing wrong, but about not being accused of doing wrong. But no, it is not patriotism and the first impulse that are the cause of accusations, but something else is hidden beneath them. Why conceal the word? Who, if not the author, should tell the holy truth? You are afraid of a deeply penetrating gaze, you fear to direct a deep gaze at anything, you love to glance at everything with indifferent eyes. You may even laugh heartily at Chichikov, perhaps even praise the author, saying: "However, he hit the nail on the head in some things, he must be a cheerful person!" And after such words, with doubled pride, you turn to yourself, and a self-satisfied smile will appear on your face, and you will add: "Indeed, strange and amusing people can be found in some provinces, and not a few scoundrels!" And who among you, full of Christian humility, does not in private, in a moment of secluded conversation with yourself, deepen within your own soul this heavy question: "Is there perhaps a part of Chichikov in me?" No, it cannot be! But then, at this moment, if a acquaintance of his who has neither a too high nor a too low rank passes by, he would immediately push his neighbor with a laugh and say: "Look, look, there’s Chichikov, Chichikov is going!" And then, like a child, forgetting all proprieties, his rank, and age, he would run after him, teasing from behind and saying: "Chichikov! Chichikov! Chichikov!"

Still, the author will be blamed by so-called patriots who quietly sit in corners, pursuing entirely unrelated occupations, amassing fortunes by planning their lives at the expense of others; but as soon as something, in their opinion, offensive to their country occurs, some book will appear that sometimes states an unflattering truth, and they will emerge from their corners like spiders seeing a fly caught in their web, and suddenly begin shouting: “Is it right to bring this to light, to announce it? After all, everything described here is ours, our very own – is that right? And what will foreigners say? Isn’t it painful to hear a bad opinion about oneself? Don’t they think, ‘Aren’t we patriots?’” Such wise remarks, especially concerning the opinion of foreigners, are difficult to counter. For instance, in a remote corner of Russia, there lived two residents. One was a family man named Kefa Mokievich, a gentle-natured man leading a slack life. He did not bother with his family; he lived more in thought and was engaged in what he called a philosophical question: “Just look at the animal, walking around the room, — he would say, — an animal is born naked. But why is it born naked? Why not like a bird, hatched from an egg? How, really, to understand the nature of things any deeper!” This was how Kefa Mokievich thought. But this was not the main point. The other resident was Mokiy Kifevich, his own son. He was considered a mighty warrior in Russia, and while his father was pondering the birth of an animal, his twenty-year-old muscular frame was bursting to break free. He could never do anything gently; if he touched someone, their hand would break, or a pimple would pop on someone’s nose. Everyone in the household, from the servant girl to the dog, would run away at his sight; he even tore up his own bed in the bedroom. This was Mokiy Kifevich, but he was a good-natured man. But this was not the main point. The main point was: “My Lord, Father Kefa Mokievich, — the servants both own and hired would say to the father, — what do you have in you, Mokiy Kifevich? He’s a nightmare to everyone!” — “Yes, he’s mischievous, mischievous, — the father would usually say, — but what can I do? It’s too late to fight him, and I’ll be accused of cruelty. He’s a proud man, let him be chided by another, he’ll calm down, but there’s public opinion, it’s the trouble! The town will find out and call him a dog. What, really, do you think, does it not hurt me? Am I not his father? Because I’m busy with philosophy and don’t have time, am I not a father? But there is a father! Father, damn them, father! Mokiy Kifevich is sitting here in my heart! — Kefa Mokievich would then hit his chest very hard with his fist and fall into a complete frenzy. — If he remains a dog, let no one in my household know it, let not me be the one to betray him.” And, showing such paternal feeling, he left Mokiy Kifevich to continue his heroics, while he returned to his favorite topic, suddenly posing a similar question to himself: “What if a elephant were hatched from an egg? The shell would be so thick, no gun could penetrate it; a new kind of firearm must be invented.” Thus, the two residents of this peaceful corner lived, appearing suddenly, like through a window, at the end of our poem, to respond humbly to the accusations of certain fervent patriots, who, at ease, pursued some philosophy or the growth of the cherished country they did not think about not doing wrong, but about not being said to do wrong. But it is not patriotism or first feelings that are behind the accusations; something else hides under them. Why conceal the truth? Who, if not the author, should say the holy truth? You fear a penetrating gaze, you are afraid to gaze deeply, you like to glance over everything with thoughtless eyes. You will even laugh heartily at Chichikov, maybe even praise the author and say, “But he’s cleverly noticed something, must be a cheerful person!” After such words, with redoubled pride, you will turn to yourself, a self-satisfied smile will appear on your face, and you will add, “And yet, agree, strange and funny people are found in certain provinces, and quite scoundrels as well!” But who among you, full of Christian humility, will not deeply, in private, in moments of solitary conversations with yourself, reflect: “Is there not a bit of Chichikov in me?” No, that’s not the case! But let someone who knows him, who has a title, but not too high and not too low, walk past him at that very moment, and he will immediately elbow his neighbor and, barely stifling a laugh, say, “Look, look, there’s Chichikov, Chichikov is walking!” And then, like a child, forgetting all propriety, due to one’s rank and age, he will run after him, mock him from behind, and say: “Chichikov! Chichikov! Chichikov!”

Still, authors are accused by so-called patriots who, while lounging in their corners, peacefully amass personal capital, setting their own destiny at the expense of others; but as soon as something offensive to the homeland appears in a book, they dart out from all corners like spiders seeing a fly caught in their web, and suddenly start shouting: "Is it right to bring this into the light? To proclaim it? After all, all that’s written here is ours, isn’t it? And what will foreigners say? Isn’t it painful to hear bad things about ourselves? Don’t they think that we are patriots?" Indeed, such astute comments, especially about the opinion of foreigners, there is nothing to counter. But there is this: two dwellers lived in a remote corner of Russia. One was a family man, named Kifa Mokievich, a gentle-natured man who led a careless life. He did not concern himself with his family; rather, his life was more oriented towards theoretical pursuits, occupied with what he called a philosophical question: "For instance, a beast," he would say, pacing in the room, "is born naked. But why naked? Why not like a bird, hatching from an egg? How can you explain that in nature? The deeper you look into it, the less you understand!" This was how Kifa Mokievich thought. But this was not the main point. The other dweller was Mokiy Kifevich, his own son. He was a sort of Russian hero, and while his father pondered the birth of beasts, Mokiy Kifevich's twenty-year-old hulking frame was eager to display his prowess. He could not do anything in moderation: a neighbor’s hand would crack or a boil would suddenly pop on someone’s nose. All in the house and the surrounding area, from the servant girl to the yard dog, would flee upon seeing him; he even broke his own bed in the bedroom into pieces. Such was Mokiy Kifevich, but he was also of a good nature. But this was not the main point. The main point was: "Alas, my noble sir, Kifa Mokievich, servants and passersby alike would say to his father, "What a Mokiy Kifevich you have! He gives no peace to anyone, such a pest!" "Yes, he is mischievous, mischievous," the father would usually reply, "but what can I do? It’s too late to fight him, and they’ll accuse me of cruelty; but he’s ambitious, and reproaches from a third party will make him behave, yet the public opinion – what a disaster! – the city will find out, call him a dog. What do you think, does it not hurt me? Am I not his father? Just because I’m busy with philosophy and sometimes can’t find time for my family, does that mean I am not a father? But, there I am, a father! A father, damn them, a father! Mokiy Kifevich is sitting right here in my heart!" Kifa Mokievich would then strike his chest violently with his fist and fall into a state of frenzy. "Even if he remains a dog, let it not be known through me, let me not be the one to expose him." And, displaying such paternal concern, he would leave Mokiy Kifevich to continue his heroics while he turned back to his favorite topic, setting himself a similar question out of the blue: "And if an elephant were to hatch from an egg, the shell would surely be thick, impenetrable by a cannonball; we need to invent a new kind of firearm." Thus, the two dwellers of a peaceful corner spent their lives, which they unexpectedly, as if from a window, looked out upon at the end of our poem. They did so to answer the accusations from some heated patriots, who, while calmly engaged in some philosophy or personal enrichment at the expense of the homeland they adored, are not concerned with whether they are doing wrong, but only with ensuring that no one accuses them of doing so. But it is not patriotism or first emotions that cause the accusations; something else lies beneath. What for is to conceal the word? Who else but the author should say the sacred truth? You fear the gaze that penetrates to the depths, you are afraid to cast a deep gaze yourself, you prefer to glaze over everything with indifferent eyes. You even laugh heartily at Chichikov, and perhaps even praise the author, saying: "He has cleverly noticed something; he must be a cheerful person!" And after such words, you will return to yourself with an even greater sense of pride, a self-satisfied smile will play on your face, and you will add: "Indeed, there are strange and humorous people in some provinces, and not a few scoundrels as well!" And who among you, full of Christian humility, will not privately, in the silence of solitude, ask: "Is there not a part of Chichikov in me?" No, never! But then, if at that moment someone familiar with him, of a rank neither too high nor too low, happens to pass by, he will immediately elbow his neighbor and, barely stifling a laugh, say: "Look, there goes Chichikov, Chichikov is coming!" And then, like a child, forgetting all decorum, fitting to his status and age, he will run after him, teasing him from behind and shouting: "Chichikov! Chichikov! Chichikov!"

Still, the author will be blamed by so-called patriots who quietly sit in corners and engage in completely unrelated tasks, accumulating their own capital by shaping their destinies on the backs of others; but as soon as something, according to their view, offensive to the homeland appears, a book emerges where sometimes bitter truths are spoken. They will emerge from all corners, like spiders seeing a fly entangled in their web, and suddenly raise a hue and cry: "Is it good to bring this to light, to proclaim it? After all, what is written here is all ours – is it good? And what will foreigners say? Is it not unpleasant to hear a bad opinion of oneself? Do they not think it painful? Do they not consider themselves patriots?" Such wise remarks, especially about the opinion of foreigners, I must admit, leave nothing to respond with. But as for this: there lived in a remote corner of Russia two inhabitants. One was a family man named Kefa Mokievich, a gentle natured man who lived in a laissez-faire manner. He did not concern himself with his family; his existence was more inclined towards contemplation, and he occupied himself with what he called a philosophical question: "Here, for instance, is an animal, " he would say while walking about the room, "an animal is born naked. Why exactly naked? Why not like a bird, hatching from an egg? How, really, one can never fathom nature, the more one delves into it!" Thus thought the inhabitant Kefa Mokievich. But this was not the main point. The other inhabitant was Mokie Kifovich, his own son. He was what is called a strong man in Russia, and when his father was occupied with the birth of the animal, his twenty-year-old broad-shouldered nature yearned to stretch itself. He could not do anything in moderation: either someone's hand would crack, or a pustule would appear on someone's nose. Everyone in the house and the neighborhood, from the chambermaid to the dog, would run away at his sight; even he had torn his own bed apart in the bedroom. This was Mokie Kifovich, but he was good-natured. But this was not the main point. The main point was: "Alas, sir, Master Kefa Mokievich, " said both the master and the servant, "what is this Mokie Kifovich of yours? No one can get a moment's peace from him, he is such a pest!" "Yes, mischievous, mischievous, " the father would often say in response, "but what can be done? It's too late to fight with him, and they'll blame me for cruelty; he is proud, if I reproach him in front of others, he will calm down, but shamelessness is the problem! The town will find out and call him a dog. Do they not think, I am not pained? Am I not a father? Do I not engage in philosophy and have other matters to attend to, so I am not a father? Well, I am a father! Father, damn them, I am a father! Mokie Kifovich is sitting right here, in my heart! " Here Kefa Mokievich would strike his chest forcefully with his fist and fall into a frenzy. "If he remains a dog, let it not be known from me, let it not be me who exposes him. No, not so! Bronze serpents and iron dogs feast at will, forever plunged into the River of Unending Suffering with no way out. The poem says: "Hear the wails of ghosts and the cries of gods, blood turbid and muddied, towering high. Countless Bullheads and Facedeers guard, ferociously, the Bridge of the River of Unending Suffering." Just as they spoke, the bridge keepers returned. Emperor Taizong was once again alarmed, nodding and sighing in sorrow, following the registrar and military governor, swiftly crossing the evil waters of the River of Unending Suffering, the realm of bitter pain. They continued on to the City of the Wrongly Executed, where they heard a clamor of voices, clearly calling out, "Li Shizhen is here! Li Shizhen is here!" Hearing his name, Taizong was terrified. He saw a horde of spectral beings, each with broken arms and bent backs, heads absent but feet present, all shouting: "Return my life! Return my life!" Taizong, panicked, hid and fled, shouting, "Mr. Cui, save me! Mr. Cui, save me!" The registrar said, "Your Majesty, these are the spirits of those who fought in sixty-four battles, conspired in seventy-two regions, and the ghosts of princes and leaders; they are all wrongfully executed, without respite or solace, unable to attain liberation. They have no money for their journey, only spirits of the homeless and hungry. Your Majesty must give them some money, and then I can help them." Taizong replied, "I have no money with me. Where could I get it?" The registrar said, "Your Majesty, in the world of the living, there is a man with a certain amount of gold and silver. I can store it for him here. If you write a contract with me as your guarantor, I can borrow this store for you and distribute it to these hungry spirits." Taizong asked, "Who is this person?" The registrar said, "He is a person from Kaifeng, Henan, surnamed Xiang, named Liang, who has thirteen stores of gold and silver here. If you borrow it, you can return it to him in the world of the living." Emperor Taizong was very pleased and agreed to take on this task. He wrote a document with the registrar, borrowing a store of gold and silver, which the military governor distributed. The registrar instructed, "You may divide the gold and silver equally and allow my lord, the Tang Grandfather, to pass. His life in the world of the living is still long. I, following the orders of the Ten Kings, will escort him back to life, and arrange a water-land assembly in the world of the living to liberate you, so you must not cause trouble." Hearing these words, the spirits, having received the gold and silver, all bowed and retreated. The registrar ordered the military governor to wave the spirit-gathering flag and led Emperor Taizong out of the City of the Wrongly Executed, onto the plain road. They drifted away. It is yet to be seen which path they took; stay tuned for the next chapter.

Copper serpents and iron dogs fight over them; eternally falling into Naraka with no way out. A poem says: Often hear the cries of ghosts and the wails of gods, Blood-mixed waves rise ten thousand feet high. Countless heads of oxen and faces of horses, Fiercely guarding the bridge of Naraka.

Just as they spoke, those bridge keepers had already returned. Emperor Taizong felt alarmed again, nodding and sighing silently, sad, following the officials, early over the foul Naraka waters and into the bitter realm of blood bowls. Ahead, they reached the city of the wrongfully dead, only to hear loud cries, clearly saying, "Li Shimin is here! Li Shimin is here!" Taizong heard their calls and was frightened. He saw a crowd of tortured souls with broken limbs and missing heads, blocking the way, all shouting: Return my life! Return my life!

Taizong hid and dodged, only calling out, "Master Chu! Save me! Master Chu! Save me!" The official said, "Your Majesty, these people are the spirits of those who fought in sixty-four battles, and those who were bandits in seventy-two places, the ghosts of princes and chieftains; they are all the victims of wrongful deaths, left without retribution, unable to ascend to the afterlife, with no money for their journey. They are all hungry ghosts. Your Majesty, if you can find some money, I can help." Taizong said, "I am here alone, where can I find any money?"

The official said, "Your Majesty, there is a person in the mortal world who has many treasures in my underworld. If Your Majesty can promise and sign a contract, and I will guarantee it, I can borrow a store of these treasures to give to these hungry ghosts, allowing them to cross."

Taizong asked, "Who is this person?"

The official said, "He is from Henan, Kaifeng Prefecture, named Xiang Liang. He has thirteen stores of treasures in my care. If Your Majesty borrows from him, you can return it in the mortal world."

Emperor Taizong was very pleased and agreed to sign a contract to borrow the treasures. He drew up a document with the official and borrowed a store of treasures, instructing the Marshal to distribute them. The official instructed, "These treasures should be shared by you for your needs, allowing our dear ancestor of Tang to pass. His life span is still long. I will take the Ten Kings' words and deliver his soul, teaching him to hold a Water and Land Festival in the mortal world to allow you all to ascend to the afterlife and never cause trouble again."

Hearing this, the ghosts received the treasures and withdrew obediently. The official ordered the Marshal to wave the banner to lead Emperor Taizong out of the city of the wrongfully dead, heading towards the broad path of Pingyang, floating away. It is unknown which path they took to leave; stay tuned for the next chapter.

Copper serpents and iron dogs feast without end in the River of Purgatory, with no way out.
