He saw a horde of spectral figures with broken limbs and missing heads, who拦住他们，齐声喊道：“还我命！还我命！”这令太宗慌张躲藏，只喊“崔先生救我！崔先生救我！”判官说道：“陛下，这些人都是一百六十四处战乱，七十二处强盗，众王子和众头目的魂灵；他们皆是枉死的冤魂，无处收管，不得超生，又无盘缠，都是孤苦饥饿的鬼魂。陛下若有钱财救济他们，我才能救得他们。”太宗说道：“寡人空身至此，何处得有钱财？”判官说道：“陛下，阳间有一人，在阴司寄放了若干金银。陛下可立约出名，我可作保，暂借一库，救济这些饿鬼，方可过去。”太宗问道：“此人是谁？”判官答道：“他是河南开封府人，姓相名良，有十三库金银在此。陛下若借用过他的，到阳间还他便了。”太宗十分欢喜，愿意出名借用。于是立了文书，借得一库金银，让太尉分发给众鬼魂。判官吩咐道：“这些金银，你们可用之度日，放过大唐祖宗过桥。他的阳寿尚早。我领了十王的旨意，送他转世，让他阳间举办水陆法会，超度你们超生，此后不再造孽。”众鬼闻言，得金银后，皆唯唯而退。判官令太尉摇动引魂幡，领太宗离城，奔向平阳大路，飘然而去。究竟从哪条路脱身，且听下回分解。

"Read it again," said Tripitaka. The monk really read it again, and the beast really felt the pain. "Stop it! Stop it! Reading it hurts me! How can this be?" Tripitaka said, "Have you finally listened to my advice?" The beast said, "I have!" "Have you forgotten your manners again?" The beast said, "No, I won't!" Though he mouthed his words, his heart harbored ill intent. He shook the needle, making it as thick as a bowl, and was about to strike Tripitaka. Hastening to help, the master repeated the spell a couple of times. The monkey fell to the ground, dropped his iron staff, and could not raise a hand. "Master, I get it now! Don't read anymore! Don't read anymore!" Tripitaka said, "How could you have such a wicked heart and strike me?" The beast said, "I did not strike you, Master. I asked you, who taught you this trick?" Tripitaka said, "It was an old woman just now who taught me." The beast grew angry and said, "There's no need to say anymore! That old woman is definitely Guanyin! How could she harm me! Let me go to South Sea and take her down!"

At about that time, as Surikov had “frozen” the child, around mid-March, I suddenly felt much better for no particular reason, and this state lasted for about two weeks. I began going out more frequently, almost every evening. I loved the March twilight, when it started to get cold and the gas lamps began to light; sometimes I would walk for miles. Once, in Six-lidded Alley, I was overtaken in the dark by some “nobleman,” whom I couldn’t quite make out; he was carrying something wrapped in paper and was wearing a bulky and grotesque overcoat, too light for the season. When he passed a lamp, ten paces in front of me, I noticed that something had fallen out of his pocket. I hurried to pick it up, for there was still enough time, as a man in a long coat had already leapt up, but he didn’t argue when he saw the object in my hands; he glanced in my direction and slipped past. The object was large, a saffron-colored leather wallet stuffed with papers, but for some reason, from my first glance, I knew that it contained nothing but money. The man who had lost it was already forty paces ahead of me and soon vanished from sight. I raced after him and tried to call out, but I could only cry “Hey!” and he didn’t turn around. Suddenly, he slipped to the left into the gate of a house. When I ran into the gate, which was very dark, there was no one there anymore. The house was of enormous size, one of those monstrosities built by con men for tiny apartments; some of these houses might have as many as a hundred apartments. When I ran through the gate, it seemed to me that someone was moving in the right, rear corner of the enormous courtyard, although I could barely make out the figure in the darkness. When I reached the corner, I saw a stairway entrance; the stairs were narrow, incredibly dirty, and completely unlit, but I could hear a man climbing up ahead, and I raced up the stairs, hoping to catch him before he found a room. That’s exactly what happened. The staircases were short, and the number was endless, so I was dreadfully out of breath; the door was opened and closed again on the fifth floor, I guessed from three floors below. It took several minutes for me to climb up, to catch my breath on the landing, to search for a bell. Finally, a woman opened the door. She was inflating a samovar in a tiny kitchen. She listened in silence to my questions but understood nothing and silently opened the door to the next room, also tiny and very low, with shabby necessary furniture and a huge bed under curtains, where “Terentyich” (so the woman called him) lay, looking inebriated. On the table, an iron nightlight burned dimly, and there was an almost empty half-gallon bottle. Lying on his back, Terentyich mumbled something to me and gestured to the next door, and the woman went away, leaving me no choice but to open that door. I did as she told me and entered the next room.

— This was exactly one minute before his death, — the prince began with readiness, carried away by the memory and, it seemed, immediately forgetting everything else, — the exact moment when he climbed the ladder and had just stepped onto the scaffold. At that moment, he glanced in my direction; I looked at his face and understood everything... However, how to describe it! I would be so, so eager for you or someone to draw it! Better still, if it were you! I thought at that very moment that the painting would be useful. You know, everything must be imagined that was prearranged, everything, everything. He was in prison and was expected to be executed at least another week; he had somehow calculated on routine formalities, that the papers would somehow go somewhere and it would be a week later. But for some reason, the case was suddenly shortened. He was sleeping at five in the morning. It was late October; it was still cold and dark at five in the morning. A prison guard came in, softly, with an attendant, and gently touched his shoulder; he propped himself up, leaned back, and saw the light: "What is it?" "At ten o'clock, the death sentence." He did not believe it while still half-asleep, began to argue that the papers would be sent out in a week, but when he woke up completely, he stopped arguing and fell silent, they said — then he said, "Still, it's hard to die suddenly..." — and fell silent again, and did not want to say anything more. Then, for three or four hours, the usual things went on: the priest, breakfast, which included wine, coffee, and beef (is this a jest? After all, what's so terrible? But, honestly, these innocent people do it from the heart and believe it is kindness), then getting dressed (you know what a criminal's getting dressed means?), and finally, being taken through the city to the scaffold... I think that at this point, he felt that he still had a long way to live while being taken there. I think he was thinking on the way: "There's still a long way to go; I'll get through this street, then the next one, then the one where the baker turns right... We'll reach the baker some time yet!" There was a crowd, noise, shouting, ten thousand faces, ten thousand eyes, — all of this had to be imagined, but the main thing was the thought: "Here are ten thousand of them, and none of them is going to be executed, while I will be!" Well, that was the prelude. The scaffold was reached by a ladder; he suddenly burst into tears on the ladder, which was a strong and courageous man, they say, and a great villain. A priest was always with him, going in the cart, talking to him; he probably did not hear much, if any. He would start to listen, but did not understand after the third word. So, probably. Finally, he started climbing the ladder; his legs were bound, and so he moved in little steps. The priest, I think, was a clever man and stopped talking, but kept offering him the cross to kiss. He was very pale at the bottom of the ladder, but as he started climbing and got onto the scaffold, he suddenly turned as white as paper, as though it were pure white writing paper. His legs must have grown weak and wobbly, and he was feeling nausea, as if something were pressing on his throat, and this made him feel as if he were tickled — had you ever felt this in fear or in very scary moments, when all reason remains, but has no power? I think that, for example, if he were certain of his death and the house was falling on him, at that moment he would suddenly desperately want to sit down, close his eyes, and wait for whatever would happen! That's when, with the beginning of this weakness, the priest, quickly, in a gesture, and without a word, placed the little silver cross right in front of his lips, a four-armed one, — he kept doing it, minute by minute. As soon as the cross touched his lips, he opened his eyes, and for a few seconds he seemed to revive, and his legs started moving again. He kissed the cross greedily, hurried to kiss it, as if trying to take something in case he needed it, just in case, but probably at that moment he was not aware of anything religious. And so it was until the last step... It is strange that very rarely do people pass out in those final seconds! On the contrary, the head lives and works violently, intensely, intensely, as a machine does when it's running; I imagine that thoughts, all unfinished, are knocking around: "Look at that — he has a wart on his forehead, the executioner's bottom button is rusted..." but at the same time, you are still aware of everything and remember everything; there is one point that you cannot forget, and you cannot pass out at that point, and everything around it, around that point, circles and whirls. And think, that until the very last quarter of a second, when the head is already lying on the chopping block, and waiting, and... knowing, and suddenly hearing above him the blade scraping! You must hear it! If I were lying there, I would deliberately listen and hear it! There might be only a tenth of a second there, but you must hear it! And imagine that, up to now, they are still arguing that when the head finally flies off, it might still know for a second, perhaps, that it has flown off, — what a notion! And what if five seconds!... Draw the scaffold so that the last step is clearly and closely visible; the criminal has stepped on it: his head, pale as paper, the priest is offering the cross, and he is stretching his blue lips eagerly, and he is looking, and — he knows everything. The cross and the head — that's the picture, the priest's face, the executioner's, his two attendants, and a few heads and eyes below, — all of this can be drawn as a background, in a haze... This is the picture.

There he glanced at me; I looked at his face and understood everything... But how can one describe it! How terribly I wished you or someone else would draw it! You yourself would do a better job! I thought at the time that it would make a useful painting. You see, everything needs to be imagined here, everything that was prepared in advance. He was in prison and was expecting the execution at least another week; he reckoned on the usual formalities, that the papers were still to go somewhere and only after a week would it come through. But then, for some reason, the case was cut short. At five o'clock in the morning, he was asleep. It was late October, and it was still chilly and dark at five o'clock. The prison warden entered, quietly and accompanied by a guard, and gently poked him on the shoulder; he stirred, propped up, saw the light, "What's this?" "Your execution is in ten hours." He did not believe it at first, started to argue that the papers would come through in a week, but when he woke up properly, he stopped arguing and fell silent, as they told it. Then he said, "It's still heavy, to be executed like that... " and fell silent again, and did not want to say anything more. Three or four hours passed for known things: confession, breakfast, to which wine, coffee, and beef were served (isn't it a joke? How cruel, and yet, indeed, these innocent people do it with all their hearts, and they believe they are being kind). Then the toilet (you know what a convict's toilet is like?), finally, they were taken through the town to the scaffold. I think that here, too, it seems as if one has an eternity left, while being taken there. I imagine he was thinking on the way: "Still so much time, there are still three streets to go; I'll go this one, then that one, where the baker turns right... we'll still get to the baker's!" There were people all around, shouting and bustling, ten thousand faces, ten thousand eyes, all of this had to be portrayed, but above all, the thought: "Here are their ten thousand faces, and none of them will be executed, but I am!" That's what had to be portrayed beforehand. The scaffold was reached by a ladder; suddenly, at the foot of the ladder, he began to cry, though he was a strong and manly man, they said, a big villain. That's how it was, no doubt. Finally, he began to climb the ladder; here his legs were tied, and so he took small steps. Indeed, there is nothing more frustrating than being, for instance, wealthy, of a respectable family, well-mannered, moderately educated, not stupid, even good-natured, and yet having no talent, no special quality, no eccentricity, not a single original idea, being simply "like everyone else." Wealth is there, but not Rothschild’s; the family name is good, but has never distinguished itself; the appearance is decent, but conveys very little; the education is decent, but you can’t figure out how to use it; there is intelligence, but no of your own; there is a heart, but no generosity, and so on and so forth in every respect. Such people exist in abundance, and perhaps even more than it seems; they are divided, like everyone else, into two main categories: some are limited, others "much more intelligent." The limited "average" person has nothing easier than to imagine himself extraordinary and original, and to delight in it without any hesitation. It took only some of our young ladies to cut their hair, put on blue glasses, and call themselves nihilists to instantly realize that putting on glasses gave them their own "convictions." It took only for one person to feel something common and good in his heart to instantly believe that no one else feels it so acutely, and that he is ahead of the general development. It took only for one person to accept a notion on someone’s word or to read a page of something incoherent to immediately believe that it was "his own thoughts," and that they sprang from his own mind. The audacity of naïveté reaches the astonishing in such cases; all of this is incredible but happens all the time. This audacity of naïveté, this unshakeable belief in oneself and one’s talent, is excellently portrayed by Gogol in the remarkable character of Lieutenant Pirogov. Pirogov does not even doubt that he is a genius, even surpassing every other genius; he does not even entertain the question, for there are no questions for him; indeed, questions do not exist for him. The great writer was eventually compelled to lash him, to appease his outraged moral sense, but seeing that the great man simply shook himself off and, after the torment, enjoyed a layered pastry, he shrugged his shoulders and left his readers in puzzlement. I always regretted that the great Pirogov was taken by Gogol in such a minor rank, for Pirogov is so self-satisfied that he has nothing easier than to imagine himself, as he gets fatter and more rotund and "higher" on the 'epaulet line,' a distinguished, for example, general; not to imagine, but simply not to doubt this: if he’s made a general, how can he not be a general? And how many of such people make terrible fiascos on the battlefield? How many Pirogovs were among our writers, scientists, propagandists? I say "were," but certainly, there are still some...

Chichikov bowed gratefully. Learning that he was headed to the notary’s office to finalize a deed of sale, Manilov offered to accompany him. Friends linked arms and walked together. At every slight elevation, hill, or step, Manilov supported Chichikov and nearly lifted him with a hand, adding with a pleasant smile, “I won’t let Pavel Ivanovich’s legs take any knocks.” Chichikov felt ashamed and didn’t know how to thank him, for he sensed that he had been a bit heavy. Thanks to these mutual courtesies, they finally reached the square where the courthouse was situated: a large three-story white stone building, likely intended to symbolize the purity of the offices occupied within; the other buildings on the square did not match the grandeur of the stone building. There was a guardhouse with a soldier standing by with a rifle, a couple of hackstands, and finally long fences with familiar inscriptions and drawings chalked or scratched on them; nothing else was visible on this secluded, or as we say, picturesque square. Heads of impartial jurors peered out from the windows of the second and third floors and then immediately retreated: probably, the head official was entering the room. Friends did not climb but rather ran up the stairs, for Chichikov, trying to avoid being supported by Manilov’s arm, quickened his pace, and Manilov, in turn, strove to prevent Chichikov from tiring, so both were quite out of breath when they entered the dark corridor. Neither in the corridors nor in the rooms did their gaze encounter any cleanliness. They did not care about it yet, and what was dirty remained dirty, lacking any attractive appearance. Fidemis (Femida) received her guests simply, in a negligee and a dressing gown. It would have been appropriate to describe the offices the heroes passed through, but the author has a strong dread of all courtrooms. Even when he passed through them in a splendid and beautified state, with varnished floors and tables, he tried to hurry through as quickly as possible, lowering and averted his eyes in humble deference, and so he knows nothing of how all this flourished and prospered. The heroes saw a great deal of paper, both rough and clean, bent heads, broad napes, coats, waistcoats of provincial cut, and even a bright gray jacket that stood out very sharply. With its head turned to one side, it almost touched the paper, busily and slowly writing some protocol on the seizure of land or the description of an estate that had been confiscated by some peaceful landowner, who was living out his days under judgment, having created wealth for himself and his children and grandchildren under his protection. From time to time, hoarse voices uttered short phrases: “Please, Fedosey Fedoseyevich, file case N368!” “You’ll always drag the official ink bottle to some place!” Sometimes a more dignified voice, undoubtedly that of a superior, was heard in command: “Here, retype it, or else I’ll take off your boots and make you sit six days without eating.” The sound of quills was loud and resembled the rumbling of several waggons loaded with twigs passing through a forest covered with dry leaves to a depth of a quarter of a verst.

Our heroes saw a lot of paper, both rough and clean, bent heads, wide napes, frock coats of provincial cut, and even a light-gray coat which stood out quite starkly, tilting its head to one side and resting almost on the paper, busily and in a flourish writing out some protocol on the extension of land or an inventory of an estate seized by some peaceful landlord who was quietly living out his life under court supervision, shielding his descendants, and occasionally heard short phrases in a hoarse voice: “Fyodor Fyodorovich, please take over matter N368!” — “You always trample the cap of the office inkwell in your journeys!” Occasionally a more dignified voice, certainly that of one of the chiefs, would command: “Here, rewrite! or else they’ll take off your boots and you’ll sit with me six days without eating.” The sound of quill pens was great and resembled that of several waggons with twigs passing through a forest overgrown with withered leaves a span high.

Chichkov felt awkward, not knowing how to thank him, for he felt somewhat heavy. "Let her then be your lover now," Leni said, "but you wouldn't miss her much if you lost her, or if you exchanged her for someone else, for instance for me." "Of course," said K., smiling, "that would be conceivable, but she has a major advantage over you: she knows nothing about my trial, and even if she were to find out, it wouldn't occur to her. She wouldn't try to persuade me to be more lenient." "That is no advantage," said Leni. "If she has no other advantages, I won't lose heart. Does she have any physical flaws?" "Physical flaws?" K. asked. "Yes," said Leni, "I have, in fact, such a small flaw, look." She stretched her middle and ring finger of her right hand apart, and the skin between them reached almost to the top joint of the short finger. K., in the darkness, did not immediately understand what she wanted to show him, so he guided his hand for him to touch. "What a natural display," K. said, and, after he had viewed her hand in full, added, "What a pretty claw!" With a kind of pride, Leni watched as K. marvelled at her two fingers, stretching them apart and closing them again repeatedly, until he finally kissed them gently and let go. "Oh!" she cried immediately, "You kissed me!" Hastily, with her knees, she climbed onto his lap. K. looked almost startled at her, now that she was so close to him, a bitter, tantalizing scent, like peppermint, wafted from her; she took his head in her hands, leaned over him and bit and kissed his neck, even bit into his hair. "You've exchanged me!" she cried from time to time, "Look, you've exchanged me now!" Her knee slipped, with a little scream she nearly fell onto the carpet, K. clutched her to hold her, and was drawn down to her. "Now you belong to me," she said.

He dozed on a bench, but his alarm continued even in his dreams. Just before he slept, he remembered that Hippolyt would kill ten people, and he chuckled at the absurdity of the thought. Around him was a beautiful, clear stillness, with only the rustling of leaves, which seemed to make everything even quieter and more secluded. He dreamt a great many dreams, all of them troubling, which made him shudder every now and then. Finally, a woman came to him; he knew her, knew her to the point of suffering; he could always name her and point her out— but strangely, her face now seemed to be quite different from what he had always known, and it pained him terribly not to recognize her. In that face was so much repentance and horror that it seemed she was a terrible criminal who had just committed a terrible crime. A tear trembled on her pale cheek; she beckoned to him with her hand and pressed a finger to her lips, as if warning him to follow her silently. His heart stopped; he did not want to recognize her as a criminal for anything in the world; but he felt that something awful, that would taint the rest of his life, was about to happen. It seemed she wanted to show him something, right there in the park. He stood up to follow her, and suddenly a light, fresh laughter sounded beside him; a hand suddenly found its way into his. He grabbed it, clutched it tightly, and woke up. In front of him stood Aglaya, laughing loudly.

A Frenchman or German would never grasp or understand all its peculiarities and differences; he would speak with the same voice and in the same language to a magnate and to a small tobacco merchant, though, of course, he would be a little more careful with the former. Not so with us: we have such sages who will speak differently to a landowner with two hundred souls than to one with three hundred; those with three hundred will speak differently to those with five hundred, and those with five hundred will speak differently to those with eight hundred—indeed, even up to a million, there will be nuances. For example, there exists an office, let us say, in a different state, and in that office there is an office director. When he sits among his subordinates, behold!—one is at a loss for words! A haughtiness and nobility of bearing! What does his face express? Simply take a brush and paint: Prometheus, resolute Prometheus! The eagle watches intently, moving smoothly and steadily. The same eagle, as soon as he leaves the room and approaches his superior's office, rushes in like a woodcock with documents under his arm, the very picture of haste. In society and at parties, where everyone is of minor rank, Prometheus will remain Prometheus, but with someone slightly higher in rank, a metamorphosis will occur, even more fantastical than anything Ovid could have imagined: he will shrink to the size of a fly, even smaller than a fly, disappearing into a grain of sand! "This can't be Ivan Petrovich," you say, looking at him. "Ivan Petrovich is taller, and this one is short and thin; he speaks loudly, rumbles, and never laughs, whereas this one—God knows what! He chirps like a bird and is always laughing." You get closer and take a look—sure enough, it's Ivan Petrovich! "Hehe," you think to yourself… But let us return to the characters. Chichikov, as we have seen, resolved not to mince words and, taking a cup of tea in his hand and adding fruit, began to speak as follows:

"Where have you come from?" Ksitigarbha asked. "The Tang Priest lost his horse in the Eagle Hawk Ravine at the Snake-Coiling Mountain and was desperate. Upon asking the local gods, they said that the bodhisattva had sent the demon dragon there to swallow the horse. So the Great Sage asked me to come and beg the bodhisattva to subdue this demon dragon and return his horse." The bodhisattva heard this and said, "This creature is the son of Ao Run, the sea king. He set fire to the palace lanterns and was condemned for disrespect to his father, facing the death penalty in the heavenly court. I personally pleaded with the Jade Emperor to take him down and teach him to be the Tang Priest's steed. Why did he devour the Tang Priest's horse? According to your words, let me go." Thus, the bodhisattva descended from his lotus throne and left the immortal cave. With Ksitigarbha, they ascended with auspicious light and arrived at South Sea. A verse serves as testimony:

The bodhisattva preaches the Perfection of Wisdom,  
Filling the Great Wall of righteousness with virtue's light.  
Greatly insightful words travel through heaven and earth,  
Sutras of true understanding save the lost.

Thus the Golden蝉can transform again,  
And the pilgrimage resumes for the true monk.  
Only the Eagle Hawk Ravine hinders our path,  
Transforming the dragon's son into a horse.

The bodhisattva and Ksitigarbha did not take long to arrive at Snake-Coiling Mountain. They lingered in the air and looked down. There, Sun Wukong was cursing by the ravine. The bodhisattva asked Ksitigarbha to call him over. Ksitigarbha descended and, without passing by the monk, went to the ravine. He called out to Wukong, "The bodhisattva is here." At this, Wukong leapt into the air and called down, "O master of seven Buddhas, compassionate ruler! Why did you scheme to harm me?"

The bodhisattva replied, "I have repeatedly endured your insolence, ruddy-ass. I saved a person to journey to the West, instructing him to save your life. Why don't you thank me for saving you, but instead quarrel with me?"

Wukong said, "You've done a terrible thing! If you released me, let me be free. You said yesterday at sea that you would have me serve the monk wholeheartedly, but you gave him a flower cap and tricked me into wearing it. You placed this golden hoop on my head and made him chant a spell, forcing me to suffer. This isn't your way of harming me!"

The bodhisattva laughed and said, "You, mischievous monkey! If you did not obey the rules, you would return to a lower realm. Had I not done this, you would have defied me again, causing trouble. This spirit must be tamed to lead you to my path."

Wukong said, "If this is so, then make me his spirit, but why do you allow the guilty demon dragon to become a spirit here, eat my master's horse, and cause chaos? This is too careless!"

The bodhisattva said, "That dragon is here because I personally requested the Jade Emperor to teach him to be the Tang Priest's steed. You see, ordinary horses cannot traverse these mountains and rivers. Only this dragon can reach the Land of Spirits. You should thank me."

Wukong said, "He fears me, hiding and not coming out. What can I do?"

The bodhisattva called out to Ksitigarbha, "Go to the ravine and call out, 'Ao Run, Dragon King's son, Third Prince, come out, the South Sea bodhisattva is here.'"

Ksitigarbha went to the ravine and called out twice. The little dragon rose from the waves, jumped out, and transformed into a human. He rode the clouds and greeted the bodhisattva in the air. "I have been waiting for you for a long time, but I did not hear anything about the journeyers."

The bodhisattva pointed to Wukong and said, "This is the Tang Priest's first disciple."

The little dragon said, "Bodhisattva, this is my rival. I was hungry yesterday and indeed ate his horse. He was overconfident and fought me until I could not hold my ground. He also threatened to hunt me down and did not mention the journey at all."

"Where do you come from?" Ksitigarbha asked. "The Tang monk lost his horse in the Eagle Devouring Ravine of Snake Coiling Mountain. This has left the Great Sage Very Difficult to Make a Move. After inquiring with the local deities, we learned that this monster sent by the bodhisattva ate the horse. Thus, the Great Sage sent me to request the bodhisattva to subdue this monster and return the horse to him." Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva said, "This creature is none other than the son of the West Sea Dragon King Ao Run. He set fire to the palace lamps and thus incurred a death sentence for rebellion. I personally interceded with the Jade Emperor, and he ordered me to teach him to be the Tang monk's mount. How did he then devour the monk's horse? According to you, I will go." The bodhisattva descended the lotus seat and left the divine dwelling, riding auspicious light to the southern sea. As proof, a poem was recited: "Sutras of the Sutras of Honey Offerings, the bodhisattva reveals kindness to fill the Great Wall of China. Marvelous words communicate with heaven and earth, the true spell saves spirits. Thus, the golden蝉 resets his shell, and the玄奘 once again takes up training. It is because the road blocks the Eagle Devouring Ravine, where the dragon's son returned to true form and became a horse. The bodhisattva and Ksitigarbha arrived at Snake Coiling Mountain shortly. They stopped the auspicious cloud in midair, looking down to observe. There, Sun Wukong was cursing by the ravine. The bodhisattva asked Ksitigarbha to call him. Ksitigarbha alighted the cloud and went straight to the ravine, calling out to the monkey, "The bodhisattva is here." On hearing this, the monkey hurriedly ascended the cloud to confront him, shouting, "You, master of the seven Buddhas, merciful lord! How did you devise a scheme to harm me!" The bodhisattva said, "I, this bold and foolish Red Ass! I have done my utmost to get a pilgrim for him, instructed him to save your life, and you did not even thank me for saving your life. Instead, you quarrel with me." The monkey said, "You have done me such a great injustice! If you released me, let me enjoy my freedom. Yesterday, you scolded me and told me to serve the monk with all my heart. Why did you send him a hat to put on my head and make me suffer? Why did you place this ring on my head and have him recite a spell to cause me pain? This is not a scheme to harm me!" The bodhisattva laughed and said, "You, monkey! If you did not obey my commands and did not wish to attain the true fruit, you would have caused more trouble by breaking free. This magic ring is to prevent you from returning to your old ways and causing more chaos. Only with this magic can you enter the path of yoga." The monkey said, "This thing is my magic ring, and yet, you sent this sinning monster to become a spirit here and let him devour my master's horse? This is letting a criminal go free, which is too cruel!" The bodhisattva said, "That dragon was placed here by me, specifically to serve the pilgrim. Ordinary horses from the East cannot withstand these rivers and mountains or reach the Holy Land of Vulture Peak. They must be this dragon for the journey to be possible." The monkey said, "Since he is so afraid of me, can't he hide better?" The bodhisattva called Ksitigarbha, "Go to the ravine and call out, 'Ao Run, Dragon King, come out, the bodhisattva of the Southern Sea is here.' He will come out." Ksitigarbha went to the ravine and called twice. The dragon flailed and leaped, surfacing and transforming into a human, flying to the air to kneel before the bodhisattva, saying, "I was saved from death by your grace. I have been waiting for a long time, and have not heard any news of the pilgrim." The bodhisattva pointed at Sun Wukong and said, "Is this not the master's great disciple?" The dragon saw and said to the bodhisattva, "Bodhisattva, this is my rival. Yesterday, I was hungry and ate his horse. He, relying on his strength, defeated me and returned. He also criticized me to the point that I dare not come out. He did not even mention the pilgrim." Sun Wukong said:

"Where have you come from?" said Jiedi. "The Tang Priest lost his horse at Eagle-Coveting Gorge in Snake-Circling Mountain. The Great Sage is at a loss as to how to proceed. When he asked the local deities, they said that a demon dragon from there swallowed the horse. The Great Sage sent me here to ask the Bodhisattva to subdue this demon dragon and return the horse to him." The Bodhisattva heard this and said, "This demon is none other than the son of Ao Ren, the lord of the Western Sea. He set fire to the pearls in the temple and, for this, his father reported him for insubordination. He was sentenced to death in Heaven. I personally pleaded with the Jade Emperor to spare his life and instructed him to serve as the Tang Priest's mount. How is it that he ate the Priest's horse? Well, go with me." The Bodhisattva descended from the lotus throne and left the仙洞, riding auspicious clouds with Jiedi until they arrived at the South Sea. There was a poem to bear witness:  
The Bodhisattva preaches the Lotus Sutra;  
Ginseng Wu fills the Great Wall with virtue.  
Mahayana sayings sound through heaven and earth;  
True mantras save even the most tormented.  
Thus, the Golden Cicada sheds its shell once more,  
And the Blessed Tang Priest undergoes another round of cultivation.  
Only because of the Eagle-Coveting Gorge does the dragon son revert to his true form and change into a horse. The Bodhisattva and Jiedi did not take long to reach Snake-Circling Mountain. They remained in the air and looked down. There, Sun Wukong was cursing at the edge of the ravine. The Bodhisattva told Jiedi to call him. Jiedi landed and went straight to the ravine, where he said, "The Bodhisattva is here." Upon hearing this, Wukong immediately leaped into the air and called down, "O Master of Seven Buddhas, merciful Lord! Why do you plot to harm me!" The Bodhisattva replied, "I, this big-headed donkey demon, this ignorant red ass! I have already gone to great lengths to save this disciple who will obtain the scriptures. I have repeatedly instructed him to save your life. Why have you not thanked me for saving your life? Instead, you complain to me!" Wukong said, "You've got me into a bad situation! You've already set me free, allowing me to be at ease and play. You said yesterday that I should serve the Priest with all my heart and soul. Why, then, did you send him a flowered hat and deceive me into wearing it and enduring pain? You put this magical headband on my head, and made the old monk recite a Tight Headband Spell over and over, causing me constant pain. This is why you're harming me!" The Bodhisattva smiled and said, "Monkey, if you don't obey the precepts and don't accept the right path, I must keep you restrained. Otherwise, you would deceive the Buddha and God again, knowing right from wrong. If you were to cause trouble again, who would subdue you? You must accept this demon as your path to Yoga." Wukong said, "If that's the case, let this be my demon. But why did you send this sinner, the demon dragon, here to wreak havoc and make him eat my master's horse? This is too much, allowing evil-doers to run free." The Bodhisattva said, "The dragon was given to me personally by the Jade Emperor to serve as the mount for the disciple who seeks the scriptures. You see, the ordinary horses from the east cannot endure the myriad waters and mountains, nor can they reach the Buddha's land in the Shansi region. You must have this dragon horse to proceed." Wukong said, "How can I endure such fear and hide forever?" The Bodhisattva called to Jiedi, "Go to the edge of the ravine and shout, 'Ao Ren Dragon King, Jade Dragon Third Prince, come out, the South Sea Bodhisattva is here.'" Jiedi indeed went to the ravine and shouted twice. The dragon plunged through the waves, jumped out of the water, and transformed into a person, floating in the clouds to the air and bowing to the Bodhisattva. "I have been waiting for a long time since I was released, but I have not heard any news of the disciple who seeks the scriptures." The Bodhisattva pointed to Wukong and said, "Is this not the Tang Priest's chief disciple?" The dragon said, "Bodhisattva, this is my enemy. I was hungry yesterday and indeed ate his horse. He took advantage of his strength and fought me to a standstill, forcing me to retreat and then refusing to let me out of my den. He never mentioned the scriptures at all." Wukong said:

"Where have you come from?" Ksitigarbha asked. "The Tang Priest lost his horse at Eagle Eagle Gorge in Snake-Coil Mountain. The Great Sage is at a loss whether to advance or retreat. After asking the local deities, it turned out that the demon dragon had swallowed it. The Great Sage sent me to ask for your help to subdue this demon dragon and return the horse." The Bodhisattva said, "This creature is the son of Ao Runtu, the king of the Western Sea. He burned the palace lights and was sentenced to death for defying his father. I interceded for him with the Jade Emperor, and he was allowed to serve the Tang Priest as his mount. How did he consume the priest’s horse? Since you say so, I will go and see." The Bodhisattva descended from the lotus platform and left his celestial abode. With Ksitigarbha, he took on divine light and came from the South Sea. There was a poem to commemorate:  
"Three Sutras of Maitreya is the name,  
Goodness fills the Great Wall, true is its fame.  
Mahayana words through heaven and earth ring,  
True dharma rescues spirits, both men and beast bring.  
Chán master escapes his shell, anew he rises.  
Xuanzang once again starts his quest.  
Eagle Eagle Gorge stops his way,  
A demon dragon takes the form of a horse’s day."  
The Bodhisattva and Ksitigarbha soon arrived at Snake-Coil Mountain. They halted in mid-air and looked down. They saw that the Great Sage was indeed calling out by the ravine. The Bodhisattva had Ksitigarbha call him. Ksitigarbha descended and approached the ravine, shouting, "The Bodhisattva is here!" The Great Sage, hearing this, leapt into the air and shouted at him, "You, the teacher of seven Buddhas, merciful king! How did you devise to harm me?" The Bodhisattva said, "I call you bold and stupid, foolish Red Ass! I have repeatedly tried to guide you, and succeeded in saving the Tang Priest. I advised him to save your life. Why do you not thank me for this life you owe me, but instead quarrel with me?" The Great Sage said, "You treated me very badly! If you had merely released me to be free, you could have gone and told the Tang Priest to leave me alone. You only recently injured me in the sea, telling me to serve the Tang Priest. Why did you send me a floral hat to wear and trick me into wearing a tighter bond on my head? Isn’t this all to harm me?" The Bodhisattva smiled and said, "You monkey! If you do not obey my command and receive the proper reward, I must bind you to stop you from going against the will of the Buddha. Otherwise, you will deceive the Buddha and cause another disaster. You must understand the benefits of following my command!" The Great Sage said, "If I am to be your bond, why are you sending the guilty demon dragon here to cause trouble, letting it devour my master’s horse? This is to release a bad man to cause evil, which is very unkind!" The Bodhisattva said, "The dragon, I personally requested from the Jade Emperor to be here to assist the Tang Priest on his journey. Think about it—how could ordinary horses from the East bear the journey over thousands of rivers and mountains and make it to the Pure Land of Buddha? Only this dragon can make the journey." The Great Sage said, "Since he fears me so much, how can I solve this?" The Bodhisattva called Ksitigarbha, "Go to the ravine and shout, 'Ao Runtu, Prince of Dragons, Youngest Son of Jade Green Dragon, come out, the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea is here.'" Ksitigarbha went to the ravine and called twice. The dragon emerged from the water, transformed into a man, and flew to the sky to bow to the Bodhisattva. "I have been waiting for your grace for a long time," the dragon said, "but I have not heard from the Tang Priest." The Bodhisattva pointed to the Great Sage and said, "Isn’t this the Tang Priest’s disciple?" The dragon said, "Bodhisattva, this is my foe. I was hungry yesterday and did indeed consume his horse. I rely on a bit of strength and fought until I was exhausted, and he cursed me until I dared not come out. He never mentioned the Tang Priest or the quest." The Great Sage:

"Where have you come from?" Jiedi asked. "The Tang Monk lost his horse at Eagle-Fearful Ravine in Snake-Coiling Mountain, and the Great Sage is at a loss whether to advance or retreat. After inquiring from the local gods, it was said that the Buddha sent a demon dragon there who swallowed the horse. The Great Sage sent this small deity to beg the Buddha to subdue the demon dragon and return his horse." Upon hearing this, the Buddha said, "This monster was originally the son of Ao Ren, the lord of the Western Sea. He set fire to the palace and burned the pearl in the throne hall, and his father reported him for treason. He was sentenced to death by the heavenly court. I personally pleaded with the Jade Emperor and obtained him, instructing him to serve as the Tang Monk's mount. How did he eat the Tang Monk's horse? Based on your words, I will go see for myself." The Buddha descended from the lotus platform, left the fairy cave, and with Jiedi riding the auspicious light, they arrived at South Sea. There was a poem to verify, saying: "The Buddha recites the honey-dew Tripitaka Sutra, and the bodhisattva propounds goodness filling the Great Wall. Great妙 verses reach the heavens, and the true words of Prajna save the spirits. Thus golden蝉 can molt again, and hence the pilgrim must undergo re-ascension. Only because the road is blocked by Eagle-Fearful Ravine does the dragon son return to his true form, transforming into a horse. The Buddha and Jiedi did not take long to arrive at Snake-Coiling Mountain. They paused the auspicious clouds in mid-air and looked down. They saw Sun Wukong roaring by the ravine. The Buddha instructed Jiedi to call him down. Jiedi landed and, without passing by the Three Baskets, went directly to the ravine and called out to Wukong, "The Buddha is here." Hearing this, Wukong hurriedly ascended to the sky and bellowed at him, "You, my seven-buddha master, compassionate and merciful lord! How did you devise a method to harm me!" The Buddha said, "I'll have you know, reckless horse spirit, crude and ignorant Red Ass! I have repeatedly tried my utmost to guide the scriptures-carrier. I advised him to save your life, yet you have not thanked me for saving your life and instead are clamoring at me!" Wukong said, "You have treated me terribly! You set me free; let me have my own free and easy time. You hurt me on the sea before, telling me to serve the Tang Monk wholeheartedly. Why did you give him a flowered hat and trick me into wearing it, making me endure the torment? You fastened this band on my head, and taught him to recite some tight-head incantation, making the old monk recite it over and over again, causing me pain over and over, which isn't you harming me?" The Buddha laughed and said, "You, this monkey! If you don't abide by the teachings, you won't obtain the true fruit. If not for this method of restraint, you would again mislead the heavens and know no good or bad! If you make such a ruckus again, who will rein you in? You must enter the path of yoga through this demonic force." Wukong said, "This matter, consider me your demonic force, but why send the guilty demon dragon here to cause trouble, making him devour my master's horse? This is allowing the wicked to do evil, which is too unjust!" The Buddha said, "That dragon was personally presented to the Jade Emperor by me, stationed here to serve the scriptures-carrier as a mount. You see that ordinary horse from the East can't endure the thousands of mountains and rivers or reach the Buddha's holy land. It must be this dragon horse to go there." Wukong said, "Given his fear of me and his hiding, what should I do?" The Buddha called to Jiedi, "Go call out by the ravine, 'Come out, Ao Ren Dragon King's jade dragon third prince, the Buddha is here.'" The small deity indeed called out two times by the ravine. That small dragon swirled the waves and leapt out of the water, transforming into a human figure, riding the clouds to the sky and bowing to the Buddha. "I have been waiting here for a long time since the Buddha saved my life, and I haven't heard any news of the scriptures-carrier." The Buddha pointed to Wukong and said, "This is the scriptures-carrier's great disciple." The small dragon saw and said, "Buddha, this is my nemesis. I was hungry yesterday and indeed ate his horse. He relied on his strength and fought me until I was weak and fled, and he taunted me until I was afraid to come out. He never mentioned the scriptures-carrier." Wukong said:

—I was passionately in love with your mother when she was still engaged, the fiancée of my friend. The prince noticed and was taken aback. He came to me in the morning at seven o'clock, woke me up. I dressed in amazement; there was silence from both sides; I understood everything. He took out two pistols from his pocket. Through a handkerchief. Without witnesses. What witnesses when, in five minutes, we are sending each other to eternity? We loaded the guns, stretched the handkerchief, stood facing each other, and pressed the pistols to our hearts and looked into each other's faces. Suddenly, tears fell in streams from both our eyes, and our hands began to shake. At the same time, for both of us! So, naturally, we embraced and fought with generosity. The prince shouted: "Mine!" I shouted: "Mine!" In short... in short... you'll have to come... to live?

If anyone had told him at that moment that he was in love, in a passionate love, he would have rejected the idea with surprise and, perhaps, even indignation. And if someone had added that Aglaya’s note was a love letter, an invitation to a romantic rendezvous, he would have been consumed with shame for that person and, perhaps, challenged him to a duel. All of this was utterly sincere, and he never doubted or entertained the slightest “doubtful” thought about the possibility of this girl’s love for him or even about the possibility of his own love for her. The idea of her loving “such a person as he” he considered monstrous. He felt it was merely a prank on her part, if there was anything at all; but he was somehow too indifferent to the prank itself and found it too much in the ordinary course of things; what he was occupied with and troubled by was something entirely different. He believed wholeheartedly what the agitated general had said the other day, that she ridiculed everyone, especially Prince. He felt no slighting or offense; in his opinion, it should have been so. The main thing for him was that he would see her again tomorrow, early in the morning, would sit next to her on a green bench, listen to the pistol being loaded, and look at her. Nothing else was needed of him. The question of what she intended to tell him and what such important matter, directly affecting him, was also flashed through his mind a couple of times. He did not doubt the existence of this “important matter” for which he was being called; he did not think about it much now, not even feeling the slightest urge to think about it.

Thus reasoning, Seliyanin finally drifted into the most distant abstractions. If Pokhify had listened, he would have learned many details pertaining to himself; but his thoughts were so engrossed with their subject that only a powerful thunderclap jolted him awake and made him look around. The entire sky was completely overcast, and the dusty postal road was sprinkled with raindrops. Finally, another thunderclap reverberated louder and closer, and the rain poured down like from a bucket. At first, it lashed the kibitka’s box obliquely in one direction, then in another, then changed its mode of attack and began to beat straight into the top of its box; droplets finally splashed into his face. This made him draw the leather curtains with two circular windows, intended for observing the roadside, and command Seliyanin to ride faster. Seliyanin, interrupted in the middle of his speech as well, realized that he really shouldn’t delay. He took off a piece of grey serge from under the yoke, put it on over his shoulders, grabbed the reins in his hands, and barked at his team, which barely shuffled its hooves, sensing a pleasant relaxation from the instructive discourse. But Seliyanin could not remember how many turns he had taken. Realizing and trying to recall the route, he guessed that he had missed a multitude of turns. Since a Russian person finds something to do in critical moments without dwelling on distant speculations, he turned right onto the first crossroad and barked: "Hey you, respected friends!" and spurred on, scarcely thinking about where the chosen road would lead.

As a Russian in a decisive moment knows what to do without wasting time on far-fetched considerations, he turned to the right onto the first crossroad and shouted: "Holla, you honored gentlemen!" and spurred on, barely considering where the chosen road would lead him.

But they had not even climbed the stairs when the painter above had flung open the door and invited K. to enter with a deep bow. The girls, on the other hand, he refused entry to; he did not want any of them to come in, despite their pleading and their attempts to force their way in, whether with or against his will. Only the hunchback managed to slip through under his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, grabbed her by the skirts, spun her around, and then sent her back to the other girls at the door, whom he had not dared to cross even while he was away. K. did not know how to judge the whole affair, for everything seemed to be happening in friendly accord. The girls at the door stretched their necks one after another towards the top, called out to the painter various jesting words that K. could not understand, and the painter laughed while the hunchback flew in his hands. Then he closed the door, bowed to K. again, held out his hand, and, introducing himself, said, "Kunstmaler Titorelli." K. gestured towards the door behind which the girls were whispering and said, "They seem to be very popular in the house." "Oh, those silly faces!" said the painter and struggled in vain to button his nightshirt at the neck. He was, after all, barefoot and only clad in a broad, yellowish linen pantaloons tied with a belt whose long end swung freely back and forth. "These silly faces are a real burden to me," he continued, now letting go of the nightshirt, whose last button had just popped off, as he fetched a chair and forced K. to sit down. "I once painted one of them—they weren’t even there today—and since then they have all been chasing me. When I am here, they only come in if I allow them, but the moment I leave, there is always at least one there. They have made a key to my door, which they pass around among themselves. It is hard to imagine how bothersome this is. For example, I come home with a lady I am supposed to paint, open the door with my key, and find the hunchback there at the little table, painting her lips red with the brush while her little sisters, whom she has to look after, run around and dirty the room in all corners. Or I come home late at night, as it happened to me yesterday—I beg your pardon, please, take into account my condition and the mess in the room—I come home late at night and want to go to bed, when something pricks my leg, and I find another one of them under the bed. I do not know why they crowd me so; you may have noticed that I do not seek to invite them to me. Naturally, this also interferes with my work. If this studio had not been provided to me for free, I would have moved out long ago." Just then, a soft and frightened voice was heard from behind the door: "Titorelli, may we already come in?" "No," answered the painter. "Not even me?" asked the voice again. "Not even me," said the painter, went to the door, and locked it.

On the other hand, he refused the girls; he would not let them in, despite their pleading and their attempts to force their way in, whether with or against his will. Only the Hunchback managed to slip through under his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, grabbed her by the skirts, spun her around, and then put her back out in front of the door among the other girls, who had not dared to cross the threshold while the painter was absent. K. did not know how to judge the whole affair, as it seemed to be taking place in a friendly agreement. The girls at the door stretched their necks one after the other upwards, shouted various jokes to the painter, which K. did not understand, and the painter laughed, while the Hunchback flew in his arms. Then he closed the door, bowed to K. once more, held out his hand, and said, introducing himself: "Painter Titorelli." K. pointed to the door behind which the girls were whispering and said: "They seem to be very popular in the house." "Ah, the masks!" said the painter and vainly tried to button his nightshirt at the neck. He was barefooted and only wearing a broad, yellow linen trousers tied up with a belt whose long end dangled freely to and fro. "These masks are a real burden to me," he continued, as he allowed the nightshirt, whose last button had just come off, to hang loosely, fetched a chair, and compelled K. to sit down. "I once painted one of them—she’s not here today—and since then they’ve been after me all the time. When I’m here, they only come in if I allow them, but as soon as I leave, then there’s always at least one there. They’ve had a key to my door made, which they pass around among themselves. One can hardly imagine how annoying that is. For example, when I come home late at night with a lady I’m painting, open the door with my key, and find the Hunchback at the little table, painting her lips red with a brush while her little siblings, whom she has to look after, are playing and dirtying the room in all corners. Or, as happened to me yesterday, I come home late at night and want to go to bed, when something bites me on the leg, I look under the bed, and draw out such a thing again. I don’t know why they crowd me like this; I certainly haven’t sought to lure them to me, as you can probably see. Naturally, I’m also disturbed in my work by this. If this studio weren’t provided to me for free, I would have moved out already." Just then, a little voice behind the door called out, soft and timid: "Titorelli, may we come already?" "No," the painter answered. "Not even me?" it asked again. "Not even me," the painter said, went to the door, and locked it.

"I do not want public success as a speaker," K. said, coming to this conclusion. "It is probably not within my reach anyway. The Judge in Charge of Investigation likely speaks much better; after all, it is part of his profession. What I want is merely the public discussion of a public malpractice. Listen: I was arrested about ten days ago. I laugh at the fact of my arrest myself, but that does not belong here. I was attacked in bed early in the night. Perhaps, as the Judge in Charge of Investigation said, such an order was not impossible, but someone else was chosen instead of one of the innocent painters in the neighboring room. The next room was guarded by two rough guards. If I had been a dangerous criminal, they could not have been more careful. Moreover, these guards were demoralized riffraff; they chattered away incessantly, wanted to be bribed, tricked me into giving up my clothes, and were trying to get money to bring me a breakfast after they had shamelessly eaten mine in front of my eyes. But that was not enough. I was led into a third room to see the supervisor. It was the room of a lady whom I greatly respect, and I had to watch her room, which had been tainted by my presence, being made a public spectacle of by the guards and the supervisor, without my fault. It was not easy to remain calm. But I managed to do so, and I asked the supervisor, who is sitting here now on the chair of the said lady in a position of utmost obtuse arrogance, why I was arrested. What did this supervisor, whom I can see now, answer? My dear sirs, he basically did not answer at all. Perhaps he really did not know anything; he had me arrested and was content with that. Moreover, he brought three low-level employees from my bank into that lady’s room, who made a mess of and touched her belongings. The presence of these employees had a second purpose: to spread the news of my arrest, damage my public reputation, and in particular, shake my position at the bank. Nothing of this succeeded. Even my landlady, a simple woman – I will name her here with honor, she is called Frau Grubach – was sensible enough to see that such an arrest does not mean more than an attempt by boys on the street who were not properly supervised. I repeat, the whole affair has only caused me inconvenience and temporary distress. But could it not have had even worse consequences?"

The incident at the station had struck both the mother and her daughters almost with terror. In her anxiety and agitation, Mrs. Prokofyevna practically ran out of the station with her daughters all the way home. In her gaze and perceptions, too much had transpired during this incident for her mind, despite the disorder and fright, to begin formulating firm thoughts. However, everyone sensed that something extraordinary had occurred, and that perhaps a certain extraordinary secret was starting to be revealed. Despite the previous assurances and explanations of Prince Sh., Eugene Pavlovich was now "exposed," accused, and formally "uncovered" in his connections with this creature. This was what Mrs. Prokofyevna and even the two elder daughters believed. The benefit from this revelation was that even more enigmas were accumulating. The girls, though partially vexed by the excessive fright and their mother's evident flight, did not trouble her with questions in the first moments of confusion. Moreover, for some reason, they thought that their sister Aglaya Ivanovna might know more about the matter than they, their mother, and Eugene Pavlovich combined. Prince Sh. was also gloomy as night and very contemplative. Mrs. Prokofyevna did not speak to him the entire journey home, and it seemed he did not notice. Adelaida tried to ask him: "About which uncle were they speaking, and what happened in St. Petersburg?" But he grumbled something vague about some inquiries and said that it was all a nonsensical affair. "There is no doubt about that!" Adelaida replied and no longer asked anything. Aglaya became unusually calm and remarked only on the road that they were running too quickly. When she turned and saw Prince Sh. chasing after them, she smiled mockingly and thereafter did not look back at him.

—"Gentlemen," the general began, "I, like everyone else, have committed less than elegant deeds in my life, but the strangest thing is that I consider the little anecdote I am about to relate to be the worst of all my life. Yet, almost thirty-five years have passed; but I could never tear myself away from the memory of a certain, as it were, heart-crawling impression. The matter, however, is rather silly: I was still a cornet at the time and a supply officer. Blood was like boiling water, and I was pinched for funds; then there was my orderly, Nikifor, who cared immensely about my household, hoarded, mended, and polished everything, and even stole, as he could, just to augment it; he was a veritable paragon of honesty and trustworthiness. Naturally, I was strict but fair. We had been stationed in a city for a while. An apartment in the suburb had been assigned to me by an old retired cornet and widow. She was probably eighty, or at least close to it. Her cottage was dilapidated and made of wood; she had no maidservant due to poverty. But, what distinguished her most, was that she had once had a large family and many relatives; some had died, others had scattered, and still others had forgotten her, while her husband had been laid to rest nearly forty-five years ago. A few years before, a niece, hunchbacked and reportedly as evil as a witch, had still been living with her. It is said she once bit the old woman on the finger, but she too had since died, leaving the old woman to struggle alone for three years. It was dull to be with her, and she was so empty that there was nothing to be gained from her. Finally, she stole my rooster. To this day, it remains a mystery, but she was the only one. We quarreled over the rooster, and then a chance arose to move to another apartment in the opposite suburb, in a large household of a bearded merchant, whom I remember now. Nikifor and I moved there happily, but we left the old woman with disgust. Three days had passed when I returned from my duties and was informed by Nikifor that "we forgot to take our saucepan from the old lady and have no bowl for soup." Naturally, I was stunned: "How could that happen? How did our saucepan end up with the old lady?" Nikifor, puzzled, continued his report, saying that when we moved out, the old lady did not return our saucepan because, as I had accidentally broken her own pot, she was keeping the saucepan for her own pot. She claimed I had proposed this to her. Such low behavior on her part, of course, put me over the edge; my blood boiled, I stood up, and rushed off. I arrived at the old lady's, already beside myself; she was sitting alone in the attic, huddled in a corner as if from the sun's rays, her hand propping up her cheek. I immediately, I must admit, let loose on her a torrent of abuse: "How dare you, and how else can you describe it?" and so on in the Russian vernacular. But I noticed something strange: she was sitting, looking at me, her eyes wide open, not a word in reply, and strangely, strangely, as if she was swaying. I finally calmed down, gazed at her, and asked, but there was no answer. I stood there in indecision for a while; the flies buzzed, the sun was setting, and there was silence. I left in utter confusion. Before I reached the door, I was summoned by the major, and later, I had to visit the company, so I did not arrive home until late evening. The first word out of Nikifor's mouth was: "Your honor, the old lady has died." "When?" "About an hour ago." This means she died right at the moment when I was reprimanding her. This thought struck me so forcefully that I hardly recovered my composure. It started to haunt me, even at night, in my dreams. I have no prejudices, but on the third day, I went to church for her funeral. In short, the more time passed, the more I dwelled on it. It was not that, but it was sometimes as if I imagined things and it would become unpleasant. The main point is this: how, in the end, did I finally understand it? First, a woman, a human being, considered humane and civilized in our time, had lived, had lived long, had finally settled down. At one time, she had children, a husband, a family, relatives; all this was buzzing around her, all these smiles; then, everything vanished, and she was left alone, like a fly carrying a curse with her for all eternity. Finally, God brought her to an end. At sunset, on a quiet summer evening, my old woman left this earth—of course, there was a moral lesson in this. And at this exact moment, instead of saying farewell, a young, desperate cornet, cussing and cursing, took her off the earth's surface with Russian obscenities for losing the saucepan! No doubt, I am guilty, and though I look back on the deed from a great distance and through the prism of changed nature, I still feel sorry for it. That is why, I repeat, it is strange to me, even more so since if I am guilty, it was not entirely; why would she choose this very moment to die? Of course, there is an excuse: the act was of a certain psychological nature, but I could not calm down until fifteen years ago when I established two permanently ill old ladies in an almshouse on my own account, with the aim of easing their last days with proper care. I wanted to leave a legacy for eternity. That's it, and that's all. I repeat that, perhaps, I may have sinned in many ways in my life, but I consider this incident to be the worst of all my life by honest reckoning.

— Gentlemen, I have indeed, as everyone has, committed unbecoming acts in my life, — the general began. — But what is strangest of all is that I myself consider the little anecdote I am about to relate to be the worst of all my life. Yet it has been almost thirty-five years; but I never could rid myself of the memory of a certain, so to speak, gnawing sensation. The matter, however, was a thoroughly silly one: I was then still a mere second lieutenant, still a recruit in the army. Blood was boiling, money was scarce. I had a trooper, Nikifor, who worried endlessly about my household, hoarded, darned, scrubbed, and even, wherever he could, stole the tiniest thing in order to increase his mistress’s possessions; he was a most trustworthy and honest man. Of course, I was strict, but fair. For a while, we were stationed in a small town. They gave me a room in the outer part of the town, at the home of an officer who had left the army and was a widow. She was about eighty, or at least looked it. The house was dilapidated, of wood, and she had no servant, owing to poverty. But what distinguished her was that she had once had a large family and many relatives; but some had died, others had dispersed, and the few relatives who remained had forgotten her; and she had been widowed more than forty years before. For a time, her niece, a hunchbacked and, it was said, evil-looking old woman, had lived with her, but she had died too, leaving the old woman to fend for herself for three years. I found her rather dull, and a rather empty life, and nothing could be extracted from her. Finally, she stole a cock from me. The matter remains unclear to this day, but there was no one else. We had a falling out over the cock, and I was rather vexed, and then it so happened that, at my request, they moved me to another room, opposite the town, in the home of a merchant with a large family and a long beard. Nikifor and I moved with gladness; but we left the old woman in anger. After three days, I returned from duty, and Nikifor reported that “we had forgotten to take our bowl from our former mistress, we have nothing with which to serve the soup.” Of course, I was taken aback: “How so? How did our bowl come to be at our former mistress’s home?” Nikifor, surprised, reported that when we were moving out, the mistress refused to give him our bowl because, as I had broken her own pot, she was withholding our bowl as a compensation. He even claimed that I had so suggested. This baseness on her part, of course, infuriated me to the last degree; blood boiled, I jumped up, and ran. I went to the old woman, nearly out of my mind; she was sitting in a dark corner, like someone who had fled the sun, resting her cheek on her hand. I immediately, you see, gave her a tongue-lashing: “You are such, you are such!” — I even used Russian. But I noticed something strange: she sat, stared at me, her eyes wide open, and did not speak a word, but stared so strangely, as if she were swaying. I calmed down and, looking at her, asked, but still no answer. I stood there undecided, the flies were buzzing, the sun was setting, and there was silence; I left in great confusion. I had not even reached home before I was summoned to a major, and then I had to visit the regiment, and I did not return home until late that evening. The first thing Nikifor said was: “Your Excellency, our former mistress is dead.” “When?” “An hour and a half ago.” This means, at the exact moment I was berating her, she passed away. This flabbergasted me; I tell you, I barely came to my senses. I even began to think about it, and it even entered my dreams. I had no prejudices, but on the third day, I went to church for the funeral. In short, as time went on, it became more and more evident to me. It is not that I thought about it, but sometimes I could imagine it, and it was unpleasant. The main thing, as I finally reasoned out, is that this woman, to use a term of our time, was human, humane, and lived a long life, settling into her lot. At one time, she had children, a husband, a family, relatives, and all of them were, as it were, bustling around her, all those smiles, and then — poof, everything was gone, and she was left alone, like a fly that has borne a curse for all time. And so, the good Lord took her to her end. At sunset, on a peaceful summer evening, my old woman took to the air, of course, with a moral lesson; and at that moment, instead of a parting tear, a young, desperate second lieutenant, in a rage, cursed her out with blue words for having lost the bowl! Undoubtedly, I was in the wrong, and even now, looking at my action from a great distance of time and with a changed nature, as if it were someone else’s, I still regret it. That is why, as I say, it is strange, and even more so, because if I am in the wrong, I am not entirely in the wrong: why did she have to die just then? Of course, the only explanation is that the act was somewhat psychological, but still, I could not be at peace until fifteen years ago, when I began to maintain, at my own expense, two bedridden old women in an almshouse with a view to giving them a proper support during the last days of their earthly life. I wanted to leave a bequest. And that’s all. I repeat that I may have sinned in many ways in life, but I consider this act the worst of all my life by honest reckoning.

— Gentlemen, as with everyone, I have sometimes done ungraceful things in my life, — began the general. — But strangest of all is that I myself consider the short anecdote I am about to recount to be the worst of my entire life. Yet it has been almost thirty-five years; yet I could never detach myself from it, even when remembering, from a certain, as it were, gnawing feeling. However, the matter is a very trivial one: I was then still only a second lieutenant and a teamster in the army. As is known, a second lieutenant: blood is boiling, and household affairs are pence. A valet, Nikifor, had come to me at the time, and he was utterly concerned with my household affairs, saving, mending, cleaning, and even stole everything he could, to increase his mistress’s household, for he was a most faithful and honest person. Of course, I was strict, but fair. It so happened that we were stationed in a town for some time. A flat was allocated to me in the suburbs by a retired lieutenant-colonel, who was a widow. She was eighty years old, or at least that is what I was told. Her house was old and shabby, wooden, and she even did not have a maid because of her poverty. But, most importantly, she was distinguished by the fact that she once had a large family and many relatives; but some had died during her lifetime, others had scattered, and others had forgotten her, while her husband had been buried forty-five years ago. She still had a niece with her, who was hunchbacked, and they said she was as evil as a witch, even once bit the old lady on the finger; but she had also died, so the old lady spent the last three years alone. Living with her was dreary and futile, so she stole a cock from me. The matter remained mysterious to this day, but no one else was to blame. Over the cock, we quarreled, and quite strongly, and just then there happened to be an opportunity for me, as a favor to me, to be transferred to another flat in the opposite suburb, in the numerous household of a certain merchant with a large beard, as I remember him. We moved with Nikifor with great pleasure, but we left the old lady with great displeasure. After three days, I returned from my lessons, and Nikifor reported to me, "Your honor, we left our bowl with the former mistress, there is no bowl to serve soup." I was, of course, shocked: "How is that, how could our bowl end up with the mistress?" Nikifor, surprised, continued to report that when we moved out, the mistress did not return our bowl because, as she said, since I had broken her own bowl, she was holding on to our bowl, and that I had supposedly offered this to her. Such baseness on her part, of course, made me lose my last nerves; blood began to boil, I jumped up and went off. I arrived at the old lady’s already in a rage; I looked, she was sitting alone in the hayloft, in a corner, as if from the sun she had retreated, and supported her cheek with her hand. I immediately, you know, poured a whole storm on her, "What, such and such a thing!" and, you know, in Russian. Only I looked, something strange presented itself: she was sitting, staring at me, her eyes bulging, and no word in answer, and strangely, strangely, she stared, as if swaying. I finally calmed down, gazed at her, asked, and she did not answer. I stood there indecisively; the flies buzzed, the sun was setting, and silence reigned; in utter bewilderment, I finally left. I had not yet reached home when I was called to the major, and then I had to visit the company, so I did not return home until well into the evening. The first words of Nikifor were: "Your honor, did you know that our mistress died?" "When?" "It was just this evening, about an hour ago." That is, at the very moment when I was reprimanding her, she passed away. This struck me so much, I can tell you, that I barely came to my senses. It began to occur to me, even in the night, and I even dreamed about it. I, of course, without prejudice, but on the third day I went to church for the funeral. In short, as time went on, it began to seem more and more so. It was not that I thought so, but sometimes I would imagine it, and it would become unpleasant. The main thing is, as I finally concluded? First of all, a woman, as it were, a human being, called a human, a gentle, creature lived, lived long, and at last settled down. She had once had children, a husband, a family, all around her, so to speak, bubbled with activity, and all these, as it were, smiles, and then—total silence, everything disappeared, and she was left alone, like... a fly, bearing a curse for eternity. And finally, God brought her to an end. In the evening, at a quiet summer sunset, the old woman took to the air, of course, with a moral lesson; and at that very moment, instead of a farewell tear, a young, reckless second lieutenant, in an uproar and with an oath, cursed her for a broken bowl! There is no doubt that I am to blame, and although I look at my actions long ago, from the remoteness of the years and the change in my nature, as someone else’s, I still continue to regret. So, I repeat, it is strange to me, and especially so, because if I am to blame, then certainly not entirely: why would she, just at that time, think of dying? Of course, there is one excuse: that the action was, in a certain sense, psychological, but I could not calm down until fifteen years ago, when I brought two permanent old ladies, on my own account, to a home for the poor, with the purpose of making their last days of earthly life more pleasant. I thought to leave this to posterity with a legacy. Well, that’s all. I repeat that, perhaps, I did many things wrong in life, but I consider this incident, by conscience, to be the worst of my entire life.

"Look at you all sitting here!" Leni called out, returning with the cup and standing in the doorway. They were really huddled close together; at the slightest turn of the head, they bumped foreheads. The merchant, though not small, still hunched, had forced K. to bow deeply if he wanted to hear everything. "Just a little longer!" K. shouted at Leni, waving his hand impatiently, still holding it over the merchant’s hand. "He wanted me to tell him about my case," the merchant said to Leni. "Tell on, tell on," she said. She spoke to the merchant affectionately but also with a hint of condescension, and K. did not like it. Now he realized the man did have some worth; at least he had experiences to share. Leni probably underestimated him. He angrily watched as Leni now took the candle the merchant had held onto the whole time, wiped his hand with her apron, and then knelt beside him to scrape off some wax that had dripped onto his trousers. "You wanted to tell me about the side attorneys," K. said, pushing Leni’s hand away without further comment. "What do you want?" Leni asked, lightly swatting at K. and continuing her work. "Yes, about the side attorneys," the merchant said, rubbing his forehead as if in thought. K. wanted to help and said, "They wanted immediate success and went to the side attorneys for that reason." "Quite right," the merchant said, but did not continue. K. thought, perhaps he did not want to speak of it in front of Leni, and gave in to his impatience for now to hear the rest, no longer pressing the merchant for more.
