"You didn't ask me my surname and given name, so how could I tell you?" said Little Dragon. "You didn't ask me where I came from, you braying devil! You shouted, 'Mind you, where I come from or where I don't, just return my horse to me!' Did you say a single 'Tang'?" said the Bodhisattva. "That monkey, always relying on his own strength, won't praise others. This time, there might be one who submits. If you ask, mention the words 'bearing scriptures' first, and you won't have to trouble your mind. They'll naturally bow to you." The Monkey King was delighted and listened intently. The Bodhisattva stepped forward, removed the gem from Little Dragon's neck, and with a willow branch dipped in sweet dew, brushed Little Dragon's body. With a breath of divine breath, she called out, "Transform!" The dragon immediately turned into the horse's skin and fur it had originally been. The Bodhisattva then instructed, "You must concentrate on eliminating your业障 (transgressions). When you accomplish your task, you will transcend the status of an ordinary dragon and receive a golden body as a reward for your virtue." Little Dragon carried the crossbeam in its mouth, heartedly agreeing. The Bodhisattva told the Monkey King to lead the dragon to see Tang Sanzang and then departed to the sea. The Monkey King held onto the Bodhisattva, refusing to let go. "I'm not going! I'm not going! The road to the West is so rugged, protecting this ordinary monk, when will I ever arrive? With all this difficulty, my life is in danger. How can I achieve any merit? I'm not going! I'm not going!" said the Bodhisattva. "You were not a person yet and you were willing to make efforts to attain enlightenment; now that you have escaped the disasters of heaven, how can you become lazy? In our path, achieving the true is through tranquility and cessation, so you must maintain sincere faith."

In our sect, true enlightenment comes from selflessness and sincerity. You must be firm in your beliefs."

"You did not ask me my surname and given name, so how could I have spoken?" said Little Dragon. "I did not ask if you were a魔 from somewhere; you roared, 'What does it matter where you came from? Just give me back my horse!' You never said a single word about Tang!" The Bodhisattva said, "That monkey is always proud, and would never praise another. This time, he may yet submit. If you ask him, mention the journey to fetch scriptures first, and you won't have to exert yourself; naturally, he will submit." The Monkey delightedly accepted this advice. The Bodhisattva stepped forward and plucked the gem from Little Dragon's neck, dipped the willow branch in the sweet dew, and brushed it over him, then blew a breath of divine breath and called, "Change!" The dragon immediately transformed into the horse's original skin, and the Bodhisattva gave him further instructions: "You must concentrate on paying off your karmic debt. Once your work is done, you will rise above the common dragon and receive a golden body and true fruit." Little Dragon, holding the withers in his mouth, silently promised to comply. The Bodhisattva instructed the Monkey to take the dragon to see the Three Sages and said, "I will return to the sea." The Monkey held back the Bodhisattva, refusing to let go. "I'm not going! I'm not going! The road to the West is so difficult, and protecting this ordinary monk, when will we ever get there? With so much suffering and hardship, my life is already in danger, how can I achieve any fruit? I'm not going! I'm not going!" The Bodhisattva said, "When you were not human and could not comprehend the path, you were still willing to cultivate; now that you have escaped the disaster of heaven, how can you suddenly become lazy? In our lineage, achieving the truth through quietude is crucial; you must have sincere faith and a true fruit."

One day, inside the cave, the Monkey King ordered his four chief lieutenants to prepare a feast and invited the Six Kings to join in the drinking, slaughtering cattle and horses, and sacrificing to heaven and earth. He instructed all the monsters to dance and sing in celebration. They all became so tipsy they were utterly drunk. After seeing the Six Kings off, he rewarded the senior and junior leaders and leaned against the iron plank bridge under the shade of the pines, falling asleep. The four chief lieutenants surrounded him, keeping quiet. Suddenly, he saw two individuals carrying a document with the name "Sun Wukong" written on it. Approaching him, they did not allow him to object and put a rope around his soul, pulling him away. The Monkey King stumbled and was dragged to the edge of a city. He gradually woke up from the alcohol, looked up, and saw a iron plaque with the three characters "Yōumíng Jì" (幽冥界) on it. Sun Wukong suddenly realized, "Yōumíng Jì is where King Yama resides. How could I be here?" The two individuals said, "Your life span in the mortal realm is over, and we, bearing the orders, have come to fetch you." Upon hearing this, the Monkey King said, "I, Old Sun, surpass the Three Realms and do not exist within the Five Elements; I am beyond their jurisdiction. Why do you come to disturb my peace?" The two plotters of death persisted, pulling him towards the city. The Monkey King was infuriated and, from his ear, pulled out a treasured item and shook it; it grew to a size like a bowl. With a slight swing, he smashed both of the plotters into a pulp. He untied himself, flung the rope aside, picked up his cudgel, and charged into the city. This caused the Bullheaded Ghosts to run in every direction, and the Horse-faced Demons to flee to the north and south. The multitude of ghost soldiers rushed to the Holy Assembly Hall and reported, "Lord! Trouble! Trouble! An eccentric雷公 (thunder god) with a tousled face has invaded!"

One day, in the cave, he instructed the four chief officers to arrange a feast, inviting the Six Kings to drink. They slaughtered cattle and horses, sacrificing to the heavens and earth, and had the various fiends dance and sing. They all drank until they were thoroughly drunk. After sending the Six Kings off, he then rewarded the big and small leaders. Leaning against the iron plank bridge under the shade of the pines, he soon fell asleep. The four chief officers surrounded and protected him, daring not to speak loudly. Suddenly, he saw in his dream two people holding a scroll with 'Sun Wukong' written on it. They approached him, refusing to listen to his protests, and tied him with ropes. The spirit of the Monkey King was snatched away in a stumbling, staggering manner, straight to the edge of a city. The Monkey King gradually sobered up, suddenly lifting his head to look, seeing a metal sign on the city wall with three characters: 'Yōumíng Jie' [幽冥界]. The Monkey King suddenly awoke, saying, "Yōumíng Jie is where the King Yama resides. Why have I come here?" The two said, "Your life on earth is now at its end. We are here to fetch you according to the decree." Hearing this, the Monkey King said, "I, the old Sun, am beyond the three realms and not among the five elements, and am not subject to his jurisdiction. How dare you come and fetch me in my drowsiness?" The two snatchers of souls continued to tug and pull, insisting on dragging him in. The Monkey King, infuriated, pulled out a treasure from his ear, waving it to be as thick as a bowl. With a slight wave of his hand, he smashed both snatchers into a pulp. He untied the ropes, threw them aside, and brandished the staff, rushing into the city. The Bull Face Devil dodged and ran, while the Horse Face Devil darted in all directions. The various ghosts hurried to the throne of the Lord of Death, reporting, "Great King! Trouble! Trouble! A furred-faced thunder deity is attacking from outside!"

Awake: a moderate, blue-gray light; glass on the walls, glass armchairs, a glass table. It soothed me, my heart stopped racing. Squeezed juice, Buddha… what absurdity? Clear: I am sick. I have never had dreams before. They say that for the ancients, this was the most normal and ordinary thing – to see dreams. Indeed: after all, their entire life was such a terrifying carousel: green – orange – Buddha – juice. But we know that dreams are a serious mental illness. And I know: up until now, my brain was a chronometer, polished and flawless, without a single speck of dust; now… yes, now precisely this: I feel something alien in my head – like a tiniest eyelash in one's eye: you feel yourself, but that eye with the eyelash – you can't forget it for a second.

And so it was that Heavenly King Li and the Third Prince led their troops to the Golden Cannon Palace. They reported, "We have followed the imperial decree to lead our troops to the mortal world, to subdue the妖仙Monkey Sun. But we were unable to defeat him due to his immense powers. We beseech Your Majesty to send more troops to eliminate him." The Jade Emperor said, "A single monster, how much power can he have? Why do you need more soldiers?" The prince stepped forward and said, "I implore Your Majesty to spare my life! That monkey uses a iron rod to defeat Thunder God and wound my arm. There is a pole outside the cave with the words 'Heavenly Saint Without Peer' inscribed. He claims that as his official title and has declared cease-fire, offering to submit. If he is not granted this title, he vows to storm the Golden Cannon Palace." Upon hearing this, the Jade Emperor was astounded, "How dare this monkey be so presumptuous! Order the troops to immediately eliminate him." Just as he was speaking, the ranks opened and the White Star descended and said, "That monkey only speaks big but does not understand hierarchy. To send troops to fight him would result in prolonged warfare without quick victory, only exhausting our forces. Better to show great mercy, and issue a decree to grant him amnesty and make him Heavenly Saint Without Peer. Simply give him a title with no salary." The Jade Emperor asked, "What is a title with no salary?" The star replied, "His title is Heavenly Saint Without Peer, but he has no duties or salary, merely to keep him occupied and free from arrogance, thus ensuring the peace of the heavens and the tranquility of the earth." The Jade Emperor agreed, and ordered a decree to be drafted and delivered by the White Star.

Then the Heavenly King Li and his Prince Third led their troops to the Golden Terrace Hall. They reported, "We were sent by Your Majesty to lead an army down to the mortal world to subdue the妖仙孫悟空. However, his powers are immense, and we were unable to defeat him. We pray that Your Majesty adds more troops to exterminate him." The Jade Emperor said, "A single demon monkey, what power can he have? Why do you need to add more troops?" The Prince then stepped forward and said, "I beg Your Majesty to spare my life! That monkey uses a metal rod and first defeated the God of Great Might. He also injured my arm. He stands outside the cave gate with a banner that reads 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' It states that this is his official title, and the fighting should cease if he wishes to surrender; if not, he will attack the Golden Terrace Hall." The Jade Emperor, upon hearing this, was astonished and said, "How dare this monkey be so audacious! Have the troops eliminate him immediately." Just then, from the ranks came out the White Star of the Northern Dipper, who said, "That monkey only knows to speak and does not know his place. If we use force to fight him, it will be hard to subdue him, and it would only exhaust our troops. Instead, Your Majesty should show great kindness and issue a decree to give him an official title, making him the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. But only give him the title and no salary." The Jade Emperor asked, "What is meant by 'no salary'?" The White Star said, "His title is Great Sage Equal to Heaven, but he does not have any duties or salary. He will be kept in the heavens and the earth to check his evil intentions and prevent him from becoming arrogant. Thus, the peace of the world will be secured, and the heavens will be clear and peaceful." The Jade Emperor said, "As you suggest," and immediately ordered an imperial edict to be issued, still commanding the White Star to deliver it.

For more than a week, the visiting gentleman had lived in the city, going from party to party and meal to meal, thus spending his time in great comfort. Finally, he decided to move his visits outside the city and pay a visit to the landowners Manilov and Sobakevich, to whom he had promised. Perhaps there was another, more pressing reason that prompted him, something more serious, closer to his heart… But the reader will learn about all this gradually, in due time, if only he has the patience to read the offered novel, which is very long and gradually expands and widens as it approaches its conclusion, which crowns the work. Selifan the coachman was instructed to have the horses ready by early morning in the familiar carriage; Petrushka was told to stay at home, keep an eye on the room and the suitcase. It would not be superfluous for the reader to acquaint himself with these two serfs of our hero. Although, of course, they are not so prominent figures, and what is called secondary or even tertiary, although the main plot and springs of the poem are not founded upon them, and touch them only occasionally and lightly… but the author loves to be extremely meticulous about everything, and even though he is himself a Russian, he wants to be as meticulous as a German. This will not take much time or space, for not much needs to be added to what the reader already knows, namely, that Petrushka walked around in a somewhat wide brown coat from his master’s wardrobe and had the usual habits of people of his rank, a large nose and mouth. His character was more of a taciturn type than a talkative one; he even had an honorable motive for education, that is, reading books, the contents of which did not trouble him in the least: whether it was the adventures of a love-struck hero, a simple primer, or a prayer book, he read them all with the same attention; if he were to come across chemistry, he would not refuse to read it. He liked not what he read, but the act of reading, or, better put, the process of reading itself, for there was always some word that would pop out of the letters, which sometimes meant something completely unexpected. This reading was more often than not done in a lying position in the vestibule, on a bed, or on a pillow that had been worn out and thinned by such use, like a pancake. Apart from his passion for reading, he had two other habits that characterized him: he did not undress to sleep, instead slept wearing the same coat in which he had left his room, and always carried with him a certain distinctive smell, his own peculiar aroma, which reminded one of a cozy room, so that it was enough for him to put his bed anywhere, even in an unused room, and simply transfer his overcoat and belongings there, and it already seemed that people had lived in this room for ten years. Chichikov, being a rather sensitive person and even a bit fussy in some cases, upon sniffing the air at the first fresh breath in the morning, only wrinkled his nose and shook his head, saying, "You, brother, I don't know, are you sweating? You should go to the bathhouse." To which Petrushka did not reply and tried to get to work on something else; or he would approach with a whip the baron’s frock coat hanging on the hook or simply clean something. What he thought when he was silent, perhaps he said to himself: "And you are good too, don't you find it boring to repeat the same thing forty times?" God knows, it's hard to know what a serf thinks in the moment when his master gives him a lesson. So, that is what can be said about Petrushka for now. Selifan was a completely different person… But the author feels very ashamed of keeping the readers so long occupied with the characters of the lower classes, knowing from experience how unwilling they are to acquaint themselves with the lower orders. Such is the Russian man: he is so eager to be above someone, even if that someone is only one rank above him, and knows that acquaintance with a count or prince is better than any close friendship. The author even fears for his hero, who is only a college councilor. Chancellors and collegiate councilors may meet him, but those who are already approaching general ranks, they may cast upon him those disdainful glances with which a proud man regards everything that kneels at his feet, or even worse, they may pass him with deathly indifference. But no matter how sorrowful these things may be, one must return to the hero. So, after giving the necessary orders the previous evening, he woke up very early in the morning, washed himself, dried himself thoroughly from head to foot with a wet sponge, which was only done on Sundays, if it happened to be a Sunday, shaved so that his cheeks became a real silk in terms of smoothness and luster, put on a fawn-colored coat with a spark and then an overcoat on large bearskins, and with the help of the inn servant, he descended the stairs and settled into the carriage. With a roar, the carriage left the inn’s courtyard and hit the street. The passing priest removed his hat, and a few ragged boys stretched out their hands, saying, "Sir, give a orphan a hand!" The coachman, noticing that one of them was a particularly avid admirer of high heels, flicked him with the whip, and the carriage began to jump over the stones. With delight, he saw a striped gate, signaling that the road was about to end, like any other kind of fare. And several times, he struck his head rather hard against the carriage floor, but finally, Chichikov rushed across soft earth. Hardly had the town receded behind them, when already, in our usual way, they started writing, and gibberish and nonsense began to appear on both sides of the road: bumps, spruce, small thin saplings, burned trunks of old trees, wild heather, and such nonsense. Along the way, there were extended villages, built like old split logs, covered in gray roofs with carved wooden decorations resembling hanging embroidered towels. A few peasants, as usual, were yawning on the benches in front of their gates in their fur coats. Women with thick faces and bandaged chests looked out of upper windows, while from the lower windows, a calf was peeping out or a blind sow was sticking out her head. In short, familiar views. Having driven fifteen versts, he remembered that here, according to Manilov, his village should be, but the sixteenth verst flew by, and the village was still nowhere in sight, and if it weren't for two peasants they came across, they might not have arrived in time.

For more than a week the stranger had been living in the city, attending parties and lunches, and thus spending his time, as they say, in a very pleasant manner. Jinguang received the imperial decree and left through the southern gate of the Heavenly Realm, pressing down the auspicious clouds to arrive at Flower and Fruit Mountain, Water Curtain Cave. He said to the monkeys, "I am an angel sent by heaven, with an imperial decree here, to request that your great king ascend. Hurry and inform him!" The little monkeys outside passed the message layer by layer until it reached the innermost part of the cave. They said, "Your great king, there is an old man outside, carrying a document, claiming to be an angel sent by heaven, who has come to summon you." When the Monkey King heard this, he was overjoyed, saying, "These past two days, I have been thinking of ascending to heaven, and now an angel has come to summon me." He called out, "Hurry and bring him in!" The Monkey King hastily straightened his robes and went to meet him outside. Jinguang entered directly to the middle, standing facing south, and said, "I am Tai Bai Jin Xing from the Western Heavens, bearing the imperial decree to summon you to heaven to receive the register of immortals." Monkey laughed and said, "Thank you, Senior Star, for coming down." He ordered, "Servants! Prepare a banquet to welcome him." Jinguang replied, "The imperial decree is in my possession, and I dare not delay; please come with me at once. I will host you more leisurely after your promotion." The Monkey King said, "Thank you for your visit, please leave! Please leave!" He immediately summoned his four main generals and instructed, "Watch over the young ones carefully, and let me ascend to heaven to see the way, so I can bring you up there to live with me." The four generals responded. The Monkey King and Jinguang ascended into the clouds, soaring high into the void. This is the elevation to a high-ranking celestial position, with a name listed in the heavenly register. It remains to be seen what position he will be granted; tune in for the next chapter.

The monkeys outside passed the message through several layers until it reached the depths of the cave, and then said, "Great King, there is an old man outside with a scroll. He says he is a celestial envoy sent by heaven, and has an imperial decree to summon you."

The Monkey King was overjoyed, saying, "These past two days, I have been considering a trip to heaven. It seems the celestial envoy has arrived just in time." He called out, "Bring the old man in quickly!" The Monkey King hurriedly dressed himself and went to greet him outside. Golden Star entered the main chamber and stood facing south, saying, "I am the Golden Star of the Western Heavens, commissioned by the Jade Emperor to summon you to heaven to receive the record of immortality." Monkey smiled and said, "Thank you, old star for your visit." He instructed, "Servants, prepare a feast to welcome him." Golden Star replied, "The imperial decree is on me, and I dare not linger; please follow me now, and we will discuss further after your promotion." Monkey replied, "Thank you for your visit, please retire! Please retire!" He then summoned the Four Guards and instructed, "Mind your duties and train the monkeys well. I shall go to heaven to take a look. When I return, I will bring you all up to live there with me." The Four Guards responded. This Monkey King and Golden Star rose to the heavens, ascending into the void, where it is: Promoted to a high position as a celestial being, listed in the register of heaven and clouds. It remains to be seen what rank and position he will receive. To be continued.

Grateful for heaven's protection, escaping from the clutches of tigers and wolves, even to die of hunger would be better than feeding those beasts. When Bo Qin's mother heard this, she called out, "Son, don't waste time talking to the elder, I have prepared simple food myself." Bo Qin asked, "Where did you get the simple food?" His mother replied, "You needn't concern yourself, I have ready-made simple food." She called her daughter-in-law to take down the small pot, heated it over the fire to remove the grease, brushed it clean, and washed it, then placed it back on the stove. First, she boiled half a pot of water for other use, then she steeped some mountain dodder leaves in water as tea. Next, she cooked millet with some dried vegetables, and placed two bowls of it on the table. The old mother turned to the Three Winds and said, "Please have your meal, this is a simple but clean and pure meal prepared by me and my daughter-in-law." The Three Winds stepped down to thank her before taking his seat. Bo Qin set up another place, laying out some saltless and unsalted tiger meat, fragrant deer meat, python meat, fox meat, and rabbit meat, chopped pieces of dried venison, all in ample portions, serving them with the Three Winds. Just as they were about to eat, they saw the Three Winds reciting scriptures with clasped hands. This frightened Bo Qin so much that he dared not touch his food, hurriedly rising to stand beside him. The Three Winds did not recite for more than a few verses before calling out, "Please have your meal." Bo Qin said, "Are you a monk who recites short prayers?" The Three Winds replied, "This is not a scripture, but a prayer for the meal." Bo Qin said, "You monks always have your own ways, even when eating you must chant."

Grateful for the Heavenly Protection, surviving the midst of tigers and wolves, even if we starve to death, it would still be better than feeding the tigers. When Mother Baochen heard this, she called out, "My son, stop chatting with the elder. I have some plain food that can serve you well." Baochen asked, "Where do you have these plain foods from?" His mother replied, "Do not worry about it, I have some plain food." She ordered her daughter-in-law to bring down a small pot, cleaned it over a fire to remove the grease, and washed it thoroughly. Then she put it back on the stove. She first heated a half pot of boiling water for other use, then added some leaves of wild almond trees, boiling them to make a tea. Next, she cooked some millet with golden beans and some dried vegetables. She placed the two bowls on the table and said to Tang Sanzang, "Elder, please partake of this plain and clean meal prepared by myself and my daughter-in-law." Tang Sanzang thanked her and sat down. Baochen then prepared another place, laying out tiger meat, fragrant deer meat, boa constrictor meat, fox meat, rabbit meat, finely chopped dried deer meat, and filling the plates and bowls. He served Tang Sanzang. As soon as they sat down, Baochen wanted to eat, but when he saw Tang Sanzang praying, he was so startled that he did not dare to touch the food. He quickly rose and stood by the side. Tang Sanzang did not recite more than a few verses before saying, "Please partake." Baochen asked, "Are you a monk who stops in the middle of his chanting?" Tang Sanzang replied, "This is not scripture, but a prayer to invite the meal." Baochen said, "Why must you religious folk have so many complications? Even eating requires chanting."

Grateful for the heavenly protection, surviving from the midst of tigers and wolves, even to starve to death would be better than feeding the tigers. When his mother heard this, she called out, "Son, don't chat idly with the elder, I have plain food ready to offer." Bao Qin asked, "Where did you get the plain food?" His mother replied, "You need not worry about that; I have some prepared." She then called his wife to fetch a small pot and, after heating and washing it several times, placed it back on the stove. First, she boiled half a pot of water for other uses, and then added some leaves of locust trees from the mountains, boiling them to make a tea. She then cooked some millet and stewed some dried vegetables, placing two bowls on the table. The old mother turned to Tripitaka and said, "Master, please accept this simple yet clean meal prepared by your servant and my daughter-in-law." Tripitaka descended and thanked them, then took his seat. Bao Qin set up another place, serving plain meat dishes without salt or sauce—tiger meat, wild boar meat, python meat, fox meat, and rabbit meat, along with chopped dried venison. He placed them in dishes and bowls, setting them before Tripitaka for the vegetarian meal. As he was about to eat, he saw Tripitaka chanting and was so startled that he could not move. He quickly stood by the side. After a few sentences, Tripitaka said, "Please." Bao Qin replied, "You're a monk with a short prayer?" Tripitaka answered, "This is not a scripture; it's a charm to invoke almsgiving." Bao Qin said, "As monks, you have so many tricks. Why do you have to recite even when eating?"

Grateful for the heavenly protection, surviving the den of tigers and wolves, even if I starve to death, it would be better than feeding the tiger. When Buqin's mother heard this, she called out, "Son, stop chatting with the elder, I have simple food to offer." Buqin asked, "Where do you get such simple food?" Grateful for the imperial favor, escaping the den of tigers and wolves, even to die of starvation would be better than feeding the tigers. When Po Qin's mother heard this, she called out, "Son, do not waste time with the elder, I have plain food ready to serve." Po Qin asked, "Where did the plain food come from?" The old mother faced Tri Seng and said, "Monk, please accept this meal, prepared personally by me and my daughter-in-law." Tri Seng descended to thank her before sitting down. Po Qin set out another place, laying out dishes of meat without salt or sauce—tiger meat, wild boar meat, python meat, fox meat, and rabbit meat—along with finely chopped dried deer meat, all set in full plates and bowls to accompany Tri Seng on his斋. And so, let the celebration cease. When I send envoys to fetch the Great Vehicle Sutra, come and make your offerings with sincerity and re-establish your merit. All the officials did as they were instructed. At that time, within the temple, the emperor asked, "Who is willing to carry out my旨意and journey to the Western Heavens to pay homage to the Buddha and seek the scriptures?" Before he could finish, a monk stepped forward and prostrated himself before the emperor. He said, "Your Majesty, though I am unworthy, I am willing to undertake this difficult task and seek the true scriptures for you, to pray for the stability of your kingdom." Emperor Taizong was overjoyed and took the monk’s hand, pulling him up. He said, "If you can be as loyal and virtuous as this, I am willing to be your brother and support you in your journey." Tripitaka humbly thanked him. Emperor Taizong was indeed very virtuous. In front of the Buddha in the temple, he bestowed upon Tripitaka the title "Imperial Younger Brother Saintly Monk" and bestowed four prostrations upon him. Tripitaka thanked him profusely, saying, "Your Majesty, what merit have I to deserve such an honor? I will risk my life to seek the scriptures until the end of the Western Heavens. If I do not reach the Western Heavens and cannot bring back the true scriptures, I will never return, nor will I escape the realms of hell." He then lit a stick of incense at the Buddha's altar, making a solemn vow. The emperor was delighted and immediately ordered the return to the capital, waiting for a propitious day to send out the imperial decree for the journey. With that, the emperor returned and the monks dispersed.

And so the festival concluded, waiting for envoys to bring the Great Vehicle Sutra, then with sincere hearts we shall rededicate ourselves to good deeds. All the officials obeyed without fail. At that time, in the temple, the emperor asked: "Who is willing to carry out my orders and journey to the Western Heavens to worship the Buddha and seek the true scriptures?" No one answered until a monk stepped forward, bowing and saying: "This monk is unworthy, but I am willing to bear this heavy task and seek the true scriptures for Your Majesty, praying for the eternal stability of our kingdom." The Tang emperor was overjoyed, and moving forward, he helped the monk rise, saying: "If you can show such loyalty and virtue, fear no long journey or rugged terrain. I am willing to be your brother." Thus, Tang Sanzang bowed his head in gratitude. The Tang emperor, indeed most virtuous, went to the Buddha's altar and bowed four times to Tang Sanzang, calling him "Imperial Brother Saint Monk." Tang Sanzang thanked him profusely: "Your Majesty, what merit or ability do I possess to receive such divine favor? This journey to the West, I will risk my life to the fullest, until reaching the Western Heavens. Should I not reach the Western Heavens or not obtain the true scriptures, I dare not return home even if I die, and will fall into the depths of hell forever." At the altar, he burned incense and swore by it. The Tang emperor was very pleased and immediately ordered the return, waiting for an auspicious day to issue the edict and depart. The imperial party then returned to their respective duties.

And let this assembly end. I shall send someone to fetch the Great Vehicle Sutra. Then, with sincere devotion, we will repair our virtuous karma. All the officials agreed without exception. At that time, inside the temple, the emperor asked, "Who is willing to carry out my instructions and go to the Western Heavens to pay homage to the Buddha and seek the scriptures?" No one stepped forward. Then, a monk stepped out and knelt before the emperor, saying, "Your humble monk is unqualified, but I am willing to serve with dog-like devotion and seek the true scriptures for your majesty, praying to ensure our royal dynasty's stability." Emperor Taizong was delighted and lifted the monk up, saying, "If you can fulfill this loyal and virtuous task without fear of long and arduous journeys, I am willing to regard you as my brother." Thus, Tripitaka bowed his head in gratitude. Emperor Taizong indeed was very virtuous, and went to the temple to offer four bows to Tripitaka in front of the Buddha, calling him "Imperial Brother Holy Monk." Tripitaka expressed his deepest gratitude, saying, "Your Majesty, what merit or ability do I have to be so honored? I will certainly devote myself to this journey, going to the Western Heavens. If I do not reach the Western Heavens and obtain the true scriptures, I shall never return home and will perish in hell." He then lit incense in front of the Buddha to make a solemn vow. Emperor Taizong was very pleased and immediately ordered the court to return. He then waited for a favorable day to issue a decree and depart, after which he returned and disbursed his officials.

And let the celebration continue. When our envoys return with the Great车辆经, we shall offer our sincere prayers and dedicate ourselves to doing good. All the officials complied without reservation. At that time, the emperor asked from within the temple: "Who among you is willing to undertake my command and journey to the Western Heaven to pay homage to the Buddha and seek the scriptures?" No one volunteered until a priest stepped forward and, bowing before the emperor, said: "Your humble monk is not talented, but I am willing to do my duty as a dog or horse and seek the true scriptures with you, Your Majesty, to ensure the stability of our royal domain." The Tang Emperor was delighted and, rising, placed his hand on the monk's shoulder, saying: "If you can be so loyal and wise, fear not the long journey and the trials of the mountains and rivers. I would be delighted to call you my brother." Xuanzang bowed in gratitude. Indeed, the Tang Emperor was very virtuous, and he went to the Buddha at the temple, bowing four times to Xuanzang and calling him "Imperial Brother, Holy Monk." Xuanzang thanked him profusely, saying: "Your Majesty, what virtue or ability do I possess that you would honor me with such favor? I shall surely dedicate myself to this journey until I reach the Western Heaven. If I fail to reach there and obtain the true scriptures, I shall not return to my homeland, and I shall fall into the abyss of hell." He then offered incense in front of the Buddha, vowing by it. The Tang Emperor was very pleased and immediately ordered his return, waiting to select a propitious day for his departure. He issued a decree and set out on his journey, thus returning to his various duties.

And so, let this celebration end for now. I will dispatch someone to fetch the Great Vehicle Sutras. Then, with sincere devotion, we will restart our good deeds. The officials all followed this. At that time, the emperor inquired within the temple, "Who is willing to carry out my旨意, to travel to the Western Heavens to worship Buddha and seek the sutras?" Before he could finish, a monk stepped forward and bowed to the emperor, saying, "Your humble monk is not talented, but I am willing to do the duty of a dog or horse, to seek the true scriptures with Your Majesty, to pray for the stability of the kingdom." Emperor Taizong was very pleased and moved forward to help the monk rise, saying, "If you can be as loyal and wise as this, fear not the long journey and the rough terrain. I am willing to be your brother." Zhu Xian bowed his head in thanks. Emperor Taizong was indeed very virtuous, and in front of the Buddha, he bowed four times to Zhu Xian, calling him "Imperial younger brother, Holy Monk." Zhu Xian thanked him endlessly, saying, "Your Majesty, what virtue or ability do I have that I could receive such divine grace? This time, I will dedicate myself and do my best, until I reach the Western Heavens. If I cannot reach the Western Heavens or obtain the true scriptures, I will not return home even if I die, and will be eternally damned in the lower realms." He then burned incense in front of the Buddha as a vow. Emperor Taizong was very delighted and immediately ordered the return to the capital, waiting for an auspicious day to issue the decree and set out on the journey. The emperor then returned, and the matter was concluded.

"Why? Why this hatred towards me now? — the prince sadly and fervently took up the question. — You know now, of course, that everything you thought was wrong. But, in any case, I thought that your hatred for me had not yet passed, and you know why? Because you tried to infringe on me, and that's why your hatred does not pass. I tell you, I remember that Parfen Rogaĭnin from that day, when we became brothers with the sign of the cross; I wrote this to you in yesterday's letter so that you would forget all this nonsense and not start talking about it with me. Why do you avoid me? Why do you hide your hand from me? I tell you that all of that, which happened then, I now consider nothing but nonsense: I know you by heart, as I did myself, for that whole day. What you imagined did not exist and could not exist. Why should our hatred exist?"

"Why? What made you so angry with me all of a sudden?" the prince took up the question sadly and fervently. "After all, you know now that everything you thought was wrong. Though I did, however, suspect that your anger toward me had not yet passed, and I wondered why. Because you had dared to challenge me, and that is why your anger does not pass. I tell you, I remember that Parfen Rogozhin, with whom I took the sign of the cross that day; I wrote about this in yesterday’s letter to make you forget all this nonsense and not to bring it up to me. Why do you avoid me? Why do you hide your hand from me? I tell you, that entire affair is now just a delusion to me: I know you as well as myself from that whole day, as if it were yesterday. What you imagined simply did not exist and could not exist. Why should our anger exist then?"

"Why? What is this sudden hostility toward me now?" the prince took up the words sadly and with fervor. "And yet, you must surely know now that everything you thought was wrong. However, I, in any case, thought until now that your hostility toward me had not faded, and I know why: because you made a bid for me, and that's why your hostility doesn't fade. I tell you, I remember that very Parmenius Rogozhin from that day we became blood brothers; I wrote you about this in my letter yesterday, so that you would forget all this nonsense and not start talking about it with me. Why do you avoid me? Why do you hide your hand from me? I tell you that all of that, what happened then, I consider to be just nonsense: I know you now as well as myself from that entire day. What you imagined did not exist and could not exist. Why should our hostility continue to exist?"

"Why? Where did this hatred of mine for you come from now?" the prince asked sadly and fervently. "After all, you now know for sure that all you thought was wrong. But, of course, I thought that your hatred toward me had not yet subsided, and I knew why: because you had attacked me. That's why your hatred does not subside. I tell you, I remember that Parfen Rogozhin with whom I was christened that day; I wrote this to you in yesterday's letter so that you would forget all this nonsense and stop mentioning it to me. Why do you shy away from me? Why do you hide your hand from me? I tell you, all that happened then is just nonsense to me: now I know you as well as myself from that entire day. What you imagined did not exist and could not exist. Why should our hatred continue to exist?"

"Why? Why such hatred toward me now?—" the prince picked up sadly and passionately. "And you know now, you know that everything you thought was false. After all, I believed, somehow, that your hatred for me had not passed, and I knew why: because you dared to provoke me, that's why your hatred doesn't pass. I tell you, I remember that Parfen Rogozhin with whom I was godfathers that day; I wrote about this in my letter yesterday, so that you would forget all this nonsense and never mention it to me. Why do you avoid me? Why do you hide your hand from me? I tell you, everything that happened then I consider mere nonsense: I know you now as well as myself from that whole day. What you imagined never existed and couldn't exist. Why should our hatred exist?"

And so, the master and his disciple rode their horses forward until they reached the temple gate, where they observed indeed a magnificent monastery. The layers of halls and pavilions were arranged in ascending order, while the three gates before them were concealed behind towering clouds of myriad colors. In front of the Five Blessings Hall, a thousand strands of red mist swirled about. Two avenues of pine and bamboo, and a grove of cypresses, lined the path. The two avenues of pine and bamboo were a perpetual haven of peace, while the grove of cypresses exuded a prideful grandeur. There was also a high bell and drum tower, and a towering pagoda. In the meditation chambers, monks were serene, and the calls of birds in the trees were tranquil. True solitude, truly secluded; true purity, truly ethereal. As the verse says: The Zen Garden of the Pure Land Conceals a Green Retreat, A Monastery's Splendor Matches Old Granny's. Truly a Pure Land so rare, A multitude of famous mountains are the monks' domain. The elder dismounted his horse, the pilgrim rested his pack, and just as they were about to enter, a group of monks emerged from the temple doors. You must see how they appeared: they wore left-side hairpin caps, donned spotless robes. They had brass rings hanging from both ears, and silk belts at their waists. They walked steadily in shoes of grass, carrying wooden fish in their hands. They recited mantras continuously, their practice of Prajna always reverting to its essence. Upon seeing them, Tripitaka stood beside the door, respectfully bowed, and greeted them. The monk hurriedly returned the bow, laughing and saying he had neglected them, asking, "Where do you come from? Please come in and we will serve you tea." Tripitaka replied, "Your disciple is an envoy from the eastern land, on a pilgrimage to the Temple of Thunder to seek scriptures. It is evening here, and I would like to stay a night at your temple." The monk replied, "Please come in, please come in." Then Tripitaka called his disciple to lead the horse inside. The monk suddenly saw the disciple's appearance, and became slightly frightened, asking, "What is that牵马 creature?" Tripitaka said, "Shh! Shh! He is impatient. If he hears you call him a creature, he will get angry. He is my disciple."

Now, they and their disciple rode on until they reached the entrance of the temple. Indeed, it was a temple. The层层殿阁, the选迭廊房, the three peaks at the outer gates were overshadowed by myriad rainbow clouds; the five blessings hall was surrounded by myriad red mists. Two rows of pines and bamboos, a grove of cypresses and pines. The pines and bamboos were pure and serene without year or age; the cypresses and pines had color and grace, unyielding and proud. They also saw the high bell and drum pavilions, the steep pagoda towers. The monks were in deep meditation, the birds' calls were leisurely in the trees. Truly isolated and quiet, truly pure and virtuous. Poem: The upper monastery of Jizhou Zen Garden hides in a green hollow, the splendor of the monastery surpasses Pujie. Indeed, there are few such pure lands in the human world, but many famous mountains are occupied by monks. The elder dismounted and the pilgrim put down his load; just as they wanted to enter, a group of monks came out from inside the gate. See their appearance: they wore left-curl hats, donned spotless robes. The copper rings hung from both ears, a silk belt around the waist. Their feet were steady on the grass path, a wooden fish in hand. They recited silently, always reciting Prajna. The monk saw them, stood by the door and bowed, greeting them. The monk hurried to return the greeting, smiling and saying that he had been neglectful and asked where they were from and invited them to enter and have tea in the guest hall. The monk said: "Please come in and take a seat, please come in and take a seat." The monk then called his disciple to bring the horse inside. The monk suddenly saw the disciple’s appearance and was somewhat frightened, asking, "Who is that pulling the horse?" The monk said: "Shh! Shh! He is very impatient, if he hears you say that, he will be angry. He is my disciple."

He and his disciple rode forward until they reached the monastery gate, where they could indeed see a temple. The层层殿阁translated as层层殿阁, or "layer upon layer of halls and pavilions," reads as follows:

Layer upon layer of halls and pavilions, 
Staircase of corridors follows suit, 
Three mountains encircle the outer gate, 
Veiled in myriad trails of rainbow clouds, 
Five Blessings Hall, 
Surrounded by myriad crimson mists, 
Two paths of pine and bamboo, 
A forest of juniper and cypress. 
Two paths of pine and bamboo, 
Fragrant and tranquil, year after year, 
Forest of juniper and cypress, 
Proud and colorful. 

They also saw the high bell and drum towers, 
And the steep pagoda. 
Monks in meditation are serene, 
Birds in the trees, their sounds leisurely. 
Truly silent, truly secluded, 
Truly void, truly pure. 
As the poem says:
In the verdant hollow of Ji Guan Monastery,
The splendid scenery outshines that of Pu Bo.
Indeed, the pure land is scarce on earth,
And many famous mountains are occupied by monks.

The elder dismounted, the disciple put down his burden, and was about to enter when a group of monks came out from the gate. You see how they appeared: 
Wearing left-siding caps, 
Wearing robes without filth. 
With bronze rings hanging from both ears, 
Wearing silk sashes around their waists. 
Walking steadily in grass shoes, 
Holding wooden fish in their hands. 
Meditating constantly in their mouths, 
All wisdom reverently held. 
Solitary and still, no dust around, 
Purified and serene, truly. 

The Tripitaka Monks stood by the door, greeted them and bowed, and the monk hurriedly returned the courtesy, smiling and saying he was sorry for not having seen them earlier. He asked, "Where are you from? Please come in and I will serve you tea in the hall." The Tripitaka Monks said, "Your disciple is an envoy from the East, on a pilgrimage to Laoren Temple to seek the scriptures. We are here as the night falls, and wish to stay here for the night." The monk said, "Please come in, come in." The Tripitaka Monks then called for the disciple to lead the horse in. The monk suddenly saw the disciple's appearance and was somewhat frightened. He asked, "Who is that leading the horse?" The Tripitaka Monks whispered, "Hush! Hush! He's easily irritated. If he hears you say what he is, he'll be angry. He's my disciple."

Now, his disciple and he rode their horses up to the entrance of the temple to take a look, and indeed it was a monastery. One could see tier upon tier of pavilions and terraces, colonnades and halls, the Three Gates flanked by towering clouds of myriad hues; in front of the Five Virtues Hall, red mists in myriad strands twined around. Two rows of pines and bamboos, one forest of cypresses and pines. The two rows of pines and bamboos were ever-so quietly, unseasoned or aged, while the forest of cypresses and pines wore colors and displays of proud and elegant beauty. They saw also the high bell and drum towers, the steep pagoda towers. Monks in quietude, meditating in their steadiness, birds in trees making idle sounds. Silence not touched by the dust, indeed a silence; purity and emptiness, truly purity and emptiness. A verse goes: "At the summit of the peak, only verdant hues of Jizhou's oasis, In competing for the best, nuns vie with the old ones. Indeed, a pure land few can find, yet on these famous mountains monks are abounding." The elder alighted his horse, and the monk put down his burden, just as they were about to enter when a group of monks walked out from the gates. You should take a look at them: they wore left-pin caps, and were in spotless robes. Brass pendants hung from their ears, and silk belts encircled their waists. Steadily they walked on, and wooden fish were held in their hands. Their mouths constantly uttered prayers, and the wisdom of Prajna Paramita they always bore in mind. Seeing this, the three sages stood beside the door, and gave their bows, greeting them; the monk responded in turn, laughing and saying that he had not seen them, asking, "Where did you come from? Please come inside and I will offer you tea in the parlor." The three sages replied, "We, your humble disciples, were sent by the Eastern Nations, on our way to the Thunder音 Temple to worship Buddha and seek the scriptures. We arrived here at twilight, and wished to stay one night under your most reverend roof." The monk said, "Please come inside and take a seat, please come inside and take a seat." The three sages then called the monk to lead the horse inside. But the monk suddenly saw the monk's appearance, and was somewhat startled. He asked, "What is that pulling the horse?" The three sages replied, "Be quiet! Be quiet! He is very quick-tempered; if he hears you say it is a certain thing, he will get angry. He is my disciple."

Now, the master and his disciple rode on horseback, approaching the temple gate to take a look. Indeed, it was a temple. To be seen were tiered halls and galleries, three majestic mountains at the outer gates shrouded in myriad rainbow clouds; before the Hall of the Five Blessings, thousand strands of red mist swirled. Rows of pines and bamboos on both sides, a grove of cypresses and pines. The rows of pines and bamboos were perpetually tranquil and serene; the grove of cypresses and pines were adorned with color and elegance. Also seen were the lofty bell and drum towers, the steep pagoda. Monks in tranquil meditation and birds singing in the trees were serene. Truly silent, truly void; truly pure, truly empty. A poem said: Deep in the verdant glen lies the temple of Vimalakirti, surpassing the magic garden in its glory. Indeed, there are few such pure lands on earth, while holy mountains are occupied by monks in abundance. The elder dismounted, and the disciple put down the burden, just about to enter when a group of monks emerged from the gate. You see, how they looked: wearing left-style caps and spotless robes, with copper earrings hanging on both sides, a sash tied around the waist, walking steadily in grass shoes, carrying a wooden fish in hand. Chanting frequently, always reciting Prajnaparamita. Seeing this, Tripitaka stood aside, bowed, and asked politely. The monk hurriedly returned the bow, smiling and saying, “Where are you from? Come inside and I will serve you tea.” Tripitaka said, “I, your disciple, am a special envoy from the Eastern Land, heading to the Pagoda of Thunder Sounds to pay homage to Buddha and seek scriptures. It is now late, and I wish to stay one night at your temple.” The monk said, “Please come in and sit, please come in and sit.” Tripitaka then called his disciple to bring the horse in. Seeing the disciple's appearance, the monk was somewhat frightened and asked, “What kind of creature is that one pulling the horse?” Tripitaka said, “Be quiet! Be quiet! He is irritable, and if he hears you say ‘creature’, he will get angry. He is my disciple.”

Well, I maintain that we do not have a single Russian socialist; there never was one, because all our socialists are either from the nobility or seminary students. Give me their books, their teachings, their memoirs, and I, not being a literary critic, will write you a convincing literary critique in which I will prove with crystal clarity that every page of their books, pamphlets, and memoirs was first written by an old Russian nobleman. Their anger, their indignation, their wit—serfdom's (even Dofamus's!); their enthusiasm, their tears—real, maybe, but still—serfdom's! Serfdom's or seminary's... You're laughing again, and you're laughing, Prince? You disagree too?

The four strong warriors replied, "This morning, we led the troops in battle with the Heavenly King, and the seventy-two cave kings and the Horned Ghost King were all captured by the gods. We survived, thus we should weep. Now that we see the Great Sage has returned unharmed from victory, we must laugh."

The Great Sage said, "Victory and defeat are common in warfare. The ancients said, 'Ten thousand killed, three thousand lost.' Even so, the leaders captured were mere beasts—tigers, leopards, wolves, and other vermin. Not one of our kind was harmed; there is no need to be vexed. Although I used a trick to drive them back, they will still camp at the foot of my mountain. Let us now hold our ground tightly, eat our fill, and sleep soundly to renew our strength. At dawn, I will show off my great power and capture these heavenly soldiers, taking my revenge on them." The four warriors and the monkeys drank a few bowls of coconut wine, then went to sleep soundly without further ado.

Just as they were debating, the True Monarch arrived and asked, "Brothers, why did he suddenly disappear?" The deities replied, "We just surrounded him, and he disappeared." Two-Feathers broadened his phoenix eyes and surveyed. Seeing that the Monkey King had transformed into a sparrow, nailed to the tree, he retracted his magical form, discarded his divine spear, and took off his slingshot. Shifting shape, he turned into a falcon and fluttered its wings, flying to pounce. Seeing this, the Monkey King took flight with a swoop, transforming into a large cormorant and soaring into the sky. Two-Feathers swiftly fluffed his feathers and morphed into a great heron, diving into the clouds to seize him. The Monkey King immediately sank lower into the stream, turning into a fish and darting into the water. Two-Feathers arrived at the stream and found no trace. Thinking to himself, "This monkey must have gone into the water; he'll surely turn into a fish or some kind of shrimp. I'll transform again to catch him." He did and transformed into a fish eagle, gliding on the surface of the lower rapids. After a moment, the Monkey King, transformed into a fish, swam downstream. Suddenly, he spotted a bird that looked like a kite, but the feathers were not blue; it seemed like a heron, but there was no topknot; it appeared like an old stork, but the legs were not red. "This must be Two-Feathers, waiting for me," thought the Monkey King, turning and darting away. Two-Feathers saw and quickly fluffed his feathers, transforming again into a red-crested grey heron, stretching its long beak, like a pair of pointed iron tongs, and came to eat the fish. The Monkey King dove underwater, transforming into a water snake and swimming near the shore, burrowing into the grass. Two-Feathers, having failed to catch the fish, saw the water agitated and a snake darting out, recognizing it as the Monkey King. He changed form again, this time into a crimson-topped grey heron, extending its long beak like a pair of pointed iron tongs, swooping to eat the snake. The snake leaped, and the Monkey King transformed once more into a flower woodcock, standing still and stupidly on a sedge meadow. Two-Feathers, seeing the monkey had transformed into such a lowly creature, and knowing that woodcocks, the dregs of all birds, are excessively lustful, and that they consort with all kinds of birds, regardless of the species, refrained from pursuing and revealed his true form. Grabbing the sling, he drew it back, and with a single shot, struck the bird on the foot.

In the midst of their shouting, the True Immortal arrived and asked, "Brothers, where did he disappear to when we surrounded him?" The gods replied, "Just here, he was surrounded, and then he disappeared." Golden-Eyed Second Lord flared his eyes to observe, seeing Sun Wukong transformed into a sparrow nailed to a tree. He then reined in his spiritual carriage, cast aside his divine spear, and let down his bow and arrows. He transformed into a falcon, flapping his wings and flying off to pounce. Seeing this, Sun Wukong spread his wings and soared up into the sky, transforming into a great cormorant and soaring upwards. Second Lord, seeing this, rapidly shook his feathers and transformed into a great sea eagle, soaring into the clouds to snatch at him. Sun Wukong, having pressed down his body, dived into the ravine and transformed into a fish, diving into the water. Second Lord reached the edge of the ravine but could not spot any trace of him. He pondered, "This Monkey must have gone underwater. He is definitely transformed into a fish or a shrimp. I will transform again to catch him." He transformed into a fish hawk, drifting along the foaming water. After a while, Sun Wukong, transformed into a fish, swam downstream and suddenly saw a bird resembling a Eurasian sparrowhawk. Its feathers were not green; it resembled a stork but had no crest; it resembled a great cormorant but its legs were not red. "He must be transforming to catch me!" — he turned and fled, darting away. Second Lord saw this and quickly shook his feathers, transforming again into a red-topped gray heron, stretching its long beak, which resembled a pair of pointed iron pincers, and swooped down to eat the fish. The fish leaped, and Sun Wukong transformed into a water snake, swimming towards the shore and diving into the grass. Seeing he could not catch the fish, Second Lord saw a water snake leap out of the water, recognized Sun Wukong, and changed his form. This time, he transformed into a red-crested gray heron, stretching its long beak and iron pincers, and dived down to eat the water snake. The water snake leaped out of the water, and Sun Wukong transformed into a great woodcock, standing steadily on the reed flat. Second Lord, seeing that Sun Wukong had transformed into a lowly bird, reasoned that woodcocks were among the most common and promiscuous of birds, indifferent to the status of other birds, whether phoenixes, swallows, eagles, or crows, and did not hesitate to approach. He revealed his original form, drew his slingshot, and with a full pull, struck the woodcock, causing it to collapse.

In the midst of the commotion, the True Palace Guardian arrived and asked, "Brothers, where did he disappear to?" The gods replied, "We were just surrounding him when he vanished." Lianglang widened his phoenix eyes and looked around. He saw the Great Sage had transformed into a sparrow, pinned to a tree, and so he withdrew his magical form, dropped his divine spear, and removed his bow. He then transformed into a sparrowhawk and spread his wings, swooping down to pounce. The Great Sage saw this and shot up into the air, transforming into a cormorant, and soared into the sky. Seeing this, Lianglang quickly shook his feathers and transformed into a great heron, diving into the clouds to seize the cormorant. The Great Sage then pressed himself back into the water, transforming into a fish, and swam into the water. Lianglang caught up to the edge of the stream but saw no trace. He thought to himself, "This monkey must have gone underwater, certainly transformed into a fish. I’ll transform once more and catch him." So he transformed into a waterfalcon, floating on the surface of the stream. After a while, the Great Sage, as a fish, swam downstream. Suddenly, he saw a bird that resembled a blue harrier, but the feathers were not blue; it resembled a heron, but there was no crest; it resembled an ibis, but the legs were not red. He thought, "This must be Lianglang, waiting for me to transform. . ." He quickly turned and flew away. Lianglang saw this and said, "This fish that swims back is like a carp, but the tail is not red; it’s like a cuttlefish, but there are no scales; it’s like a blackfish, but the head lacks a star; it’s like a crucian, but there are no scales on the cheeks. He must have seen me and turned back. . ." He flew forward, pecking the fish. The Great Sage sprang out of the water and transformed into a water snake, swimming close to the shore and diving into the grass. Seeing that he could not catch the fish, Lianglang saw a snake in the water and recognized the Great Sage. He quickly changed back to his original form, transforming into a red-topped gray heron, stretching out a long beak resembling a pair of tweezers, and swooped down to eat the snake. The snake leapt and transformed into a pheasant, standing limply in a marsh. Seeing the pheasant, Lianglang thought, "This is the lowest and most promiscuous bird, associating with all kinds of other birds—rarely with phoenixes or swans. . ." So he did not bother to pursue it but reappeared in his true form, walking over and picking up his bow, drawing it back and letting fly, striking the pheasant on its heel.

In the midst of the commotion, the True Immortal arrived and asked, "Brothers, where did he disappear to?" The deities replied, "We had him surrounded just now, but he vanished." Two-starred Rear General flared his phoenix eyes to search, seeing the Great Sage transformed into a sparrow, stuck on a tree. He then reined in his magical form, cast aside his divine spear, and removed his sling, transforming into a sparrow hawk and fluttering his wings as he flew forward to catch it. The Great Sage saw this and, with a swish of his wings, transformed into a cormorant, rising into the sky. Two-starred Rear General saw this and quickly shook his feathers, transforming into a great heron, soaring into the clouds to seize the cormorant. The Great Sage then pressed his body back into the stream, transforming into a fish and dived into the water. Two-starred Rear General arrived at the edge of the stream, but found no trace of him. He thought to himself, "This monkey must have gone into the water, for sure transformed into some kind of fish. I'll transform once more to catch him." And indeed, he transformed into a fish eagle, drifting on the surface of the lower rapids. After a while, the Great Sage, transformed as a fish, swam downstream and noticed a flying creature that appeared to be a green kite, feathers not green; or a heron, lacking a crest; or an old stork, legs not red. "He must have transformed to catch me," he thought, and immediately turned and fled. Two-starred Rear General saw this and exclaimed, "The fish that turned around, resembles a carp, but its tail is not red; or a perch, but its scales are not spotted; or a black fish, but it has no star on its head; or a carp, but it has no scales. Why did it turn around when it saw me? It must be the monkey!" He pursued the fish, pecking at it. The Great Sage dashed out of the water, transforming into a water snake and slithering toward the shore, where he burrowed into the grass. Two-starred Rear General, having failed to catch the fish, noticed a snake dart out of the water. Recognizing the Great Sage, he swiftly turned and transformed into a crimson-topped gray heron, extending its long beak, resembling a pair of pointed iron tongs, to seize the water snake. The water snake leaped, transforming into a flower quail, standing woodenly on a reed flat. Two-starred Rear General, recognizing the lowly nature of the flower quail, which is the most base and lustful bird among birds, ignored it and reverted to his original form, approaching to take his sling, filling it to the brim, and firing a shot that struck the flower quail on its heel.

While they were arguing, the True Deity arrived and asked, "Brothers, where have you lost him?" The deities replied, "We just surrounded him, and now he’s gone." Two-Winged Deity widened his phoenix eyes to search, saw the Great Sage had transformed into a sparrow pinned to a tree, and then retracted his magic form, laid aside his divine spear, and removed his slingshot. He changed into a sparrow hawk, flapped his wings, and flew to attack. The Great Sage, seeing this, instantly took flight and transformed into a cormorant, soaring into the sky. Two-Winged Deity hurriedly shook his feathers and transformed once more into a great sea eagle, diving into the clouds to pursue. The Great Sage then pressed his body down, diving into the ravine, and transformed into a fish, diving into the water. When Two-Winged Deity reached the edge of the ravine, he saw no trace of him. He thought to himself, "That monkey must have dived into the water. He’ll surely transform into a fish or some kind of shrimp. I’ll have to change again to catch him." Indeed, he transformed into a fish hawk, floating on the surface of the downstream water. After a moment, the Great Sage, transformed into a fish, swam downstream. Suddenly, he spotted a flying bird, resembling a hawk but not entirely, with a crown not like a stork, with legs not like an old crane. He thought, "This must be Two-Winged Deity waiting for me!..." He turned around and swam back, feigning flight. Two-Winged Deity saw this and thought, "The fish that swims back is likely a carp; the tail isn’t red. It’s probably a perch; the scales aren’t spotted. It’s not a black carp; there’s no star on its head. It’s not a crucian carp; there are no barbels on its cheeks. He’s surely that monkey!" He pursued and pecked at the fish. The Great Sage leaped out of the water, transformed, and became a water snake, gliding towards the shore, and diving into the grass. Seeing that he couldn’t catch the fish, Two-Winged Deity noticed a water snake darting away from the water, recognizing the Great Sage. He quickly transformed into a red-crested gray heron, stretching out a long beak like a pair of pointed iron tongs, to eat the water snake. The water snake leaped and transformed into a flower cuckoo, standing dazed on a reed field. Seeing that the bird was lowly—cuckoos were the most humble and promiscuous birds, regardless of whether they were orioles, swallows, eagles, or crows—Two-Winged Deity did not pursue, but revealed his original form, walked over, picked up his sling, and shot the flower cuckoo, hitting it hard on the heel.

The thought of the trial would not leave him. He had already thought about writing a defense brief and submitting it to the court. He wanted to include a short biography and explain, for each important event, the reasons for his actions, whether they should be condemned or approved according to his current judgment, and provide the relevant reasons. The advantages of such a defense brief over the mere defense provided by the lawyer, who, as it turned out, was far from perfect, were undoubtedly considerable. K. did not know what the lawyer was doing; not much, apparently, as the lawyer had not summoned him to his office for a month, and K. had not had the impression at any of the earlier meetings that this man could do much for him. The lawyer had, in fact, hardly questioned him. And here there was much to question. The main thing was to ask questions. K. had the feeling that he himself could ask all the necessary questions. The lawyer, however, instead of asking questions, told his own stories or sat silently opposite, leaned slightly forward over the desk, pulled a whisker within his beard, and looked down at the carpet, perhaps right at the spot where K. had lain with Leni. From time to time, he gave K. some empty warnings, like those given to children. Such useless and boring speeches, which K. had no intention of paying a single penny for in the final settlement. After he had sufficiently humiliated K., the lawyer usually started to cheer him up a bit. He told him that he had already, in many similar cases, either completely or partially won. Cases that, although perhaps not as difficult in reality as this one, seemed outwardly even more hopeless. A list of these cases he kept in a drawer in his desk – he knocked on some drawer – and he could not show the briefs, as they were secret. Nevertheless, he now had the great experience he had acquired through all these cases, which would be to K.’s advantage. He had immediately started to work and the first brief was almost ready. It was very important, as the first impression made by the defense often determined the direction of the proceedings. Unfortunately, he had to point out to K. that sometimes the first briefs were not even read in court. They were simply put into the file and the clerk was told that in the meantime the examination and observation of the accused were more important than any writing. The clerk added that if the litigant became persistent, the documents would be examined along with all the files, of course, including this first brief, when all the material had been gathered. Unfortunately, this was also mostly not the case; the first brief was usually set aside or lost, and even if it remained until the end, it would hardly be read, as the lawyer, however, only learned through rumor. All of this was regrettable, but not entirely without justification. K. should not overlook the fact that the proceedings were not public; the court could, if it deemed it necessary, hold them in public, but the law did not stipulate that public hearings were required. As a result, the court documents, especially the indictment, were inaccessible to the accused and his defense, so one did not know in general, or at least did not know precisely, what the first brief was directed against. It could therefore only contain something of relevance to the case by chance. Only real and conclusive submissions could be made later, once the individual charges and their justification became clear or could be deduced during the accused’s examination. Under these circumstances, the defense was naturally in a very unfavorable and difficult position. But this was intended. The law did not actually allow for the defense, but only tolerated it, and there was even debate over whether this could be read into the relevant law. There were thus, strictly speaking, no court-recognized lawyers; all those who appeared as lawyers in this court were essentially side lawyers. This naturally diminished the standing of all lawyers, and if K. were to visit the court offices next time, he could see for himself the lawyer’s room. He would likely be shocked. The narrow, low chamber to which they were confined showed the contempt with which the court viewed these people. The room was lit only through a small hole that was so high that one had to seek out a colleague to lift one up to see where the smoke from the nearby chimney, which blackened one’s face, was coming from. There was a hole in the floor of this room – to give another example of these conditions – that had been there for more than a year, not large enough for a person to fall through, but big enough for one to sink to one’s knee. The lawyer’s room was on the second attic floor; so, if one fell in, the leg would hang into the first attic floor, right in the corridor where the parties waited. It is not exaggerated to call these conditions of the lawyer’s room scandalous in the eyes of the lawyers. Complaints to the administration were not effective, and it was strictly forbidden for lawyers to make any changes to the room at their own expense. But this treatment of the lawyers had its justification. The court wanted to eliminate the defense as much as possible and put everything on the accused. This was not a bad standpoint in principle, but it was entirely mistaken to conclude from this that the lawyers were not needed for the accused in this court. On the contrary, they were more needed here than in any other court. The proceedings were not only secret in front of the public but also secret in front of the accused. Naturally, as far as possible, but to a very large extent possible. The accused also had no access to the court documents, and it was very difficult to infer from the interrogations the documents underlying them, especially for the accused, who was, of course, involved and had many worries that distracted him. Here, the defense intervened. The accused was generally not present during interrogations, so they had to seek the accused out and, as soon as possible, and preferably at the door of the interrogation room, investigate the interrogation and, often from the vague reports, extract the relevant information. But the most important thing was not this, for not much could be learned in this way, even though a capable man would learn more than others. The most important thing remained the personal relationships of the lawyer; they contained the main value of the defense. K. had already observed from his own experiences that the lowest level of the court organization was not entirely perfect and had negligent and corrupt employees who made the strict sealing of the court vulnerable. Here, the majority of lawyers entered, were corrupted and questioned, and even cases of documents being stolen were known to have occurred. It is undeniable that, in this way, some were given surprisingly favorable results for the accused in the short term, and these little lawyers were proud of this and attracted new clients. However, for the further progress of the case, it meant either nothing or something not good. Only honest personal relationships were of real value, and this meant with higher officials, who naturally meant officials of the lower ranks. Only through them could the progress of the case, even at first only imperceptibly, but more and more distinctly, be influenced. Only a few lawyers had such relationships, and K.’s choice was very fortunate. Perhaps only one or two other lawyers could demonstrate similar relationships as Dr. Huld. He, however, did not concern himself with the society in the lawyer’s room and had nothing to do with it. The connection with the court officials, however, was close. Dr. Huld did not even have to go to court; he waited in the antechambers of the judges for their unexpected appearance and achieved, depending on their mood, only apparent success or not even that. No, K. had seen for himself that the officials, even high-ranking ones, came of their own accord, willingly gave information, even if it was open or at least easily deducible, discussed the next steps of the proceedings, and even in individual cases were convinced and accepted the foreign view. Of course, one should not trust them too much in this respect, even if they openly announced their new, favorable intentions for the defense; they might go straight to their office and give a court decision the next day that was precisely the opposite and might be even harsher on the accused than their first intention, which they claimed to have abandoned. Against this, one could not defend oneself, because what was said in private remained private and could not be publicly deduced, even if the defense was not also striving to maintain the favor of the gentlemen. On the other hand, it was indeed correct that the gentlemen did not only join the defense out of benevolence or friendship but were, to a certain extent, dependent on it. Here, the disadvantage of a court organization that even at its inception fixed the secret court came into play. The officials lacked a connection with the public for which they were originally intended, and they were well equipped for ordinary, middle-level cases, which rolled along almost automatically on their own and needed only a push now and then. But in the case of particularly simple or particularly difficult cases, they were often at a loss, for they were constantly confined to their law, and did not have a proper sense of human relationships, which they lacked particularly in such cases. Then they turned to the lawyer for advice, and a servant carried the usually secret documents behind them.
