One day, Queen Mother of the West hosted a banquet, opening her treasure hall, and a feast of peaches was held in the Paochou pond. She ordered the red-robed fairy, the white-robed fairy, the green-robed fairy, the black-robed fairy, the purple-robed fairy, the yellow-robed fairy, and the jade-green fairy to each carry a flower basket to the peach grove to pick peaches for the gathering. The seven robed fairies stopped at the entrance of the peach grove. There, they saw the peach grove's land god, the earth guards, and the two officials of the Celestial Treasury, all standing guard. The fairies approached and said, "We are here by the Queen Mother's command to pick peaches and hold a banquet." The land god said, "Fair ladies, please hold your horses. This year is not like past years. The Jade Emperor has dispatched the Great Sage Equal to Heaven to oversee everything. You must first inform the Great Sage and only then may you enter the grove." The fairies asked, "Where is the Great Sage?" The land god replied, "The Great Sage is inside, resting under the pavilion due to drowsiness." The fairies said, "In that case, let us seek him out; we cannot delay." The land god and the fairies then entered together. They searched for the Great Sage, but he was nowhere to be found. Only his clothes remained on the pavilion, and no one knew his whereabouts. After looking everywhere, they could not find him. It turned out that the Great Sage had played for a while, eaten a few peaches, and turned into a two-inch-tall person, sleeping under the thick leaves of a tree. The seven fairies said, "We have come by command, but we cannot find the Great Sage, so how can we return empty-handed?" A celestial official nearby said, "Since you fair ladies have come by command, there's no need to hesitate. The Great Sage is used to wandering freely; he must have gone out to meet friends. You can go ahead and pick the peaches; we will relay your message to him." The fairies did as they were told and picked the peaches from the trees. First, they picked two baskets from the front trees, then three baskets from the middle trees; when they reached the back trees, they saw that the fruit was sparse, with only a few green-skinned peaches. The ripe ones had already been eaten by the Monkey King. The seven fairies looked around. In the south branch, they saw a half-red, half-white peach. The green-robed fairy pulled the branch down, and the red-robed fairy picked the peach, then raised the branch up. It turned out that the Great Sage had changed form and was sleeping on that branch. He was awakened by their actions. The Great Sage immediately revealed his true form and, from his ear, pulled out his golden cudgel, which grew to the size of a bowl, and said, "Who dares to come and steal my peaches!" The seven fairies were so frightened that they knelt down and said, "Great Sage, please do not be angry. We are not monsters. We are fair ladies sent by the Queen Mother to pick peaches for a banquet and to open the treasure hall, to hold a feast of peaches. We arrived and saw the land god and the others at the peach grove. We could not find the Great Sage. Afraid that we might be late for the Queen Mother's command, we did not wait for the Great Sage and instead came to pick the peaches first. We hope you will forgive us." The Great Sage said, "Please rise. Whom is the Queen Mother inviting to this banquet?" The fairies said, "As in the past, the guests are the Buddha and the bodhisattvas and arhats from the Western Heavens, South Guanyin from the Southern Pole, the Venerable of Deep Benevolence from the East, the immortals from the Ten Continents and the Three Isles, the Venerable of the Northern Pole, the Venerable of the Central Pole, and the five elders of the five directions. There are also the Five Dwarves, the Three Pure Ones and the Four Immortals from the Upper Eight Palaces, the immortals from the Middle Eight Palaces, and the immortals from the Lower Eight Palaces. All the lesser and greater deities in all the palaces and temples of the heavens will be attending the peach feast." The Great Sage laughed and said, "Do they invite me too?" The fairies said, "We have not heard anything about it." The Great Sage said, "I am the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. If they invite me old Sun to sit at the head of the table, why not?" The fairies replied, "This is the custom of the previous gathering. We do not know what the rules are for this one." The Great Sage said, "That is right. I should not blame you. You may wait here. I will go first to find out what the plan is and whether they will invite old Sun."

Finally, around half past eleven, the prince was left alone; his head ached. Kolja, who had helped him change his wedding attire for everyday clothes, was the last to leave. They parted warmly. Soon, almost no one was left in the house: Burdovsky had gone to see Hippolyt, Keller and Lebedev had gone somewhere. Only Vera Lebedeva stayed for a while longer in the rooms, hastily restoring them to their ordinary state. She went to check on the prince before leaving. He was sitting at the table, his elbows resting on it and his hands covering his head. Quietly approaching him, she touched his shoulder. The prince looked at her in bewilderment for a moment, as if trying to recall something; but once he remembered and understood, he suddenly became extremely agitated. However, everything was resolved by an intense and passionate plea to Vera to have the first car knock on his door at seven the next morning. Vera agreed; the prince began to ardently urge her not to tell anyone about it; she promised and then, just as she was about to leave, he stopped her for the third time, took her hands, kissed them, then kissed her on the forehead, and in some sort of extraordinary manner said to her: "See you tomorrow!" He had barely undressed during the night but, however, had slept. In his opinion, he could return that same day. It turned out, therefore, that he found it necessary and fitting to inform her at that moment that he was setting off for the city.

Approaching the intersection of Cucumbers and Gardens streets, he himself was surprised by his extraordinary agitation; he did not expect his heart to be beating so painfully. One house, possibly by its peculiar appearance, began to attract his attention from a distance, and the prince remembered that he had said to himself: "This, no doubt, is the very house." With unusual curiosity he approached to verify his hunch; he felt that it would be particularly unpleasant for him if he was right. The house was large, gloomy, three-story, devoid of any architecture, its color a dirty green. Some, but only a few, houses of this kind, built at the end of the last century, survived almost unchanged in these streets of St. Petersburg (where everything changes so quickly). Built solidly, with thick walls and extremely few windows; in the lower floor, sometimes windows with bars. Mostly, on the ground floor, there was a money changer's shop, which the coppersmith who worked in the shop rented out above. Both outside and inside, it was somehow inhospitable and dry, as if everything were hiding and concealing itself; it was hard to say why this impression was created by the very look of the house. The architectural combinations of lines, of course, have their own mystery. Almost exclusively merchants live in these houses. Approaching the gate and looking at the inscription, the prince read: "The House of the Hereditary Honorable Citizen Rogozhin."

Yesterday, after meeting you, I went home and imagined a painting. Artists depict Christ based on the gospel accounts; I would paint him differently: I would show him alone, as his disciples sometimes left him alone. I would have him with only a small child. The child played beside him; perhaps it was telling him something in its childlike language. Christ listened, but now he was lost in thought; his hand, absent-mindedly, remained on the child’s fair head. He looked into the distance, toward the horizon; a great thought, as vast as the world, rested in his gaze; his face was sad. The child fell silent, rested its head on His knees, and, propping its cheek with its hand, looked up at Him with a thoughtful stare, as children sometimes do. The sun is setting... This is my painting! You are innocent, and in your innocence lies your perfection. Oh, only remember this! What does it matter to you about my passion for you? You are now mine, and I shall be at your side for the rest of my life... I shall soon die.

The child fell silent, rested his elbows on Christ's knees, and, supporting his cheek in his hand, raised his head and looked at him pensively, just as children sometimes do when lost in thought. The sun was setting... This is my picture! You are innocent, and in your innocence is all your perfection. Oh, only remember this! What does it matter to you about my passion for you? You are now mine, and I will be by your side for the rest of my life... I am about to die.

Yesterday, after meeting you, I went home and conjured up a painting. Painters depict Christ according to the gospel accounts; I would have painted him differently: I would have portrayed him alone, with his disciples sometimes leaving him alone. I would have left him alone with only a small child. The child played beside him; perhaps it was telling him something in its childlike language. Christ listened, but now he had become lost in thought; his hand, absentmindedly, lingered on the child's fair head. He looked into the distance, into the horizon; a great thought, as vast as the world, rested in his gaze; his face was somber. The child fell silent, resting its elbows on Christ's knees, propping up its cheek in its hand, and stared at him intently, lost in thought as children sometimes do. The sun was setting... This is my painting! You are innocent, and in your innocence lies all your perfection. Oh, remember this! What does it matter to you about my passion for you? You are now mine, and I will be by your side for the rest of my life... I shall soon die.

The guests returned by the same loathsome route to the house. Nоздрев led them into his study, where, however, there were no signs of the usual furnishings—books or papers; only sabers and two guns hung on the wall—300 rubles for one and 800 for the other. The son-in-law inspected these and shook his head. Then came out Turkish daggers, one of which bore an inscription that was wrong: "Master Savely Siberian." Next was a mechanical organ. Nоздрев played with it for them. The organ played pleasantly enough, but in the middle of it, it seemed something had happened, for the mazurka ended with the refrain: "Malburg rode off to war," and this refrain unexpectedly ended with a familiar waltz. Nоздрев had long since stopped playing, but there was a small reed in the organ that would not calm down and whistled for a long time on its own. Then came out pipes—wooden, clay, hemp-stuffed and not stuffed, covered with leather and not covered, a chubuk with a amber mouthpiece, a recently won one, a cigarette pouch embroidered by some countess who had fallen head over heels in love with it at a post station, with her fingers, in her words, the most subtile superfluousness—words that, presumably, meant the highest point of perfection. Having chewed tobacco, they sat down to a table just past five o'clock. It was clear that dinner did not play a major role in Nоздрев's life; the dishes did not count much: some were burnt, some were completely uncooked. It seemed the cook was guided more by inspiration, tossing in whatever came to hand: if pepper was by the stove, he sprinkled it, if cabbage was at hand, he stuffed it in, poured in milk, ham, and beans—whatever, as long as it was hot, and some flavor would come out. But Nоздрев himself helped himself to the wine. Before the soup was brought, he had already poured his guests each a large glass of port and another of the so-called "governor's cut," because in provincial cities there was no simple cut. Nоздрев then ordered a bottle of Madeira, which, he said, was better than any marshal had drunk. The Madeira did indeed burn in the mouth, for merchants, knowing the taste of the gentry, who loved good Madeira, had adulterated it with reckless absinthe, or sometimes even with imperial vodka, hoping that the Russian stomach could take it. Nоздрев then ordered another special bottle, which, according to him, was a combination of Burgundy and Champagne. He poured it earnestly into both glasses, to the left and to the right, to the son-in-law and to Chichikov; Chichikov, however, noticed in passing that he did not add much to his own glass. This made him cautious, and as soon as Nоздрев started to talk or poured for his son-in-law, he immediately tipped his glass into his plate. Soon the rye berries were served, which, according to Nоздрев, had the perfect taste of cream, but to his surprise, the smell of shivusha was noticeable in it. Then they drank some balm, with a name so hard to remember that even the host himself called it by a different name in the next moment. Dinner was long since over, and the wine had been tried, but the guests still sat at the table. Chichikov did not want to talk to Nоздрев about the main subject in the presence of the son-in-law. After all, the son-in-law was a stranger, and the subject required a private and friendly conversation. Moreover, the son-in-law seemed to be in no danger, for he seemed to have drunk enough and was now sitting on a chair, snorting constantly. Chichikov noticed that he himself was not in a secure state and eventually asked to be excused to go home, but in such a lazy, sluggish voice as if he were urging a horse with clamps to put on a harness.

The guests returned by the same nasty road to their home. Novdshev led them to his study, where, however, there was no trace of what usually is found in studies, namely books or papers; only sabres and two guns were hung on the walls—one for three hundred and the other for eight hundred rubles. His son-in-law, after a look around, merely shook his head. Then the Turkish daggers were shown, on one of which had been carelessly carved: "Master Savely Siberian." Next came the music box. Novdshev turned the handle a few times for them. The music box played pleasantly, but in the middle of it, something seemed to go wrong, and the mazurka ended with a song: "Malabrug went to war," and the "Malabrug went to war" inexplicably gave way to a familiar waltz. Novdshev had long stopped fiddling, but the music box had one very lively flute that wouldn’t quiet down, and it whistled for a long time all by itself. Then came the pipes—wooden, earthen, hemp-wrapped, un-wrapped, covered with leather and uncovered, a pipe with an amber mouthpiece, recently won, a tobacco pouch embroidered by a countess who had fallen in love with it up to the tips of her fingers, which he said were the most exquisite superfluity, a word that apparently meant the highest point of perfection. After partaking of some walnuts, they sat down to the table at five o’clock. It was clear that dinner was not the main event in Novdshev’s life; the dishes played no significant role: some things were overcooked, others were barely done. It seemed that the cook was guided more by inspiration and put on whatever came to hand: if pepper was nearby, he sprinkled it; if cabbage, he stuffed it in; he poured in milk, ham, or beans—merely get it hot, and the taste would come. But Novdshev went in for wine: before the soup was brought, he had already poured port and champagne into large glasses for the guests, and another kind for his son-in-law, for there is no simple champagne in provincial cities. Novdshev ordered a bottle of Madeira, which he said was better than any made by a marshal. The Madeira seemed to burn in the mouth, as the merchants, knowing that the gentry loved good Madeira, had fortified it with rum, or at times even with imperial vodka, hoping that Russian stomachs would bear it all. Then Novdshev ordered a special bottle, which he said was a blend of burgundy and champagne. He poured it in both glasses, right and left, for the son-in-law and for Pichikov; but Pichikov, somehow glancing at it, noticed that he was not pouring much for himself. This made him cautious, and as soon as Novdshev started talking or poured for his son-in-law, he tipped his glass into a plate. It was not long before an apple brandy was brought, which Novdshev said had the perfect taste of cream but in which, to his amazement, one could hear the sivuiska in all its force. Then they drank some balsam with a name so hard to recall that even the host himself called it something different the next time. Dinner had been long over, and the wines had been well drunk, but the guests were still sitting at the table. Pichikov in no hurry wanted to discuss the main topic with Novdshev in the presence of the son-in-law. After all, the son-in-law was a stranger, and the subject required a private and friendly discussion. However, the son-in-law was certainly not a dangerous man, as he seemed to have drunk his fill and, sitting on a chair, was every moment yawning. Pichikov noticed that he was in an unsound state and started to excuse himself to go home, but in such a lazy and languid voice that it was as if he were unhooking reins from a horse with a pair of tongs.

The guests returned by the same repulsive way to their home. Zotov led them into his study, in which, however, there were no signs of what is usually found in studies—books or papers. Only sabers and two guns hung there—300 rubles for one and 800 for the other. The son-in-law, after inspecting everything, only shook his head. Then Turkish daggers were shown, one of which had been mistakenly inscribed with the words: "Master Savely Siberian." Next came a hand organ. Zotov turned some dials right there. The organ played nicely, but in the middle of it, it seemed something went wrong, as the mazurka ended with the song, "Malybrug went to the march," and "Malybrug went to the march" was unexpectedly followed by a familiar waltz. Zotov had long stopped fiddling, but one reed in the organ was very vivacious and would not quiet down, so it whistled on its own for a long time. Then came out pipes—wooden, clay, hemp-wrapped, unwrapped, leather-covered, and not covered, with a bit of amber in the mouthpiece, recently won, a chemise embroidered by some countess who had fallen head over heels in love with it at a post station, where, according to his words, her fingers were the most supple in the entire world—a word that, apparently, meant the highest point of perfection to him. After smoking a pipe, they sat down to the table around five o'clock. It was clear that dinner was not the mainstay of Zotov's life; the dishes did not play a large role: some were overcooked, some were barely simmered. It seemed that the cook followed some inspiration, putting down whatever came to hand: whether there was pepper nearby, he sprinkled it; if cabbage appeared, he stuffed it in; he plopped in milk, ham, and lentils—basically, if it was hot, that was fine, and some taste would likely come out. However, Zotov was very liberal with the wine: before they even served the soup, he had poured a large glass of port and another for his son-in-law, because in provincial towns there was no simple sort of wine. Zotov therefore ordered a bottle of Madeira, which, he claimed, was better than which the marshal had ever drunk. The Madeira really burned in the mouth, for merchants, knowing that gentry loved good Madeira, generously mixed it with rum, and sometimes even added imperial vodka, hoping that Russian stomachs would hold it. Zotov then ordered another special bottle, which he said was both Burgundy and Champagne together. He poured very earnestly into both glasses, right and left, to the son-in-law and Chichikov; Chichikov noticed, however, somewhat casually, that he did not add much to his own glass. This made him cautious, and as soon as Zotov started to talk or poured for the son-in-law, he immediately tipped his glass into his plate. In a short time, rowanberry was brought to the table, which Zotov said had the perfect taste of cream, but in which, to everyone's amazement, the skidudushki was present in full force. Then came a balsam, which had such a name that it was hard to remember, and even the host himself called it by another name on another occasion. Dinner was long over, and the wine had been tasted to the limit, but the guests still sat at the table. Chichikov did not want to discuss the main issue with Zotov in the presence of the son-in-law. After all, the son-in-law was a stranger, and the topic required a private and friendly conversation. Moreover, the son-in-law was unlikely to be a dangerous person, as he seemed to have drunk his fill and, sitting on a stool, was constantly snorting. Noticing that he was in no stable state himself, he finally asked to go home, but with such a sluggish and lazy voice as if he were trying to drag a halter on a horse by using tweezers.

The guests returned by the same loathsome way to the house. Nazdrev led them to his study, in which, however, there was no trace of what usually is in studies, namely books or papers; there hung only sabres and two guns—one cost three hundred and the other eight hundred rubles. The son-in-law, after inspecting them, only shook his head. Then Turkish daggers were shown to them, one of which, by mistake, had been inscribed: "Master Savely Siberian." Following this, a music box was exhibited. Nazdrev began to show them something there. The music box played without much displeasure, but in the middle of it, something seemed to have happened, for the mazurka ended with a song: "Malbrough Went to the Campaign," and "Malbrough Went to the Campaign" unexpectedly ended with some long-familiar waltz. Nazdrev had long stopped fiddling, but there was one reed in the music box that was very lively and would not quiet down, and it whistled on and on. Then pipes were brought—wooden, clay, flax-wrapped, unlit, wrapped in leather, and unwrapped, a pipe with an amber mouthpiece, recently won, a pocket purse embroidered by some countess who, at a post station, fell deeply in love with it, whose hands, according to him, were the very highest pinnacle of elegance—perhaps a term that meant for him the highest point of perfection. Having had a bite of a rouble, they sat down at the table at five o'clock. It seemed that lunch did not occupy a central place in Nazdrev's life; the dishes played no great role: some things were overcooked, some were simply not cooked. It was clear that the cook was guided more by inspiration and put down the first thing that came to hand: whether pepper was standing beside him, he sprinkled it; whether cabbage had fallen to his hands, he stuffed it in; whether milk, sausages, or lentils were at his disposal, he doused them in; in a word, pour in whatever was hot, and flavor would follow. Meanwhile, Nazdrev made a point of the wine: before the soup had even been served, he had already poured a large glass of port and another type of liqueur for both guests because, in provincial and district cities, there was no such thing as simple liqueur. Nazdrev therefore ordered a bottle of madeira, of which, he said, no field marshal had ever tasted a better. The madeira indeed burned in the mouth, for the merchants, knowing that the gentry loved good madeira, fortified it heavily with rum, and sometimes poured in czar's vodka, hoping that Russian stomachs would withstand everything. Then Nazdrev ordered a special bottle brought, which, he said, was both Burgundy and champagne combined. He poured very earnestly into both glasses, first to the son-in-law and then to Chichikov, who noticed, though fleetingly, that he himself was not pouring any extra. This made him wary, and as soon as Nazdrev started talking or poured for the son-in-law, he immediately tipped his glass into his plate. In a short while, a rowanberry cordial was brought to the table, which Nazdrev said had the perfect taste of cream, but in which, to his amazement, the sivuishi was heard at full strength. Then they drank a certain balm whose name Chichikov found hard to recall, and even the host called it by a different name another time. Lunch had been over for a long time, and the wine had been thoroughly sampled, but the guests still sat at the table. Chichikov had no wish to talk to Nazdrev about the main matter in the presence of the son-in-law. After all, the son-in-law was a stranger, and the matter required a private and friendly conversation. Anyway, the son-in-law was likely not a dangerous man, for he seemed to have had his fill and, sitting on a chair, snored at regular intervals. Noticing that he himself was in no fit state, he finally began to take leave of the house, but in such a lazy and listless voice that, in Russian, it would be as if he were hooking the reins on the horse with a pair of forceps.

The guests returned by the same nasty road to their house. Novodrev led them into his study, though there were no signs of what is usually found in studies—books or papers. Only sabres and two guns hung on the walls—one for three hundred and the other for eight hundred rubles. His son-in-law, after a cursory look, shook his head. Then Turkish daggers were shown, one of which had been incorrectly inscribed: “Master Savely Siberian.” Next came a merry-go-round. Novodrev was turning it for them; the merry-go-round played quite pleasantly, but in the middle of it, it seemed something had happened, for the mazurka ended with a song: “Malibrug set out on a campaign,” and this, in turn, unexpectedly ended with an old waltz. Novodrev had long stopped fiddling with it, but there was a whistle in the machine that wouldn’t settle down, and it whistled for a long time. After that, pipes were displayed—wooden, earthen, bunched, smoked and unsmoked, leather-bound and not bound, one with a resinous mouthpiece, won not long ago, a tobacco pouch embroidered by a countess who had fallen in love with it to the point of being willing to bite her fingers off, according to his own words, it being the peak of perfection—a word, apparently, meaning the highest possible point of perfection. They smoked and, at half-past four, settled down to the table. Apparently, dinner did not play a primary role in Novodrev’s life; the dishes did not matter much: some were overcooked, and some were not cooked at all. Evidently, the cook worked more from inspiration, throwing in the first thing that came to hand: whether pepper was to his hand or cabbage—this was stuffed in, whether he had milk or pork or beans—put in the latter, no matter what, as long as it was hot, and the taste would do, to be sure. However, Novodrev was very fond of wines: before the soup was even served, he had already poured port wine and another kind of wine into a large glass for his guests and his son-in-law, for in provincial towns there was no simple kind of wine. Novodrev ordered a bottle of Madeira brought in, better of which he had never drunk, not even a field marshal. The Madeira, indeed, set the mouth alight, for merchants, knowing the tastes of the gentry who loved good Madeira, had heavily fortified it with rum, and sometimes they added czar’s vodka, hoping that the Russian stomach would take it. Then Novodrev ordered another bottle to be brought in, which, as he said, was a combination of Burgundy and Champagne. He poured very generously into both glasses, on both sides, to his son-in-law and Chichikov; Chichikov noticed, however, that he did not give himself much. This made him cautious, and as soon as Novodrev started talking or poured wine for his son-in-law, he tipped his glass into a plate. Very soon, a box of quince jelly was brought in, which Novodrev said had a perfect taste of cream but had quince flavor in it as well, which was astonishing. Then they drank some balsam, of which the name was hard to recall, and even the host himself called it by a different name the next time. Dinner was over long ago, and the wine was sampled, but the guests were still seated at the table. Chichikov had no intention of broaching the main subject with Novodrev in front of his son-in-law; after all, his son-in-law was a stranger, and the matter required a private and friendly conversation. Besides, his son-in-law seemed not to be a dangerous person; he had drunk to his fill, it seemed, and was sitting on a chair, snoring every few minutes. Noticing that he himself was not in a good state, he finally started to leave, but in such a lazy and sluggish voice that it was as if he were dragging himself home on a rope.

— Well, don’t celebrate just yet, wait a bit more, — the nephew retorted resentfully, — he’s happy about it. I came to him, my lord, to this place, and confessed everything; I behaved honorably, I didn’t spare myself; I cursed myself before him as much as I could, and here everyone was a witness. To occupy this spot on the railroad, I must somehow equip myself, because I’m in tatters. Look at my boots! Otherwise, I couldn’t show up at the place, and if I didn’t appear on time, someone else would take it, and then I’d be back at the equator and find another place someday. Now, I’m asking him for only fifteen rubles, and I promise I’ll never ask again, and on top of that, I’ll pay him the entire debt, down to the last kopek, during the first three months. I’ll keep my word. I can sit on bread and kvass for months, because I have a character. In three months, I’ll earn seventy-five rubles. With the old debt, I’ll owe him only thirty-five rubles, so I’ll have enough to pay. Well, let him impose any interest rate he wants, damn it! Does he not know me? Ask him, my lord: did I pay him back before when he helped me? Why doesn’t he want to now? He got angry because I paid this other officer, and there’s no reason for it! That’s how this man is, for himself and for others!

— Well, don't rejoice just yet, wait and see, — the nephew cried crossly. — He’s glad about it. I came to him, your lordship, here, and confessed everything; I acted honorably, I didn’t spare myself; I cursed myself before him as much as I could, and here we are all witnesses. To take up this position on the railroad, I must somehow be properly dressed, for I am entirely in rags. Just look at my boots! Otherwise, I cannot show up for the place. And if I don’t show up on time, someone else will take it, and then I’ll be back on the equator, and I’ll find another place sometime. Now I am asking him for only fifteen rubles, and I promise never to ask again and that I will pay him back the whole debt in three months. I will keep my word. I know how to sit out for months on meager rations because I have character. In three months, I will earn seventy-five rubles. With the old debt, I will owe him only thirty-five rubles, so I will have the means to pay. Why, for God’s sake, can’t he just decide on any interest rate he wants! Does he not know me at all? Ask him, your lordship: when he used to help me, did I ever pay him back or not? Why does he not want to do it now? He’s angry that I paid that lieutenant, that’s all! What a man this is, for himself and for others!

— Well, don’t crow yet, wait a bit, — the nephew grumbled, hurt. — He’s just delighted. I came to him, your Highness, and confessed everything here; I acted nobly, I didn’t spare myself; I abused myself before him to the best of my ability, and all these witnesses are here to prove it. — Here’s the deal! You haven’t got the whole story, my lord... here... Moreover, she’s convinced I love her with a passion, swear to you, and you know, I suspect she loves me too, in her way. There’s a saying: “I hit the one I love.” She’ll spend her life thinking of me as the jack of clubs, (maybe that’s what she wants) and will still love me in her way; she’s made up her mind about that, she’s the kind of person. She’s a remarkably Russian woman, I’ll tell you; but I’ve got a surprise for her. The scene with Varya yesterday happened by accident, but it’s to my advantage: she now sees and believes in my devotion and that I’ll sever all my connections for her. So we’re not fools, are we. By the way, do you think I’m a chatterbox? Prince, I may indeed be doing a bad thing by confiding in you. But precisely because you’re the first nobleman to have shown up, I went to you, so to speak, I mean that literally. You’re not upset about the other day, are you? I may be saying what’s in my heart for the first time in two years. There are so few honest people; none is more honest than Ptiycyn. Are you perhaps laughing at me, or not? Rogues love honest people, you didn’t know that? And you know, I... But tell me honestly, why am I a rogue? What do they all call me behind her back, that I’m a rogue? And you know, even behind her back and hers, I call myself a rogue! That’s how rotten I am!

—"And here's the rub! You gentlemen know nothing of the situation... There's more to it than that... And she's convinced that I love her to distraction, I swear to you, and you know, I strongly suspect that she loves me too, in her own way, you know the saying: I love him, I beat him. She'll spend her whole life thinking of me as the jack of clubs (maybe that's what she needs) but will still love me in her own way; she's preparing for that, that's the kind of character she is. She's a remarkably Russian woman, I'll tell you; and I'm cooking up a surprise for her. That scene with Varvara happened by accident, but it worked to my advantage: she now sees and is convinced of my loyalty, and that I'll sever all my ties for her. So, we're not fools, you can be sure. By the way, do you think I'm a chatterbox? I, your Highness, may indeed be doing something wrong by confiding in you. But precisely because you were the first honorable person to come along, I lashed out at you, or rather, ‘lashed out’—don't take it figuratively. You're not angry about what happened yesterday, are you? I may have said my heart's truest words for the first time in two whole years. There are so few honest people here; Pti͡osin is the most honest. Do you think you're laughing or not? Villains love honest people, you didn't know that? And yet... And to be honest, do you think I'm a villain? What do they all call me after her? And, you know, even I call myself a villain after them and her! That's how viciously vicious I am!

— But that’s the rub! You’re not privy to everything, Your Highness... here... And, besides, she’s convinced I love her to distraction, I swear to you, and, you see, I strongly suspect she loves me, in her way, you know the saying: I love him, I hit him. She’ll spend her whole life thinking of me as the jack of hearts (though that may be just what she needs), but will still love me in her way; she’s prepared for that, and that’s just who she is. She’s a very Russian woman, I’ll tell you that; but I’m preparing a surprise for her. That scene with Varia the other day happened by accident, but to my advantage: now she’s seen and believes in my devotion and that I’ll sever all my connections for her. So we’re not fools, are we? By the way, don’t you think I’m a chatterbox? I, Your Highness, may indeed be doing something wrong by confiding in you. But because you’re the first nobleman I’ve come across, I lashed out at you, so to speak. Don’t take that literally. You’re not angry about that scene from yesterday, are you? I’ve never said my heart out like that in two years. There are simply so few honest people here; Petrinsky is the most honest of them all. Are you laughing at me, or not? Look, how he is obviously engrossed in his own matters and sits there.” K. did not even have the will to argue; the intention of the girl might have been good, aiming to distract him or give him the chance to gather himself, but the means were wrong. “I had to explain his laughter to you,” said the girl. “It was offensive.” “I believe he would forgive much more offensive remarks if I take you out in the end.” K. said nothing, did not even look up, he endured that the two were discussing him as if he were an object, and it even pleased him. But suddenly, he felt the hand of the information giver on one arm and the girl’s on the other. “Come on, you weak man,” said the information giver. “Thank you both very much,” said K., surprised and happy, and took the foreign hands to the places where he needed the most support. “It looks like this,” said the girl softly into K’s ear as they approached the corridor, “that it particularly pleases me to put the information giver in a good light, but believe me, I want to tell the truth. He does not have a hard heart. He is not obliged to lead sick parties out, but he does it, as you see. Perhaps none of us is hard-hearted, we would all like to help, but as judicial officials, we are easily perceived as hard-hearted and not wanting to help. I suffer from it.” “Would you like to sit here for a moment?” asked the information giver, they were already in the corridor and in front of the defendant, whom K. had spoken to earlier. K. almost felt ashamed in front of him; he had stood so upright in front of him before, now he needed two to support him, and the information giver balanced his hat on spread fingers; his hairstyle was destroyed, and the hair hung in the sweaty forehead. But the defendant seemed not to notice any of this; humbly, he stood before the information giver, who looked over him, and tried to excuse his presence. “I know,” he said, “that the processing of my requests cannot happen today. But I came anyway; I thought I could wait here. It’s Sunday, I have the time and I am not disturbing.” “You don’t need to apologize for that,” said the information giver, “your consideration is praiseworthy, you are taking the space despite not being necessary, but I will not prevent you from following the process as long as it does not bother me. When I have seen people neglecting their duties shamefully, I have learned to have patience with people like you. Sit down.” “Listen to how he talks to the parties,” whispered the girl. K. nodded, but was immediately startled as the information giver asked again, “Would you like to sit down here?” “No,” said K., I do not want to rest. He had said it with the utmost certainty, in reality, it would have felt very good to sit down. He was seasick. He felt as if he were on a ship in heavy seas. The water seemed to crash against the wooden walls, the hissing sound from the depths of the corridor was like the surging of water, and the corridor swayed, as if the waiting parties were being lowered and raised on both sides. The calm of the girl and the man, who led him, was even more incomprehensible. He was at their mercy, if they released him, he would fall like a plank. From their small eyes, sharp glances went back and forth, and K. felt their regular steps, without joining them, for he was almost carried from step to step. Finally, he realized they were talking to him, but he did not understand, he only heard the noise that filled everything and the persistent high tone, like from a siren. “Louder,” he whispered with his head lowered, ashamed, for he knew they had spoken loudly enough, even if incomprehensible to him. Finally, a fresh breeze came, as if the wall in front of him had been torn away, and K. heard someone say next to him, “First he wants to leave, but then you can tell him a hundred times that this is the exit, and he won’t move.” K. realized that he was in front of the exit door, which the girl had opened. It felt as if all his strength had suddenly returned, to catch a taste of freedom; he took a step onto the staircase and bid farewell to his companions, who were bending down to him. “Thank you,” he repeated, shook both hands, and only let go when he thought he saw that, accustomed to the office air, they could barely endure the relatively fresh air from the stairs. They could barely answer, and the girl would have fallen if K. had not closed the door very quickly. K. then stood still for a moment, combed his hair with the help of a pocket mirror, picked up his hat, which lay on the next staircase – the information giver had probably thrown it – and ran down the stairs with such freshness and long strides that he almost feared this turn. Such surprises his otherwise well-established health had never brought to him before. Was his body perhaps preparing to revolutionize and start a new process, when the old one was so easily endured? He did not entirely dismiss the idea of consulting a doctor at the next opportunity, at least he wanted to – in which he could counsel himself – to make better use of the coming Sunday mornings than this one.

But the man did not follow the instruction, instead keeping his hands calmly in his pockets and laughing loudly. "See," he said to the girl, "I have indeed hit the right mark. See, prince, I whisper to you: between us and Eugeny Pafalavič not a single word has been said, do you understand? We are not connected in any way, — but such a word could be said, and even soon, and even perhaps very soon! And just to destroy! And why and for what — I do not understand! —"Hit him!" Nozdryov cried, rushing forward with an apple branch, all aflame with heat and drenched in sweat as though he were storming a fortress. "Hit him!" he shouted in the same voice he would use during a great attack, yelling at his platoon: "Boys, forward!" as some desperate lieutenant, whose overwrought valor had gained him such notoriety that an order was given to hold him by the hands during hot engagements. Time passed swiftly, but it was the seventh day of the major assembly. Again, Tang Sanzang presented a memorial requesting the emperor to offer incense. The two of them went to the temple. It was truly a chance encounter with old acquaintances, and Prajna returned to its original place. Entering the temple, what they saw was indeed a great and powerful country, surpassing Shāyā and far exceeding Jetavana and Śrāvasti. A series of divine sounds resounded brightly, and the chants echoed loudly. The Bodhisattva arrived at the platform of Vaiśravana and indeed saw the form of the wise and clear Jin Chanzi. There was a poem: "Calm and clear, not a speck of dust, Great Dharma sits on the high stage. The souls of the dead come in the dark, and the wise listen to the teachings on the bustling streets. Donations come as needed, the heart distant, treasures emerge随意 at will, doors of concealment open. Seeing this teaching of boundless law, people of all ages are filled with joy." Another poem said: "Traveling through the world to the lecture hall, encountering familiar, unpretentious souls. Discussing thousands of matters at present, and the merits of many eons. The cloud of teaching flows, covering all mountains and peaks, the network of doctrine fills all of space. Counting the life of a person, returning to good thoughts, petals of falling red rain from the sky." The abbot on the stage recited the Sutra for Delivering the Dead and the Tranquil Nation Talisman, and then announced the Encouragement to Practice Sutra. The Bodhisattva stepped forward, clapping the treasure platform and shouting loudly, "Monsignor, you only know the small vehicle teachings, can you discuss the great vehicle?" I have the three treasures of great vehicle Buddhism, which can elevate the dead to heaven, can deliver the suffering, can cultivate a life of boundless joy, and can achieve no coming or going."

A range of heavenly voices sounded clear and resounding, and the chanting of Buddha was loud. The Bodhisattva approached the multitude around the precious pagoda and truly saw the form of Wisdom Golden蝉. The poem said: All things are clear and without speck of dust, Grand Sutra Master sits on the high platform. Silent dead cross to the beyond, Listeners come from the bustling markets. Generous offerings should match the moment, The treasury opens at will. In the discourse on boundless wisdom, Old and young all put on a happy face. Another poem said: Through the cosmos in the law hall, Meeting acquaintances, not ordinary but refined. Talking about thousands of matters in front, Discussing countless accomplishments behind. Dharma clouds hang like a mountain spread, Net of doctrine fills the vast sky. Surveying life, return to virtuous thought, Falling flowers rain red. The monk on the platform recited the Sutra for Liberating Souls, spoke of The Seal of Heavenly Defense, and then declared the Scroll Encouraging Merit. The Bodhisattva came forward and loudly called, "Monsieur Monk, you only understand the Lesser Vehicle teachings but do not understand the Greater Vehicle?" Hearing this, Tripitaka was greatly pleased, leaped down from the platform, and said to the Bodhisattva, "Venerable Father, my disciple was disrespectful, too guilty. Seeing the gathered monks, they all talk about Lesser Vehicle teachings, but I do not know the Greater Vehicle." The Bodhisattva said, "Your Lesser Vehicle teachings cannot liberate the dead, only to blend in with the mundane world. I have the Three Baskets of the Greater Vehicle Buddhism, which can liberate the dead to ascend to heaven, rescue people from suffering, cultivate countless lives, and remain nowhere coming and going."

Time passed in the blink of an eye, and it was the seventh day of the grand assembly. Again, Tripitaka submitted a memorial to the Tang emperor, requesting permission to light the incense. At this time, sounds of goodness filled the land. Emperor Taizong immediately prepared his carriage, accompanied by the officials, the eunuchs, and the imperial relatives, arriving early at the temple. All the people in the city, regardless of their rank or status, went to the temple to listen to the sermon. The Bodhisattva and Woodress said, "Today is the day of the Water and Land Dharma Assembly, with a seven-day continuous session, it is already enough. We will混杂在众人之中，一则看这次法会怎么样，二则看金蝉子是否有缘穿我的宝物，三则也听听他讲的是哪部经法。” The two then entered the temple. It was indeed a case of meeting old acquaintances, and Prajna returned to its original abode. Entering the temple and viewing the scene, it truly was a heavenly kingdom, surpassing Śrāvastī, surpassing Jetavana, and not inferior to the Dharma halls of the highest monasteries. The sounds of immortals were clear and resounding, and the voices of Buddha’s praise were loud. The Bodhisattva approached the Mucalinda Platform, and truly saw the golden蝉相。Poem: "All phenomena are clear and without a speck of dust, great ceremony with Tripitaka seated on the high platform. Solving the afterlife for lonely souls in the dark, high cultivators come to listen in the market. Offering according to needs, the path far removed, caves opening at will, treasures revealed. Delighting in the exposition of boundless teachings, old and young all release joy in their hearts." Another poem: "Traveling through the world of Dharmas in the lecture hall, meeting familiar friends, not ordinary and kindred spirits. Telling of myriad matters in the present, discussing countless meritorious deeds of eons past. Dharmic clouds unfurled, vast and encompassing all mountains, teaching nets spread across the vast expanse of space. Counting life's path back to good intentions, flowers falling like rain, red and flowing." The monk on the stage recited for a while the Sutra for the Salvation of Departed Souls, then discussed the Seal of Heavenly Treasure for Pacifying the State, and finally declared the Sutra for Urging Merit and Virtue. The Bodhisattva approached, clapped on the precious platform, and shouted loudly, "Master, you can only talk about the Lesser Vehicle teachings, can you talk about the Greater Vehicle?" Upon hearing this, Tripitaka was greatly delighted and leaped down from the platform. Bowing to the Bodhisattva, he said, "Master, disciple was negligent, much sin. Seeing the assembly of monks, they all speak of Lesser Vehicle teachings, but do not know how the Greater Vehicle is." The Bodhisattva said, "Your Lesser Vehicle teachings cannot save the dead to ascend to heaven, only allowing them to blend with the secular and keep a low profile. I have the Three Treasures of Greater Vehicle Buddhism that can save the dead to ascend to heaven, rescue those in difficulty from suffering, cultivate limitless longevity, and achieve unarrival and non-departure."

To his complete humiliation, the teacher’s students and their parents had neither heard of Natasha Filippovna nor of his impending marriage yesterday or today. Instead, they all rushed out to gape at him as a wonder. The entire numerosous family of the teacher—starting from the fifteen-year-old girls and down to the seven-year-olds—stormed after their mother, surrounded him, and gaped at him with open mouths. Following them came a bony, jaundiced aunt in a black veil, and finally, the grandmother of the family appeared, an old woman in glasses. The teacher very much requested that he be allowed to enter and sit down, which the prince promptly did. He immediately guessed that they knew perfectly well who he was, and that they knew very well that his wedding should have taken place yesterday, and were dying to ask him about it and about this wonder that now he was asking them about Natasha Filippovna, who must now be with him in Pavlovsk. They were being tactful. In brief strokes, he satisfied their curiosity about the wedding. Astonishment, gasps, and exclamations ensued, so he was compelled to tell them almost everything, the main points being, of course. Finally, the prudent and agitated ladies decided that they had to first and foremost make contact with Rogozhin and get the whole story from him. If he was not at home (which they would find out for sure) or he did not want to tell them, they should go to the Semenovsky Regiment, to a lady, a German, known to Natasha Filippovna, who lived with her mother: perhaps Natasha Filippovna, in her excitement and desire to hide, had spent the night with them. The prince rose, completely crushed; it was said later that he had “paled terribly”; indeed, his legs almost gave way. Finally, through the awful racket, he made out that they were agreeing to act together with him and were asking for his city address. He had no address; they advised him to stay at some inn. The prince thought it over and gave the address of his former hotel, the very same one where he had had a fit five weeks earlier. He then went back to Rogozhin.
